(Sūrat Āl ʿImrān is Madanī, and it has two hundred verses.)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ ﴿Allah — there is no god but He.﴾ It has already been established that these opening letters (al-fawātiḥ) cannot be single letters such as ṣād, qāf and nūn, nor can they be equivalent to a single word such as ḥā MīM, ṭā SīN and yā SīN, which are equivalent to Qābīl and Hābīl; nor like ṭā SīN MīM, which is equivalent to Dārā bi-Jird, as Sībawayh mentioned in al-Kitāb. Therefore the way of pronouncing them is merely to name them, with their final letters quiescent in pause, whether they are taken as names or recited in the manner of enumeration. Even though two quiescent letters come together, this is certainly tolerated in the context of pausing. Thus the proper way with this opening is to pause upon it and then begin with what follows it, as Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) did according to the transmission from ʿĀṣim. As for the fatḥah found in it according to the well-known reading, it is merely the vowel of the hamzah of the Divine Name (Allāh), which was transferred onto the Mīm in order to indicate that the hamzah is still present, since its omission is not for continuous recitation but for lightening. Thus, by keeping its vowel, it is in the status of a present letter that begins the utterance, and the Mīm, by the vowel belonging to another letter, is in the status of pausing on a quiescent letter rather than a vowelled one, as is imagined and objected to on the grounds that this is not customary in speech. It has also been said: it is a vowel for the meeting of two quiescent letters, namely the Yā, the Mīm and the Lām of the Divine Name after the fall of its hamzah. You are aware that its fall is conditioned upon its occurrence in continuous speech, and you have understood that the quiescence of the Mīm is a pausal quiescence which necessitates cutting it off from what follows and requires the hamzah to remain in its state. This is unlike the case of particles and indeclinable nouns that are built upon quiescence, for their proper state is to be connected to what follows both in form and in usage; therefore the hamzah of connection falls away from them and their final letters are vowelled to resolve the meeting of two quiescent letters. Then, if they are taken as an enumerated sequence, they have no place in grammatical analysis (iʿrāb), like all the opening letters. If they are taken as a name for the sūrah, their position is either nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, or accusative, by supposing a verb suitable to the context, such as "mention" (dhakkir), "recite" (iqraʾ) or the like. As for nominative as the subject (mubtadaʾ), or accusative by supposing a verb of oath, or genitive by supposing its particle, none of these is admissible, because what follows them is not suitable to be a predicate nor to be an oath sworn upon it. The noble Name is the subject (mubtadaʾ), and what follows it is its predicate, and the sentence is a fresh statement, meaning: He is the One deserving of worship, and none other.

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿The Living, the Self-Subsisting.﴾ It is another predicate of it, or of an omitted subject, meaning: He is the Living, the Self-Subsisting, and none other. It has been said: it is an adjective of the subject, or an appositive to it, or to the first predicate; or it is the predicate, and what precedes it is a parenthetical insertion between the subject and its predicate, clarifying what the noble Name implies; or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from it. In any case, it serves as evidence that the entitlement to worship is exclusive to Him, glorified and exalted, because al-Ḥayy (the Living) means the One who remains, against whom there is no path to death and annihilation, and al-Qayyūm (the Self-Subsisting) means the One who constantly stands in managing and preserving creation. Necessarily, the exclusivity of these two attributes to Him, exalted is He, entails the exclusivity of the entitlement to worship to Him, exalted is He, since it is impossible for them to be realised without these two.

It has been narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Greatest Name of Allah is in three sūrahs: in Sūrat al-Baqarah, ﴿Allah — there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾; in Āl ʿImrān, ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Allah — there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾; and in Ṭā Hā, ﴿And faces shall be humbled before the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾." It has also been narrated that the Children of Israel asked Mūsā (peace be upon him) about the Greatest Name of Allah, and he said: "The Living, the Self-Subsisting." It is also related that ʿĪsā (peace be upon him), when he wished to revive the dead, would supplicate: "O Living, O Self-Subsisting." It is said that Āṣif ibn Barkhiyā, when he brought the throne of Bilqīs, invoked this. It was also recited as al-Ḥayyu al-Qayyām. This is a refutation of those who claimed that ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) was a lord, for it has been narrated that the delegation of Najrān came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), sixty riders among them, including fourteen men of their nobles: three of them were their great men to whom their affairs returned: their leader and the holder of their counsel, al-ʿĀqib, whose name was ʿAbd al-Masīḥ; their second, their minister and adviser, al-Sayyid, whose name was al-Ayham; and their third, their scholar, bishop and head of their schools, Abū Ḥārithah ibn ʿAlqamah, of the Banū Bakr ibn Wāʾil. The kings of Rome had honoured him, appointed him, and esteemed him because of what they witnessed of his knowledge and his diligence in their religion, and they built churches for him. When they left Najrān, Abū Ḥārithah rode his mule, and his brother Kurz ibn ʿAlqamah was beside him. While Abū Ḥārithah's mule was walking, it stumbled, and Kurz said: "Ruin to the farthest one," meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Abū Ḥārithah said to him: "Rather, may your mother be ruined." Kurz said: "Why, brother?" He said: "By Allah, he is the Prophet whom we were awaiting." Kurz said to him: "Then what prevents you from him, while you know this?" He said: "Because these kings gave us much wealth and honoured us; if we believed in him, they would take all of it from us." This matter settled in Kurz's heart and he concealed it until he embraced Islam, and he would relate this. They came to Madīnah and then entered the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after the ʿAṣr prayer, wearing striped Ḥibarāt garments: robes and fine mantles. One of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) who saw them said: "We have never seen a delegation like them." When their prayer time came, they stood to pray in the mosque. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Leave them." So they prayed facing east. Then those three spoke with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: at one time, "ʿĪsā is Allah, because he used to revive the dead, heal the sick, inform of the unseen, and create from clay the form of a bird, then breathe into it and it flies." At another time: "He is the son of Allah, since he had no known father." At yet another time: "He is the third of three," based on His saying, exalted is He: "We have done and We have said," and had He been one, He would have said "I have done and I have said." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "Submit." They said: "We submitted before you." He (ﷺ) said: "You lie. What prevents you from Islam is your claim that Allah has a son." They said: "If he has no son of Allah, then who is his father?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do you not know that there is no child except that it resembles its father?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Do you not know that our Lord is Living and does not die, while ʿĪsā is subject to annihilation?" They said: "Yes." He (peace be upon him) said: "Do you not know that our Lord is Self-Subsisting over every thing, preserving it and providing for it?" They said: "Yes." He (peace be upon him) said: "Does ʿĪsā possess anything of that?" They said: "No." He (peace be upon him) said: "Do you not know that nothing is hidden from Allah, exalted is He, on earth or in heaven?" They said: "Yes." He (peace be upon him) said: "Does ʿĪsā know any of that except what He taught him?" They said: "Yes." He (peace be upon him) said: "Do you not know that our Lord fashioned ʿĪsā in the womb however He willed, and that our Lord does not eat, drink or excrete?" They said: "Yes." He (peace be upon him) said: "Do you not know that his mother carried ʿĪsā as a woman carries, and bore him as a woman bears her child, then he was nourished as a child is nourished, then he ate food, drank drink and excreted waste?" They said: "Yes." He (peace be upon him) said: "How then can this be as you claim?!" They fell silent and refused except obstinacy. So Allah, exalted and majestic, sent down from the beginning of the sūrah up to nearly eighty-odd verses, confirming what he (peace be upon him) argued against them with, answering their doubts, and establishing the truth about which they dispute.

﴿He has sent down to you the Book﴾, that is, the Qur'an. He referred to it by the generic noun (ism al-jins, "generic noun") to indicate that it surpasses the rest of the individual books in possessing the perfections of the genus. It is as though it alone deserves to be called "the Book," to the exclusion of all others, as is suggested by the explicit naming of the Torah and the Gospel. The form *nazzala* (the intensive form of the verb) indicates gradual revelation (tanjim, "revelation in stages"). The placing of the adverbial phrase *'alayka* before its object is for the sake of the emphasis on what is placed first and the building of suspense toward what is delayed. The sentence may be a new independent statement (isti'naf), or another predicate of the Glorious Name, or it may itself be the predicate. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿There is no god but He﴾, is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD, "interjected phrase") or a circumstantial clause (hal). His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾, is either an adjective or a substitution (badal), as has already been explained.

It was also read as *nazzala* with the lighter form (takhfif, "the single-consonant reading") and *al-Kitabu* in the nominative. In that case it is apparent that the sentence is independent, though it has been said that it may be a predicate with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning: "the Book has come down from Him."

﴿With the truth﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (hal) either of the subject or of the object, meaning: He sent it down in a manner that is true in its revelation, in accordance with what it is; or accompanied by justice in its rulings; or by truthfulness in its reports, among which are the report of the Oneness (of God) and what follows it, and His promise and threat; or by what establishes that it is from God Exalted through clear proofs.

﴿Confirming﴾ is a circumstantial phrase of the Book by agreement, on the assumption that His saying ﴿with the truth﴾ is a circumstantial phrase of the subject of *nazzala*. As for the assumption that it is a circumstantial phrase of the Book, then according to the one who permits multiple circumstantial phrases without conjunction or substitution, it is a circumstantial phrase of it after another circumstantial phrase. According to the one who prohibits this, it has been said that it is a circumstantial phrase of the place of the first circumstantial phrase by way of substitution. It has also been said that it is from the concealed pronoun in the prepositional phrase, because in that case it bears a pronoun, as it stands in place of its governing element which bears it; so it is a nested circumstantial phrase (hal mutadakhilah). In every case it is an emphatic circumstantial phrase. The benefit of restricting the revelation with it is to urge the People of the Two Scriptures to believe in what was sent down, and to alert them to the obligation of this, for belief in what confirms necessarily entails belief in what it confirms.

﴿For what is before it﴾ is an object of *muSaddiqan* (confirming), and the *lam* is a support for strengthening the operation of the verb, like in ﴿He is an accomplisher of what He intends﴾. That is, confirming what came before it of the previous books. This implies their presence and the full manifestation of their matter among people, and its confirmation of them in calling to faith and monotheism, in declaring God Mighty and Majestic free from what is unbefitting His glorious station, and in commanding justice and goodness; and likewise in the reports of the prophets and the past nations, and likewise in its being revealed in the description mentioned in them. Likewise in the laws that do not differ with the difference of nations and eras, this is apparent and beyond doubt. As for the laws that differ according to the difference of these, then it is because the rulings of each one of them come down as the wisdom of legislation requires with respect to the particular circumstances of the nations obligated by them, containing the benefits appropriate to their situation.

﴿And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾ is a specification of what is before it, and a demonstration of the elevated status of its place, as an affirmation of what precedes it and a preparation for what follows it, for by this the standing of what it confirms rises in eminence and distinction, and it increases in hearts in acceptance and reverence; and the condition of whoever disbelieved in both of them becomes more monstrous in its heinousness, and entails what will be mentioned of severe punishment and retribution. That is, He sent them both down all at once upon Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both. They were not mentioned by name because the discussion concerns the Two Books, not the ones upon whom they were sent down. Both are non-Arabic names: the first is Hebrew, and the second is Syriac. This is supported by the reading with a *fatha* on the *hamza* of *al-Injil*, for *if'il* is not among the morphological patterns (abniyah, "word-patterns") of the Arabs. And seeking to derive their etymologies from *al-warā* (offspring) and *al-najl* (lineage) is far-fetched.

﴿مِن قَبْلُ﴾ يتعلق بـ﴿أَنزَلَ﴾، أي: أنزلهما من قبل نزول الكتاب، والتصريح به مع ظهور الأمر للمبالغة في البيان.

﴿هُدًى لِّلنَّاسِ﴾ في موضع النصب على أنه علة للإنزال، أي: أنزلهما لهداية الناس. أو على أنه حال منهما (الحال، أي المفعول الثاني للتوضيح)، أي: أنزلهما حال كونهما هدى لهم. والإفراد لأنه مصدر، جُعلا نفس الهدى مبالغة، أو حُذف منه المضاف، أي: ذوي هدى. ثم إن أُريد هدايتهما بجميع ما فيهما من حيث هو جميع، فالمراد بالناس الأمم الماضية من حين نزولهما إلى زمان نسخهما. وإن أُريد هدايتهما على الإطلاق، وهو الأنسب بالمقام، فالناس على عمومه؛ لأن هدايتهما بما عدّ الشرائع المنسوخة من الأمور التي يصدقهما القرآن فيها، ومن جملتها البشارة بنزوله وبمبعث النبي ﷺ، تعم الناس قاطبة.

﴿وَأَنزَلَ الْفُرْقَانَ﴾ "الفرقان" في الأصل مصدر كالغفران، أُطلق على الفاعل مبالغة (أي على الفارق بين الحق والباطل). والمراد به هنا: إما جنس الكتب الإلهية، عُبِّر عنها بوصف شامل لما ذُكر منها وما لم يُذكر، على طريق التتميم بالتعميم، إثر تخصيص بعض مشاهيرها بالذكر، كما في قوله عز وجل: ﴿فَأَنبَتْنَا فِيهَا حَبًّا﴾ ﴿وَعِنَبًا﴾ إلى قوله تعالى: ﴿وَفَاكِهَةً﴾. وإما نفس الكتب المذكورة أُعيد ذكرها بوصف خاص لم يُذكر فيما سبق، على طريقة العطف بتكرير لفظ الإنزال، تنزيلًا للتغاير الوصفي منزلة التغاير الذاتي، كما في قوله سبحانه: ﴿وَلَمَّا جَاءَ أَمْرُنَا نَجَّيْنَا هُودًا وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ بِرَحْمَةٍ مِّنَّا وَنَجَّيْنَاهُم مِّنْ عَذَابٍ غَلِيظٍ﴾. وإما الزبور، فإنه مشتمل على المواعظ الفارقة بين الحق والباطل، الداعية إلى الخير والرشاد، الزاجرة عن الشر والفساد. وتقديم الإنجيل عليه مع تأخره عنه نزولًا لقوة مناسبته للتوراة في الاشتمال على الأحكام والشرائع، ولشيوع اقترانهما في الذكر. وإما القرآن نفسه، ذُكر بنعت مادح له بعد ما ذُكر باسم الجنس، تعظيمًا لشأنه، ورفعًا لمكانه، وقد بيّن أولًا تنزيله التدريجي إلى الأرض، وثانيًا إنزاله الدفعي إلى السماء الدنيا، أو أُريد بإنزال القدر المشترك العاري عن قيد التدريج وعدمه. وإما المعجزات المقرونة بإنزال الكتب المذكورة، الفارقة بين المحِق والمبطل.

﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا بِآيَاتِ اللَّهِ﴾ وُضع موضع الضمير العائد إلى ما فُصّل من الكتب المنزلة أو منها، ومن المعجزات، وآياتٍ مضافةٍ إلى الاسم الجليل، تعيينًا لحيثية كفرهم، وتهويلًا لأمرهم، وتأكيدًا لاستحقاقهم العذاب الشديد، وإيذانًا بأن ذلك الاستحقاق لا يُشترط فيه الكفر بالكل، بل يكفي فيه الكفر ببعض منها. والمراد بالموصول: إما أهل الكتابين، وهو الأنسب بمقام المحاجّة معهم، أو جنس الكفرة، وهم داخلون فيه دخولًا أوليًّا. أي: إن الذين كفروا بما ذُكر من آيات الله الناطقة بالحق، لاسيما بتوحيده تعالى وتنزيهه عما لا يليق بشأنه الجليل، كلًّا أو بعضًا، مع ما بها من النعوت الموجبة للإيمان بها، بأن كذّبوا بالقرآن أصالةً وبسائر الكتب الإلهية تبعًا، لأن تكذيب المصدِّق موجب لتكذيب ما يصدِّقه حتمًا، وأصالةً أيضًا بأن كذّبوا بآياتها الناطقة بالتوحيد والتنزيه، وآياتها المبشرة بنزول القرآن ومبعث النبي ﷺ، وغيّروها.

﴿لَهُمْ﴾ بسبب كفرهم بها.

﴿عَذَابٌ﴾ مرفوع، إما على الفاعلية من الجار والمجرور، أو على الابتداء، والجملة خبر ﴿إِنَّ﴾، والتنوين للتفخيم، أي: أيُّ عذاب!

﴿شَدِيدٌ﴾ لا يُقدَّر قدرُه. وهو وعيد جيء به إثر تقرير أمر التوحيد الذاتي والوصفي، والإشارة إلى ما ينطق بذلك من الكتب الإلهية، حملًا على القبول والإذعان، وزجرًا عن الكفر والعصيان.

﴿وَاللَّهُ عَزِيزٌ﴾ لا يُغالَب، يفعل ما يشاء ويحكم ما يريد.

﴿ذُو انتِقَامٍ﴾ عظيم، خارج عن أفراد جنسه. وهو افتعال من النِّقمة، وهي السطوة والتسلط، يقال: انتقم منه إذا عاقبه بجنايته. والجملة اعتراض تذييلي مقرِّر للوعيد (p-6) ومؤكِّد له.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 5:

﴿Indeed, nothing is hidden from Allah, neither on the earth nor in the heaven.﴾ This is a resumed statement (isti'naf) brought forth to show the vastness of His knowledge, and His encompassing of all that is in the world of existing things, among which is what proceeds from them of disbelief and transgression, both secretly and openly, following the statement of His perfect power and might. It serves as a reinforcement of the preceding threat (wa'id) and as an alert that gaining knowledge of some unseen matters, as was the case with Jesus, peace be upon him, is far from reaching the rank of the divine attributes. He (exalted and majestic is He) expressed His knowledge by what was mentioned, by saying it is not hidden from Him, as in His saying (glorified is He): ﴿Nothing is hidden from Allah, neither on the earth nor in the heaven.﴾ This indicates that His knowledge (exalted is He) of what is known to Him, even if it is in the furthest hidden ends, is not of such a nature that any trace of concealment could accompany it in any way, as is the case with the knowledge of created beings; rather, it is in the utmost clarity and manifestness. The negated clause is the predicate of inna, and the repetition of the predication (isnad) serves to strengthen the judgment. The word fi ("in") is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of shay' ("thing"), emphasizing its generality, which is derived from its occurrence in the context of negation; that is: nothing whatsoever is hidden from Him that exists on the earth or in the heaven, whether that existence is by way of being settled within them or being a part of them. It has also been said that it is connected to "yakhfa" ("is hidden"). He expressed the whole world by these two because they are its two regions. The earth is mentioned before the heaven to show concern for the affairs of its inhabitants, and the placing of the negative particle between them indicates an ascent from the lower to the higher, in terms of nearness and distance from us, which call for differentiation in relation to our knowledge.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 6:

As for His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying: ﴿He it is Who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾, it is a resumptive clause (jumla musta'nifa), expressing some of the rulings of His being the Sustainer (qayyumiyya) and of the states of creation proceeding through the stages of existence according to His will, which is founded upon far-reaching wisdoms. It confirms the completeness of His knowledge, while also providing further clarification of His relation to things before they enter into existence, necessarily so, since the knowledge of the Exalted requires knowledge of the various forms that follow from the shaping, which follows from the will, before they come to be, in degrees. The word "fi" (in) is connected to "yusawwirukum" or to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial state (hal) of the object pronoun, meaning: He shapes you while you are in the wombs as a lump of flesh (mudgha). "Kayfa" is an object of "yasha'", and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), either from the subject of "yusawwirukum," meaning: He shapes you being according to His, the Exalted's, will, that is, willing; or from its object, meaning: He shapes you being according to His, the Exalted's, will, following it in accepting the differing states, from being drops of semen, then clots of blood, then lumps of flesh, unformed and then formed, and in being characterized by the various attributes of maleness and femaleness, beauty and ugliness, and other attributes. In this is evidence of the falsity of the claim of those who asserted the lordship of Jesus, peace be upon him, and he is among the sons of the Nasut (human nature), who turn through these stages according to the will of the Creator, the Mighty and Majestic, and the extent of the feebleness of their intellects is not hidden.

It has also been read as "taṣawwarakum" in the past form of the tafa''ul pattern, meaning: He formed you for Himself and for His worship.

﴿There is no god but He﴾, since none is characterized by any of the great affairs mentioned that are specific to divinity, so that his divinity could be supposed.

﴿the Mighty, the Wise﴾, the one perfect in power and wisdom, and for this reason He creates you in the wondrous pattern mentioned.

(p-7)﴿He it is who sent down to you the Book﴾. This begins the refutation of their doubts, which arose from what the Qur'an stated about the description of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him). It comes as a resumption (istiʾnāf) following the statement that lordship and its basis belong exclusively to Allah, the Exalted, time and again, and that everyone else is subdued under His dominion and subject to His will. It is said: "The delegation of Najran said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Do you not claim, O Muhammad, that ʿĪsā is the Word of Allah and a spirit from Him?' He (ﷺ) said: 'Yes.' They said: 'That is enough for us.'" So He censured their deviation and their trial, and He explained that the Book is founded upon firm principles and built upon branches resting on them, speaking the truth and decisively refuting the error in which they are. By "sending down" (inzāl) is meant the common notion, stripped of any indication of whether it was gradual or not. The definite article in "the Book" (al-kitāb) is for a known referent, and placing the prepositional phrase ("to you") before it serves to draw attention to the care given to the matter of his (ʿĪsā's) glad tidings, by honouring the act of sending down upon him, and to create anticipation for what was sent down. When the soul is made to wait for something whose natural place is at the front, especially after an indication of its high rank or benefit, it remains expectant of it, so that when it arrives it settles in the soul with full firmness, and so that its division into its two parts follows directly.

﴿From it are verses﴾. The prepositional phrase ("from it") is the predicate, and "verses" (āyāt) is the subject, or vice versa, with an interpretation whose verification has already passed in His words: ﴿And among the people is one who says…﴾ (2:8). The first is more in accordance with the rules of grammar (ṣināʿa, the discipline of Arabic grammar and syntax). The second is more appropriate to the eloquence of the meaning, since the primary intent is the division of the Book into the two known categories, not that they are "from the Book." So reflect on this. The sentence is either a new (resumptive) clause, or it lies in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) qualifying "the Book": that is, He who sent down the Book in this state, namely divided into clear (muḥkam) and ambiguous (mutashābih) verses. Alternatively, the prepositional phrase alone is the circumstantial element, and "verses" is raised by it as its agent.

﴿Clear﴾ (muḥkamāt) is a description of "verses": that is, their meaning is definitive in its indication. What is meant is that their wording is firm and protected from possible or confused readings.

﴿They are the mother of the Book﴾. That is, they are its foundation and its core, to which the others are referred. Thus by "the Book" is meant all of it, and the genitive construction is in the sense of "in," as in "one of ten" (wāḥid al-ʿashara), not in the sense of "of" (lām), since that would make "the Book" refer to what is other than the clear verses. This sentence is either a description of what precedes it or a new clause. He used the singular "mother" (umm) although the verses are many, because the purpose is to show that each one of them is a foundation, or to show that all of them are like a single verse, as in His words: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ (21:91). It is also said that the singular is used instead of the plural, as in the words of the poet:

*By it are the carcasses of the Ḥaṣrā, as for their bones, they are white, and as for their skin, it is hard.*

That is: "as for their skins."

﴿And others﴾ (wa-ukhar) is a qualifier of a deleted noun coordinated with "verses," that is: "and verses others." It is the plural of "ukhrā," and it is not declined because it is a descriptive adjective deviated from "ākhar" or from "ākhar" in a general sense. ﴿Ambiguous﴾ (mutashābihāt) is a qualifier of "others." In reality, it qualifies the deleted noun, meaning: they are capable of multiple meanings that resemble one another, none of which is distinguished from the others in deserving to be intended by them. The matter is not made clear except through careful reflection and refined contemplation. So ambiguity, in reality, is a quality of those meanings, and it is attributed to the verses in the manner of describing the indicator by the quality of what it indicates. It is also said: since it is a characteristic of similar matters that the intellect fails to distinguish between them, everything the intellect cannot reach was called ambiguous, even if that was not due to resemblance. This is just as the term "problematic" (mushkil) originally applied to what enters among its like and its counterparts without its specific identity being known, and then it was applied to everything obscure, even if its obscurity was not from that aspect. This was made to be so in order to display the excellence of the scholars and to increase their eagerness to strive in reflecting upon these verses and in acquiring the sciences upon which the derivation of the correct rulings intended by them depends. Through this, and through exhausting their minds in extracting their refined aims and their fitting meanings, they attain lofty ranks, and they ascend by means of harmonizing them with the clear verses, arriving at certainty and tranquillity, toward distant ladders.

As for His words, mighty and majestic: ﴿Alif Lām Rā. A Book whose verses have been made firm﴾ (11:1), its meaning is that they were protected from the incursion of defect or from abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one), or they were supported with decisive proofs indicating their truth, or they were made wise because they contain the sublime and profound wisdoms. And His words, exalted be He: ﴿A Book, similar in its parts, oft-repeated﴾ (39:23), mean that its parts are similar: some of them resemble others in the soundness of meaning, the eloquence of composition, and the truth of what they indicate.

﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾: that is, inclination away from the truth toward vain desires. Al-Rāghib (al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī) said: "Zaygh is inclination away from uprightness toward one of the two sides." In making their hearts a place of deviation there is an intensification of their turning away from the paths of guidance and of their persistence in evil and corruption.

﴿They follow what is ambiguous of it﴾: turning away from the clear verses, that is, they cling to the outward appearance of the ambiguous part of the Book, or to a false interpretation, not seeking the truth after having believed that it is from Allah, the Exalted, but rather:

﴿seeking discord﴾: that is, seeking to mislead people from their religion through doubt, confusion, and contradicting the clear by the ambiguous, as was reported about the delegation.

﴿And seeking its interpretation﴾: that is, seeking to interpret it according to what they desire of misguided interpretations, while in fact they are far from that rank. This is His statement, mighty and majestic: ﴿None knows its interpretation except Allah and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾ (3:7, the part following this). The phrase "seeking its interpretation" is a circumstantial clause from a pronoun, so that "they follow" is understood by the final cause, meaning: they follow the ambiguous in order to seek its interpretation, while in fact it is specific to Him and to those of His servants whom He has granted success in it, those firmly grounded in knowledge, meaning those who are established and rooted in it and did not waver on slippery footholds. In the causal clause "for seeking its interpretation" rather than "its interpretation itself," and in stripping "interpretation" of any description of correctness or truth, there is an indication that they have no share in interpretation at all, and that what they seek is not an interpretation whatsoever, not that it is an incorrect interpretation for which its holder might be excused.

Whoever pauses at ﴿except Allah﴾ explains the ambiguous as what Allah, mighty and exalted, has kept to His own knowledge, such as the duration of the world, the time of the Hour, and the special properties of numbers such as the number of the guardians of Hell (cf. 74:30). Or it is what a decisive proof indicates that its apparent meaning is not intended, without indicating what is intended by it.

﴿They say: "We believe in it"﴾: that is, in the ambiguous. The lack of mention of their belief in the clear verses is either because it is evident, or because it refers to the Book as a whole. The sentence on the first reading is a resumptive clause clarifying the state of those firmly grounded, or a circumstantial clause from them. On the second reading, it is the predicate of His words: ﴿and those firmly grounded﴾.

His words: ﴿Each is from our Lord﴾ are part of what is said, confirming and emphasizing what precedes. That is: each one of them, the ambiguous and the clear, is sent down from Him, exalted be He, with no contradiction between them. Or it means: "We believe in it and in its truth as He intends it."

﴿And none remembers﴾ properly.

﴿except those of understanding﴾: that is, the pure minds, free from inclining toward vain desires. This is a concluding statement brought from Him, exalted be He, in praise of those firmly grounded for their quality of mind and good reflection, and an indication of what made them ready to be guided to its interpretation: the stripping of the intellect from the veils of the senses. The connection of this noble verse to what precedes is that it is a response to what the Christians clung to, such as His words: ﴿and His word which He cast to Mary, and a spirit from Him﴾ (4:171), in a general manner. The detailed response will come with His words: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of ʿĪsā before Allah is like the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ (3:59).

﴿Our Lord, let not our hearts deviate﴾ is part of the speech of those firmly grounded in knowledge. That is, do not let our hearts swerve from the path of truth to follow the ambiguous (al-mutashabih) by an interpretation (ta'wil) You do not approve of. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The heart of the son of Adam lies between two of the fingers of the All-Merciful. If He wills, He makes it firm upon the truth, and if He wills, He makes it swerve from it." It has also been said that its meaning is: do not test us with trials in which our hearts would deviate.

﴿after You have guided us﴾ means: to the truth and the correct interpretation, or to belief in both kinds of verses. The word "ba'da" (after) is in the accusative, governed by "let not deviate," as an adverb of time (zarf). The word "idh" stands in the genitive position as its object, having come out of its adverbial function. The meaning is: after the time of Your guiding us. It has also been said that "idh" here has the meaning of "an" (that).

﴿and grant us from Yourself﴾: both prepositional phrases depend on "grant." The first has been placed first for a reason already mentioned many times. The second may be attached to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (hal) of the object, meaning: existing from You. The "min" here indicates the figurative starting point. "Ladun" is originally an adverb meaning the first limit of time, place, or other entities. Examples include "min ladun Zayd" (from the presence of Zayd). It is not synonymous with "'inda" (with), since it may be a non-essential element (fadlah), and likewise "ladى." Some grammarians restrict it to adverbs of place. It may be followed by a pure noun of time, as in his saying:

The shivering runs through my back
from the midday until the afternoon.

It is never entirely separated from the idea of annexation (idafah). Most often it is annexed to nouns, but it may also be annexed to "an" with its clause, as in his saying:

We have not severed, from the time that you took our guardianship,
the kinship of one with kin, nor the right of a Muslim.

That is: from the time of Your guardianship over us. It may also be annexed to a nominal sentence, as in his saying:

Remember his blessings from the time you were a youth.

It is also annexed to a verbal sentence, as in his saying:

We have stayed from the time you made peace with us, and your death,
so let there be no inclination among you toward dissension.

It is rarely free of "min," as in the last two verses.

﴿mercy﴾: abundant mercy, which brings us near to You and by which we succeed in Your presence; or it means success in remaining steadfast upon the truth. The postponement of the explicit object after the two prepositional phrases is for a reason already mentioned many times: giving attention to what is placed first, and creating suspense toward what is delayed. When something that should be first is delayed, the soul remains awaiting its arrival, especially when it is signaled that it is one of the benefits by the particle "li" (for). When it is finally presented, it settles in the soul with the greatest firmness.

﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾: this is a reason for the request or for granting what is asked. The word "anta" (You) is either the subject of a nominal sentence, a separating pronoun (fasl), or an emphasis of the subject of "inna" (indeed). The absolute form "al-Wahhab" (the Bestower) is used so that it includes every gift. In it is an indication that guidance and misguidance are from Him, Exalted, and that He bestows favors by what He grants to His servants without anything being obligatory upon Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 9:

﴿Our Lord, indeed You are the Gatherer of mankind for a Day﴾ That is, the Day of the Reckoning, or the Day of Recompense. The governed noun has been omitted and the governing noun (the one that is annexed to it) has been put in its place, to make it terrifying and to emphasize the awfulness of what takes place in it.

﴿about which there is no doubt﴾ That is, concerning its occurrence and the occurrence of what is in it of the resurrection, the reckoning and the recompense. Their purpose by this is to show the completeness of their need for mercy, and that it is the most excellent aim in their eyes. The emphasis serves to display the completeness of the tranquility and the strength of certainty they have regarding the conditions of the Hereafter.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in the promise﴾ This is a justification for the content of the emphasized sentence, or for the negation of doubt and the emphasis mentioned earlier. The manifestation of the Majestic Name, together with the shift (iltifat) of speech, serves to bring out the completeness of the glorification and reverence arising from mention of the awesome, dreadful Day. This differs from what is at the end of the noble surah, for that is a station of asking for favour, as will come. It also serves to indicate the reason for the ruling, since divinity (uluhiyyah) is incompatible with failing in a promise. It has also been permitted that the sentence is an utterance from Him, Exalted, to confirm the saying of those firmly grounded in knowledge. "Al-Mi'ad" (the promise) is a verbal noun, like "al-Mi'qat" (the appointed time). The Wa'idiyyah (the Mu'tazilite-leaning proponents of the threat doctrine) used it as evidence, (p-10) and it is answered that the threat against sinners is conditional upon the absence of pardon, by detailed proofs, just as it is, by consensus, conditional upon the absence of repentance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾. After he had explained the true religion and monotheism, mentioned the states of the Books that speak of it, and explained the matter of the Great Qur'an and the manner in which the firmly grounded scholars believe in it, he began to explain the state of those who disbelieve in it. What is meant by the relative pronoun is the category of disbelievers in general, encompassing all their kinds. It was also said: the delegation of Najran, or the Jews of Banu Qurayza and Banu al-Nadir, or the polytheists of the Arabs.

﴿Will never avail them﴾, i.e., will never benefit them. It is also read with the masculine form (yughni) and with the letter ya' quiescent (tughnī, as a dialectal/ grammatical variant) (jiddan) owing to the difficulty of the vowel on the letters of prolongation.

﴿their wealth﴾ which they expend in procuring benefits and warding off harms.

﴿nor their children﴾, those through whom they gain victory in important matters and upon whom they rely in pressing calamities. The placing of children after wealth, with the negative particle inserted between them, is either due to the nobility of children in removing distresses, or because wealth is the first resource to which one resorts when calamities descend.

﴿against God﴾, i.e., against His punishment, exalted is He.

﴿in anything﴾, i.e., in anything at all. It was also said: the word "min" (from) carries the sense of "in exchange for" (badal), and the meaning is: in exchange for God's mercy or in exchange for His obedience, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth﴾, i.e., in exchange for the truth. And from it is the poet's saying: "And the fortune of the man of wealth does not benefit him from you, i.e., his fortune does not benefit him in exchange for your favor," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is not your wealth nor your children that bring you near to Us in position﴾. You know that the possibility that their wealth and children could take the place of God's mercy or His obedience is something that does not occur to anyone's mind such that it would need to be addressed by negating it. The first interpretation is the most fitting for denouncing the state of the disbelievers and magnifying their affair, and the most suitable with what follows it, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those are the fuel of the Fire﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So God seized them﴾. That is: those characterized by disbelief are the firewood and fuel of the Fire with which it is kindled. If the intent is to describe their state at the kindling, then the choice of the nominal sentence serves to indicate the certainty and establishment of the matter; otherwise, it signals that the reality of their state is that, and that their outward conditions are as nothing, so they, while in this world, are the very fuel of the Fire. This contains, in indicating the complete entanglement of them with the Fire, what is not hidden. The word "hum" (they) may be a subject (mubtada'), or a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl). The sentence is either a resumptive sentence confirming the failure of wealth and children to avail, or it is conjoined to the predicate of "inna". Whichever it is, it specifies the punishment from which he explained their wealth and children would not avail them at all. It is also read "wuqud al-nar" with a dammah on the waw, and it is a verbal noun, meaning: the people of its fuel.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 11:

﴿كَدَأْبِ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ "Al-da'b" (habit, practice): a verbal noun from da'aba fi al-'amal, meaning to exert oneself in work and become weary of it; its usage became predominant in the sense of condition, state, and custom. The position of the "kaf" (like) is in the nominative case, as it is the predicate of an elided subject. The accusative has also been permitted, governed either by ﴿لَنْ تُغْنِيَ﴾ (will not avail) or by "al-waqud" (fuel), meaning: they will not avail them just as they did not avail those, or the fire will be kindled by them just as it was kindled by those. You know that what is mentioned in the explanation of "al-da'b" is only denial and seizure, without any reference to failure to avail, especially if "min" is taken in the sense of "substitution" as the one who permitted this holds. Nor is it about kindling the fire, which would then be read as a causal clause, and that is contrary to the apparent meaning. Moreover, on the assumption of the accusative governed by "lan tughniya," it would necessitate separating the governor from the governed by a foreign element, namely His words, exalted is He: ﴿وَأُولَئِكَ هم وقُودُ النّارِ﴾ (and those are the fuel of the Fire), unless it is made a resumptive clause conjoined to the predicate of "inna." Therefore the correct reading is the nominative as a predicate, meaning: the habit of these people in disbelief and in not being saved from the seizure of God Most High and His punishment is like the habit of the family of Pharaoh.

﴿والَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ That is: those before the family of Pharaoh from the disbelieving nations. The relative pronoun is in the genitive case, conjoined to what precedes it. His words, exalted is He: ﴿كَذَّبُوا بِآياتِنا﴾ (they denied Our signs) are an explanation and elaboration of their habit, which they practised, in the manner of a resumptive clause built on a question, as if it were said: "How was their habit?" So it was said: "They denied Our signs." His words, exalted is He: ﴿فَأخَذَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ (so God seized them) are an explanation of their habit that was done to them, meaning: so God seized them and punished them, and they did not find any escape from the might of God Most High. Thus the habit of these disbelievers is also like their habit. It has been said that "they denied, etc." is a circumstantial clause from the family of Pharaoh and those before them, with "qad" implied, meaning: the habit of these is like the habit of those, and they have denied, etc. As for it being a predicate of the relative pronoun, as has been said, this detracts from the splendour of the noble composition, and the shift to the first person first, to proceed according to the ways of Majesty, and to the third person second, by mentioning the Divine Name to nurture awe and instil reverence.

﴿بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾ If by them is meant their denial of the signs, then the "ba'" (with) indicates causation, introduced for emphasis on what the "fa'" (so) conveys of the causal link of what precedes to what follows. If by them is meant all their other sins, then the "ba'" indicates accompaniment, introduced to show that they had other sins, meaning: He seized them while they were burdened with their sins, not repenting of them, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿وَتَزْهَقَ أنْفُسُهم وهم كافِرُونَ﴾ (and their souls depart while they are disbelievers). "Dhanb" (sin) originally means that which follows and comes after; and crime was called "dhanb" because it follows, that is, its punishment follows its doer.

﴿واللَّهُ شَدِيدُ العِقابِ﴾ (and God is severe in punishment) is a concluding statement confirming the meaning of what precedes it of seizure, and a completion of it.

**﴿Say to those who disbelieve﴾**: the intended ones are the Jews, based on what has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both: "When the Jews of Medina saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prevail over the polytheists on the day of Badr, they said, 'By Allah, he is truly the unlettered Prophet whom Moses gave good tidings of, and his description is in the Torah,' and they intended to follow him. But some of them said, 'Do not hasten until we see another of his encounters.' Then, on the day of Uhud, they doubted. They had a treaty with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for a fixed period, and they broke it. Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf set out with sixty riders to the people of Mecca, and they resolved together to fight the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then this was revealed." Also from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) struck Quraysh at Badr and returned to Medina, he gathered the Jews in the market of Bani Qaynuqa' and warned them that what had befallen Quraysh might befall them. They said, 'Do not let it deceive you that you met a people who were inexperienced in war and so you gained an advantage over them. If you fight us, you will know that we are the (real) men,' and then this was revealed." That is, say to them.

**﴿You will be overcome﴾**: definitely, soon, in this world. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, fulfilled His promise by the killing of Bani Qurayzah, the expulsion of Bani al-Nadir, the conquest of Khaybar, and the imposition of the jizya (poll tax) on others besides them. This is among the clearest proofs of prophethood. As for what has been related from Muqatil, that it was revealed before Badr, and that the relative pronoun refers to the polytheists of Mecca, and that for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them on the day of Badr, "Indeed Allah will overcome you and gather you to Hell, and wretched is the resting-place," then this leads to the severing of the noble verse from what follows it, since it was revealed after the battle of Badr.

**﴿And you will be gathered﴾**: that is, in the Hereafter.

**﴿to Hell﴾**. The two verbs are also read with the letter "ya'" (third person), on the basis that he (peace be upon him) was commanded to convey to them, in his own words, what Allah the Exalted had informed of their threat, as if it were said: "Convey this statement to them."

**﴿And wretched is the resting-place﴾**: either it is part of what is said to them, or it is a new sentence to magnify the horror of Hell and the dreadfulness of the state of its people. The object of the dispraise is omitted (p-12), that is: "And wretched is the resting-place, Hell," or "and what they prepared for their own souls."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 3, verse 13:**

﴿There has certainly been for you﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath (qasam), and it is part of the speech that was commanded to be delivered. It was brought in to confirm and establish the content of what precedes it. The address is also to the Jews. The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is the predicate of *kana* (was), with *kana* being defective (naqisa, a linking verb). Because the phrase comes between *kana* and its subject, the feminine marker is dropped (tark al-ta'nith), as in the verse of poetry:

*"If a man is deceived by one of you women after me and after you in this world, he is indeed deluded."*

The feminine marking here is not real, or the phrase is connected to *kana* with *kana* being complete (tamma, not requiring a predicate). It is placed before its subject because, as has been noted many times, this emphasizes what is placed first and creates anticipation for what is delayed. The meaning is: By God, there has certainly been for you, O you who are deceived by their number and their equipment.

﴿A sign﴾ (ayah), a great sign indicating the truth of what I say to you: you will be defeated.

﴿In two groups﴾ (fi fi'atayn), that is, two companies or two parties. The defeated one of the two was relying on its large numbers and was self-satisfied with its might, and what befell it has befallen it. So what befalls you will befall you. The adverbial phrase is in the nominative case as an attribute (sifa) of *ayah*. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as the predicate of *kana*. The first adverbial phrase is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of *ayah*, [namely] ﴿they met﴾ (iltaqata), in the position of the genitive as an attribute of the two groups. That is: they met in battle on the day of Badr.

﴿A group﴾ (fi'ah) is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: one of them is a group, as in the verse:

*"When I die, people will be two factions: one gloating, and another praising what I used to do."*

That is: one of them is gloating and the other is praising. And as in the verse:

*"Until, when the star rose in the darkness and the herbage was left, twisted and reaped..."*

The sentence, together with what is conjoined to it, is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) confirming what is in the two groups as a sign. The words of God, ﴿fighting in the way of God﴾, are in the nominative position as an attribute of a complete group, as if it were said: a believing group. But in its place is mentioned, from the rulings of faith, what suits the context, as praise for them, and as a reckoning of their fighting, and as an announcement that it is the basis for the realization of the sign, which is the seeing of the few as many. It has also been read as *yuqatilu* (he fights), treating *fi'ah* as meaning a people or a company.

﴿And another﴾ (wa ukhra) is a descriptive modifier (na't) of an omitted subject conjoined to what was omitted from the first sentence. That is: and another group. It is indefinite, whereas by analogy it should be definite like its counterpart, because it is clear that the distinction applies to the dual just mentioned, and there is no need for definition. The words of God, ﴿disbelieving﴾ (kafirah), are the predicate of the omitted subject. The reason this group is not described by what corresponds to the description of the first group is to remove their fighting from the level of consideration, and as an announcement that they did not take up the fight because of the terror and awe that had seized them. It has also been said: each of the two conjoined elements is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in *iltaqata*, and what follows them is a description. So there must be an omitted pronoun referring back to the substituted element, which justifies describing the substitute with a sentence lacking its pronoun. That is: a group of them fights, etc., and another group is disbelieving. It is also permissible that each of them is a subject and what follows them is the predicate: one group of them fights, etc., and another group is disbelieving. It has also been said: each of them is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: among them is a group that fights, etc.

It has been read as *fi'atin* in the genitive as a partitive substitution (badal ba'd min kull) for "two groups." It has already been noted that a pronoun referring back to the substituted element must be present, and this is called a detailed substitution (badal tafsili), as in the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azza:

*"I was like one with two legs: one healthy, and one which time struck, so it was paralyzed."*

It has also been read as *fi'atan* etc. in the accusative, either for praise, or for blame, or as a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in *iltaqata*. As if it were said: they met, believing and disbelieving. Then *fi'atan* and *ukhra* serve as a preparatory introduction (tawti'a) to what is in fact the circumstantial qualifier, since the intended purpose of the mention is the description of the two.

As in your saying: "Zayd came to me as a righteous man."

﴿They see them﴾ (yarawnahum), that is: the last group makes the first group appear. The choice of the plural form indicates that the seeing encompasses each individual of the group. The sentence is in the nominative position as a descriptive attribute of the last group, or it is a resumptive sentence clarifying how the sign occurred.

﴿Twice their number﴾ (mithlayhim), that is: twice the number of the observers, approximately two thousand. For they were approximately one thousand, and they were nine hundred and fifty fighters, led by 'Utba ibn Rabi'a ibn 'Abd Shams, and among them were Abu Sufyan and Abu Jahl. Among them were one hundred horses and seven hundred camels, and of weapons of every kind an uncountable number.

It is related on the authority of Muhammad ibn Abi al-Furat, on the authority of Sa'd ibn Aws, that he said: The polytheists captured a man from the Muslims, and they asked him: "How many were you?" He said: "Three hundred and some tens." They said: "We did not see you except that you were doubling against us, or twice the number of those we saw." That is, six hundred and some twenty, whereas they were three hundred and thirteen men: seventy-seven men from the Emigrants (Muhajirun), and two hundred and thirty-six from the Helpers (Ansar), may God be pleased with them all. The standard-bearer of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and of the Emigrants was 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him), and the standard-bearer of the Helpers was Sa'd ibn 'Ubada al-Khazraji. In the army there were ninety camels and two horses, one of which belonged to al-Miqdad ibn 'Amr, and the other to Marthad ibn Abi Marthad, and six coats of mail and eight swords. The total of those martyred on that day from among the Muslims was fourteen men: six from the Emigrants and eight from the Helpers, may God be pleased with them all. God, Mighty and Majestic, showed them thus, despite their paucity, so that [the enemy] would be awed and would shrink from fighting them, as a reinforcement (madad) from Him, glorified is He, just as He reinforced them with the angels, peace be upon them. This occurred at the meeting of the two groups, after He had made them appear few in their eyes when they first saw each other, so that they would be emboldened against them and would not flee from the outset, when fleeing would have saved them.

It has also been said: the first group makes the last group appear twice their own number, even though they were three times as many, so that they would stand firm and be reassured by the promised victory in the words of God: ﴿If there are among you a hundred steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾.

The first explanation is the better one, because seeing twice their number, which was not specified on the side of the believers, is not the case: rather, what occurred was the seeing of an equal number, or even less than that. For it is related that Ibn Mas'ud (may God be pleased with him) said: "We looked at the polytheists and saw them doubling against us, then we looked at them again and we did not see them exceed us by even one man." Then God, Exalted, made them appear few in their eyes even more, until they saw them as a small number, fewer than themselves. Ibn Mas'ud (may God be pleased with him) said: "They were made to appear few in our eyes on the day of Badr, until I said to a man beside me: 'Do you see them as seventy?' He said: 'I see them as a hundred.' Then we captured one of them and we said: 'How many were you?' He said: 'A thousand.'"

So if the intended meaning were that the believers would see the polytheists as fewer than their actual number, as in the Surah of al-Anfal, then their seeing of them as fewer than themselves would be more worthy of mention as a sign than seeing them as twice their number. Moreover, demonstrating the effects of God's power and wisdom to the disbelievers, by showing them the few as many and the weak as strong, and by casting terror into their hearts because of this, is more fitting as a sign for them and as a proof against them, and closer to the acknowledgment of the addressees of this, because of their great mixing with the disbelievers who witnessed the situation. Likewise, the connection of the verb to its agent is stronger than its connection to its object. Therefore, making the nearer of the two previously mentioned items the agent and the more distant one the object is, whether the sentence is taken as a descriptive attribute or as a resumptive sentence, better than the reverse. This is what the eloquence of the revelation requires according to the reading of the majority. It is not appropriate to make the address to the polytheists of Mecca, as has been said. As for making the threat a reference to the defeat at Badr, as they have explicitly stated, it is evident and has no concealment. As for making it a reference to another defeat, then the group that witnessed that awesome sign are the ones addressed at that time. So referring to them once as an unspecified group and another time as a described group, and then attributing the seeing to them, while attributing it to the addressees would be more effective in establishing the proof and more fitting for rebuke, is something for which there is no need. By this it becomes clear the status of making the second address to the believers.

As for the reading *tarawnahum* with the second-person address (ta' al-khitab), its apparent meaning, even if it directs the second address to the polytheists, is not decisive in that regard. For even if the final difficulty is removed by it, the first one remains as it is. Perhaps the seeing of the polytheists was treated as the seeing of the Jews, because of the unity between them in disbelief and their agreement in word, especially after the covenant and pact that took place between them through Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. So the seeing is attributed to them as an intensification of the explanation and to confirm that such a situation befell them. So reflect. It has also been said: the intended meaning is all the disbelievers, and there is no doubt about its soundness and correctness. It has also been read as *yurawnahum* and *turawnahum* in the passive voice from the causative (min al-irada), meaning: God shows them (yurihim) or shows you (yurikum) thus.

﴿Visible sight﴾ (ra'y al-'ayn) is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid) for *yarawnahum* if the seeing is by the eye. Or it is an analogical verbal noun (masdar tashbihi) if the seeing is of the heart, meaning: a manifest, unveiled seeing, operating in the manner of seeing with the eye.

﴿And God strengthens﴾, that is: He reinforces.

﴿With His help whom He wills﴾: that He strengthens him without the intermediary of ordinary means, just as He strengthened the fighting group in His way with the victory mentioned. This is part of the speech that was commanded to be delivered.

﴿Indeed in that﴾ refers to what was mentioned of seeing the few as many, which entails the victory of the few, who lacked equipment, over the many, who complained of their weapons. The sense of distance in the demonstrative is to announce the great distance of the status of what is pointed to in excellence.

﴿Surely a lesson﴾ ('ibrah): *al-'ibrah* is a form from *al-'ubur* (crossing over), like *al-rikbah* from *al-rukub* (riding) and *al-jilsah* from *al-julus* (sitting). Its meaning is admonition (al-i'tiz), for it is a kind of crossing over, that is: a great lesson existing.

﴿For people of insight﴾ (li-ulī al-abṣār): for those with minds and discernment. It has also been said: for those who see them. This is either part of the speech subsumed under the saying, confirming what precedes it by way of a concluding statement (tadhyil), or it comes from Him, Exalted, confirming His words upon him, peace and blessings be upon him.

﴿Zuyyina lil-nas﴾ (It has been made attractive to people) is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaʼnaf, a new sentence not grammatically dependent on what precedes it). It is brought to explain how trivial worldly pleasures and their various kinds are, to make people averse to them, and to direct their desires toward what is with God, following the explanation that these things benefit none of the disbelievers who used to take pride in them. By "people" (al-nas) is meant the human race as a whole.

﴿Hubb al-shahawat﴾ (the love of desires). "Al-shahwa" is the soul's inclination toward what it wants. Here what is meant is "al-mushtahayat" (the desired things), and it is expressed as "al-shahawat" to emphasize that they are desired and sought after, as if they were the desires themselves. Alternatively, it indicates their immersion in loving them, to the point that they loved their desired objects, as in God's words, ﴿Indeed, I have loved the love of good﴾. Or it is a way of disparaging them, since desire is base and blameworthy, one of the qualities of beasts. "Al-muzayyin" (the one who makes attractive) is God, glorified and exalted, since He is the Creator of all actions and motives. The wisdom behind this is to test them. God, exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them﴾, and so on. Such adornment is a means to attaining the happiness of both abodes when its pursuit follows the noble Shariʻa, and a means to the continuation of the species. The passive form (al-majhul) "zuyyina" was chosen in keeping with the customs of divine majesty, and it has also been read in the active voice. It has been said that "al-muzayyin" is Satan, since the context of the noble verse is one of censure of these things. Al-Jubba'i distinguished between permissible things, attributing their adornment to God Most High, and forbidden things, attributing their adornment to Satan.

﴿Min al-nisaʼ wal-banin﴾ (of women and sons). It is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) describing "al-shahawat", and "min" here explains it in meaning. It has also been said that "min" indicates the category (li-bayan al-jins). Women are mentioned before sons because of their prominence in the meaning of desire, for they are the snares of Satan. Daughters are not mentioned because love for them is not consistently found in the same way.

﴿Wal-qanatir al-muqantara﴾ (and heaped-up piles of gold and silver). "Qinṭar" is the plural "qanatir" and means a great amount of wealth. It has been said to be one hundred thousand dinars, or the filling of a bull's hide, or seventy thousand, or forty thousand mithqal, or eighty thousand, or one hundred ratl, or one thousand two hundred mithqal, or two thousand dinars, or one hundred mana, one hundred ratl, one hundred mithqal and one hundred dirham, or the blood-money for a soul. There is disagreement over whether its pattern is "fiʻlal" or "fiʻnal". The word "al-muqantara" is derived from it for emphasis, like the saying "badra mubdara" (a purse emptied out). It has also been said that "al-muqantara" means well-secured and fortified, or abundant and piled up, one part on another, or buried, or minted and stamped.

﴿Min al-dhahab wal-fiddah﴾ (of gold and silver) is either an explanation of "al-qanatir" or a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿Wal-khayl﴾ (and horses) is coordinated with "al-qanatir". It has been said that "khayl" is a collective noun with no singular form from its own root, like "qawm" and "rahṭ", whose singular is "faras" (horse). It has also been said that its singular is "kha'il", derived from "khuyala" (vanity, pride).

﴿Al-musawwama﴾ means "al-muʻallama", marked, from "al-sawma" (a mark), or "al-mar'iyya", pastured, from "asama al-dabba" and "sawwamaha" when one releases and lets the animal graze freely, or "al-muthamhama", perfect in form.

﴿Wal-anʻam﴾ (and livestock) means camels, cattle and sheep.

﴿Wal-harth﴾ (and tillage) means crops, a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle (bi-maʻna al-mafʻul).

﴿Dhalika﴾ (that) means what has been mentioned of the aforementioned things.

﴿Mataʻ al-hayat al-dunya﴾ (the enjoyment of the life of this world) means what is enjoyed in the life of this world for a few days, after which it quickly perishes.

﴿Wallahu ʻindahu husn al-maʼab﴾ (and God, with Him is the best return). "Husn al-marjiʻ" means the good place of return. This indicates that nothing among what has been enumerated has a praiseworthy outcome. Repeating the predication by making the divine name (al-jalala) the subject, and predicating a locative sentence of it, adds emphasis and magnification, and heightens the encouragement toward what is with God, mighty and majestic, of lasting bliss, and the discouragement from the pleasures of this world and its fleeting good things.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 15:

﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something better than that?﴾ After He had explained, in summary, the state of the adornments of the worldly life, and mentioned what is with Him, Exalted is He, of good return, He commanded His Prophet ﷺ to elaborate on that summarized matter for the people, as an intensification of encouragement. The address is to everyone, and the hamza (interrogative particle) is for confirmation, meaning: "Shall I inform you of what is better than those pleasures that were detailed and made attractive to you?" The vagueness of "something better" serves to magnify its matter and to create eagerness for it. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For those who are God-conscious with their Lord are gardens﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining that vague matter, either with ﴿gardens﴾ as the subject and the prepositional phrase as the predicate, or with ﴿gardens﴾ raised by it as the agent, according to those who do not require that the preposition depend on a preceding element, as explained in its proper place. By taqwa is meant devoting oneself wholly to God, Exalted is He, and turning away from all else, as indicated by the attributes that follow. The attaching of the attainment of the gardens and what follows of the varieties of goods to it is to encourage its attainment and steadfastness in it. "With" (ʿinda) is in the accusative as a circumstantial element (ḥāl) from ﴿gardens﴾, or it is related to what the prepositional phrase is related to, in the sense of "being situated," indicating the complete loftiness of the rank of the gardens and the sublimity of their tiers. The mention of the title of Lordship together with the attachment to the pronoun of the God-fearing is to show increased kindness toward them.

It has been said: the lām is related to "something better," and likewise the adverbial phrase, and ﴿gardens﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause explains "something better." This is supported by the reading "gardens" in the genitive as an apposition to "something better." It is not hidden that linking the informing and explaining to what is better, for a particular group, may give the impression that there is another better thing for others.

﴿Flowing﴾ is in a position of nominative or genitive as an attribute of ﴿gardens﴾ according to the two readings.

﴿Beneath them rivers flow﴾ is related to ﴿flowing﴾. If by ﴿gardens﴾ is meant the trees themselves, as is apparent, then their flowing beneath them is evident; and if by them is meant the totality of the land and trees, then it is by consideration of its apparent part, as its detailed explanation has passed several times.

﴿Abiding therein﴾ is a presumed circumstantial element from the pronoun implied in "for those who," and the operating element is the sense of "being situated" contained in it.

﴿And pure spouses﴾ is conjoined to ﴿gardens﴾, meaning: cleansed of what is loathsome in women, of bodily and natural conditions.

﴿And approval﴾: the tanwin is for magnification. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from God﴾ is related to an omitted element that occurs as its attribute, emphasizing the grandeur conveyed by the tanwin; meaning: approval, and what approval, whose measure no one can estimate, is from God, Mighty and Majestic. It has also been read with the rā' vowelled with a ḍamma.

﴿And God is Seeing of the servants﴾, both of their deeds, so He rewards and punishes according to what befits them; or Seeing of the states of those who are God-conscious, and for that reason He has prepared for them what has been mentioned. In this is an indication that they are the ones deserving to be named by the name "servant."

Those who say, ﴿Our Lord, we have indeed believed﴾ (الَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ رَبَّنا إنَّنا آمَنّا), is in a place of raising (مَحَلِّ الرَّفْعِ, mahall al-raf', the nominative position). It is the predicate (khabar) of a deleted subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), as if it had been said: "Who are those pious ones who attain these noble honours?" Then it was said: "They are those who..." and so on. It may also be in the accusative by way of praise, or in the genitive as a follower of ﴿the pious﴾ (الْمُتَّقِينَ) as a descriptive adjective (نَعْتًا, na't) or an appositive (بَدَلًا, badal), or likewise following ﴿the servants﴾ (الْعِبادِ). The first is more apparent.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And Allah is Seeing of the servants﴾ (وَاللَّهُ بَصِيرٌ بِالْعِبادِ), in this case, is a parenthetical clause (مُعْتَرِضَةٌ, mu'taridah) and an emphasis of the sentence, to show that their faith arises from a great desire and perfect eagerness.

In the ordering of the supplication by their saying, ﴿So forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, upon mere faith, there is an indication that faith alone is sufficient to merit forgiveness and protection from the Fire.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 17:

﴿The patient⁠﴾ — this is on the reckoning that the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is in a nominative position, in which case it is put in the accusative by way of praise, with the implied verb "I mean" (a'ni). As for the reckoning that it is in a accusative or genitive position, then it is a qualifier (na't) for it. What is meant by patience (al-sabr) is patience in the hardships of acts of obedience, in adversity and affliction (al-ba'sa' wa'l-darra'), and at the time of battle (hina'l-ba's).

﴿And the truthful⁠﴾ — in their words, their intentions and their resolutions.

﴿And the obedient⁠﴾ — those who persist in acts of obedience and are constant in acts of worship.

﴿And the spending⁠﴾ — spending their wealth in the way of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And those who seek forgiveness at dawn⁠﴾ — Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: that is, those who pray at dawn (al-asḥar). From Zayd ibn Aslam: they are those who pray the dawn prayer in congregation. Al-Hasan said: they prolonged the prayer until the pre-dawn (al-sahar), then they sought forgiveness. Nafi' said: Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, would spend the night in worship, then he would say, "O Nafi', has dawn come?" I would say, "No," so he would return to prayer. When I said, "Yes," he would sit, seeking forgiveness from Allah and supplicating until morning. From al-Hasan: they used to pray at the beginning of the night until, when the pre-dawn came, they began supplication and seeking forgiveness. The specification of the pre-dawn hours for seeking forgiveness is because supplication at that time is closer to being answered, since worship then is more arduous, the soul is purer, and the spirit is more gathered, especially for those who strive. The placing of the conjunction "wa" (and) between the enumerated attributes serves to indicate the independence of each of them and their perfection in each, or the difference of those described by them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 18:

﴿God bears witness that He﴾ with the hamza vowelled with a fatha, meaning "that He," or "on the basis that He."

﴿There is no deity but Him﴾: that is, He made His oneness clear by setting up the cosmic proofs in the horizons and in the souls, and by sending down the legislative verses that speak to this. He expressed this with the word "witness" by way of metaphor (istiʿara, the transfer of a word from its literal to a figurative sense), to indicate its strength in establishing what is sought and to signal the rebuke of the one who denies it. It has also been read as "innahu" with the hamza vowelled with a kasra. This is either by treating "shahida" (bore witness) as if it were "qala" (said), which takes a direct quotation, or by making the clause a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ), with the verb governing His words, "Indeed the religion [with God is Islam]," on the reading of "anna" with a fatha, as will come. It has also been read as "shuhadaʾa lillah" (witnesses for God) with an accusative ending, as a circumstantial state (hal, an accusative describing the condition of the subject) of those mentioned, or as an accusative of praise (madḥ). It has also been read with a nominative ending, as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtadaʾ), and its ultimate parsing is nominative of praise, meaning: they are witnesses for God. "Shuhadaʾ" is either the plural of "shahid," like "ẓurafaʾ" is the plural of "ẓarif," or the plural of "shahid" in the sense of "shaʿirs" for "shaʿir."

﴿And the angels﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf, coordination) to the Majestic Name, with the bearing of witness taken in a figurative sense that includes acknowledgment and belief, by way of the generality of the metaphor. That is: they acknowledged this.

﴿And those of knowledge﴾: that is, they believed in Him and argued for Him with the proofs mentioned, the cosmic and the legislative. It was said: the intended ones are the prophets, peace be upon them. It was said: the Emigrants and the Helpers. It was said: the learned believers among the People of the Book, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his peers. It was said: all the learned believers who knew His oneness, exalted be He, through decisive proofs. As for their being in the nominative case according to the last two readings, it was said that it is by coordination with the pronoun in "shuhadaʾ," because of the separation (faṣl) between them. But you know that this, on the accusative reading as a state, leads to restricting the condition of those mentioned to the witnessing of the angels and those of knowledge, and there is not much benefit in that. So the correct view then is that their nominative case is by inception (ibtidaʾ, beginning a nominal sentence), and the predicate is omitted because the speech indicates it, meaning: and the angels and those of knowledge are witnesses to this. You may also take the two readings as an accusative or nominative of praise, and then the coordination to the concealed pronoun becomes good in every case.

His words, exalted be He, ﴿standing in justice﴾: that is, upholding justice in all His affairs. This is an explanation of His perfection in His acts, following the explanation of His perfection in His essence. Its accusative case is a state (hal) from God, as in His words, ﴿and it is the truth, confirming﴾. It was permissible to make it singular despite the impermissibility of "came Zayd and ʿAmr riding" because there is no ambiguity, as in His words, ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift﴾. Perhaps its being placed after the two coordinated items is to indicate the elevation of their rank and the nearness of their station, and the haste toward establishing the testimony of monotheism, showing concern for its matter and exalting its position. The secret of placing it before the two coordinated items, together with what it contains of indicating His originality in bearing witness to it, is as was mentioned in His words, ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord﴾. Or it is ﴿from whom﴾, which is the more apparent. The governing element in it is the meaning of the sentence, that is: singularly. It is most fitting that it be so because it is an emphasizing state, or it is an accusative of praise. It was said that it is an adjective (ṣifa) of the negated item, meaning: there is no god standing in justice, and so on. The separation between them is of the kind of their broad usages. It is included in what is witnessed to if it is made an adjective or a state of the pronoun, or an accusative of praise from it. It has also been read as "al-qaʾim bil-qisṭ," as an apposition (badal) of "huwa," so the separation between them necessarily occurs as it does with the adjective, or as the predicate of an omitted subject. It has also been read as "qayyiman bil-qisṭ."

﴿There is no deity but Him﴾ is a repetition for emphasis, and for extra attention to knowing the proofs of monotheism and the judgment concerning it after establishing the argument, and so that His words, exalted be He, may follow it:

﴿the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾, so that it is known that He is the one described by these two. The order is that knowledge of His power precedes knowledge of His wisdom, exalted be He. Their nominative case is by apposition (badal) from the pronoun, or by adjectival description (waṣfiyya) of the subject of "shahida," or as predicates (khabariyya) of a concealed subject. It has been related regarding its virtue that he, peace be upon him, said: "Its companion will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and God, Mighty and Majestic, will say: Indeed My servant has a covenant with Me, and I am most worthy of fulfilling covenants. Admit My servant into the Garden." This is evidence of the excellence of the science of the foundations of religion and the nobility of its people. It is related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that around the House there were three hundred and sixty idols, and when this noble verse was revealed, they fell down prostrate. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran. Al-Kalbi said: Two rabbis (aḥbar) of the rabbis of al-Sham came to the Prophet (ﷺ). When they saw Medina, one of them said: How much this city resembles the description of the city of the Prophet who will emerge at the end of time. When they entered upon him, peace be upon him, they recognized him by the description. They said to him, peace be upon him: "Are you Muhammad?" He (ﷺ) said: "Yes." They said: "And are you Ahmad?" He, peace be upon him, said: "I am Muhammad and Ahmad." They said: "Indeed we ask you about something, and if you inform us of it, we will believe in you and affirm you." He, peace be upon him, said: "Ask." They said: "Inform us about the greatest testimony in the Book of God, Mighty and Majestic." So God, exalted be He, revealed this noble verse, and the two men embraced Islam.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 19:
