﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (jumla musta'nifa) emphasizing the first: that is, there is no religion pleasing to Allah the Exalted other than Islam, which is monotheism (tawhid) and adherence to the noble Shari'a. From Qatada, that it is: the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and the affirmation of what has come from Allah the Exalted. It has also been read as "Indeed the religion with Allah is surely Islam" (lalIslam). It has also been read as "Indeed the religion" etc., as an apposition (badal) of "annahu": it is a badal al-kull (whole-for-whole apposition) if Islam is interpreted as faith or as what faith includes, and a badal al-ishtimal (apposition of inclusion) if it is interpreted as the Shari'a; or [it is read] that "shahida" governs it, on the reading of "innahu" with a kasra, as has been indicated.

﴿And those given the Book did not differ except after knowledge had come to them﴾ This was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians when they abandoned the Islam with which the Prophet ﷺ came and denied his prophethood. Referring to them by the relative pronoun, and making the giving of the Book a clause attached to it, serves to increase the censure of their condition, for disagreement by one who has been given that which removes it and cuts off its root is at the utmost of ugliness and reprehensibility. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿except after knowledge had come to them﴾ is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of states or the most general of times; that is: they did not differ in any state or at any time except after they knew that it is the truth from which there is no turning away, or after they knew the reality of the matter and became capable of knowing it through clear proofs and manifest signs. In this there is an indication of the extent of their deep immersion in error beyond which there is no greater, for disagreement after attaining that level is not something that issues from a sensible person. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿out of envious rivalry among themselves﴾ means: out of envy existing among them and seeking leadership, not from doubt or obscurity in the matter; this is censure following censure.

﴿And whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah﴾ That is: in His signs which state what was mentioned, that the religion with Allah the Exalted is Islam, and does not act in accordance with their requirement, or in any sign of His, exalted is He, such that what we are concerned with enters it in the first place.

﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ This stands in place of the answer to the conditional, as its cause: that is, whoever disbelieves in His signs, exalted is He, He will requite and punish him soon, for indeed He is swift in reckoning; that is, His reckoning will come soon, or that will be accomplished quickly. The explicit mention of the Majesty (al-Jalala) serves to instill awe and bring in dread. And in the arrangement of punishment upon disbelief in His signs, exalted is He, in general, without specifying the particular circumstance of them, namely that their disbelief came after the giving of the Book and after gaining awareness of what is in it, and that this was out of rebellion, is an indication of the complete severity of their punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 20:

﴿Then if they argue with you﴾, i.e., concerning whether the religion with Allah is Islam, or they dispute with you about it after you have presented the proofs to them.

﴿Then say: "I have submitted my face"﴾, i.e., I have sincerely devoted my self, my heart, and my whole being. He expressed it by the face because it is the most noble of the outward limbs, the locus of the powers and senses, and the gathering place of most of what worship consists of, such as prostration and recitation, and by it one turns toward everything.

﴿to Allah﴾, associating no partner with Him in it, and this is the upright religion upon which the proofs rest, and to which the signs and the messengers, peace be upon them, have called.

﴿and whoever follows me﴾ is a conjunction with the attached pronoun in "I have submitted," and this is permissible because of the intervening separation, which serves the function of emphasis by a detached pronoun; i.e., "and those who follow me have submitted," or it is an object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu, the object indicating the one accompanied).

﴿And say to those who were given the Book﴾, i.e., from the Jews and the Christians. The relative pronoun was placed in the position of the pronoun in order to maintain the parallelism between the two attributes of the conjoined groups.

﴿and to the unlettered﴾, i.e., those who have no Book, from among the polytheist Arabs.

﴿Have you submitted?﴾ following me as the believers did, for there has come to you from the clear proofs what necessarily requires and demands it without doubt. So have you submitted and acted upon its requirement, or are you still in your disbelief? This is like the saying of one who has summarized a matter for his companion and left no path of clarification and explanation unexplored, asking: "Have you understood it?" in the manner of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ (5:91), following the detailing of the deterrents from indulging in wine and gambling. In it is what is not hidden of belittling them, reproaching them for obstinacy and lack of fairness, and rebuking them for dullness and dullness of wit.

﴿Then if they submit﴾, i.e., as you have submitted. It was not stated explicitly, as in His saying: ﴿If they believe in the same as you believed in﴾ (2:137), to close the door entirely to applying the name of Islam to anything else.

﴿then they are guided﴾, i.e., they have succeeded with the greatest share and been saved from the precipices of misguidance.

﴿But if they turn away﴾, i.e., they turn away from following and from accepting Islam.

﴿then upon you is only the conveyance﴾ serves in place of the answer, i.e., they have not harmed you at all, for upon you is only the conveyance, and you have done so in the most complete manner. It is narrated that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse to the People of the Book, they said: "We have submitted." Then he (peace be upon him) said to the Jews: "Do you testify that Jesus is the Word of Allah, His servant, and His messenger?" They said: "God forbid." And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said to the Christians: "Do you testify that Jesus is the servant of Allah and His messenger?" They said: "God forbid that Jesus should be a servant." And that is the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿But if they turn away﴾.

﴿And Allah is All-Seeing of the servants﴾, knowing all their conditions. This is a concluding statement containing both promise and warning.

﴿Those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter﴾, as in your saying: "The Shaytan (Satan), beware of him, is a clear enemy." And according to the first view, it is a resumptive sentence (istinaf, a new sentence that begins a fresh clause). The demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah) is the subject (mubtada'), and the sense of distance contained in it indicates how far their affair has gone in misguidance and how remote their standing is in the awfulness of their condition. The relative pronoun (al-ladhina) together with what is within the scope of its clause is the predicate (khabar). That is: "those who are characterized by those ugly attributes," or "those afflicted with the worst condition, who" had their deeds, the righteous acts and good deeds they performed, rendered void, so that no trace of them remains in either abode. Rather, cursing and disgrace remain for them in this world, and a painful punishment in the Hereafter.

﴿And they have no helpers﴾, who would help them against God's might and His punishment in either of the two abodes. The plural form is used in consideration of the word ما (ma), and the word لا (la) is placed opposite it to negate the multiplicity of helpers from each one of them individually, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the wrongdoers have no helpers﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 23:

﴿Have you not considered﴾: an expression of wonder directed at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or at everyone who is capable of seeing, regarding the condition of the People of the Book and the evil of their conduct; and a confirmation of what preceded, that their disagreement regarding Islam occurred only after knowledge of its truth had come to them. That is: Have you not looked?

﴿at those who were given a portion of the Book﴾: that is, the Torah, with the lam (in "al-Kitab") being for specific reference. Taking it to refer to the genus of divine books is an extension of the distance, since the full closeness of the reference would then be complete only by including the Torah among them. The reason is that the basis of the censure and wonder is their turning away from being judged by what they were called to, and they were called only to the Torah. What is meant by "that which they were given" from it is what was made clear to them in it of knowledge and rulings, among which is what they knew of the descriptions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the truth of Islam. The expression "a portion" (nasib) indicates the complete particularity of this to them and that it is a right of theirs which must be observed and acted upon in accordance with its requirement. The indefiniteness in it is for magnification, and taking it to mean belittlement does not fit the context of emphasizing the ugliness of their condition.

﴿They are called to the Book of Allah﴾: which they were given a portion of, namely the Torah. The use of the apparent noun in place of a pronoun is to make response obligatory, and its attribution to the Majestic Name is to honor it and to affirm the obligation of referring to it. The sentence is a resumptive clause clarifying the place of the wonder, arising from a question that emerged from the beginning of the speech, as if it were said: "What do they do, so that he looks at them?" And it was said: "They are called to the Book of Allah, the Exalted." It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the relative pronoun.

﴿so that He may judge between them﴾: and this is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered their houses of study and invited them to faith. Nu'aym ibn 'Amr and al-Harith ibn Zayd said to him: "What religion are you upon?" He, peace be upon him, said: "The religion of Ibrahim." They said: "Ibrahim was a Jew." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Between us and you is the Torah, so come to it." They refused. It was also said: it was revealed concerning stoning, about which they disagreed. It was also said: the Book of Allah is the Qur'an, for they knew that it was the Book of Allah and did not doubt it. It was read as "liyuhkama" in the passive voice, in which case the disagreement among them is that some of them embraced Islam, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his like, and the others opposed them.

﴿Then a party of them turns away﴾: an expression of astonishment at their turning away after their knowledge of the obligation to return to it.

﴿while they are averse﴾: either it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "a party," as it is specified by the description, meaning: they turn away from the assembly while they are averse in their hearts; or it is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad), meaning: they are a people whose habit is aversion from the truth and persistence upon falsehood.

(p-21) ﴿Dhalika﴾ (That) refers to what has passed of turning away and aversion, and it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿bi-annahum﴾, meaning: it occurs because of the fact that they [did so].

﴿They said: "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days."﴾ (Despite) their committing sins and engaging in disobedience.

﴿Except for a few numbered days﴾: this is the length of their worship of the calf. Their belief in this became firmly established, and they made the calamities easy for themselves.

﴿And what they used to fabricate deceived them in their religion﴾: from their saying that, and what resembles it from their saying that "our fathers, the prophets, will intercede for us," or that "God the Exalted promised Ya'qub, peace be upon him, that He would not punish his descendants except for the fulfilment of an oath (tahillat al-qasam)." For this reason they committed the abominable acts that they committed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 25:

﴿How then﴾ is a rebuke to their stated claim mentioned above, and a refutation of what deceived them into magnifying what will befall them and exaggerating the terrors that will overtake them. That is: how then will their state be?

﴿When We gather them for a Day﴾ means: for the recompense of a Day.

﴿about which there is no doubt﴾ means: concerning its occurrence and the occurrence of what is in it. It is narrated that the first banner raised on the Day of Resurrection among the banners of disbelief will be the banner of the Jews, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will disgrace them before all witnesses, and then He will order them to the Fire.

﴿and every soul will be paid in full what it has earned﴾ means: the recompense of what it has earned, without any deficiency at all, as they claim. The word "earned" (al-maksub) has been placed in the position of its recompense (jaza'uhu) to indicate the complete connection and inseparability between the two, as if they were one thing. This also indicates that worship is not nullified, and that the believer is not eternally abiding in the Fire, because the full payment of the recompense for his faith and his deeds cannot take place in the Fire nor before entering it; therefore it occurs after deliverance from it.

﴿and they﴾ means: all people, indicated by "every soul."

﴿will not be wronged﴾ by an increase in punishment or a reduction in reward; rather, to each of them is given the measure of what he earned.

﴿Say: O Allah﴾. The *mim* (in *Allahumma*) is a substitute for the vocative particle, which is why the two do not occur together. This is among the distinctive features of the Majestic Name, as is its being preceded by the definite article, the elision of its hamza, and its taking the oath particle *ta'* (of *taallah*). It is also said that its origin is *ya Allah ummana bi-khayr*, meaning "direct us toward good" (*umma* being "to aim at" or "to intend"). It was then shortened by dropping the vocative particle, the object of the verb, and its hamza.

﴿Owner of Sovereignty﴾: that is, the owner of sovereignty in its entirety, absolutely, with true ownership, such that You dispose of it as You will, in bringing into being and annihilating, giving life and causing death, punishing and rewarding, without any partner and without any one who can prevent You. This is a second vocative according to Sibawayh (the grammarian), since the *mim* in his view prevents the word from being an adjective (*wasfiyya*).

﴿You give sovereignty﴾: this explains some aspects of the disposal that the ownership of the King requires, and confirms that His ownership is exclusively real, belonging to Him, Exalted, in truth, while the ownership of others is by way of metaphor. This is indicated by the choice of *itaʾ* (giving), which is simply bestowing, over *tamlik* (making someone a possessor), which would signify the establishment of ownership in reality.

﴿to whom You will﴾: that is, giving it to him.

﴿And You take away sovereignty from whom You will﴾: that is, removing it from him. The first "sovereignty" is real and general, and its being owned is real, while the other two are metaphorical and particular, and their attribution to their possessors is metaphorical. It has also been said that the first sovereignty is general and the other two are parts of it, so reflect on this. It has also been said that what is meant by sovereignty is prophethood, and taking it away is transferring it from one people to another.

﴿And You exalt whom You will﴾: that You exalt him in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both, by granting victory and success.

﴿And You abase whom You will﴾: that You abase him in one of the two, or in both, without any hindrance from another and without any resistance.

﴿In Your hand is all good﴾: the definiteness of *al-khayr* (the good) is for generality, and the fronting of the predicate is for restriction. That is: by Your power is all the good, not by the power of anyone other than You. You dispose of it by withholding and extending as Your will requires. The good is singled out for mention because it is decreed in itself, whereas evil is decreed incidentally, since every particular evil includes a general good, or because the occurrence of evil involves some participation by its doer in general, as it is a recompense for his deeds. The good, however, is pure bounty. Or it is for observing good manners, or because the discussion concerns it.

It is related that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) dug the trench in the year of the Confederates and divided among every ten men of the people of Madinah forty cubits, and they began digging it, a rock emerged from the bottom of the trench like a hill, on which the iron tools had no effect. So they sent Salman to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to inform him. He came, peace be upon him, took the pickaxe from him, and struck it a blow that split it, and from it a flash of light emerged that illuminated what lay between its two lava-fields, as if a lamp were in the middle of a dark house. So he said "God is great," and the Muslims said "God is great" with him. He said: "The palaces of al-Hirah appeared to me from it, as if they were the fangs of dogs." Then he struck a second time and said: "The red palaces of the land of the Romans appeared to me from it." Then he struck a third time and said: "The palaces of San'a appeared to me, and Gabriel informed me that my community will prevail over all of them, so rejoice." The hypocrites said: "Do you not marvel? He promises you and gives you false hopes, and tells you that from Yathrib he sees the palaces of al-Hirah and the cities of Kisra, and that they will be conquered for you, while you are digging the trench out of fear and cannot even come out." Then this verse was revealed.

﴿Indeed You are over all things competent﴾: this is a reason for what preceded and a confirmation of it.

﴿You cause the night to enter into the day﴾, that is, You make it enter into it by having one follow the other, or by shortening the first and lengthening the second.

﴿And You cause the day to enter into the night﴾, according to one of the two interpretations.

﴿And You bring the living out of the dead﴾, that is, You bring animals into existence from their constituent matter or from the sperm-drop. It has also been said: You bring the believer out of the disbeliever.

﴿And You bring the dead out of the living﴾, that is, You bring the sperm-drop out of the animal. It has also been said: You bring the disbeliever out of the believer.

﴿And You provide for whom You will without account﴾. Abu al-'Abbas al-Muqri said: The word *hisab* (account, reckoning) occurs in the Qur'an in three senses. In the sense of *ta'ab* (toil, exertion): the Exalted said, ﴿And You provide for whom You will without account﴾. In the sense of *'adad* (number): the Exalted said, ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾. And in the sense of *mutalaba* (demand for accountability): the Exalted said, ﴿So confer [favor] or withhold, without account﴾. The *bāʾ* (the preposition "bi") is connected to an omitted element which occurs as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative, a word describing the state of the doer or the object at the time of the action), and it is either a state of the subject of *tarzuqu* (provides) or of its object. In this is an indication that whoever is able to perform such great acts, which bewilder minds and understandings, then His power to strip sovereignty from the non-Arabs and humble them, and to bestow it upon the Arabs and make them honored, is the easiest of all easy things.

From 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the Opening of the Book (al-Fatihah), the Verse of the Throne, and two verses from Al 'Imran, ﴿Allah witnesses that there is no deity except Him﴾ up to His saying, ﴿Indeed, the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam﴾, and ﴿Say, O Allah, Owner of sovereignty﴾ up to His saying, ﴿without account﴾, are suspended (hanging) between the Throne and Allah the Exalted, with no veil between them and Allah. They say, 'O Lord, will You send us down to Your earth and to those who disobey You?' Allah the Exalted says, 'I have sworn that no one will recite you after every prayer except that I will make Paradise his abode, in exchange for what he did, and I will settle him in the enclosure of holiness, and I will look at him with My eye every day seventy times, and I will fulfill for him seventy needs, the least of which is forgiveness, and I will protect him from every enemy and envier, and I will give him victory over them.'"

And in some books: "I am Allah, the King of kings. The hearts of kings and their forelocks are in My hand. If the servants obey Me, I make them a mercy for them; and if the servants disobey Me, I make them a punishment upon them. So do not occupy yourselves with cursing the kings, but turn in repentance to Me, and I will incline them toward you." This is the meaning of his saying, peace be upon him: "As you are, so will you be ruled over."

(p-23)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 28:

﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies﴾ They were forbidden from allying with them due to kinship, or pre-Islamic (jahiliyya) friendship, or similar causes of companionship and association, as in His glorified saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ and the Exalted saying: ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾, so that their love and their hatred are for none but Allah the Exalted, or for seeking their help in the raid and in all other religious matters.

﴿rather than the believers﴾ This is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: going beyond the believers to them, whether exclusively or jointly. In it is an indication that they (the believers) are the worthiest of alliance, and that in allying with them there is a sufficient alternative to allying with the disbelievers.

﴿And whoever does that﴾ meaning: taking them as allies. The expression of it as a verb (fa'l) is for brevity, or to convey the sense of repugnance by mentioning it.

﴿then he has nothing from Allah﴾ meaning: nothing of His allegiance, the Exalted.

﴿in anything﴾ It is correct that the name of alliance (wilaya) be applied to it, for allying with two mutual enemies is something that hardly falls within the realm of occurrence. He (the poet) said:

"You wish my enemy, then you claim that I am your friend; the foolishness is not far from you."

The sentence is parenthetical (i'tiradiyya). His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except when you fear from them a fear﴾ is, in the form of the second-person address by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of circumstances, and the governing element is the verb of prohibition, with the address being taken into account in it, as if it were said: Do not take them as allies, outwardly or inwardly, in any circumstance, except the circumstance of your taking precaution.

﴿from them﴾ meaning: on their part.

﴿a precaution (taqah)﴾ meaning: a precaution, or a thing that must be guarded against, with the verbal noun standing in the place of the object (maf'ul). For then it is permissible to show allegiance in that situation, while the soul remains content with enmity and hatred and awaits the removal of the impediment, so that the staff may be stripped (of its bark) and what is in the heart may be revealed, as 'Isa, upon him be peace, said: "Be moderate and walk on the side." The original form of "taqah" is "wuqyah"; then the waw was changed to ta' as in "takhamah" and "tuhmah," and the yaa' was changed to alif. It has also been read as "tuqyah."

﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾ meaning: His holy essence. The permissibility of using the word "nafs" to mean the essence applied to Him, glorified is He, without any reciprocity (mushakala), is not a matter of dispute among the earlier scholars, though some of the later verifiers have stated that it is not permissible, even if the essence is intended by it, except by way of reciprocity. In it is a threat whose magnitude is not hidden. The mention of the "nafs" serves to announce that He has a terrible punishment, for which the dangers posed by the disbelievers are regarded as nothing.

﴿And to Allah is the final return﴾ a concluding statement confirming the content of what precedes it and establishing that it will certainly occur.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 29:

﴿Say: Whether you conceal what is in your breasts﴾ of the inner thoughts, among which is the allegiance to the disbelievers.

﴿or reveal it﴾ among yourselves.

﴿Allah knows it﴾, and so He will call you to account for it when you return to Him. The priority given to concealment over disclosure has already been explained (its secret) in the commentary on His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whether you reveal what is in your souls or conceal it﴾, and His words, exalted is He: ﴿He knows what they keep secret and what they make known﴾.

﴿And He knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾ is a resumptive statement, not conjoined to the answer of the conditional clause, and it is of the type of mentioning the general after the specific, for emphasis and affirmation.

﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾, so He is able to punish you in a manner beyond which there is no greater, if you do not desist from what you have been forbidden. The use of the noble Name in the place of a pronoun serves to cultivate awe and to magnify the gravity of the matter. It is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to what precedes, clarifying His words: ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾, namely that His holy Essence, distinguished from all other essences that are characterized by what none of them is characterized by, is characterized by essential knowledge that encompasses all objects of knowledge, and by essential power that encompasses all things within its scope, such that nothing whatsoever escapes His dominion.

﴿The Day every soul finds﴾: that is, of the accountable souls.

﴿whatever good it has done present﴾: before it, by the command of God the Exalted. In it there is an awe-inspiring force that is absent from the phrase "present" (ḥāḍiran) on its own.

﴿and whatever evil it has done﴾: this is conjoined to "whatever it has done" (mā ʿamilat), and presentation (al-iḥḍār) applies to it too. However, it is singled out for mention with regard to good, to signal that good is intended for its own sake, and that the presentation of evil is one of the requirements of the legislative wisdom (al-ḥikmah al-tashrīʿiyyah).

﴿would wish﴾ (tawaddu): this verb governs the adverbial phrase of time (al-ẓarf). The meaning is: it would wish and long, on the Day it finds its records of deeds, of good and evil, or their recompenses, presented.

﴿that between it and that﴾: that is, between it and that Day.

﴿were a distant term﴾: because of the extremity of its terror. The attribution of this wish to every soul, whether or not it had committed evil deeds, or whether it was purely devoted to good, indicates, to an extent that is not hidden, the full grievousness of that Day and the horror of its arrival. May God Almighty grant us refuge from that.

It is also permissible for the accusative of "the Day" (yawma) to be as a direct object (mafʿūl bihi), by the implied verb "remember" (uḏkurū). Then "would wish" (tawaddu) is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "every soul," or a resumptive statement (istiʾnāf) built upon a question. That is: "Remember the Day every soul finds whatever good and evil it has done present, wishing that between it and that [Day] were a distant term." Or, as if a questioner said, when they were commanded to remember that Day: "What will happen then?" So it was answered: "It would wish that between it and [that Day] were..." etc. Alternatively, "you find it" is restricted to "whatever good it has done," and "would wish" is the predicate (khabar) of "whatever evil it has done," and "mā" is not conditional, because of the nominative case of "tawaddu." The reading "waddat" (with feminine ending) is also attested, in which case it is permissible for "mā" to be conditional. However, taking it as a predicate is more apt in meaning, because it is a narration of a past state, and more consistent with the well-known reading.

﴿And God warns you of Himself﴾: this is a repetition of what preceded and a restatement of it, but not merely for emphasis. Rather, it conveys what the words of His Exalted and Majestic saying convey: ﴿and God is Compassionate toward the servants﴾. Namely, His warning comes from His compassion toward them and His vast mercy; or, His compassion toward them does not prevent the realization of what He warned them of regarding His punishment. His warning is not founded upon forgetting the attribute of compassion, but is realized together with its realization too, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿O man, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾. Thus the sentence, on the first view, is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtirāḍ), and on the second view, a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The repetition of the Majestic Name serves to nurture awe.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 31:

﴿Say: If you love Allah, then follow me.﴾ Love (al-mahabba) is the soul's inclination toward a thing because of a perfection it has perceived in it, such that it drives the soul to whatever brings it closer to that thing. When the servant knows that true perfection belongs only to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that every perfection he sees in himself or in others is from Allah, through Allah, and toward Allah, his love is for none but Allah and is in Allah. This necessarily entails the desire to obey Him and the eagerness for what brings him closer to Him. For this reason love has been interpreted as the desire for obedience, and it has been made to entail following the Messenger (ﷺ) in his worship and being eager to comply with him.

﴿Allah will love you﴾ means: He will be pleased with you.

﴿and forgive you your sins﴾ means: He will remove the veils from your hearts by overlooking what has passed from you. Thus He brings you near to the court of His might and settles you in the neighborhood of His holiness. He expressed this by "love" through metaphor (al-isti'ara) or figurative language by association (al-mushakala).

﴿And Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ means: toward whoever seeks His love through obedience to Him and draws near to Him through following His Prophet, peace be upon him. This is a concluding phrase (tadhyil, a closing statement that confirms what precedes it) that affirms the preceding sense while adding the promise of mercy. Placing the august Name in the position of the pronoun indicates that the attribute of divinity entails forgiveness and mercy.

It was narrated that it was revealed when the Jews said: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved." It was also said: it was revealed concerning the delegation of Najran when they said: "We worship the Messiah out of love for Allah, exalted is He." And it was said: it was revealed concerning people who claimed in his time, peace be upon him, that they love Allah, so they were commanded to make their words true through action.

Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them): "The Prophet (ﷺ) stopped before the Quraysh while they were in the Sacred Mosque prostrating to idols, on which they had hung ostrich eggs and put earrings in their ears. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O assembly of Quraysh, you have opposed the religion of Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both.' The Quraysh said: 'We only worship them out of love for Allah, the Exalted, so that they may bring us near to Allah in closeness.' Then Allah, the Exalted, said to His Prophet, peace be upon him: ﴿Say: If you love Allah﴾, the Exalted, and worship idols so that they bring you near to Him, ﴿then follow me﴾." That is: follow my law and my sunnah, and Allah will love you. For I am His Messenger to you and His proof against you.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 32:**

﴿Say: Obey Allah and the Messenger﴾, that is, in all commands and prohibitions. This includes obedience through following him (ﷺ) in the first place. The use of the explicit name (izhar, "explicit mention") instead of a pronoun (idmar, "concealment by pronoun"), through the shift of person known as iltifat (a shift in grammatical address), serves to specify the aspect (haythiyyah) under which obedience is due and to indicate its cause. The obedience commanded is obedience to him (ﷺ) insofar as he is the Messenger of Allah, not insofar as he is himself. There is no doubt that the title of Messengership is one of the things that makes obedience obligatory and motivates it.

﴿But if they turn away﴾: this may be part of what is said in the command, in which case it is the present tense in the second person, with one of the two tā' elided, i.e. تَتَوَلَّوْا (tatawallaw, "you turn away"). Or it may be a separate statement, following from it and coming from Allah, the Exalted, in which case it is the past tense in the third person. Leaving out the possibility of obedience, as in His saying ﴿But if they submit﴾, hints that obedience is not expected from them.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the disbelievers﴾: the negation of love is a kinayah (an allusion or figure of speech) for His hatred of them and His wrath against them, that is, He is not pleased with them and does not commend them. The use of the explicit noun (izhar) instead of a pronoun (idmar) serves to generalize the ruling to all disbelievers, and to indicate its cause, since His wrath against them is because of their disbelief. It also announces that turning away from obedience is disbelief, and that His love, Mighty and Majestic is He, is specific to the believers.

**Qur'an 3:33:** ﴿Indeed, God chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of Imran over all the worlds.﴾

When God Exalted had explained that the religion acceptable to Him is Islam and monotheism, and that the disagreement of the People of the Two Books concerning it arises only from rebellion and envy, and that attaining His good pleasure, forgiveness and mercy depends on following the Messenger (ﷺ) and obeying him, He began to establish his prophethood and his being from the people of the ancient House of Prophethood. He first explained the exalted rank of all the Messengers, peace be upon them, and then followed this with mention of the origin of the affair of Jesus, peace be upon him, and his mother, and the manner of his call to people to monotheism and Islam. This was to establish the truth and to nullify what the People of the Two Books hold concerning the two of them, of excess and deficiency. Then He explained the invalidity of their disputation about Abraham, peace be upon him, and their claim to belong to his religion, and He declared his lofty station free of what they adhere to, namely Judaism and Christianity. Then He stated explicitly that all the Messengers, peace be upon them, are callers to the worship of God, Mighty and Majestic, alone and to obedience to Him, and are exempt from any possibility of calling to the worship of themselves or others, whether angels or prophets. He also stated that all their nations are commanded to believe in whoever comes to them as a messenger confirming what is with them, to establish the obligation of believing in the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his Book, which confirms what lies before it of the Torah and the Gospel, and the necessity of obeying him, as will come in detail.

Adam, peace be upon him, is singled out for mention because he is the father of humankind and the origin of prophethood. The same applies to Noah, peace be upon him, for he is the second Adam. As for the mention of the family of Abraham, it is to encourage those who acknowledge their being chosen to believe in the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), and to incline them toward acknowledging his being chosen, by way of his being one of their company, along with what has passed of the indication that he, peace be upon him, is of ancient lineage in prophethood, from the company of the chosen and the righteous. As for the mention of the family of Imran alongside their inclusion in the family of Abraham, it is to show special concern for establishing the matter of Jesus, peace be upon him, because the disagreement about his affair is so deeply entrenched. Attributing election to the nearer father is a stronger indication of its being realized in the family, and this is what necessitated adding the family to Abraham rather than to Noah and Adam, peace be upon them.

"Istifa' (election)" means taking what is pure of a thing, like "istisfa'" (selecting the purest). By it is depicted God's choosing for them holy souls and what befits them of spiritual qualities and bodily perfections, which entail the Messengership, in the person of the chosen one himself, as with all the Messengers, peace be upon them, or in one who is connected to him and arises from him, as with Mary. It has been said: God chose Adam, peace be upon him, by creating him with His own hand in the best form, by teaching him the names, by causing the angels to prostrate to him, and by settling him in the Garden. He chose Noah, peace be upon him, by making him the first to abrogate (*naskh*, the replacement of a ruling by a later one) the laws, since before that marriage with close relatives had not been forbidden; by lengthening his life; by making his offspring the ones who remained; by answering his supplication concerning the disbelievers and the believers; and by carrying him upon the surface of the water. By "the family of Abraham" is meant Isma'il and Isḥaq and the prophets from their descendants, among whom is the Prophet (ﷺ). As for the election of the Prophet (ﷺ) himself, it is understood from the election of them by way of priority. Its not being explicitly stated is to indicate that it needs no mention, due to the full fame of his matter in *khullah* (close friendship with God), and his being the leader of the prophets and the exemplar of the Messengers, peace be upon them, and because the election of his family came by his own supplication, in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from among themselves﴾, and so on. For this reason he, peace be upon him, said: "I am the answer to the prayer of my father Abraham."

As for "the family of Imran": Jesus and his mother Mary, daughter of Imran son of Matan son of Azar son of Abi Bur son of Rabb Babil son of Salyan son of Yuhanna son of Yushiya son of Amun son of Manasha son of Hizqiya son of Ahaz son of Yuthim son of Uzziyahu son of Yahuram son of Yahushafat son of Asa son of Rahba'am son of Sulayman son of Dawud, peace be upon them, son of Bisha son of Awfidh son of Bu'az son of Salmun son of Nahshun son of Amyudhab son of Ram son of Hasrun son of Baris son of Yahudha son of Ya'qub, peace be upon him. It has also been said that the family of Imran means Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, the two sons of Imran son of Yasar son of Qahath son of Lawi son of Ya'qub, peace be upon him. Between the two Imrans there are one thousand eight hundred years. Accordingly, the election of Jesus, peace be upon him, would then be by inclusion in the family of Abraham, peace be upon him. The first view is the more apparent, as evidenced by its being followed by the story of Mary and by the election of Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, by their being clearly included in the string of the family of Abraham, peace be upon him.

By "the worlds" is meant the people of each one's time; that is, He chose each of them over the worlds of his own time.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 34:

﴿Dhurriyyatan﴾ is in the accusative, either as an apposition (badaliyyah) to the two (al-Al, i.e., Adam's house and the house of Imran), or as a circumstantial accusative (hal) from them both. The explanation of its derivation (ishtiqaq) has already passed in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And of my descendants﴾, and His words: (p-27) ﴿some of them from others﴾ are in the accusative place as an attribute (sifah) of "dhurriyyatan". That is: He chose the two families in a state in which they were descendants, linked in succession, some branching from others in lineage, as is indicated by the explicit mention of their being descendants. It has also been said: "some of them from others" means in religion. Thus the implication (istimalah) in the first aspect is an approximation (taqribiyyah), and in the second it is a proof (burhaniyyah).

﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of the sayings of His servants.

﴿All-Knowing﴾ of their deeds, both the manifest and the hidden; so He chooses from among them, for His service, whoever's uprightness is evident in word and deed, in the manner of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Allah knows best﴾, where He places His message. The sentence is a concluding remark (tadhyil) confirming the content of what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 35:

﴿When the wife of ʿImrān said﴾ is in the place of the accusative as an object (maf'ūl bihi) of a verb that is implied, in the manner of a resumption (isti'nāf), to establish the choosing of the family of ʿImrān and to explain its manner. That is: "Mention to them the time when she said..." etc. The reason for directing the reminder to times has passed several times, although the intended thing is the reminding of the events that occurred in them. It has also been said: it is in the accusative of time (ẓarf) relating to what precedes it, meaning: He is All-Hearing of her spoken words and All-Knowing of her intention which she kept hidden. It has also been said: it is a time-adverb for the meaning of "choosing" indicated by the mentioned verb "chose," as if it were said: "and He chose the family of ʿImrān when she said" etc. So this is the conjoining of sentences to sentences, not the conjoining of single words to single words, so that the choosing of all of them would necessarily be at that time. The wife of ʿImrān is Ḥannah daughter of Fāqūdhā, the grandmother of ʿIsā, peace be upon him. ʿImrān son of Yaṣhar had a daughter named Maryam, who was older than Mūsā and Hārūn, peace be upon them both. So it is thought that what is meant is his wife, but this is not so. For the matter of the guardianship of Zakariyyā, peace be upon him, requires that she was the wife of ʿImrān son of Māthān, because he, peace be upon him, was a contemporary of his, and he had married Ishā', the sister of Ḥannah, the mother of Yaḥyā, peace be upon him. As for his saying, peace be upon him, concerning Yaḥyā and ʿĪsā, peace be upon them both: "They are two maternal cousins." It is said: its interpretation is that the word "sister" is often applied to a sister's daughter, and on this basis he, peace be upon them both, made them two cousins. It has also been said: Ishā' was the sister of Ḥannah on the mother's side and the sister of Maryam on the father's side, on the basis that ʿImrān first married the mother of Ḥannah, who bore him Ishā', then he married Ḥannah, on the basis of the permissibility of marrying stepdaughters in their law, and she bore Maryam. So Ishā' was the sister of Maryam on the father's side and her maternal aunt, since she was the sister of Ḥannah on the mother's side. It is related that she was an aged, barren woman. Then one day, while she was in the shade of a tree, she saw a bird feeding its young, so she yearned for offspring and wished for one, and she said: "O Allah, I have a vow to You: if You grant me a child, I will dedicate it as charity to Bayt al-Maqdis, so that it will be among its servants." This vow was legitimate among them for boys. Then ʿImrān died while she was pregnant. At that time, her saying: ﴿My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb﴾ must be understood as a repetition, to confirm her vow and to remove it from the form of a conditional to the form of an unconditional statement. The mention of the attribute of lordship, which indicates the bestowal of what is good for the one being nurtured, together with its attachment to her pronoun, serves to set in motion the chain of answering. For this reason it has been said: when a servant wishes his supplication to be answered, let him call upon Allah by the names and attributes suitable to it. The emphasis of the sentence serves to show the intensity of desire regarding its content, and the placing of the prepositional phrase first serves to show full concern with it. The child is referred to with "what" only to obscure its matter and its inadequacy to the rank of rational beings.

﴿Dedicated﴾ meaning: freed for the service of Bayt al-Maqdis, occupied by no other matter, or devoted to worship. Its accusative is as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the relative pronoun in "nadhartu" (I vowed). It has been said: it is a state of its pronoun in the relative clause, and the governing element is the sense of "settling" (istiqrār), for it is in the force of "what has settled in my womb." It is not hidden that what is intended is restricting her action to dedication so that nearness to Him, exalted is He, may be achieved thereby, not restricting what has no bearing on her, namely the settling in her womb.

﴿So accept from me﴾ meaning: what I have vowed. Acceptance (taqabbul) is taking a thing with approval. In reality this is a request for a child, since acceptance cannot be conceived without the existence of the accepted thing; rather it is for a male child, since a female is not accepted (for this purpose).

﴿Indeed You, You are the All-Hearing﴾ of all things heard, of which among them are my humbling and my supplication.

﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of all things known, of which among them is what is in my heart, and nothing else. This is a reason for the request for acceptance, not in the sense that His being All-Hearing of her supplication and All-Knowing of what is in her heart makes acceptance possible in general, but in the sense that His knowledge of the soundness of her intention and her sincerity necessitates it, out of grace and kindness. The emphasis of the sentence serves to display the strength of her certainty in its content. The restriction of the two attributes of hearing and knowledge to Him, exalted is He, serves to display that her supplication is specific to Him, exalted is He, and that the cord of her hope is entirely cut off from anything other than Him, as an exaggeration in humble entreaty and supplication.

﴿فَلَمّا وضَعَتْها﴾ means: when she gave birth to it, that is, what was in her womb. The pronoun referring to it is feminine because the context calls for showing its femaleness, and because it is treated as within the scope of the conditional (*shart*), since the response (*jawab*) of "lamma" (when) is built upon it, as I intend. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿قالَتْ رَبِّ إنِّي وضَعْتُها أُنْثى﴾ ("She said: My Lord, I have given birth to it as a female") is not based on giving birth to some child in general. It is as if it were said: "When she gave birth to a girl, she said," and so on. It has also been said that the feminine form is used because what was in her womb was female in God's knowledge, or because it is interpreted as "the pregnancy," "the soul," or "the living being." You should know that considering any of what was mentioned within the scope of the conditional does not serve as the basis for the response being attached to it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿أُنْثى﴾ ("female") is a emphatic circumstantial (*hal*) clause from the pronoun, or a substitute (*badal*) for it. Its feminine form is for the purpose of hastening to present what had overtaken her of the disappointment of hope, or because of the interpretation mentioned earlier as "the pregnancy" or "the living being." In that case, the circumstantial clause is explanatory. She said it out of grief and regret over the failure of her hope and the reversal of her expectation, since she had hoped to bear a male. For this reason she had vowed it dedicated (*muharraran*) to the service of the sanctuary (*sidana*). The emphasis is to refute her false belief.

﴿واللَّهُ أعْلَمُ بِما وضَعَتْ﴾ ("And God knows best what she had given birth to") is a glorification on the part of God, exalted is He, of what she had given birth to, and an magnification of its status, and a statement that she was ignorant of its true worth. That is: God knows best the thing she gave birth to and the great matters attached to it, and that He made it and its son a sign for the worlds, while she was unaware of that. The sentence is a parenthetical interjection (*i'tiradiyya*). It has been read as "وَضَعْتَ" (you gave birth) as an address from God to her, meaning: you do not know the worth of this granted one and what God placed in it of exalted rank and lofty station. It has also been read as "وَضَعْتُ" (I gave birth) in the first person, with an *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person) from address to third person, to show the utmost reverence. In that case it is an apology from her to God, since she has brought forth a child unfit for the service she had vowed, or it is a consolation to herself, in the sense that perhaps God has a secret and a wisdom in it, and perhaps this female is better than a male. The reason for the *iltifat* is then clear.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَلَيْسَ الذَّكَرُ كالأُنْثى﴾ ("And the male is not like the female") is another interjection, explaining what was in the first about the magnification of the subject and the raising of her status. The *al-* (the definite article) in "al-dhakar" and "al-untha" is for previous reference (*al-'ahd*). That is: the male she was seeking, and imagining in him perfection, at best would be like one of the custodians, unlike the female who was granted to her, for the scope of her knowledge and her wish cannot encompass what is in it of great matters. This is according to the first two readings. As for the last interpretation of the last reading, its meaning is: the male is not like this female in excellence, but rather lower than her. As for the first interpretation, its meaning is: an emphasis on the apology by explaining that the male is not like the female in excellence, distinction, and suitability for serving those who worship in the sanctuary, for they are far removed from that. Thus the *al-* is for the category (*li-l-jins*).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَإنِّي سَمَّيْتُها مَرْيَمَ﴾ ("And I have named her Maryam") is coordinated (*'atf*) on ﴿إنِّي وضَعْتُها أُنْثى﴾. Her purpose in presenting it to the Knower of the unseen is to draw near to Him, exalted is He, and to seek protection (*'isma*) for her. Indeed, "Maryam" in their language means "the worshipper." Al-Qurtubi said: its meaning is "servant of the Lord." It also expresses that she has not retracted her intention, even though what she gave birth to was female, and that even if she is not suited to the custodianship of the House of the Holy Place (Bayt al-Maqdis), then let her be among the female worshippers in it.

﴿وَإنِّي أُعِيذُها بِكَ﴾ ("And I seek refuge for her in You") is coordinated on "innī sammaytuhā." The form of the present tense (*mudari'*) indicates continuity, that is: I entrust her to Your protection. It has been read with a fatha on the ya' of the speaker (*ya' al-mutakallim*) in the places that are followed by a hamza with a damma, except in two places: "بِعَهْدِي أُوفِ" (I will fulfill My covenant) and "آتُونِي أُفْرِغْ" (bring me, I will pour it out).

﴿وَذُرِّيَّتَها﴾ ("and her offspring") is coordinated on the pronoun. Placing the prepositional phrase before it serves to highlight the full concern for it.

﴿مِنَ الشَّيْطانِ الرَّجِيمِ﴾ ("from Satan, the accursed") means: the expelled one. The root meaning of *rajm* is pelting with stones. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no newborn who is born except that Satan touches him at the moment of his birth, so he starts crying out from his touch, except Maryam and her son." Its meaning is that Satan seeks to lead astray every newborn, such that he is affected by him, except Maryam and her son, for God protected them both through the blessing of this seeking of refuge.

﴿فَتَقَبَّلَها﴾ means that He took Maryam and accepted her in the vow in place of a male child.

﴿رَبُّها﴾ means her Owner and the One who brings her to her fitting perfection, and in this there is an honour for her that is not hidden.

﴿بِقَبُولٍ حَسَنٍ﴾ It has been said: the *ba'* (بِ) is extra (*za'idah*), and *qabul* (قَبُولٌ) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) emphasising the preceding verb with the additional letters removed, meaning: He accepted her with a good acceptance. The commentator turned away from the apparent sense to indicate that the acceptance came together with perfect pleasure and agreed with a special care (*al-'inayah al-dhatiyyah*). The form *tafa''ala* (تَفَعَّلَ), by its original usage, suggests effort and that the act goes against the nature of the doer, though what is meant of it regarding God, exalted is He, is what follows from it of complete strength and abundance of the act. It has also been said: *qabul* (قَبُولٌ) is that by which a thing is received, like *su'ut* (سَعُوطٌ, nasal drops) and *ladud* (لَدُودٌ, a drench) for what is put into the nose or the mouth. This means His singling her out by placing her in the position of a male in the vow, and no female had been accepted before her; or it means that her mother handed her over immediately after birth, before she grew up and became fit for the service (*al-sidanah*, guardianship of the sanctuary). It is narrated that when Hannah (حَنَّةُ) gave birth to her, she wrapped her in a cloth, carried her to the mosque, and placed her with the rabbis, the sons of Aaron (هارُونُ), who were in Bayt al-Maqdis like the keepers of the Ka'bah (الحَجَبَةُ). She said to them: "Take this offering (*al-nadhirah*)", so they competed for her, because she was the daughter of their leader and the master of their sacrifices, since the family of Mathan (ماثانُ) were the chiefs and kings of the Children of Israel. It has also been said: they found her affair and the affair of 'Isa (عِيسى) (peace be upon him) in the divine books, so Zakariyya (زَكَرِيّا) (peace be upon him) said: "I have the greater right to her, since her aunt is with me." But they refused except by lot, and they were twenty-seven. They went to a river and cast their pens into it, and the pen of Zakariyya floated while the pens of the others sank, so he took charge of her. It has also been said: it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) and there is a hidden genitive construction (*mudaf muqaddar*) in it, meaning: He accepted her with one who has good acceptance, that is, with a matter that has good acceptance. It has also been said: *taqabbala* (تَقَبَّلَ) here means *istaqbala* (اسْتَقْبَلَ, to receive), like *taqassa* (تَقَصّى) meaning *istaqsa* (to investigate fully) and *ta'ajjala* (تَعَجَّلَ) meaning *ista'jala* (to hasten), meaning: He received her at the beginning of her affair, when she was born, with a good acceptance.

﴿وَأنْبَتَها﴾ is a metaphor for raising her (*tarbiyatuha*) with what sets her right in all her conditions.

﴿نَباتًا حَسَنًا﴾ is a verbal noun emphasising the verb mentioned, with the additional letters removed. It has also been said: it is rather for a hidden verb agreeing with it, its estimate being: "so she grew a good growth."

﴿وَكَفَّلَها زَكَرِيّا﴾ means: He made Zakariyya (peace be upon him) her guardian (*kafil*) and surety for her welfare, standing in charge of her affairs. This was not by way of revelation but in the manner of the detail mentioned, for his desire (peace be upon him) to be her guardian, the floating of his pen, the sinking of their pens, and all the other matters that happened among them are all signs of His power, exalted is He. It is read *"iksulha"* (اكْفُلْها, imperative). It is read *"Zakariyya'"* (زَكَرِيّاءَ) with a fatha and with the madd. It is read with the *fa'* lightened and with a kasra, and *"Zakariyya'"* (زَكَرِيّاءُ) with a damma as a long vowel. It is read *"wa-taqabbalha rabbaha"* and *"anbitha"* and *"kaffilha"* in the imperative form in all of them, and *"rabbaha"* (رَبَّها) in the accusative as an invocation, meaning: "So accept her, O her Lord, and raise her with a good upbringing, and make Zakariyya her guardian," so this is a specification of the direction of the upbringing. It has been said: he (peace be upon him) built for her a *mihrab* (مِحْرابٌ) in the mosque, meaning an upper chamber reached by a ladder. It has also been said: the *mihrab* is the most noble of the places of sitting and its foremost part, as though she was placed in the most noble spot in Bayt al-Maqdis. It has also been said: their mosques were called *al-mahareeb*. It is narrated that no one would enter upon her except him alone, and when he went out he would lock seven doors upon her.

﴿كُلَّما دَخَلَ عَلَيْها زَكَرِيّا المِحْرابَ﴾ The placing of the adverbial phrase before the subject is to show complete care for her affair. The word *al-mihrab* (المِحْرابَ) is in the accusative by extension (*al-tawassu'*). The word *kullama* (كُلَّما) is an adverb on the basis that *ma* is a verbal (*masdariyyah*) particle; the time is either omitted or is an indefinite noun described by a following clause whose meaning is "the time"; the returning pronoun is omitted, and the governing element in it is its answer (*jawab*), meaning: every time he entered upon her, or every time he entered upon her in it.

﴿وَجَدَ عِنْدَها رِزْقًا﴾ means: he found with her a kind of provision not usual, for such things would descend from Paradise. He would find with her summer fruit in winter and winter fruit in summer, and she never suckled at a breast.

﴿قالَ﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) built upon a question, as though it was asked: "What did Zakariyya (peace be upon him) say upon witnessing this sign?" So it is said: he said: ﴿يا مَرْيَمُ أنَّي لَكِ هَذا﴾ meaning: "O Maryam, from where does this come to you, this which does not resemble the provisions of this world, while the doors are locked against you?" This is a proof for the permissibility of *karamah* (كَرامَةٌ, miraculous favour) for the saints (*awliya'*). Whoever denies it makes this a *irhas* (إرْهاصٌ, a preparatory sign) and a foundation for the prophethood of 'Isa (peace be upon him). As for making it a miracle (*mu'jizah*) for Zakariyya (peace be upon him), this is rejected by the fact that the matter was unclear to him (peace be upon him). He addressed her (peace be upon him) in this way although she was far from the rank of being addressed, because he knew from what he witnessed that she was supported by God with knowledge and power.

﴿قالَتْ﴾ is a resumptive sentence as before, as though it was asked: "What did Maryam do while she was young, having no ability to understand the question or to give a reply?" So it is said: she said: ﴿هُوَ مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾ meaning: "So do not be amazed and do not think it unlikely."

﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشاءُ﴾ that He should provide for whomever He wills.

﴿بِغَيْرِ حِسابٍ﴾ meaning: without measure, because of its abundance, or without any merit, as a bounty from Him, exalted is He. This is the justification for it being from God. It is either part of their speech, in which case it is in the accusative place (*mahall al-nasb*), or it is part of His speech, mighty and majestic is He, in which case it is a resumptive sentence.

It is narrated that Fatimah al-Zahra' (فاطِمَةُ الزَّهْراءُ) (may God be pleased with her) gave the Messenger of God (ﷺ) two loaves and a piece of meat. He returned with them to her and said: "Come here, my little daughter." She uncovered the tray, and behold, it was full of bread and meat. He said to her: "From where is this for you?" She said: "It is from God; indeed God provides for whomever He wills without measure." The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "Praise be to God who has made you like the mistress of the Children of Israel." Then he gathered 'Ali, al-Hasan, al-Husayn and all his household (may the good pleasure of God be upon them all), and they ate and were satisfied, and the food remained as it was, so she gave generously to her neighbours.

(p-31)

﴿Hunalika﴾ (At that point) is a new, independent statement and a separate narrative, placed within the account of Maryam because of the strong connection and close intertwining between them. Its inclusion also confirms the purpose for which the account of Maryam was given, namely to show the chosen status of the family of ʿImran, since the distinction of some relatives is evidence of the distinction of others. "Huna" is an adverb of place, "al-lam" (the lam) indicates distance, and "al-kaf" (the kaf) is for address. The meaning is: in that place, where he (Zakariyya) was sitting beside Maryam in the mihrab (the prayer niche), or at that time, since "huna," "thamma," and "haythu" may be used metaphorically for time.

﴿Da'a Zakariyya rabbahu﴾ (Zakariyya called upon his Lord). When he saw Maryam's miraculous favour from God and her station with Him, he desired that he too should have from Ishaʿ (Elisabeth) a child like the child of Hannah in nobility and favour with God Almighty, even though she was barren and aged, just as Hannah was. It is also said that when he saw fruits out of their season, he became alert to the possibility that an aged barren woman could bear a child from a decrepit old man, so he turned to supplication without delay. This is indicated by placing the adverbial phrase before the verb, not in the sense that this alone was the cause of turning to supplication, but that it was a final part of the complete cause, of which his advanced age, the weakness of his strength, and his fear of his relatives (mawali) were also parts, as explained in Surat Maryam.

﴿Qala﴾ (He said). This is an explanation of the supplication and a statement of its manner, and it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis).

﴿Rabbi hab li min ladunka﴾ (My Lord, grant me from Yourself). Both prepositional phrases are connected to "hab" (grant), because their meanings differ: the "li" (lam) is the complement of "hab," and "min" indicates the starting point metaphorically. That is: give me from the pure power of Yours, without an ordinary intermediary.

﴿Dhurriyyatan tayyibatan﴾ (a good offspring), as You granted to Hannah. It is also permissible for "min" to be connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (hal) modifying "dhurriyyatan," meaning: existing from You. "Al-dhurriyyah" (offspring) is nasl (progeny); it applies to the singular and plural, male and female. The intended meaning here is a single child, so the feminine form of the adjective is due to the feminine form of the noun it modifies, as in the words of one who said:

"Your father is a caliph, another woman bore him...
and you are the caliph of that perfection."

This applies when it is not intended to refer to a specific individual. If a specific individual is intended, it is not permissible to treat the word grammatically in that way, as in names like Talha and Hamza. So one may not say "Talha came and Hamza went" (using feminine verbs for these male names).

﴿Innaka sami'u al-du'a'﴾ (Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication), that is, the One who answers it. This is a justification for what precedes it and an initiation of the chain of answering.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 39:

﴿Then the angels called to him﴾. The one who called was Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, as the recitation of one who reads it (with the singular, fa-nadahu Jibril) makes clear. The plural is used as in the saying, "So-and-so rides horses and wears garments, and he has nothing but one horse and one garment." Al-Zajjaj said: That is, the call came to him from this category of beings, namely the angels. It has also been said: Since Jibril, peace be upon him, was their chief, the call was expressed with the term for the group, out of honour for him. It has also been said: A chief must have followers, so the calling was attributed to all of them, although it came from him alone. It has been read as fa-nadahu with imala (vowel inclination).

﴿while he was standing﴾. This is a circumstantial clause (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject) from the object of the calling. It confirms what the fa (then) conveys, namely that the good news came immediately after the supplication. As for His, may He be exalted, words ﴿praying﴾, it is either a description of "standing," or a second predicate according to those who hold that the second predicate may be a clause, as in His, may He be exalted, words ﴿then behold, it was a serpent, moving swiftly﴾. Or it is another circumstantial clause from the same subject, on the view that there are several such clauses, without conjunction or apposition. Or it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun hidden in "standing." As for His, may He be exalted, words ﴿in the sanctuary﴾, that is, in the mosque, or in the chamber of Maryam, it is connected either to ﴿praying﴾ or to ﴿standing﴾. This applies on the assumption that ﴿praying﴾ is a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in ﴿standing﴾, because the governing element and the circumstance then are one thing, so no intervening foreign element is required, as would be required on the other possibilities.

﴿that God gives you good news of Yahya (John)﴾. That is: that God [...]. It has been read with a kasra on the hamza, on the assumption of an implied "saying," or treating the calling as having the status of such, since it is a kind of it. It has been read yubshiruka from the causative form (ibshar), and yabshuruka from the triliteral form. Whichever reading is adopted, this statement to its end should be understood as relating, in its own wording, what God, may He be glorified and exalted, said, following the method of His words: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God﴾, etc. This is indicated by his (peace be upon him) returning the answer directly to Him, may He be exalted, not through the angel. The departure from attributing the good news to the royal "we" (nun al-'azama), as occurred in Surat Maryam, is to follow the customs of majesty, as in the saying of the caliphs, "The Commander of the Faithful orders you to such and such." It is also to indicate that what is related there of the calling, the good news, and the dialogue that follows was all through the mediation of the angel, as a report from Him, glorified is He, and not directly, as is the obvious reading. By this the unity of meaning of the two noble surahs becomes clear, so reflect. "Yahya" is a non-Arabic name, and even if it is treated as Arabic, its diptotic status (non-declension) is due to definiteness and the pattern of a verb. It is reported from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father: "He was named Yahya because God gave him life through the (barren) womb of his mother." Qatada said: Because God gave life to his heart through faith. Al-Qurtubi said: His name in the earlier Book was Hayy (Living), and there must be an implied noun to which the circumstance refers, namely: "with the birth of Yahya," for good news does not relate to entities themselves.

﴿confirming﴾. A circumstantial clause, anticipated, from Yahya.

﴿a word from God﴾. That is: [confirming] Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him. He was called "a word" because he came into being by the word "Be" without a father, so he resembled the wondrous things which belong to the realm of command. "From" (min) is for the beginning of the end, metaphorically, and is connected to an omitted element that stands as a description of "word," that is: a word proceeding from Him, may He be exalted. It has been said: He was the first to believe in him and to confirm that he was the Word of God and a spirit from Him. Al-Suddi said: The mother of Yahya met the mother of Isa and said, "O Maryam, did you perceive my pregnancy?" Maryam said, "I too am pregnant." She said, "I have found that what is in my belly prostrates to what is in your belly." That is the meaning of His words ﴿confirming a word﴾, etc. Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: Yahya was six months older than Isa, peace be upon them both. It has been said: three years older. He was killed shortly before the raising of Isa, peace be upon them both. In any case, there was a long period between the birth of Yahya and the good news of him, since Maryam gave birth when she was thirteen years old, or ten years old. It has been said: "a word from God" means: a book of God, called a word just as the poem of al-Huwaydara is called "the word of al-Huwaydara."

﴿and a master﴾. Conjoined to ﴿confirming﴾, that is: a chief who leads his people and surpasses them in nobility. He was superior to all people, for he did not commit a sin nor intend an act of disobedience. How great is such mastery, how lofty it is.

﴿and chaste﴾. Conjoined to what precedes, that is: one who exerts great effort in restraining the self and withholding it from desires while having the capacity. It is reported that in his youth he passed by some children who invited him to play, and he said, "For play was I not created."

﴿and a prophet﴾. Conjoined to what precedes, following from the praiseworthy qualities that were enumerated.

﴿from among the righteous﴾. That is: arising from among them, because he was from the lineage of the prophets, peace be upon them, or being one of those well known for righteousness, as in His, may He be exalted, words ﴿and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾. By righteousness is meant what exceeds the minimal righteousness that is absolutely necessary in the station of prophethood, reaching its utmost levels. On this is based the supplication of Sulayman, peace be upon him: ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 40:

﴿Said he﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) answering a implied question, as if it were said: "What did Zakariyya, peace be upon him, say at that time?" So it is said: he said, ﴿"My Lord"﴾. The angel did not address the one calling out to him as the one directly speaking to him, even though that was by way of relating from Him, may He be exalted. Rather, he followed the manner of his earlier supplication, out of exaggeration in humble entreaty and intimate conversation, and in earnest devotion to Him, may He be exalted, and as a precaution against what the address of the angel might suggest, namely the delusion that His knowledge, glorified is He, of what proceeds from him depends upon an intermediary, just as the standing of humans upon what proceeds from Him, glorified is He, depends upon an intermediary in most circumstances, even though it does not depend upon one in some of them.

﴿"How can there be for me a boy?"﴾ In this there is an indication that he had been informed, at the time of the glad tidings, that the child would be a boy, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"We give you glad tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya"﴾. "Anna" means "how" or "from where," "kana" is complete (taamma), and "anna" and "al-lam" are both related to it. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the subject is, as has been mentioned many times, for the sake of giving attention to what is fronted and creating anticipation for what is delayed. That is: how or from where will a boy come to me? It is also permissible for the "lam" to be related to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) of "ghulam," since if it were delayed it would be an attribute of it; or [kana is] defective (naqisa) with its subject being an explicit noun and its predicate either ("anna" and "al-lam" related to an omitted element, as mentioned) or it is the predicate, and "anna" is in the accusative of place (zarfiyya).

﴿"And my wife is barren"﴾ — "ataqir" meaning one who has barrenness (ʿuqr). This is also a circumstantial clause (hal) of the "ya" of "li" according to those who permit multiple circumstantial clauses, or of the "ya" of "balaghani," meaning: how can that be for me? The situation being that I and my wife are in a state utterly contrary to it. He, peace be upon him, said this despite having previously supplicated for it and the strength of his certainty in God's power over it, especially after his witnessing, peace be upon him, the previous signs, out of magnifying God's power, glorified is He, and marveling at it, and counting His favor upon him in that matter, mighty and majestic is He, not out of considering it unlikely. It has also been said: rather, that was out of considering it unlikely, since between the supplication and the glad tidings there were sixty years, and he had forgotten his supplication, and this is far-fetched. It has also been said: that was a question about how it would come about.

﴿"Thus"﴾ refers to the verbal noun (masdar) of "yafʿalu" in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿"God does what He wills"﴾, that is: whatever He wills to do of wondrous acts that break customary patterns. So "Allah" is the subject, "yafʿalu" its predicate, and the "kaf" is in the accusative place, as it is originally an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: God does what He wills to do, an act like that wondrous act and marvelous creation, which is the creation of a child from an aged, frail man and a barren old woman. It was fronted before the governing element to convey restriction in relation to what is lower than the thing indicated. The "kaf" is considered superfluous (muqhamah) to emphasize the grandeur conveyed by the demonstrative noun. Its verification has already been discussed in the interpretation of His saying: ﴿"And thus We have made you a middle nation"﴾. Or it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the implied verbal noun, being definite, meaning: He does the act being like that. Or it is in the nominative place, as a predicate, and the divine name is the subject, meaning: in the manner of this marvelous affair is the affair of God, exalted is He. And ﴿"He does what He wills"﴾ is an explanation of that vague affair. Or "thus" is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: the matter is thus, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"God does what He wills"﴾ is its explanation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 41:

﴿He said: "My Lord, appoint for me a sign."﴾ That is: a sign (ʿalāma) by which I may know the fulfilment of what is asked and the occurrence of the conception. He asked for it because conception (al-ʿulūq) is a hidden matter that cannot be ascertained, so he wished that Allah the Exalted would make him aware of it, so that he might receive that magnificent blessing with thanksgiving from the moment it came about, and not delay it until it became apparent in the usual manner. It is likely that this question came a long time after the glad tidings, since by then there appeared what has been mentioned of the difference between the ages of Yahya and ʿIsa, peace be upon them both, being six months or three years, because the appearance of the sign occurred immediately after its being specified, according to His the Exalted's saying in Surat Maryam: ﴿So he came out to his people from the prayer niche and revealed to them﴾, and the verse [continues]. Except that the exchange between Zakariyya and Maryam may have taken place when she was of advanced age, and she has been counted among those who spoke in infancy, in accordance with her saying that is related [in the Qur'an]. The "ja'l" (appoint) here is creative (ibdāʿī), the preposition "li" (for me) is connected to it, and its fronting (al-taqdīm) is for what has been repeatedly mentioned, namely the attention given to what is fronted and the arousing of curiosity about what is postponed. Or it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "ayatan" (a sign). It has also been said: it carries the meaning of "taṣyīr" (making/rendering), which requires two objects: the first being "ayatan" and the second being "li" (for me), and the fronting is because there is no justification for "ayatan" to be a subject (mubtada') when the sentence is resolved into a subject and predicate, other than fronting the prepositional phrase; so their status does not change after the entry of the abrogating particle (al-nāsikh).

﴿He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to people﴾, that is: that you will not be able to speak to them.

﴿for three days﴾, that is: consecutive days, corresponding to His the Exalted's saying in Surat Maryam: ﴿for three nights, sound﴾, while being able to remember and glorify [Allah]. Its sign was made to be this so that the period would be devoted to the remembrance of Allah the Exalted and to thanking Him, discharging the right of the blessing. It is as if it were said: the sign of the attainment of the sought-after and the arrival of the blessing is that you should restrain your tongue except for thanking Him for it. The best answer is that which is derived from the question itself.

﴿except by gesture﴾, that is: by signalling with a hand, a head, or the like. Its root meaning is movement; one says "irtamaza", i.e. he moved, and from it the sea is called "al-rāmūz". This is a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ) because a gesture is not of the kind of speech, or a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil), given that by speech is meant that by which the intended meaning is understood, and there is no doubt that gesture is of that kind. It has been read "ramazan" with two fatḥas, as the plural of "rāmiz" like "khadam", and with two ḍammas as the plural of "rumūz" like "rusul", as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of both him and the people together, in the sense of "mutarāmizayn" (signalling to one another), like his saying:

"Whenever you meet me as two individuals, the fleshy parts at your buttocks tremble and are startled."

﴿And remember your Lord﴾, that is: during the days of confinement, in thanks for the bestowal of favour and grace, as the mention of the title "Lord" (al-rubūbiyya) indicates.

﴿much﴾, that is: a great remembrance, or for a great period of time.

﴿And glorify [Him]﴾, that is: glorify Him, the Exalted, or perform glorification.

﴿in the evening﴾, that is: from midday to sunset. It has been said: from the afternoon until the passing of the first part of the night.

﴿and at dawn﴾, from the break of dawn until forenoon.
