It has been said: the intended meaning of glorification is prayer, as evidence by its being restricted to a time, as in His the Exalted's saying: ﴿So glory be to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾. It has also been said: it is the oral remembrance, just as the intended meaning of remembrance is the remembrance of the heart. It has been read "al-abkār" with a fatḥa on the hamza, as the plural of "bakar" like "saḥar" and "asḥār".

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 42:

﴿And when the angels said﴾ This begins an explanation of the remaining rulings concerning the chosen status of the family of 'Imran, following a reference to some of the virtues of their relatives, namely Zakariyya and Yahya, peace be upon them both, because the context calls for them, as will be pointed out. The verb is also recited with the masculine form (dhakkara). The intended "angels" here is Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, and what is involved in this has already been discussed. The word "idh" (when) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb that is conjoined to the implied verb preceding it, the narrative being conjoined to a narrative. It is said that it is conjoined to the earlier temporal clause, namely His saying: "when the wife of 'Imran said," and it is governed by the same governing word, so reflect on this. That is, "and mention also, among the evidences of their being chosen, the time when the angels, peace be upon them, spoke."

﴿O Maryam﴾ The repetition of the address serves to indicate increased attention to the rulings of chosen status that are related, and to draw attention to their being independent and distinct from the earlier rulings. For these are among the rulings of physical upbringing suited to Maryam's state in childhood, whereas these belong to the category of spiritual upbringing (p-35) through the legal obligations connected with her state in adulthood. It is said that they spoke to her directly, as an honour for her, or as an early sign (irhas) of the prophethood of 'Isa, peace be upon him, because of the consensus (ijma') that God, exalted is He, did not appoint a woman as a prophet. It is also said that they inspired her.

﴿Indeed God has chosen you﴾ first, in that He accepted you from your mother with a good acceptance, and did not accept any other female; and He raised you in the care of Zakariyya, peace be upon him; and He provided for you from the provision of Paradise; and He singled you out with noble honours.

﴿and purified you﴾ that is, from what is found repellent in conditions and actions, and from what the Jews slandered you with, through the speech of the infant.

﴿and chosen you﴾ last.

﴿above the women of the worlds﴾ by His granting you 'Isa, peace be upon him, without a father, which was not granted to any other woman, and by making you both a sign for the worlds. Accordingly, it is fitting that the mention of this exchange precede the mention of the good news of 'Isa, peace be upon him, because of what has been repeatedly noted, namely the indication that each of the two deserves to be mentioned independently. Had the external sequence been observed, it would have been understood that everything is one thing. It is also said that the two instances of "chosen" refer to one and the same choosing, and the repetition is for emphasis and to clarify who chose her above them. In that case there is no difficulty regarding the order of the noble arrangement, since "chosen" is then taken to refer to what was mentioned first, and this exchange is placed before the good news of 'Isa, peace be upon him, as an indication that before that she was abundantly devoted to acts of obedience and worship as she had been commanded, striving in them, turning wholly toward God, exalted is He, devoted to Him, stripped of the attributes of humanity, and prepared for the outpouring of the Spirit upon her.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 43:

﴿O Mary﴾ The repetition of the vocative serves to signal that the intended address is what follows it, and that what precedes it, the reminder of blessings, was a preparation for mentioning it and an encouragement to act upon its requirement.

﴿Devote yourself (iqnutī) to your Lord﴾ That is: stand (in prayer), or prolong standing in prayer, for Him, exalted is He. The mention of the title of His lordship (rubūbiyyah) for her serves to indicate the reason for the obligation to comply with the command.

﴿And prostrate yourself and bow with those who bow﴾ She was commanded to pray in congregation by mentioning its pillars, as an emphasis on the obligation to observe it and to signal the excellence of each of them and their fundamental nature. The mention of prostration before bowing is either because the order in their law was thus, or because prostration is the best of the pillars of prayer and the furthest degree of humility. This does not require that the external order be thus; rather, what is fitting for it is ascent from the lower to the higher. Or it is so that "bow" (irka'ī) is paired with "those who bow," to signal that those who have no bowing in their prayers are not worshippers. As for what has been said, that the conjunction wa (and) does not necessitate order, its outcome is correctness, not preference. The command with the last two pillars is stripped of what the first was restricted by, because the purpose is to restrict the command to prayer by this, and she has done so, since she restricted the first of its pillars by it. It has also been said that the intended meaning of qunūt is the continuation of acts of obedience, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing?﴾ and that by prostration is meant prayer, because of what has passed that it is the best of its pillars, and by bowing is meant humility and submissiveness. It was said: when she was commanded to this, she stood in prayer until her feet swelled and blood and pus flowed from them.

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (That) is a demonstrative referring to the wondrous matters mentioned earlier. The sense of distance in it serves to draw attention to the exalted status of what is referred to and the high rank it holds in virtue. It is a mubtada' (subject), and its khabar (predicate) is the words of the Exalted: ﴿مِن أنْباءِ الغَيْبِ﴾ (is among the news of the unseen), meaning: it is among the reports related to the unseen. (The sentence is resumptive, mustanifah, and has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis).) The words of the Exalted ﴿نُوحِيهِ إلَيْكَ﴾ (We reveal it to you) form an independent sentence that explains the first. It has also been said that the khabar is the second sentence, and ﴿مِن أنْباءِ الغَيْبِ﴾ is either related to "نُوحِيهِ" (nuhihi, "We reveal it"), or is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) of its pronoun, meaning: "We reveal it from among the news of the unseen," or "We reveal it while it is part of the news of the unseen." The use of the present tense (the form of the future-oriented verb) indicates that the revelation has not yet ceased.

﴿وَما كُنْتَ لَدَيْهِمْ﴾ (And you were not with them): that is, with those who disagreed and contended over the upbringing of Maryam (Mary). This affirms and establishes that it is revelation, in the manner of mockery toward those who deny it, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَما كُنْتَ بِجانِبِ الغَرْبِيِّ﴾ (And you were not on the western side) and so on.

﴿وَما كُنْتَ ثاوِيًا في أهْلِ مَدْيَنَ﴾ (And you were not dwelling among the people of Madyan) and so on. The means of knowing such events and occurrences is either witnessing or hearing, and their absence is certain for them. Thus there remains only the possibility of direct observation, which is impossible by necessity, so it is negated as a form of mockery toward them.

﴿إذْ يُلْقُونَ أقْلامَهُمْ﴾ (when they cast their pens): a ẓarf (adverbial of time) related to the istiqrar (the implied verb of being located) that governs "لَدَيْهِمْ" (with them). "Aqlāmahum" (their pens) means their arrows, the ones with which they cast lots. It has also been said that they cast lots with their pens with which they used to write the Torah, seeking blessing (tabarruk).

﴿أيُّهم يَكْفُلُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ (which of them would take charge of Maryam): this is related to an omitted verb indicated by "يُلْقُونَ أقْلامَهُمْ" (they cast their pens), meaning: they cast them, looking on, or in order that they might know which of them would take charge of her.

﴿وَما كُنْتَ لَدَيْهِمْ إذْ يَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾ (And you were not with them when they disputed): that is, concerning her affair, competing for her guardianship, as was mentioned earlier. The repetition of "وَما كُنْتَ لَدَيْهِمْ" (you were not with them), even though the purpose is already established, is by linking "إذْ يَخْتَصِمُونَ" (when they disputed) to "إذْ يُلْقُونَ" (when they cast), as in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿نَحْنُ أعْلَمُ بِما يَسْتَمِعُونَ بِهِ إذْ يَسْتَمِعُونَ إلَيْكَ وإذْ هم نَجْوى﴾ (We know best what they listen to when they listen to you, and when they confer privately). This indicates that each of the two matters, his (ﷺ) absence at the casting of the pens and his absence at the dispute, independently serves as testimony to his prophethood (ﷺ). This is especially so if their dispute is understood to mean their contention before the casting of lots, for the change in the order of mention confirms this.

﴿When the angels said﴾ This begins the account of Jesus, peace be upon him. It is a *badal* (substitution) for "when the angels said" above, and is in the accusative case through its governing word. What lies between them is an *i'tiraḍ* (parenthetical insertion), brought in to confirm what preceded it and to draw attention to its independence and to its being worthy of being counted on its own among the signs of prophethood. The conjunction is omitted between them on the basis that the addressee is the same, and to indicate that the two addresses are concurrent or close in time. It was said: it is accusative, governed by an implied verb that is conjoined to its governing word. It was said: it is a *badal* for "when they dispute," as if it were said: "You were not present in that long period, one part of which saw the dispute and another part of which saw this address," indicating his, peace be upon him, comprehensive knowledge of the details of Maryam's circumstances from beginning to end. The speaker is Gabriel, peace be upon him, and the plural form is used because of what has passed.

﴿O Maryam, indeed Allah gives you glad tidings of a word from Him﴾ "Min" (from) is used figuratively for the starting point, and it is connected to an omitted word that serves as an adjective of "a word," meaning: a word existing from Him, mighty and majestic.

﴿his name﴾ The pronoun referring to "the word" is masculine because it stands for a masculine referent. It is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is ﴿the Messiah﴾. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Isa﴾ is a *badal* of it or an *'atf al-bayan* (explicative apposition). It was said: it is another predicate. It was said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject. It was said: it is accusative, governed by an implied "I mean," for praise. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿son of Maryam﴾ is an adjective of Isa. It was said: the intended meaning of the "name" is that by which the named is distinguished from others. In that case, the predicate is the three together, since it is what distinguishes him, peace be upon him, from all others. "Al-Masih" is his title, peace be upon him, and it is one of the honorable titles, like "al-Siddiq." Its origin in Hebrew is *mashiha*, and its meaning is "the blessed." "Isa" is an arabicized form of *Yeshua*. The attempt to derive both from *al-mash* (wiping) and *al-'is* (a color) is subject to dispute. The explanation that he was wiped with blessing, or with what purifies him from sins, or that Gabriel wiped him, peace be upon them both, or that he wiped the earth and did not stay in one place, or that he, peace be upon him, would wipe one afflicted with a disease so he would be healed, and that in his complexion there was *'is*, meaning whiteness with a reddish tinge like a mark on water. It is said "son of Maryam" although the address is to her, to draw attention to the fact that he would be born without a father, so he is not ascribed to anyone except his mother. With this, she was preferred over the women of the worlds.

﴿and honored in this world and the Hereafter﴾ *Wajih* means one who has standing (*jah*), which is strength, protection, and nobility. It is a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier) *muqaddarah* (anticipated) from "a word." Although it is indefinite, it is suitable for the *hal* to be attached to it, and its masculine form is by consideration of the meaning. Honor in this world is prophethood and precedence over people; in the Hereafter it is intercession and high rank in Paradise.

﴿and among those brought near﴾ That is, near to Allah, mighty and majestic. It was said: it refers to his being raised to the heavens and his companionship with the angels. It is conjoined to the first *hal*, and His saying, exalted is He, is conjoined to it:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 3, verse 46:**

﴿He will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity﴾. That is, he will speak to them while being a child and while being a grown man (*kahl*), with the speech of the prophets and without any difference. "*al-mahd*" (المَهْدُ) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) that has been used as the name of what is prepared for the infant, that is, what is smoothed out from its resting place. It has been said that he was raised up as a young man, and the meaning of "and in maturity" is that he will speak as a grown man after his descent. The mention of his different and contrasting states indicates that he is far removed from divinity.

﴿And he is among the righteous﴾: this is another circumstantial clause (*hal*) coordinated with the earlier states, or it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun (*damir*) in "*yukallimu*" (يُكَلِّمُ).

"Qalat" (she said) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon an implied question, as if it were said: "What did Maryam say when the angels said to her what they said?" So it was answered: she said, supplicating to her Lord: ﴿My Lord, how can there be﴾, i.e., how can it be, or from where can it be?! ﴿for me a child﴾, in the manner of ordinary astonishment and wonder, and magnifying the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has also been said: it was in the manner of a question and inquiry, as to whether it would be through marriage or otherwise. The verb "yakunu" may be complete (taammah), with "anna" (how/from where) and "al-lam" (for me) both connected to it; and the postponement of the subject (fa'il) after the prepositional phrase is due to the concern with what is brought forward and the arousing of interest in what is delayed. It is also permissible for "al-lam" to be connected to an elided element that stands as a circumstantial clause (hal) of "walad" (child), since if it were postponed it would be a qualifier (sifah) of it. Or it may be defective (naqisah), with its subject being "walad," and its predicate either "anna," with "al-lam" connected to a hidden element standing as a circumstantial clause, as was mentioned; or the predicate is "anna," which is in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarfiyyah).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And no human has touched me﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) that confirms the astonishment, i.e., and the state I am in is one incompatible with childbearing.

"Qala" (he said) is a resumptive clause as previously explained, and the speaker is Allah, exalted is He, or Jibril, upon him be prayers and peace.

﴿Thus Allah creates what He wills﴾. The discussion of its grammatical analysis is as was mentioned in the story of Zakariyya exactly, except that the use of "yakhluqu" (creates) here in place of "yaf'alu" (does) there is because the birth of the virgin without a human having touched her is more wondrous and more strange than the birth of a barren old woman from a decrepit old man. Thus the verb "creation," which indicates origination (al-ikhtira'), was more fitting to this context than the general verb "doing," and for this reason He followed it with an explanation of its manner, so it was said: ﴿When He decrees a matter﴾ among matters, i.e., He wills a thing, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾. The root meaning of "qada'" is judgment and decisiveness; it is applied to the divine will that is definitive and linked to the existence of a thing, because it necessarily brings it about (al-battah). It has also been said: it means the command, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾, so that He says to it only, "Be."

﴿Then it is﴾ without delay. This, as you see, is an illustration of the perfection of His power, exalted is He, and the ease with which the things willed come to be as His will requires; and a depiction of the swiftness of their occurrence by means of the obedience known of the commanded one to the strong, obeyed commander; and a clarification that He, exalted is He, just as He is able to create things gradually through customary causes and materials, is able to create them at once without any need for any of the causes or materials.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 48:

﴿And He will teach him the Book﴾ That is: the writing, or the category of divine books.

﴿And the wisdom﴾ That is: the sciences and the refinement of character.

﴿And the Torah and the Gospel﴾ Singling them out by mention, on the assumption that by "the Book" is meant the category of revealed books, is for the sake of increasing their excellence and their distinction over others. The clause is a conjunction upon ﴿He will give him glad tidings﴾, or upon ﴿honourable﴾, or upon ﴿He creates﴾, or it is an independent statement brought to console her heart and to remove what concerned her of fear of blame, since she knew that she would give birth without a husband. It has also been read as "wa-nu'allimuhu" with the nun.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 49:

﴿And a messenger to the Children of Israel﴾ is in the accusative (manṣūb) by a concealed verb whose meaning is implied, and it is conjoined (maʿṭūf) to "yuʿallimuhu" (﴿He will teach him﴾). That is, "and He will make him a messenger to the Children of Israel," meaning all of them. Some Jews said that he was sent only to a specific people. Then it was said: he was a messenger during his childhood; and it was said: after reaching maturity. The first of the prophets of the Children of Israel was Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the last of them was ʿIsa, peace be upon him. It was also said that the first of them was Musa and the last of them was ʿIsa, peace be upon them all.

His, may He be exalted, saying ﴿that I have come to you﴾ is the object (maʿmūl) of "rasūlan" (messenger), because it contains the sense of speaking. That is, "a messenger speaking that I have come…" It was also said that it is in the accusative by a concealed verb governed by a concealed saying, conjoined to "man yuʿallimuhu." That is, "and he says: I have been sent as a messenger, that I have come to you…" It was also said that it is conjoined to the previous states (al-aḥwāl al-sābiqa), and the fact that they are in the third person (ghayba) does not harm this, even though this is in the first person (takallum), because of what you have understood: that it contains the sense of speaking. It is as if it were said: "while he is honorable and a messenger speaking that I have come…"

It was read "wa-rasūlin" (in the genitive), conjoined to "kalima" (word). The bāʾ in His, may He be exalted, saying ﴿with a sign﴾ is connected to a deleted element that serves as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the agent (fāʿil) of the verb, with the bāʾ indicating accompaniment (mulābasa). The tanwīn (nunation) is for magnification, not for unity, because their number and abundance are evident. It was read "bi-āyātin" (with signs) or "bi-jiʾtukum" (with "I have come to you"), with the bāʾ indicating transitivity. The "min" in His, may He be exalted, saying ﴿from your Lord﴾ denotes the starting point of the source (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya), figuratively, and is connected to a deleted element that serves as a qualifier (ṣifa) of "āya" (sign). That is: "I have come to you accompanied by a great sign from your Lord," or "I have brought you a great sign from Him, may He be exalted." Mentioning the attribute of lordship (rubūbiyya) together with the addition to the pronoun of the addressees serves to emphasize the obligation of compliance with the commands that will follow.

His, may He be exalted, saying ﴿that I create for you from clay something like the form of a bird﴾ is an apposition (badal) of His saying ﴿that I have come to you﴾. Its position (maḥall) is accusative by removing the preposition according to Sibawayh and al-Farrāʾ, and genitive according to the opinion of al-Khalil and al-Kisāʾi, or it is an apposition of "āya" (sign). It was also said that it is accusative by a verb to be estimated, that is, "I mean that I create…" It was also said that it is nominative, being the predicate of an implied subject, that is, "it is that I create for you…" It was read with a kasra on the hamza ("innī"), as a resumptive new sentence (istiʾnāf), meaning: "I determine for you," that is, for the purpose of achieving your faith and repelling your denial of me, from the clay (ﷺ) something like the form of a bird.

﴿Then I breathe into it﴾: the pronoun refers to the kāf (the "you" of "I create for you"), that is, into that thing which resembles the form of a bird. It was read "fa-anfukhu fīhā" (then I breathe into it), with the pronoun referring to the estimated form, that is, "I create for you from clay a form like the form of a bird, then I breathe into it."

﴿Then it becomes a bird﴾, living and flying like the rest of the birds.

﴿By the permission of God﴾, by His command, may He be exalted. By this, peace be upon him, indicated that its giving of life is from God, may He be exalted, and not from him. It was said: he created nothing other than the bat. It is reported that when he claimed prophethood and displayed the miracles, they demanded of him the creation of a bat, so he took clay, shaped it, and breathed into it, and behold, it flew between heaven and earth. Wahb said: it would fly as long as people were looking at it, and when it disappeared from their eyes, it would fall dead, so that it would be distinguished from the creation of God, may He be exalted. It was said: they only asked for the creation of a bat because it is the most perfect of birds in its creation and the most eloquent proof of power, for it has teats and teeth, it menstruates, becomes pure, and gives birth like other animals; it laughs as a human laughs; it flies without feathers; it cannot see in the light of day or in the darkness of night, and it only sees at two times: an hour after sunset and an hour after the break of dawn. It was also said: he created several kinds of birds.

﴿And I heal the blind man﴾, that is, the one born blind, or the one whose eye has been wiped (smooth).

﴿And the leper﴾, the one afflicted with leprosy (baraṣ). The Arabs never shrank from anything as they shrank from it. It is also called "waḍaḥ." The specification of these two ailments is because they are among those that defeated physicians, and they were at the height of skill in his time, peace be upon him. So God, may He be exalted, showed them a miracle of that kind. It is reported that he, peace be upon him, would sometimes have thousands of the sick gathered around him: whoever was able would come to him, and whoever was not able, he, peace be upon him, would go to them; and ʿIsa, peace be upon him, healed nothing except by supplication.

﴿And I give life to the dead by the permission of God﴾. He repeated it for emphasis, to repel the suspicion of anyone who imagined divinity (lāhūtiyya) in him. Al-Kalbi said: he, peace be upon him, would give life to the dead by saying "Yā Ḥayyu, yā Qayyūm" (O Living, O Self-Subsisting). He brought back ʿAzar, who was his friend, and he lived and had a child. He passed by the son of an old woman who was dead, so he called upon God, may He be exalted, and he got down from his bier alive, returned to his family, remained alive, and had children. The daughter of the Tenth (?) he brought back to life, and she bore children after that. They said: "You bring back to life one who was recently dead, so perhaps they did not die but were struck by a swoon; so bring back to life for us Sam son of Nuh." He said: "Show me his grave," and they did so. He stood at his grave and called upon God, mighty and majestic, and he rose from his grave with his head grey. He, peace be upon him, said: "How did you turn grey, when there was no grey hair in your time?" He said: "O Spirit of God, when you called me, I heard a voice saying: 'Answer, Spirit of God!' I thought the Hour had come, and from the terror of that I turned grey." Then he asked him about the agony of death (nazʿ). He said: "O Spirit of God, its bitterness has not left my throat." Between him and his death there were more than four thousand years. He said to the people: "Believe him, for he is the prophet of God." Some of them believed in him, and others denied him, saying: "This is magic; show us a sign." So he said: "O so-and-so, you ate such-and-such, and O so-and-so, such-and-such was hidden for you." That is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses﴾, that is, of the unseen matters of your circumstances about which you have no doubt. It was read "tadhkhirūna" with a dhāl and a light pronunciation (taʾkhīf).

﴿Surely in that﴾ refers to the great matters mentioned.

﴿is indeed a sign﴾, a great one. It was read "la-āyātin" (signs).

﴿for you﴾, indicating the truth of my messengership with a clear indication.

﴿if you are believers﴾: the answer of the conditional is deleted, because the meaning is directed toward it, or because what is mentioned indicates it, that is, "you will benefit from them," or "if you are among those from whom faith can come, they will show you the truth of my messengership and the belief in it."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 50:**

﴿And confirming what was before me of the Torah﴾ (p-40) It is coordinated (*'atf*, grammatical coordination) with the implied element on which His words *"with a sign"* depend, meaning: "I have come to you accompanied by a sign, etc..."

﴿And confirming what was before me﴾ etc... Or it is coordinated with *"a messenger"* according to the three possibilities, for *"confirming"* (*musaddiqan*) carries the sense of speaking, as in *"a messenger"* (*rasulan*). That is: "and He makes him a confirmer who speaks, that I confirm etc..." Or: "and he says, I was sent as a messenger, that I have come to you etc., and confirming etc." Or: "while being a confirmer who speaks, that I confirm etc." Or it is in the accusative by an implied verb indicated by ﴿I have come to you﴾, meaning: "and I have come to you as a confirmer etc." His words ﴿of the Torah﴾ are either a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the relative pronoun, with the governing element being *"confirming"*; or from its implied pronoun in the adverbial phrase that functions as a relative clause, with the governing element being the implied "being settled" (*al-istiqrar*) in the adverbial phrase, or the adverbial phrase itself, since it stands in the place of a verb.

﴿And to make lawful for you﴾ is the object of an implied element indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "and I have come to you in order to make lawful for you etc." It was said: it is coordinated with the meaning of *"confirming"*, like the saying of people: "I came to him apologizing and seeking his pleasure," as if it were said: "I have come to you so that I may confirm, and to make lawful for you etc." It was also said: it is coordinated with *"with a sign,"* meaning: "I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, and to make lawful for you."

﴿some of what was forbidden to you﴾ means: in the law of Moses, peace be upon him, such as fats, the fatty parts (*thurub*), fish, camel meat, and work on the Sabbath. It was said: he made lawful for them some fish and birds that have no scales (*siss'isa*). There is disagreement concerning the making lawful of the Sabbath. It is also read as *"harrama"* (with the active form), with the subject being what was before me, or Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is also read as *"haruma"* on the pattern of *"karuma,"* and this indicates that his law abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation) some rulings of the Torah. This does not undermine his being a confirmer of it, since abrogation is in reality an explanation and a specification in terms of time. The placement of the object after the prepositional phrase is for the reason mentioned repeatedly before: hastening to mention what pleases the addressees, and creating anticipation for what has been delayed.

﴿And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾ that bears witness to the truth of my messengerhood. It is also read as *"with signs"* (*bi-ayatin*, plural).

﴿So fear Allah﴾ in not accepting it and in opposing what it indicates.

﴿And obey me﴾ in what I command you and forbid you, by the command of Allah, Exalted is He. That sign is my word.

Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is the straight path. ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ رَبِّي ورَبُّكم فاعْبُدُوهُ هَذا صِراطٌ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾ It is the plain truth on which all the messengers unanimously agreed, so it is a clear sign that he (may blessings and peace be upon him) is among them.

It is also read "Anna Allaha" with a fatha, in apposition (badal) to "ayah" (sign), or with the implied sense "I have brought you a sign" that Allah is my Lord and your Lord.

His words, ﴿فاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وأطِيعُونِ﴾ ("So fear Allah and obey me"), form a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ). Apparently it repeats what came before, meaning: "I have brought you a sign after a sign, of what I have mentioned to you: the creation of birds, the healing of the blind and the leper, the raising of the dead, the telling of hidden things, and other things, such as my birth without a father, my speaking in the cradle, and other things." The first (the signs) serves to lay the groundwork for the proof, and the second (the message) serves to bring it close to the ruling. For this reason, his words, ﴿فاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ﴾, are connected to it with the particle "fa" (so). The meaning is: since I have brought you the manifest miracles and the clear signs, then fear Allah by not opposing Him, and obey me in what I call you to.

The meaning for the one who reads "wa li-anna Allaha rabbi wa rabbukum fa-u'buduhu" with a fatha is like His words, exalted is He, ﴿لإيلافِ قُرَيْشٍ﴾ ("For the familiarity of the Quraysh") etc. Then he began the call and alluded to it in a general statement, saying: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ رَبِّي ورَبُّكُمْ﴾, indicating that the completion of the theoretical faculty (al-quwwah al-nazariyyah, the intellectual faculty of knowing) is by correct belief whose ultimate aim is tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness). He said: ﴿فاعْبُدُوهُ﴾, indicating the completion of the practical faculty (al-quwwah al-'amaliyyah, the faculty of action), for it necessarily entails obedience, which is carrying out the commands and refraining from the prohibitions. Then he confirmed this by making clear that combining the two matters is the path witnessed to be upright. Its parallel is his words, may blessings and peace be upon him: "Say: I believe in Allah, then be upright."

(p-41) **﴿So when Jesus perceived their disbelief﴾**: this begins an account of the outcome of his situation, peace be upon him, following the mention of a part of it through the report of the angels. The **fa'** here is the *fa' fasiha* (the "eloquent *fa'*," which signals an unstated intermediate step); it makes clear that everything the angels had said has come to pass and has passed from potential into actuality, as I have explained. This is like His words, exalted is He, **﴿Then when he saw it settled beside him﴾** after His words **﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you﴾**. It is as if it were said: she carried him, bore him, and so it was, such and such. Some say: *dhayta wa dhayta* (such and such). The details were not mentioned because the report of the angels is sufficient, to signal that there is no failure, and out of confidence in what was explained in the other passages. As for the omission of the rest of his circumstances, peace be upon him, from the chain of narration, this is either out of concern for them or because they do not suit the context of good tidings, since they contain mention of his hardships, peace be upon him, and his struggle with plots. By *ihsas* (perceiving) is meant a strong apprehension that operates like direct observation, and by *kufr* (disbelief) is meant their persistence in it, their obstinacy, and their stubborn rejection of it, together with their determination to kill him, peace be upon him, as the perceiving indicates. This is because the verb is used in such contexts when its object is something feared and hated, as in His words, mighty and majestic is He, **﴿So when they perceived Our might, behold, they fled from it﴾**. The word **min** ("from") is connected to **ahassa** ("perceived"), and the pronoun attached to it refers to the Children of Israel; that is, the perceiving began on their part. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the direct object, as has been mentioned more than once, serves to give attention to what is fronted and to create suspense for what follows. Some say it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) for *al-kufr*.

**﴿He said﴾**: that is, he addressed his companions, not all the Children of Israel, as in His words **﴿as Jesus, son of Mary, said to the disciples﴾**, and the verse continues. His words, exalted is He, **﴿So a party of the Children of Israel believed, and a party disbelieved﴾**, are not explicit that the address was directed to all of them; rather, it suffices that the call reached them.

**﴿Who are my helpers?﴾** *Al-ansar* is the plural of *nasir* (helper), like *ashraf* is the plural of *sharif* (noble).

**﴿to God﴾** is connected to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the *ya'* (my), meaning: "Who are my helpers, heading toward God, seeking refuge in Him?" Or it is connected to **ansari** ("my helpers") containing the sense of "addition," as if it were said: "Who are those who ascribe themselves to God, mighty and majestic is He, and help me as He helps me?" Some say *ila* here means *fi* ("in"), that is, "in the way of God." Some say it means *li* ("for"). Some say it means *ma'a* ("with").

**﴿He said﴾**: this is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*), following a question that naturally arises in the mind, as if it were said: "What did they say in reply to him, peace be upon him?" And it is said: "He said."

**﴿The disciples (al-hawariyyun)﴾**: this is the plural of *hawari*. It is said: "So-and-so is the *hawari* of so-and-so," meaning his chosen one and his pure companion, from *al-hawar*, which is pure whiteness. From this comes *al-hawariyyat* for the urban women, because of the purity and clarity of their complexions. The companions of Jesus, peace be upon him, were called by this name because of the purity of their intentions and the cleanness of their inner selves. It is said: because of the traces of worship and its lights upon them. It is said: they were kings who wore white garments. This is because one of the kings prepared a meal and gathered the people for it, and Jesus, peace be upon him, was over a dish from which he kept eating without it diminishing. They mentioned this to the king, who summoned him, peace be upon him, and said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "Jesus, son of Mary." So he abandoned his kingdom and followed him together with his relatives, and those are the disciples. It is said: they were fishermen who caught fish and wore white garments. Among them were Shim'un, Ya'qub and Yuhanna. Jesus, peace be upon him, passed by them and said to them: "You catch fish; if you follow me you will become those who catch people for eternal life." They said: "Who are you?" He said: "Jesus, son of Mary, servant of God and His messenger." So they asked him for a miracle. Shim'un had cast his net that night and caught nothing. So Jesus, peace be upon him, commanded him to cast it into the water again, and he did, and so much fish gathered in the net that it nearly tore. They sought help from the people of another boat, and they filled both boats. At that, they believed in Jesus, peace be upon him. It is said: they were twelve men who believed in him, peace be upon him, and followed him. Whenever they were hungry they would say: "We are hungry, O Spirit of God," and he would strike the earth with his hand, and from it would come forth for each one two loaves of bread. And whenever they were thirsty they would say: (p-42) "We are thirsty," and he would strike the earth with his hand, and water would come forth from it, and they would drink. Then they said: "Who is greater than us?" He, peace be upon him, said: "Greater than you is one who works with his hand and eats from his earnings." So they began washing garments for wages, and so they were called disciples (*hawariyyun*). It is said: his mother entrusted him to a dyer. One day the dyer wanted to occupy himself with some of his affairs, and he, peace be upon him, said to him: "Here are garments of various kinds; I have assigned to each of them a specific mark; dye them in those colors." The dyer went away, so he, peace be upon him, placed them all in one vat and said: "Become, by God's leave, as I wish." When the dyer returned and asked him, he told him what he had done. He said: "You have ruined my garments!" He said: "Stand up and look." So he began taking out a red garment, a green garment and a yellow garment, until he had brought out all of them in the best condition, as he had intended. The onlookers were amazed by him and believed in him, peace be upon him, and they were the disciples. Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that some of these twelve disciples were kings, some were fishermen, some were launderers, and some were dyers. All of them were called disciples because they were the helpers of Jesus, peace be upon him, his supporters, and those sincere in obedience to him and love for him.

**﴿We are the helpers of God﴾**: that is, the helpers of His religion and His messenger.

**﴿We have believed in God﴾**: this is a resumptive sentence functioning as the reason for what precedes it, since belief in Him, exalted is He, necessitates supporting His religion, defending His allies, and fighting His enemies.

**﴿And bear witness that we are Muslims﴾**: that is, sincere in faith, submitting to what you require of us in supporting you. They asked him, peace be upon him, to testify to this on the Day of Resurrection, the day when the messengers, peace be upon them, bear witness for their nations and against them, signaling that the aim of their purpose is eternal happiness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 53:

﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down﴾: a supplication (tadarru') to God, Mighty and Majestic, and a presentation of their state to Him, Exalted, after presenting it to the Messenger, in exaggeration of making their matter manifest.

﴿And we have followed the Messenger﴾: that is, in everything he brings and leaves of the matters of religion (ummur al-din), so that following him in support (al-ittiba' fi al-nusrah) enters into it as a primary inclusion.

﴿So register us among the witnesses﴾: that is, among those who bear witness to Your oneness (wahdaniyyah), or with the prophets who bear witness for their followers, or with the community of Muhammad, upon him be prayer and peace, for they are witnesses over mankind entirely. This is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object of "uktub-na" (register us).

﴿وَمَكَرُوا﴾ That is: those among the Jews whom Jesus, peace be upon him, knew to be disbelievers, who appointed someone to kill him secretly (ghilah).

﴿وَمَكَرَ اللَّهُ﴾ by raising Jesus, peace be upon him, and casting his likeness upon the one who intended to assassinate him, so that he was killed. Scheming (al-makr), in its origin, is a stratagem by which one brings another to harm. It cannot be attributed to Him, glorified is He, except by way of mushakalah (a rhetorical convention in which a term is used for something else because of its association with it). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that when the king of the Children of Israel intended to kill him, peace be upon him, Jibril, peace be upon him, commanded him to enter a house that had a small opening (rawzanah). Jibril then lifted him through that opening to the heaven. The king said to a wicked man among them: "Go in to him and kill him." He entered the house, and Allah, mighty and majestic, cast Jesus' likeness upon him. He came out and informed them that there was no one in the house. They killed him and crucified him.

It is also said: he, peace be upon him, gathered the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) one night and advised them, then said: "One of you will disbelieve in me before the rooster crows, and will sell me for a small sum of money." They went out and dispersed. The Jews were seeking him, and one of them became a hypocrite and said to them: "What will you give me if I guide you to the Messiah?" They set for him thirty dirhams. He took them and guided them to him. Allah, mighty and majestic, cast upon the hypocrite the likeness of Jesus, peace be upon him, and raised Jesus to the heaven. They seized the hypocrite, while he was saying: "I am your guide," but they did not heed his words, and they crucified him. Then they said: "His face resembles the face of Jesus, and his body resembles the body of our companion. If this is Jesus, where is our companion? And if this is our companion, where is Jesus?" Thus a great fighting broke out among them.

It is also said: when the one who was crucified was crucified, Maryam came, and with her a woman whom Allah, exalted is He, had cured of madness through the supplication of Jesus, peace be upon him. The two of them began weeping over the crucified one. Then Allah, exalted is He, sent down Jesus, peace be upon him, and he came to them and said: "Why are you weeping?" They said: "Over you." He said: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, raised me, and nothing but good has befallen me. This is merely something that was made to resemble me for them."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: the Jews tortured the disciples after the raising of Jesus, peace be upon him, and inflicted great hardship upon them. This reached the king of the Romans, and the king of the Jews was among his subjects. He was told: "A man from the Children of Israel, one of those under your command, used to tell them that he was the Messenger of Allah, and he showed them the reviving of the dead, the healing of the blind and the leper, and he did such and such." He said: "Had I known that, I would not have let them be between them and him." Then he sent for the disciples, took them from their hands, and asked them about Jesus, peace be upon him. They informed him, and he pledged allegiance to them upon their religion. He took down the crucified one, concealed him, and took the wood (of the cross), honoring it. Then he waged war against the Children of Israel and killed a great multitude of them. From him the origin of Christianity among the Romans emerged. Then after him came another king called Tatyus, who attacked Bayt al-Maqdis about forty years after the raising of Jesus, peace be upon him. He killed and took captives, and he left in the city of Bayt al-Maqdis not a stone upon another. At that time Quraydhah and al-Nadir left for the Hijaz.

The people of histories (ahl al-tawarikh) said: Maryam conceived Jesus, peace be upon him, when she was thirteen years old, and she gave birth to him at Bayt Lahm, in the land of Urshalim, sixty-five years after Alexander's conquest of the land of Babylon. Allah, exalted is He, revealed to him at the age of thirty, and raised him to Himself from Bayt al-Maqdis on the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr) in the month of Ramadan, when he was thirty-three years old. His mother lived six years after his raising.

﴿واللَّهُ خَيْرُ الماكِرِينَ﴾ the most powerful of them in scheming, the most effective of them in plotting, and the most capable of them in inflicting harm from where it is not expected. The placing of the Divine Name (al-Jalalah) in the position where a pronoun would be expected serves to inspire awe. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil) that affirms what precedes it.

﴿Idh qāla Allāh﴾ (when Allah said) is an adverbial complement (ẓarf) governed either by *makr Allāh* (the scheming of Allah) or by an implied verb such as *waqaʿa dhālika* (that happened).

﴿Yā ʿĪsā innī mutawaffīka﴾ (O ʿIsa, indeed I will take you in full). The meaning is: *mustawfī ajalika* (taking in full your term), and *mu'akhkhiruka ilā ajalika al-musammā* (deferring you to your appointed term), protecting you from their killing; or *qābiḍuka mina al-arḍ* (seizing you from the earth), from *tawaffaytu mālī* (I received my property in full). Or it means *mutawaffīka nā'iman* (taking you while you are asleep), since it is narrated that he was raised while asleep. It is also said: *mumītuka fī waqtika baʿda al-nuzūl min al-samāʾ* (causing you to die at your time after descending from the sky), and *rāfiʿuka al-ān* (raising you now). Or: *mumītuka min al-shahawāt al-ʿāʾiqa ʿani al-ʿurūj ilā ʿālam al-malakūt* (causing you to die to the desires that prevent ascent to the world of the malakut, the divine dominion). It is also said: Allah caused him to die for seven hours, then raised him to the sky, and this is the view of the Christians. Al-Qurtubi said: The correct view is that Allah raised him without death or sleep, as al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said, and this is the choice of al-Tabari, and it is the correct view, from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. The origin of the story is that when the Jews resolved to kill him, peace be upon him, the disciples, who were twelve men, gathered in a room. Al-Masih entered upon them through the niche of the room, and Iblis informed all the Jews about them. Four thousand men of them mounted and surrounded the door of the room. Al-Masih said to the disciples: "Which of you will go out and be killed and be with me in Paradise?" One of them said: "I will, O Prophet of Allah." He threw upon him a woolen cloak and a woolen turban, gave him his staff, and the likeness of ʿIsa, peace be upon him, was cast upon him. He went out to the Jews, and they killed him and crucified him. As for ʿIsa, peace be upon him, Allah clothed him with feathers and light, and dressed him in light, and cut off from him the desire for food and drink. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I will take you in full﴾. He flew with the angels. Then, when his companions saw that, they split into three groups. One group said: "Allah was among us, then He ascended to the sky," and they are the Yaʿqubiyya. Another group said: "The son of Allah was among us for as long as Allah willed, then Allah raised him to Himself," and they are the Nestorians (al-Nusturiyya). Another group of them said: "The servant of Allah and His messenger was among us for as long as Allah willed, then Allah raised him to Himself," and these are the Muslims. Then the two disbelieving groups allied against them and killed them, and Islam remained obliterated until Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿Wa rāfiʿuka ilayya﴾ (and raising you to Me), that is, to the place of My honour and the abode of My angels.

﴿Wa muṭahhiruka mina alladhīna kafarū﴾ (and purifying you from those who disbelieved), that is, from the evil of their company, the impurity of their companionship, and the defilement of their association.

﴿Wa jāʿil alladhīna ittabaʿūka﴾ (and placing those who followed you). Qatadah, al-Rabiʿ, al-Shaʿbi, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: they are the people of Islam who affirmed him and followed his religion from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), as opposed to those who denied him and lied about him from among the Christians.

﴿Fawqa alladhīna kafarū﴾ (above those who disbelieved). These are those who schemed against him, peace be upon him, and whoever follows their way from the Jews, for the people of Islam are above them, dominant in might, strength, and proof. It is also said: they are the disciples, so their superiority should be understood as the superiority of the Muslims by virtue of their unity in Islam and monotheism. It is also said: they are the Romans. It is also said: they are the Christians. Thus, *ittibāʿ* (following) here means merely profession and love; otherwise those disbelievers are far removed from being his followers, peace be upon him.

﴿Ilā yawm al-qiyāma﴾ (until the Day of Resurrection) is the limit of the *jaʿl* (placing) or of the *istiqrār* (settledness) implied in the adverbial complement. It does not mean that the placing or the superiority ends at that time and the disbelievers are freed from humiliation. Rather, it means that the Muslims will prevail over them until that limit, and after it Allah will do with them what He wills.

﴿Thumma ilayya marjiʿukum﴾ (then to Me is your return). That is, your return by resurrection. *Thumma* (then) indicates delay. Placing the prepositional phrase first (*ilayya*) serves restriction (qaṣr), which conveys the emphasis of promise and threat. The pronoun refers to ʿIsa, peace be upon him, and others among his followers and those who disbelieved in him, using the prioritizing of the addressed over the absent within the *iltifāt* (shift of grammatical person), for this is more eloquent in giving glad tidings and warning.

﴿Fa aḥkumu baynakum﴾ (then I will judge between you), on that day, immediately after your return to Me.

﴿Fīmā kuntum fīhi takhtalifūn﴾ (concerning that over which you used to differ), that is, concerning matters of religion. *Fīhi* is connected to *takhtalifūn* (you differ), and placing it before the verb is for the sake of observing the *fawāṣil* (verse-endings).

﴿As for those who disbelieve, I will punish them with a severe punishment.﴾ This is an explanation of the judgment that falls between the two groups and a detailing of its manner. It begins with the state of the disbelievers, because the thrust of the speech is to threaten them and to deter them from the disbelief and obstinacy they are upon.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾ is related to "أُعَذِّبُهُمْ" (u'adhdhibuhum, "I will punish them"). It does not mean that each of the two punishments, the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, is inflicted and initiated separately, but rather that the whole of them is completed on that Day. It has been said that the meaning is more general than the worldly and the otherworldly.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾ is an end point (ghayah) for the superiority (al-fawqiyyah, "being above"), not for the making (al-ja'l, "appointing"). The return (al-rujū') is deferred from the making, and it is unbounded, not from the bounded superiority, following the pattern of your saying: "I will lend you the use of this house for a month, then I will bestow upon you a robe of honour (khil'ah)," so that the bestowing of the robe is delayed beyond the lending, not beyond the month.

﴿And they will have no helpers﴾ who will rescue them from the punishment of Allah, exalted is He, in both abodes. The plural form corresponds to the plural pronoun, meaning: none of them has a single helper. (p-45)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 57:

﴿As for those who believed﴾ in what I have been sent with.

﴿And did righteous deeds﴾ as is the habit of the believers.

﴿He will pay them their wages in full﴾ That is, He will give them their rewards completely. Perhaps the shift to the third person (ghayba) is to signal the difference between the two sources, punishment and reward, in terms of majesty (jalal) and beauty (jamal). It is also read as "fa-nuwaffihim" (We will pay them), in keeping with the customs of greatness and magnificence.

﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾ That is, He hates them. This metonymy (kinaya) is widespread in all languages and functions as if it were the literal meaning. The mention of wrongdoing (zulm) serves to indicate that by their disbelief they transgress and exceed the limits, placing disbelief in the place of gratitude and faith. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to what precedes it, confirming its meaning.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 58:

﴿Dhalika﴾ (That) is a reference to what preceded of the account of ʿIsa (peace be upon him), and the sense of distance in it serves to indicate the greatness of the matter referred to and the remoteness of its rank in nobility, and that it is, in the clarity of the matter and the prominence of its status, like something witnessed and seen with the eye. It is the subject (mubtada'), and His, Mighty and Majestic is He, saying ﴿We recite it﴾ is its predicate (khabar). His, Exalted is He, saying ﴿to you﴾ is connected to "we recite it." His, Exalted is He, saying ﴿from the signs﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the accusative position, or a predicate after a predicate, or it is the predicate and what lies between them is a circumstantial clause from the demonstrative noun; or "dhalika" is the predicate of an implied subject, i.e., the matter is that. And "natluhu" (We recite it) is a circumstantial clause, as has passed. The form of the present tense is either to bring the scene into presence, or it is on its literal meaning, since the recitation has not yet been completed.

﴿And the Wise Reminder﴾ i.e., the one containing wisdoms (al-hikam), or the one made firm (al-muhkam), protected from the entry of any flaw into it. What is meant by it is the Qur'an. So ﴿min﴾ (from) is partitive, or it is a particular part of it, so "min" is explicative. It has been said: it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), so ﴿min﴾ is inceptive.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 3, verse 59:

﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus﴾ means: his wondrous state, which, in its strangeness, is arranged within the category of likenesses.

﴿with Allah﴾ means: in His decree and judgment.

﴿is like the likeness of Adam﴾ means: like his amazing state, about which no doubter doubts and no disputant disputes.

﴿He created him from dust﴾ is an explanation of what was left vague in the likeness, a detailing of what was stated briefly in it, a clarification of the comparison by showing the point of resemblance between them, and a cutting off of the root of the opponents' doubts. The denial of Jesus's creation without a father, by one who acknowledges the creation of Adam peace be upon him without a father or a mother, is hardly sound. The meaning is: He formed his body from dust.

﴿Then He said to him, "Be"﴾ means: He brought him into existence as a human being, as in His saying, ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾. Or it means He decreed his formation from dust and then formed him. It is permissible for ﴿thumma﴾ (then) to indicate a delay in the report rather than a delay in what is reported.

﴿and he was﴾ is a narration of a past state. It was reported that the delegation of Najran said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, "Why do you revile our companion?" He said, "And what do I say?" They said, "You say he is a servant." He said, "Yes, he is the servant of Allah, His Messenger, and His word which He cast to the virgin, the chaste." They became angry and said, "Have you seen a human being without a father? Since you concede that he has no human father, it must be that his father is Allah." So the Prophet peace be upon him said, "Adam peace be upon him had neither a father nor a mother, and it does not follow from that that he is a son of Allah, glory be to Him and exalted. So likewise is the case of Jesus peace be upon him."

﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾ is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical topic), i.e., it is the truth, namely what We have related to you of the account of ʿIsa, upon him be peace, and his mother. The prepositional phrase (*zarf*) is either a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), meaning "being from your Lord," or a second predicate, meaning "being from Him, exalted is He." It is said that they are a subject and predicate, i.e., the truth mentioned is from God, exalted is He. The mention of the title of Lordship (*rubūbiyya*) together with the attribution to the pronoun of the addressee is to honor him, peace be upon him, and to indicate that the sending down of these true verses, which speak to the reality of the matter, is a nurturing for him, peace be upon him, and a kindness toward him.

﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾ concerning that. The address is either to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the manner of stirring and urging, to increase firmness, and to convey that doubting in what is to be avoided is such that one should be forbidden from it even one who can hardly conceive of issuing it, so how about one who is about to doubt; or it is addressed to everyone who is fit to be addressed.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 61:**

﴿Whoever disputes with you﴾ about it, i.e., among the Christians, since they are the ones who take up disputation.

﴿concerning it﴾, i.e., concerning the matter of ʿIsa (Jesus), peace be upon him, and his mother, claiming that he is not in the state described.

﴿after the knowledge has come to you﴾, i.e., that which necessitates it with certainty from the clear signs; they heard that from you and yet did not refrain from what they were upon of error and misguidance.

﴿Then say﴾ to them:

﴿"Come"﴾, i.e., come forward with resolve and determination.

﴿"Let us call our sons and your sons"﴾. Mention of the sons suffices without mention of the daughters, because it is evident that they are dearer than them; as for the women, their attachment is of another kind.

﴿"And our women and your women, and ourselves and yourselves"﴾, i.e., let each of us call upon himself, his dearest family members, and those closest to his heart, to the mubahala (mutual imprecation), and urge them to it. Placing them before the self during the mubahala, which is among the matters of peril and likely destruction, even though a man risks himself for them and fights in their defense, indicates the complete security of his peace be upon him and his full trust in his affair and the strength of his certainty that no trace of harm will befall them in this at all. This is the secret of giving precedence to his side, peace be upon him, over the side of those addressed in each of the preceding and the following, while observing the original form of the expression, for the non-speaker follows.

﴿"Then let us invoke"﴾, i.e., let us mutually invoke, by each of us cursing the liar among us. "Al-buhla" (with a dammah or a fatḥah) means the curse, and its root is abandonment; it has in its usage the sense of their saying: "I left the she-camel (bahaltu al-naqa)," i.e., I left her without a tether.

﴿"And so let us lay the curse of God upon the liars"﴾. This is coordinated with ﴿let us invoke﴾ and explains its meaning. It is reported that when they were called to the mubahala, they said: "Let us return and consider." When they were alone, they said: "To al-ʿAqib," and their leader, ʿAbd al-Masih, said: "What do you see?" He said: "By God, you know, O company of Christians, that Muhammad is a sent prophet, and he has brought you the decisive word concerning the affair of your companion. By God, no people have ever invoked a prophet and then their elder lived or their young grew up. If you do it, you will surely be destroyed. If you refuse except to cling to your religion and remain upon what you are upon, then make peace with the man and depart to your lands."

«So they came to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he had gone out embracing al-Husayn, holding the hand of al-Hasan, with Fatimah walking behind him and ʿAli behind her, may God be pleased with them all, and he was saying: "When I supplicate, say Amen." The bishop of Najran said: "O company of Christians, I see faces which, if they asked God, Exalted, to remove a mountain from its place, He would remove it. So do not invoke, lest you perish, and there will not remain on the face of the earth a Christian until the Day of Resurrection." They said: "O Abu al-Qasim, we have decided not to invoke you, and to leave you upon your religion while we remain upon ours." He ﷺ said: "If you refuse the mubahala, then embrace Islam, and you will have what the Muslims have and you will bear what the Muslims bear." They refused. He, upon him be peace, said: "Then I will fight you." They said: "We have no strength to fight the Arabs, but we will make a peace agreement with you on condition that you do not attack us, nor frighten us, nor turn us back from our religion, on condition that we pay you every year two thousand garments: a thousand in Safar and a thousand in Rajab, and thirty coats of mail of iron." So he made peace with them on that basis, and he said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, destruction had already hung over the people of Najran. Had they invoked, they would have been transformed into monkeys and swine, and the valley would have burst into flame upon them, and God would have uprooted Najran and its people, even the birds upon the treetops, and the year would not have passed over the Christians, all of them, until they perished."»

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 62:

﴿Indeed, this﴾ i.e., what has been related of the story of Jesus and his mother, peace be upon them both.

﴿is indeed the true narrative﴾, apart from what is other than it of the falsehoods of the Christians. So it is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl, the pronoun of separation), and the lam has entered upon it because it is closer to the subject than to the predicate, whereas its original place is to enter upon the subject. It has also been read as "lahwa" with the ha' sukūn (silent), and ﴿al-qaṣaṣ﴾ is the predicate of inna, and "al-ḥaqq" is its attribute; or it is a subject, ﴿al-qaṣaṣ﴾ is its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of inna.

﴿And there is no god except Allah﴾ — here the "min" of comprehensiveness (min al-istighrāqiyya) is explicitly stated, as an emphasis of the refutation of the Christians in their trinitarianism.

﴿And indeed Allah, He is the Mighty﴾, the One capable of all things that are capable of being done.

﴿the Wise﴾, the One who encompasses all known things; no one shares with Him in power and wisdom, so as to share with Him in divinity.

﴿Then if they turn away﴾ from monotheism and from accepting the truth that has been related to you, after they have witnessed those luminous proofs and shining demonstrations.

﴿then indeed Allah is All-Knowing of the corrupters﴾ That is, of them. The reason the phrase was placed where it stands is to signal that turning away from monotheism and from the truth from which there is no escape, after the proofs have been established, is corruption of the world, and in it is a severity of threat that is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 64:

﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we will not worship except Allah and not associate anything with Him and not take one another as lords instead of Allah."﴾ This is a command to address the People of the Two Scriptures (ahl al-kitabayn). It is also said: it is addressed to the delegation of Najran. And it is also said: it is addressed to the Jews of Madinah.

﴿Come to a word that is equitable between us and you﴾, a word on which the Messengers and the Books do not differ, and it is ﴿that we will not worship except Allah﴾, i.e., that we single Him out in worship and devote worship sincerely to Him.

﴿And not associate anything with Him﴾, i.e., not make anyone other than Him a partner with Him in deserving worship, and not consider anyone worthy of being worshipped.

﴿And not take one another as lords instead of Allah﴾, by saying "Uzayr is the son of Allah" and "al-Masih is the son of Allah," and by not obeying the rabbis (al-ahbar) in what they introduced of prohibition and permission, because each of us is a human like us. It is narrated that when the verse ﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords instead of Allah﴾ was revealed, 'Adi ibn Hatim said: "We did not worship them, O Messenger of Allah." He (ﷺ) said: "Did they not make lawful for you and make unlawful for you, and you follow their word?" He said: "Yes." He (ﷺ) said: "That is it."﴾ ﴿Then if they turn away﴾ from what you have called them to of monotheism and abandoning association.

﴿Then say﴾, i.e., say to them, you and the believers:

﴿Bear witness that we are Muslims﴾, i.e., the proof has become binding upon you, so acknowledge that we are Muslims, not you; or acknowledge that you are disbelievers in what the Books have spoken and upon which the Messengers, peace be upon them, agreed. — Note: Observe what has been taken into account in this narrative of exaggeration in guidance and good gradation in argumentation, where first he explained the circumstances of 'Isa (peace be upon him) and the states contrary to divinity that befell him; then he mentioned the manner of his calling people to monotheism and Islam. When their obstinacy appeared, they were called to mubahalah (mutual invocation of curse) with a kind of miracle; then when they turned away from it and submitted only partially, they were called to what 'Isa (peace be upon him), the Injil, and all the other prophets (peace be upon them) and the Books agreed upon; then when its futility also became apparent, he was commanded to say to them: "Bear witness that we are Muslims."

O People of the Scripture (ﷺ)... wait, correction: this address is to the People of the Book, namely the Jews and the Christians.

"O People of the Book" (ya ahl al-kitab), referring to the Jews and the Christians.

"Why do you argue about Abraham?" That is, about his religion (millah) and his law (shari'ah). The Jews and the Christians disputed about Abraham, peace be upon him, each of them claiming that he was of them, and they brought their dispute before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), whereupon this verse was revealed. The meaning is: why do you claim that he, peace be upon him, was of you?

"And the Torah was not revealed," to Moses, upon him be prayers and peace.

"And the Gospel," to Jesus, upon him be prayers and peace.

"Except after him," since between Abraham and Moses, peace be upon them both, there were a thousand years, and between Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, there were two thousand years. How, then, could any sensible person utter such a thing?!

"Will you not then use your reason?" That is: will you not reflect, so that you would not understand the falsehood of your doctrine? Or do you say this without realizing its falsehood?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 66:

﴿Ha antum ha'ulaa'﴾ (Behold, you are these people) is a sentence composed of a subject and a predicate. It is introduced by the particle of alerting (harf al-tanbih), then clarified by a resumptive sentence (jumla musta'nafa) to indicate the utter heedlessness of them, meaning: you are these foolish people, in that ﴿you argued about that of which you have knowledge﴾, in the sense of "since you found it" in the Torah and the Gospel.

﴿Then why do you argue about that of which you have no knowledge﴾ at all, since there is no mention of the religion of Abraham in either of the two Books, definitively. It has been said that "ha'ulaa'" is in the sense of "alladhi" (who), and ﴿hajajtum﴾ (you argued) is its relative clause (silah). It has also been said that "ha'antum" originally was "a'antum" in the form of a question for wonder (ta'ajjub), and the hamza was changed into a ha'.

﴿And Allah knows﴾ what you argued about in it, or everything, so that this enters into it as a primary inclusion (dukhul awwali).

﴿And you do not know﴾, meaning: the point of dispute, or some of the things of which that is part.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 67:

﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian.﴾ This is an explicit statement of what the established proof (al-burhan) has declared.

﴿But he was a ḥanīf﴾ — that is, one who inclined away from all the deviant beliefs (al-‘aqa'id al-zai'gha) entirely.

﴿Muslim﴾ — that is, one who submitted (munqadan) to God, Exalted is He. The intended meaning is not that he was upon the religion of Islam, for otherwise the obligation would be shared (lashtaraka al-iltizam).

﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ — this is an allusion (ta'ridh) that they (the polytheists) are polytheists, by their saying: "'Uzayr is the son of God," and "the Messiah is the son of God." And it is a refutation of the polytheists' claim that they were upon the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 68:

﴿Indeed, the closest of people to Abraham﴾ means: the nearest of them to him and the most particularly connected to him.

﴿are those who followed him﴾ means: in his time.

﴿and this Prophet and those who believe﴾ because they agree with him in most of what was legislated for them originally. It has been recited (qira'a) as "والنَّبِيَّ" with a fatha (naṣb), coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the pronoun in "اتَّبَعُوهُ" (the pronoun in "they followed him"), and with a kasra (jarr), coordinated with "إبْراهِيمَ" (Abraham).

﴿And Allah is the Guardian (walī) of the believers﴾ He helps them and rewards them with the best for their faith. The specific mention of the believers serves so that the ruling is established for the Prophet (ﷺ) by way of indication of the text (dalālat al-naṣṣ).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 69:

﴿Some of the People of the Book wish that they could lead you astray﴾ (p-49) It was revealed concerning the Jews when they invited Hudhayfah, 'Ammar and Mu'adh to Judaism, and "law" (*law*) here has the meaning of "an" (that).

﴿And they lead astray none but themselves﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*), brought to indicate the complete firmness and steadfastness of those addressed upon the upright religion they hold, meaning: leading astray does not pass beyond them, and its harm returns only to them, because their punishment is thereby doubled. It has been said: "And they lead astray none but their like," but this is rejected. His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And they are not aware﴾ means: of the fact that the harm of it is specific to them and its injury falls upon them.

O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God, while you bear witness?

That is, [in the signs] which the Torah and the Gospel have spoken of and which point to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ).

"While you bear witness": that is, while you yourselves testify that they are the signs of God, or [it means] "with the Qur'an," while you bear witness to his description in the two Books, or you know, through the miracles, that he is true.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 71:

﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you clothe the truth with falsehood﴾ by your distortion and by presenting falsehood in the guise of truth, or by being negligent in distinguishing between them. It is also read "tulabbisūna" with a shadda (tashdid), and "talbasūna" with a fatha on the ba', meaning: you wear the truth together with falsehood, as in his saying ﷺ: "Like one who wears two garments of falsehood" (ka-lābisi thawbay zūr).

﴿And conceal the truth﴾ i.e., the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his description.

﴿while you know﴾ i.e., its being true.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 72:

﴿And a group of the People of the Book said﴾: they were their leaders and those who corrupted their followers.

﴿Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe﴾: that is, display belief in the Qur'an revealed to them.

﴿The beginning of the day﴾: that is, its first part.

﴿And disbelieve﴾: that is, display the disbelief in it that you hold.

﴿Its end﴾: appearing to them, as hypocrites, that you believed in it at first sight without reflection, then reflected on it, came to know the flaw in your initial opinion, and so turned back from it.

﴿Perhaps they﴾: that is, the believers.

﴿Will return﴾: from what they hold of belief in it, just as you returned. The intended "group" is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and Malik ibn al-Sayf, who said to their companions when the qibla was changed: "Believe in what has been revealed to them concerning the prayer toward the Ka'bah, and pray toward it at the beginning of the day, then pray toward the Rock at its end, perhaps they will say, 'They are more knowledgeable than us, and they have returned, so they will return.'" It is also said that they were twelve men of the rabbis of Khaybar who agreed among themselves to enter Islam at the beginning of the day and say at its end: "We examined our Book and consulted our scholars, and we did not find Muhammad to have the description that was mentioned in the Torah," perhaps his companions would doubt him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 73:

﴿And do not believe﴾, i.e., do not affirm with inner assent of the heart (taṣdīq qalbī).

﴿except for those who follow your religion﴾, i.e., except for the people of your religion. Or: do not openly show your faith at the start of the day, except to those who were upon your religion before, for their return is more hopeful and more important.

﴿Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God﴾. He guides whom He wills with it to faith and makes him firm in it.

﴿that someone be given the like of what you were given﴾ is related to something omitted, i.e., (p-50) you devised that and said, "That someone be given the like of what you were given." Or it is related to "do not believe," i.e., do not show your faith, lest someone be given the like of what you were given. Except to your partisans, and do not spread it to the Muslims, lest their steadfastness increase, nor to the polytheists, lest it lead them to call them to Islam. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tirāḍ) that conveys that their scheming is not profitable in any way. Or the predicate of "inna" is "the guidance of God," with "guidance" (al-hudā, هدى) being a substitute (badal) for "al-hudā" in the first part. It has been read as "a-an yu'tā" as a rebuking interrogative (istifhām taqrī'ī), which supports the first interpretation, i.e., "Is it because someone is given the like of what you were given that you devised...?" It has also been read as "an" (أن) being a negation, so it is part of the speech of the group, i.e., "And do not believe except for those who follow your religion," and say to them, "No one is given the like of what you were given."

﴿or they argue with you before your Lord﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "that someone be given" according to the first two interpretations. According to the third, its meaning is: until they argue with you before your Lord and refute your argument. The "waw" is a pronoun referring to "aḥad" (someone), because it has the sense of a plural, since what is meant by it is other than their followers.

﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills, and God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾. This is a refutation of them and a nullification of what they claimed, with a dazzling proof.

**﴿He singles out for His mercy whom He wills﴾**, i.e., He makes His mercy exclusive to **﴿whom He wills. And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾**. Both are a *tadhyil* (concluding appendage) to what precedes, confirming its meaning.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 75:**

﴿And among the People of the Book﴾ is the beginning of an explanation of their treachery regarding wealth, after the explanation of their treachery regarding religion. The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada', inchoative), as its verification was discussed previously in the tafsir (exegesis) of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among the people is one who says﴾, and so on. Its predicate (khabar) is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you﴾. The intent here is to describe their being characterized by the content of the conditional clause, not that they themselves are the particular persons mentioned. It is as if it were said: some of the People of the Book are such that if you entrust them with a qintar, that is, a large amount of wealth, they will return it to you, like Abdullah ibn Salam, to whom a man from Quraysh entrusted one thousand two hundred uqiyya of gold, and he returned it to him.

﴿And among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you﴾, like Finhas ibn Azura, to whom another man from Quraysh entrusted a dinar, and he denied it. It has also been said: those who are trustworthy with much are the Christians, since trustworthiness is prevalent among them, and those who are treacherous with little are the Jews, since treachery is prevalent among them.

﴿except while you are standing over him﴾ is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh) with an unrestricted general object, either of states or of times. That is: he will not return it to you in any state or at any time, except while you remain standing over him, or at a time during which you remain standing over him, insistently demanding it through legal claim and the establishment of proof.

﴿That﴾ refers to the abandonment of returning, indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿will not return it﴾, and the notion of distance in the demonstrative is for announcing their utmost extremity in evil and corruption.

﴿because﴾ means: by reason of the fact that.

﴿they say: "There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered"﴾ means: regarding the matter of those who are not from the People of the Book.

﴿blame﴾ means: reproach and censure.

﴿and they speak falsehood against Allah﴾ by their claiming that.

﴿while they know﴾ that they are liars and fabricators against Allah, Exalted is He. That is because they regarded the wronging of those who opposed them as permissible, and they said: "No prohibition regarding them was placed in the Torah."
