It has also been said: the Jews dealt with men from Quraysh, and when those men embraced Islam, the Jews demanded their dues from them, saying: "Your right has lapsed because you abandoned your religion," and they claimed that this was so in their book.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said, when this verse was revealed: "The enemies of Allah have lied. There is nothing from the time of ignorance that is not under my feet except trustworthiness, for it is to be returned to the righteous and the wicked."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 76:

﴿Bala﴾ (Yes, indeed) is an affirmation of what they denied, meaning: yes, there is a way over them concerning them.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever fulfils his covenant and fears God, then indeed God loves those who fear Him﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming the sentence which "bala" (yes, indeed) has taken the place of. The pronoun in the genitive, referring to ﴿man﴾ (whoever) or to God Exalted, and the generality of ﴿al-muttaqin﴾ (those who fear God) stands in place of the returning pronoun from the consequent back to ﴿man﴾ (whoever). It also indicates that taqwa (God-consciousness, fear of God) is the criterion of the matter, general to fulfilling covenants and other than it, including performing obligations and abstaining from prohibitions.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 77:

﴿Indeed, those who sell﴾ i.e., who exchange and take (in return).

﴿the covenant of Allah﴾ i.e., in exchange for what they covenanted upon: faith in the Messenger (ﷺ) and fulfilling the trusts.

﴿and their oaths﴾ and what they swore by, such as their saying: "By Allah, we shall surely believe in him and surely support him."

﴿for a small price﴾ that is, the transient goods of this world.

﴿Those﴾ are the ones described with those ugly attributes.

﴿have no share﴾ i.e., no portion.

﴿in the Hereafter﴾ of its bliss.

﴿Allah will not speak to them﴾ i.e., in a way that would please them, or with anything at all. Rather, what takes place of questioning, rebuke and reproach during the reckoning comes from the angels, peace be upon them. Or it means they will not benefit from the words of Allah Most High and His signs. The apparent meaning is that it is a metaphor for the intensity of His anger and wrath, we seek refuge in Allah from that, because of the Most High's saying: ﴿nor will He look at them on the Day of Resurrection﴾. For it is a figure of speech for disdain toward them and displeasure with them, which is derived from the metaphor concerning one of whom looking is permissible, because whoever values a person turns toward him and gives him the regard of his eyes. Then it became common until it became an expression for esteem and kindness even when there was no looking at all. Then, concerning One of whom looking is not permissible, only the meaning of kindness was used, as a figure for what was a metaphor for that concerning whom looking is permissible. And ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is connected to both verbs, and in it is an amplification of the threat.

﴿nor will He purify them﴾ i.e., He will not praise them, or He will not cleanse them from the filth of sins.

﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾ for what they did of disobedience. It was said: this verse was revealed concerning Abu Rafi', Lubaba ibn Abi al-Haqiq and Huyayy ibn Akhtab, who distorted the Torah, altered the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and took bribes for that. It was also said: it was revealed concerning al-Ash'ath ibn Qays, when there was a dispute between him and a man over a well, and they brought their case before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said to him: "Your two witnesses or his oath." Al-Ash'ath said: "Then he will swear and not care." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever swears an oath by which he claims property to which he is not entitled, while he is a liar in it, will meet Allah while He is angry with him." It was also said: it concerns a man who displayed merchandise in the market and swore that he had bought it for a price he had not actually paid for it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 78:

﴿And indeed among them﴾ i.e., among the Jews who distort (the Scripture).

﴿A group﴾ such as Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Malik ibn al-Sayf, and their likes.

﴿Who twist their tongues with the Book﴾ i.e., they twist them in its recitation, inclining them away from what was revealed toward the distorted (text), or they bend them with something resembling the Book. It is also read "yulawwuna" (with the doubled letter, from the verb lawwā, to twist), and "yalūna" (with the waw that is pronounced with a damma changed into a hamza, then lightened by dropping it and transferring its vowel to the preceding consonant, which is quiescent) (p-52).

﴿So that you may think it﴾ i.e., the distorted (text), indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿they twist﴾, and so on. It is also read with the letter yā' (yaḥsabūhu, "they may think it"), in which case the pronoun refers to the Muslims.

﴿To be from the Book﴾ i.e., to be part of it. His words, exalted is He: ﴿And it is not from the Book﴾ are a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the object pronoun, meaning: and the state of affairs is that it is not from it in reality, and also in their own belief.

﴿And they say﴾, along with what was mentioned of twisting and distortion, in the manner of explicit statement, not by allusion and indirect hint.

﴿It is﴾ i.e., the distorted (text).

﴿From Allah's presence﴾ i.e., it was revealed from Allah's presence.

﴿And it is not from Allah's presence﴾ is a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun of the subject in the predicate, meaning: and the state of affairs is that it is not from His presence, exalted is He, in their own belief as well. In this there is an emphasis on their condemnation, the disgracefulness of their affair, and the perfection of their audacity that is not hidden, and the mention of the Glorious Name and of the Book in the place of the pronoun serves to magnify what they undertook in saying (this).

﴿And they speak falsehood against Allah while they know﴾ that they are liars and fabricators against Allah, exalted is He. This is an emphasis and a recording against them of lying about Allah and deliberately doing so. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: They are the Jews who came to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and they altered the Torah and wrote a book in which they changed the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then Qurayza took what they had written and mixed it with the Book that was in their possession.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 79:

﴿It is not for a human﴾ is a refutation of their fabrication against the prophets, peace be upon them, when the Christians of Najran said: "Indeed, Jesus, peace be upon him, commanded us to take him as a lord," far be it from him, peace be upon him. It is also a refutation of it immediately after the refutation of their fabrication against Allah, glorified is He. That is: it is not correct and not proper for anyone. The phrase "for a human" was used to indicate the cause of the ruling, for humanness is incompatible with the matter that the disbelievers attributed to them.

﴿that Allah should give him the Book﴾, the Book that speaks the truth, commands monotheism, and forbids associating partners with Allah.

﴿and the wisdom﴾: understanding and knowledge, or wisdom, which is the Sunnah and prophethood.

﴿then he should say﴾: that human, after Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has honored him with what He mentioned of the honors, made him know the truth, and informed him of his lofty affairs.

﴿to the people, "Be servants to me"﴾: the prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element that is an attribute of "servants," meaning: servants who are existing [as such].

﴿besides Allah﴾: it is connected to the word "servants," because of the verbal sense within it, or it is a second attribute of it. It may also be a circumstantial element (ḥāl), since the indefinite noun is specified by the qualifier. That is: exceeding Allah, Exalted is He, whether this is by independent worship or by partnership, for exceeding is certainly realized in both. It is said: "Abu Rafi' al-Qurazi and the Najrani leader said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Do you want us to worship you and take you as a lord?' He, peace be upon him, said: 'God forbid that anything other than Allah, Exalted is He, be worshipped, or that we command the worship of other than Him, Exalted is He. I was not sent with that, nor was I commanded with it.' Then it was revealed." It is also said: "A man from the Muslims said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we greet you as some of us greet one another. Should we not prostrate to you?' He, peace be upon him, said: 'It is not fitting that anyone be prostrated to besides Allah, Exalted is He. But honor your Prophet and recognize the truth for its people.'" ﴿But rather, be﴾: that is, but rather he says, "Be..."

﴿rabbaniyyin﴾ (devoted to the Lord): "rabbānī" is a relative noun derived from "rabb" (Lord) with the addition of the alif and nun, like "liḥyānī" and "riqbānī." It denotes one who is perfect in knowledge and action, and who holds very firmly to obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and to His religion.

﴿because you have been teaching the Book and because you have been studying﴾: that is, because of your persistence in teaching the Book and studying it, meaning reciting it. The making of the predicate of "kāna" a present-tense verb is to convey continuous renewed action, and the repetition of "bimā kuntum" is to signal that each of the continuity of teaching and the continuity of recitation is independently a virtue and a means of attaining rabbaniyyah. The placing of teaching before studying is either to increase its honor over studying, or because the first address is to their leaders and the second is to those beneath them. It has been read as "taʿlamūna" in the sense of "knowing" (ʿālimīn), "tudarrisūna" from "tadrīs" (teaching), and "tudrisūna" from "idrās," with the meaning of "tadrīs," like "akrama" in the meaning of "karuma." It is also permissible that the well-known reading also carries this meaning, on the estimate of "bimā tadrusūnahu ʿalā al-nās" (by what you teach it to the people).

﴿And He would not order you to take the angels and the prophets as lords﴾, with the verb in the accusative (naṣb) as a conjunct (ʿaṭf) of "then he would say" (thumma yaqūla). The particle "lā" (not) is redundant (mazīdah), used to emphasize the sense of negation in His words, ﴿It is not for a human﴾. That is: it is not for a human that Allah should give him prophethood, and then he should order people to worship himself, and order them to take the angels and the prophets as lords. The insertion of the corrective clause (istidrāk) between the two conjoined elements serves to hasten to establishing the truth by stating what befits His status and what it is fitting to proceed from Him, right after exonerating Him from what does not befit His status and cannot proceed from Him.

As for what has been said, that the "lā" is not redundant, in the sense that it is not for him to order worship of himself, nor to order taking his equals as lords, but rather he forbids it, and that is lower than worship, so that the corrupt nature of this interpretation entails what was mentioned concerning the insertion of the corrective clause between the two conjoined sentences, since, in that case, the two are in the status of a single sentence. Likewise His words, ﴿Would He order you to disbelief﴾, for it is explicit that the intent is to clarify the negation of both matters intentionally, not to clarify the negation of the first on account of the negation of the second. The reading in the nominative (qirāʾat al-rafʿ), as a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf), and the permissibility of the circumstantial (ḥāliyyah) status by postulating a subject (mubtadaʾ), i.e., "and he does not order you" to its end, support this, and its corruption is clear for what you have just understood.

His words, ﴿after you have submitted﴾, indicate that the address is to the Muslims, and they are the ones seeking permission to prostrate to him, upon him be peace.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 81:

﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb addressed to the Prophet ﷺ; that is: "Remember the time when Allah, exalted is He, took their covenant."

﴿"Whatever I have given you of Book and wisdom, and then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what is with you, you shall surely believe in him and surely help him."﴾ It has been said: it is to be taken at its apparent meaning, and if this is the ruling for the Prophets, peace be upon them, then the nations are more fitting and more deserving of it. It has also been said: its meaning is that the covenant was taken from the Prophets and their nations, and mention of the latter is dispensed with by mention of the former. It has also been said: the attribution of the covenant to the Prophets is an attribution to the agent, and the meaning is: "And when Allah took the covenant which the Prophets had confirmed upon their nations." It has also been said: what is intended is the sons of the Prophets, with the omission of the noun, and they are the Children of Israel; or He called them "Prophets" in mockery of them, because they used to say, "We are more deserving of prophethood than Muhammad ﷺ, for we are the People of the Book and the Prophets were from among us." The lam in ﴿لَما﴾ (lam) serves as an introduction to an oath, because taking a covenant carries the sense of obtaining an oath, and "ma" (ma) may be conditional; "you shall surely believe" (لَتُؤْمِنُنَّ, latu'minunna) stands in place of the answer to both the oath and the condition, and it may also be declarative. It has been read as "li-ma" with a kasra, on the basis that "ma" is verbal (maṣdariyya), meaning: "because of my giving you some of the Book, then because of the coming of a confirming Messenger, Allah took the covenant that you shall surely believe in him and surely help him." Or it is relative, and the meaning is: "His taking of what I have given you, and a confirming Messenger has come to you for it." It has been read as "lammā" with the sense of "when I gave you," or "lam min ajli mā ātaytukum" (for the sake of what I gave you), on the basis that its original form is "lamin mā," which by assimilation had one of the three mīms dropped due to heaviness.

﴿He said﴾: that is, Allah, exalted is He, after He had taken the covenant.

﴿"Do you acknowledge?"﴾ regarding what has been mentioned.

﴿"And take upon that My burden (iṣrī)?"﴾ That is, My covenant; it is so called because it is bound (yu'ṣar), that is, tied fast. It has been read with a damma on the hamza, either as a dialect form like ʿibar and ʿabr, or as the plural of iṣār, which is that by which something is bound.

﴿They said﴾: a resumptive clause built upon a question, as if it were said: "What did they say at that?" So it was said: "They said, 'We acknowledge.'" And the taking of the burden was not mentioned, being sufficed by this.

﴿He said﴾, exalted is He.

﴿"Then bear witness"﴾: that is, let some of you bear witness against others to the acknowledgment. It has also been said that the address in it is to the angels.

﴿"And I am with you among the witnesses"﴾: that is, I too am a witness to your acknowledgment and your bearing witness. The use of "with" (ma'a) addressing those spoken to is because they are the direct performers of the testimony in reality, and in it is emphasis and warning of no small measure.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 82:

﴿Then whoever turns away﴾ i.e., turns away from what has been mentioned.

﴿after that﴾ — after the covenant and the emphatic affirmation through acknowledgment and testimony. Thus the sense of distance in the demonstrative ("after that," dhalika) serves to magnify the covenant.

﴿those﴾ is a demonstrative referring back to "whoever" (man). The plural is used in light of the meaning, just as the singular in "turns away" (tawalla) is used in light of the wording. What is contained in it of the sense of distance serves to indicate the extent of their wrongdoing and the remoteness of their station in evil and corruption. That is: ﴿those﴾ — the ones who turn away, characterized by the ugly qualities.

﴿are the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqun)﴾ — those who rebel and go out of obedience among the disbelievers. For the fasiq of every group is one who exceeds the limit.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 83:

﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?﴾ It is coordinated (ʿatf) with something implied (muqaddar), meaning: "Do they then turn away and seek other than the religion of Allah?" The object is placed first (taqdim al-maf'ul) because its denial is what is intended; or it is coordinated with the preceding sentence. The hamzah (interrogative particle) is placed between the two for denunciation (inkar). It has also been read with the second-person ta' (ta' al-khitab), on the assumption of: "And say to them." ﴿And to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) that serves to reinforce the denunciation (wakadat al-inkar).

﴿Willingly and unwillingly﴾ meaning: obediently, by reflection and following the proof (tawaʿan), or unwillingly, by the sword and by witnessing what compels one to Islam, such as the lifting of the mountain, the onset of drowning, and approaching death; or choosing freely like the angels and the believers, and subjugated like the disbelievers, for they are able to refrain from what has been decreed upon them.

﴿And to Him they will be returned﴾ meaning: whoever is in them both. The plural is used in consideration of the meaning. It has also been read with the second-person ta', and the clause is either coordinated with what precedes it, in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, or it is a resumed sentence (mustaʾnifah) brought for warning and threat (tahdid wa waʿid).

﴿قُلْ آمَنّا بِاللَّهِ﴾ is a command to the Messenger (ﷺ) to inform, on his own behalf and on behalf of the believers with him, that they believe in what has been mentioned. The plural pronoun in His words, ﴿وَما أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْنا﴾ ("and what has been sent down to us"), which refers to the Qur'an, is used either because it was also sent down to them, through its being conveyed to them, or because what is attributed to one member of a group may be attributed to all of them. Or it refers to him alone, and this is the more fitting reading given what follows. The use of the plural is to show the greatness of his rank (peace be upon him) and the elevation of his station, by commanding him to speak on his own behalf in the manner of kings. It is also possible that the command is general, and that the singular form is used to honour him (peace be upon him) and to indicate that he (peace be upon him) is the foundation in this matter, as in His words, ﴿يا أيُّها النَّبِيُّ إذا طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّساءَ﴾ ("O Prophet, when you divorce women").

﴿وَما أُنْزِلَ عَلى إبْراهِيمَ وإسْماعِيلَ وإسْحاقَ ويَعْقُوبَ والأسْباطِ﴾ ("and what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes"): this refers to the scrolls. The verb nazala (to descend) is construed with "ila" (to) because it ends with the messengers, and it is construed with "ʿala" (upon) because it comes from above. Whoever claims a distinction, that "ʿala" is used because the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and "ila" because the address is to the believers, has overreached. Do you not see His words, ﴿بِما أُنْزِلَ إلَيْكَ﴾ ("in what has been sent down to you"), and so on, and His words, ﴿آمِنُوا بِالَّذِي أُنْزِلَ عَلى الَّذِينَ آمِنُوا﴾ ("believe in what has been sent down to those who believe"), and so on? The reason the revelation given to the Messenger (ﷺ) is mentioned before what was given to the other messengers (peace be upon them), although it came down to him later, is that it is the one best known to them and the standard by which the others are measured. "Al-Asbat" is the plural of sibt, which means grandson, and what is meant by them are the grandchildren of Jacob (peace be upon him) and his twelve sons and their descendants, since they are the grandchildren of Abraham (peace be upon him).

﴿وَما أُوتِيَ مُوسى وعِيسى﴾ ("and what was given to Moses and Jesus"): this refers to the Torah and the Gospel, and to all the clear miracles that were brought by their hands, as is indicated by the choice of the verb ītāʾ (giving) over inzāl (sending down), which is specific to the Book, and by singling out the two of them for mention, since the discussion is with the Jews and the Christians.

﴿والنَّبِيُّونَ﴾ ("and the prophets") is conjoined to Moses and Jesus (peace be upon them both). That is: and what was given to the prophets, among those mentioned and others.

﴿مِن رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ("from their Lord"): the Books and the miracles.

﴿لا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أحَدٍ مِنهُمْ﴾ ("we make no distinction between any of them"): unlike the way of the Jews and the Christians, who believed in some and disbelieved in others. Rather, we affirm the truth of the prophethood of each of them and the validity of what was sent down to them in their time. The text does not explicitly deny distinction between the Books, because that is implied by what was mentioned; its detailed treatment has already passed in the commentary on His words, ﴿لا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أحَدٍ مِن رُسُلِهِ﴾ ("we make no distinction between any of His messengers"). The hamza in "aḥad" is either original, in which case it is a noun coined for whoever is fit to be addressed, and which is the same for singular, dual, plural, masculine and feminine, which is why "bayn" (between) may validly precede it, as in the phrase "al-māl bayn al-nās" (wealth is among the people). Or it is substituted from a waw, in which case it has the same meaning, and its generality comes from its occurring in the context of negation. The validity of "bayn" preceding it is based on an omitted conjoined term, which is clear from context, meaning: between one of them and another, as in the verse of al-Nabigha:

"Between the good when he came safely, and Abu Hajar, there were only a few nights,"

that is, between the good and between me.

﴿وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ ("and we are submitting to Him"): that is, we are subservient to Him, or we are sincere to Him, the Exalted, with our souls, not making any associate with Him in them. In this there is an implicit contrast with the faith of the People of the Book, for they are far removed from this.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 85:

﴿Whoever seeks other than Islam﴾, that is, other than tawhid (monotheism, the affirmation of God's oneness) and submission to the judgment of God, the Exalted, like the conduct of the overt polytheists (mushrikun), and like those who claim to affirm tawhid while associating partners with Him, such as the People of the Two Books (ahl al-kitabayn).

﴿as a religion﴾ that he adopts. It is in the accusative because it is the object of "yabtaghi" (seeks). "Ghayra al-Islam" (other than Islam) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from it, since it was originally an attribute of it; when it was placed before it, it took the accusative as a circumstantial clause. Alternatively, "dinan" is the object, and "ghayra al-Islam" is a circumstantial clause. Or "dinan" is a specification (tamyiz) because of the vagueness in it, or it is an apposition (badal) for "ghayra al-Islam."

﴿then it will never be accepted﴾ from him, that is, that (religion) will never be accepted at all; rather, it will be rejected in the most severe and most reprehensible manner. As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and he in the Hereafter will be among the losers﴾, it is either a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the genitive ("minhu," from him) or a new resumptive sentence with no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis), meaning: among those who fall into loss. The meaning is that the one who turns away from Islam and seeks other than it is devoid of benefit and falls into loss by nullifying the sound natural disposition (fitrah) upon which people were created. The placing of rejection and loss upon the mere seeking indicates that the condition of one who adopts a religion other than Islam and is content with it is even more dreadful and reprehensible. It has been argued from this that faith (iman) is Islam, since if it were other than it, it would not be accepted. The reply is that the verse negates the acceptance of every religion that differs from it, not the acceptance of everything that differs from it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 86:**

﴿How will Allah guide﴾ to the truth (p-56) ﴿a people who disbelieved after their belief﴾. It has been said: they were ten men who apostatized after they had believed and joined (the polytheists) in Makkah. It has also been said: they were the Jews of Qurayza and al-Nadir and whoever followed their religion, who disbelieved in the Prophet (ﷺ) after they had been believers in him before his mission (ba'th).

﴿And they testified that the Messenger is true, and the clear proofs had come to them﴾. This is an expression of astonishment at Allah guiding them, for one who deviates from the truth after it has become clear to him is immersed in misguidance and far from right guidance. It has also been said that this is a negation and a denial of guidance for them, and that this implies that the repentance of the apostate is not accepted. The words of Allah Most High, ﴿and they testified﴾, are a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on their "belief" (īmān), considering it as resolved into a verbal clause, as in the words of Allah Most High: ﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity and who lend to Allah﴾ etc. For it has the force of saying "after they had believed," or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "disbelieved," with "qad" implied. This is evidence that acknowledgment by the tongue is outside the reality of faith (īmān).

﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, i.e., those who wronged themselves by neglecting reflection (naẓar) and by placing disbelief in the place of belief. How much more so one who has been brought the truth, recognized it, and then turned away from it. The clause is either parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyyah) or circumstantial (ḥāliyyah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 87:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to those mentioned, in view of their being characterized by the abominable attributes that preceded, and the sense of distance in it (for the reason mentioned many times) is the subject (mubtada'). The words of the Exalted: ﴿their recompense﴾ are a second subject (mubtada' thani). The words of the Exalted: ﴿that upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels and of mankind, all together﴾ are its predicate (khabar), and the whole clause is a predicate for ﴿those﴾. This by its explicit wording indicates the permissibility of cursing them, and by its implicit meaning negates the permissibility of cursing others. Perhaps the distinction between them and others is that they have had a seal set upon their hearts, are barred from guidance, and are utterly despairing of mercy, unlike others. By "mankind" is meant the believers, or everyone, for the disbeliever also curses one who denies the truth and apostatizes from it, but he does not recognize the truth in its specific reality.

Abiding eternally therein (khalidina fiha): in the curse, or the punishment, or the Fire, even though none of them is mentioned, since the context points to them.

﴿Their punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved﴾: that is, they will not be given respite (yumhalun).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 89:

﴿Except those who repent after that﴾, i.e., after the apostasy (irtidad).

﴿And make amends﴾, i.e., they repair what they corrupted, or they enter into righteousness (salah).

﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, so He accepts their repentance and bestows His favor upon them. This is a justification (ta'lil) for what the exception (istithna') indicates. It has been said: it was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Suwayd, when he regretted his apostasy and sent to his people asking them to inquire whether there was any repentance for him. His brother al-Hilas sent to him the verse, so he returned to Medina and repented.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 90:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief﴾ like the Jews, who disbelieved in Jesus, peace be upon him, and in the Gospel, after believing in Moses, peace be upon him, and in the Torah; then they increased in disbelief when they disbelieved in Muhammad, may blessings and peace be upon him, and in the Qur'an. Or [it refers to] those who disbelieved in him, peace be upon him, after they had believed in him before his mission (ba'tha); then they increased in disbelief by persisting in opposing him, reviling him, barring others from belief, and breaking the covenant. Or [it refers to] people who apostatized and joined Makkah, then increased in disbelief by saying, "We await for him the vicissitudes of fate (rayb al-manun), or we return to him and feign hypocrisy by displaying belief."

﴿Their repentance will never be accepted﴾ Because they do not repent except when they are on the verge of destruction, so the absence of their repentance is expressed by the non-acceptance of it, as an intensification concerning their state and a depiction of their condition in the form of the condition of those who have despaired of mercy. Or because their repentance would be nothing but hypocrisy, given their apostasy and their increase in disbelief; for this reason the particle fa' (then) does not enter into it.

﴿And those are the astray﴾ those who are firmly fixed in error.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold, even if he were to ransom himself with it﴾. Since dying in disbelief is the cause of the impossibility of the ransom being accepted, the particle *fa'* (the connective "then") is added here to signal this causal link. *Mil'u al-shay'* (the filling of a thing) is what the thing is filled with. *"Dhahaban"* is a *tamyiz* (specifying accusative, explaining the noun it follows).

It is also read in the nominative, *"mil'u"*, in which case it is either a *badal* (substitute) for *mil'* or the *khabar* (predicate) of an omitted subject. *"Wa-law iftada"* is construed according to meaning (*mahmul 'ala al-ma'na*), as if it had been said: "never will a ransom be accepted from any of them, even if he were to ransom himself with the filling of the earth in gold." Or it is *ma'tuf* (conjoined) on an implied element whose sense is: "never will the filling of the earth in gold be accepted from any of them, even if he were to give it in charity in this world, and even if he were to ransom himself with it from the punishment in the Hereafter." Or the intended meaning is "even if he were to ransom himself with its like," as in His saying: ﴿And if those who did wrong had all that is on the earth, and the like of it with it﴾. The *mithl* (like) may be omitted while still being intended, because two like things are judged as one thing.

*"Ulā'ika"* (those) is a demonstrative referring to those mentioned, in consideration of their being characterized by the abominable attributes mentioned.

﴿For them is a painful punishment﴾, *alīm* meaning painful. The demonstrative *ism al-ishara* is the *mubtada'* (subject), and the prepositional phrase (*al-zarf*) is its *khabar* (predicate). Because it relies on the subject, *"'adhabun alim"* is raised as the *fā'il* (agent).

﴿And for them there are no helpers﴾, meaning in averting the punishment from them or in lightening it. *"Min"* is *mazida* (extra, emphatic), for *istighraq* (comprehensive negation). The plural form is used in consideration of the pronoun (*al-damir*), meaning: there is not a single helper for any one of them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 92:

﴿You will never attain righteousness﴾ "Nal" (نالَ) from "nayl" (نَيْلًا), meaning to reach or attain, when one reaches it. The address is to the believers, and it is an independent statement brought to explain what benefits the believers and is accepted from them, following the explanation of what does not benefit the disbelievers nor is accepted from them. That is: you will never reach the reality of righteousness (al-birr), for which the competitors compete, nor will you attain its level, nor will you join the company of the righteous; or, you will never attain the righteousness of God Most High, which is His reward, His mercy, His good pleasure, and His Garden.

﴿until you spend﴾ That is, in the way of God, Mighty and Majestic, desiring what is with Him. The "min" (مِن) in His words, ﴿of what you love﴾ (مِمّا تُحِبُّونَ), is partitive (tab'idiyyah), and the reading of one who recites "ba'da ma tuhibbun" (بَعْضَ ما تُحِبُّونَ) supports it. It has also been said that it is explicative (bayaniyyah), and "ma" (ما) is relative or descriptive, meaning: of what you desire and what pleases you of the noblest of your wealth and what is dearest to you, as in His words, ﴿Spend of the good things you have earned﴾; or of what includes them and other deeds and one's very life (al-muhjah), with spending meaning absolute giving. In this there is an indication of the difficulty of attaining righteousness that is not hidden. The predecessors, may God be pleased with them, when they loved something, would make it for God, Mighty and Majestic. It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, "Abu Talha came and said, 'O Messenger of God, the dearest of my wealth to me is Bayraha'. So place it, O Messenger of God, where God shows you.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'Bakh, bakh! That is profitable wealth (mal rayih aw rabih), and I think you should make it for the near relatives.' So he distributed it among his relatives." And "Zayd ibn Harithah came with a horse of his which he loved and said, 'This is for the way of God.' So the Messenger of God ﷺ mounted Usama ibn Zayd upon it. It seems Zayd felt something in himself and said: 'I only intended to give it in charity.' The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'Indeed God Most High has accepted it from you.'" It is said: in this is evidence that spending the dearest wealth on the closest relatives is more excellent. ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, wrote to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari to buy for him a slave girl from the captives of Jalula on the day the cities of Kisra were conquered. When she came to him, he was pleased with her (p-58) and said: "God Most High says: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of what you love﴾," and he freed her. It is narrated that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz had a slave girl, of striking beauty, belonging to his wife, and ʿUmar was desirous of her, and he had asked her for her several times but she did not give her to him. Then, when he assumed the caliphate, she adorned her and sent her to him, and said: "I have given her to you, O Commander of the Faithful, so let her serve you." He said: "From where did you acquire her?" She said: "I brought her from the house of Abu ʿAbd al-Malik." So he investigated how she had come into her possession, and it was said: "Indeed, Fulan the governor had debts, and when he died she was taken from his estate." So he investigated the condition of the governor, summoned his heirs and satisfied them all by giving them the money. Then he turned to the slave girl, whom he loved intensely, and said: "You are free for the sake of God Most High." She said: "Why, O Commander of the Faithful? You have removed from her affair every doubt." He said: "Then I am not of those who restrain the self from desire."

﴿And whatever you spend of anything﴾ "Ma" (ما) is conditional and jussive for "tunfiquu" (تُنْفِقُوا), governing it in the object position, and "min" (مِن) is partitive, attached to an omitted element that is a description of the conditional noun, meaning: whatever kind of thing you spend, being one of the things; for the singular in such a position stands in the place of the plural. It has also been said: the place of the prepositional phrase is accusative as a specification (tamyiz), meaning: whatever thing you spend, good that you love or bad that you dislike.

﴿indeed God is knowing of it﴾ This is a justification for the answer of the condition, occupying its place, meaning: He will recompense you according to it, whether good or bad, for indeed He, Most High, is Knowing of everything you spend with complete knowledge, such that nothing of His essence and attributes is hidden from Him. The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for the sake of observing the rhyme (fawasil). In this there is encouragement to spend what is good and a warning against spending what is bad, which is not hidden.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 93:**

﴿كُلُّ الطَّعامِ﴾ That is: every individual food, or every kind of food.

﴿كانَ حِلا لِبَنِي إسْرائِيلَ﴾ That is: lawful (ḥalālan) for them. The word ḥill (ḥil) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as an adjective, and for this reason it is used in the same form for the singular and the plural, and for the masculine and the feminine, as in His saying, ﴿they are not lawful for them﴾ (لا هُنَّ حِلٌّ لَهُمْ).

﴿إلا ما حَرَّمَ إسْرائِيلُ عَلى نَفْسِهِ﴾ This is an exceptive (istithnāʾ) that is connected (muttaṣil) to the noun of kāna: that is, all foods were lawful for the Children of Israel except what Israel (i.e., Ya'qub, peace be upon him) forbade for himself, namely the flesh of camels and their milk. It is said: he had sciatica, so he vowed that if he were healed he would not eat the food he loved most, and that was the one he loved most. It is also said: he did that for treatment, on the advice of physicians. Those who permit the Prophet to exercise ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) cite this, while the opponent may say that this was by permission from God Most High in it, so it is like its prohibition from the outset.

﴿مِن قَبْلِ أنْ تُنَزَّلَ التَّوْراةُ﴾ This is connected to His saying, ﴿was lawful﴾ (كانَ حِلا), and there is no harm in placing the exception between them. It is also said: it is connected to ﴿forbade﴾ (حَرَّمَ). In this view, restricting his (peace be upon him) prohibition to the time before the revelation of the Torah adds no further benefit. That is: everything other than the excepted item was lawful for them before the Torah was revealed, containing the prohibition of what was forbidden to them because of their wrongdoing and their transgression, as a punishment for them and a tightening upon them. This is a rebuttal of the Jews' claim of innocence regarding what His saying condemned them for: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who judaized, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾, and His saying: ﴿And to those who judaized We forbade every animal with claws﴾, the two verses. They said: "We were not the first to whom it was forbidden; it was forbidden to Noah, Abraham and those after them, until the matter reached us, so it was forbidden to us just as it was forbidden to those before us." It is also a rebuke to them for denying abrogation (naskh) and for attacking the claim of the Messenger (ﷺ) that he agreed with Abraham (peace be upon him) in making lawful the flesh of camels and their milk.

﴿قُلْ فَأْتُوا بِالتَّوْراةِ (p-59) فاتْلُوها﴾ He (peace be upon him) was commanded to argue against them with their own book, which states clearly that the prohibition of what was forbidden to them was a new prohibition that followed from their wrongdoing and transgression: whenever they committed one of the sins they had perpetrated, a type of good things was forbidden to them as a punishment, and they are commanded to bring it out and recite it, so as to silence them, put them to shame, and expose their lie. The name of the Torah is made explicit because the sentence is a speech addressed to the Jews, disconnected from what precedes it.

His saying, ﴿if you are truthful﴾ (إنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ), means: in your claim that this is an ancient prohibition. The apodosis of the conditional is omitted, since what is mentioned indicates it: that is, if you are truthful, then bring the Torah and recite it, for your truthfulness would definitely compel you to do so. It is reported that they did not dare to bring out the Torah, so they were confounded and returned humbled. In this there is a clear proof of the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ) and of the permissibility of abrogation, which they deny, and this is not hidden. The sentence is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafah) that confirms what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 94:

﴿Then whoever fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ That is: he invents it against Him, glorified is He, by claiming that He prohibited what has been mentioned before the revelation of the Torah to the Children of Israel and to the nations that preceded them.

﴿after that﴾ After what has been mentioned of their being commanded to bring the Torah and recite it, and the rebuke and confutation that resulted from it. The restriction "after that" serves to indicate the utmost ugliness (of the act).

﴿then those﴾ This is a demonstrative referring to the relative pronoun (alladhi/man) in consideration of its being characterized by what is in the sphere of the relative clause. The plural is used in consideration of its meaning, just as the singular is used in the relative clause in consideration of its wording, and the sense of distance contained in it is to announce the remoteness of their rank in misguidance and transgression. That is: "then those," who persist in fabrication after the reality of the situation has become manifest and the arena of argument and disputation has become too narrow for them.

﴿they are the wrongdoers﴾ Those who go to excess in wrongdoing and aggression, and who go far in both. The sentence is a new (independent) clause with no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical case), brought from His side, glorified is He, to explain the completeness of their obstinacy. It has also been said: it is in the place of the accusative, included under the saying, as a conjunction (ʿatf) upon His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then bring the Torah﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 95:

﴿Say: "God has spoken the truth."﴾ That is: the truthfulness of God, exalted is He, has become manifest and established regarding what was revealed concerning the matter of the prohibition. It is also said that it refers to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew﴾ and so on. Or [it means] He spoke the truth in every matter of affairs, and this is included in that by primary inclusion. And in it there is an allusion to their clear lie.

﴿Then follow the religion of Abraham﴾ That is: the religion of Islam, which is in origin the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him. For you were not following his religion as you claim. Or [it means]: follow the like of his religion, so that you may be freed from Judaism, which has compelled you to distortion, obstinacy, and fabricating falsehoods in order to level out base worldly aims, and has obliged you to prohibit good things that were lawful for Abraham, peace be upon him, and those who followed him. The "fa" (then) indicates that the manifestation of His truthfulness, exalted is He, necessitates following and abandoning what they were upon.

﴿Hanifan﴾ That is: inclining away from all the deviant religions.

﴿And he was not among the polytheists﴾ That is: in any matter of his religion, in principle and in its branches. In it there is an allusion to the polytheism of the Jews, and an explicit statement that he, peace be upon him, had absolutely no religious connection with them. The purpose is to show that the Prophet (ﷺ) is upon the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him, in its fundamentals, because he calls only to monotheism and to disavowal of every object of worship other than Him, glorified and exalted is He. The sentence is a concluding remark (tadhyil) to what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 96:

﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾ opens the explanation of their disbelief in another part (p-60) of the rites of his religion, peace be upon him, following the explanation of their disbelief in the matter of all foods being lawful to him, peace be upon him. It is narrated that they said: "Bayt al-Maqdis is greater than the Ka'bah, because it is the place of migration of the prophets and it is in the holy land." The Muslims said: "Rather, the Ka'bah is greater." This reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this was revealed. That is: indeed, the first House established for worship and made a place of devotion for them, and the one who established it is Allah, the Exalted. The reading in the passive voice supports this, but the reading in the active voice is also attested. The words of the Exalted: ﴿that at Bakkah﴾ are the predicate of "inna" (indeed). It is described with a definite noun although its subject is indefinite, because it is specified by two things: the annexation and the descriptive clause after it. That is: the House that is at Bakkah, meaning, in it. The omission of the qualified noun has an evident grandeur. "Bakkah" is a dialectal variant of Makkah, for the Arabs interchange the letters "ba'" and "mim," as in their saying: "darbatu lazibin" and "lazimin," and "al-namit" and "al-nabit" as the name of a place in al-Dahna', and their saying: "amrun rathibun" and "rathimun," "sabbada ra'sahu" and "sammadaha," and "aghbatat al-humma" and "aghmatat." It is also a name of the sacred land, from "bakka," meaning to crowd, because of the crowding of people in it. It is narrated from Qatadah: "the people crush one another (yabukku)," or because it crushes the necks of tyrants; that is, it breaks them. No tyrant intended it except that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, destroyed him. It is said: "Bakkah" is the name of the central part of Makkah. It is said: it is the name of the place of the House. It is said: it is the name of the Mosque itself, and Makkah is the name of the whole city. This is supported by the fact that "al-tabakk," meaning crowding, occurs only at the circumambulation. It is said: "Makkah" is the name of the Mosque and the place of circumambulation, and "Bakkah" is the name of the city, based on His saying: ﴿at Bakkah, blessed﴾. It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, was asked about the first House established for mankind, and he said: "The Sacred Mosque, then Bayt al-Maqdis." He was asked: "How far apart are they?" He said: "Forty years." It is said: the first to build it was Ibrahim, peace be upon him. It is said: Adam, peace be upon him. We have already covered what is in it of opinions in the commentary on Surat al-Baqarah. It is said: it is the first House established in nobility, not in time.

﴿Blessed﴾, abounding in good and benefit, because of what is gained by one who performs Hajj and 'Umrah to it, makes i'tikaf near it, and circumambulates around it, of reward and expiation of sins. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed in the adverbial phrase, because the estimate is: "the one at Bakkah is it," and the governing element in it is the verb of stability (istiqrar) estimated within the adverbial phrase.

﴿And a guidance for the worlds﴾, because it is their qibla and place of worship, and because in it are wondrous signs indicating the great power of Allah, the Exalted, and the far-reaching depth of His wisdom, as He said.

﴿فِيهِ آياتٌ بَيِّناتٌ﴾ [In it are clear signs], evident ones, such as the deflection of birds from flying over the House across the ages, and the wild predators coexisting with their prey within the Sacred Precinct without attacking them, and Allah the Exalted's subduing of every tyrant who intends harm to it, like the companions of the Elephant. The clause is either explanatory of the guidance (al-huda) or a separate circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿مَقامُ إبْراهِيمَ﴾ [the station of Abraham]: that is, the imprint of his feet, upon him be peace, in the rock upon which he, upon him be peace, would stand when raising the stones to build the Ka'bah, at its elevation, or when washing his head. It is related that he, upon him be peace, came visiting from al-Sham to Makkah, and the wife of Isma'il, upon him be peace, said to him: "Descend until I wash your head." He did not descend, so she brought him this stone and placed it under his right side, and he placed his foot upon it until she had washed the right side of his head. Then she turned it to his left side until she washed the other side, and the imprint of his two feet remained upon it. This phrase is either: (a) a subject (mubtada') whose predicate has been omitted, meaning "among them is the station of Abraham"; or (b) a substitute (badal) for ﴿آياتٌ﴾, a substitute of part for whole (badal al-ba'd min al-kull); or (c) an explicative apposition ('atf bayan), either taken as a singular on account of its being equivalent to many signs, due to the prominence of its status and the strength of its indication of the power of Allah the Exalted and of the prophethood of Abraham, upon him be prayer and peace, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿إنَّ إبْراهِيمَ كانَ أُمَّةً قانِتًا﴾ [Indeed Abraham was a nation, devoutly obedient]; or on account of its comprising many signs, for each of these is a sign: the imprint of his two feet in a solid rock, his sinking into it up to the ankles, the softening of some rocks but not others, its preservation apart from the rest of the signs of the prophets, upon them be peace, and its being safeguarded despite the great number of enemies for thousands of years, being an independent sign. This is supported by the reading in the singular (al-qira'ah 'ala al-tawhid). It may also be understood from His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَمَن دَخَلَهُ كانَ آمِنًا﴾ [and whoever enters it is safe]. Although it is a new independent sentence (jumlah mustanifah ibtida'iyyah) or a conditional sentence (shartiyyah), it is in effect equivalent to saying "and [He made] secure whoever enters it," so it is in meaning and outcome conjoined to "the station of Abraham." It is not hidden that the dual is a type of plural, so this suffices; or it may be said that two of those signs were mentioned, and the mention of the rest was omitted to indicate their abundance. The meaning of "made secure whoever enters it" is: making him secure from being harmed, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿أوَلَمْ يَرَوْا أنّا جَعَلْنا حَرَمًا آمِنًا ويُتَخَطَّفُ النّاسُ مِن حَوْلِهِمْ﴾ [Have they not seen that We made a sanctuary secure while people are being snatched from around them?]. This was through the supplication of Abraham, upon him be peace: ﴿رَبِّ اجْعَلْ هَذا البَلَدَ آمِنًا﴾ [My Lord, make this city secure]. A man could commit every offence and then take refuge in the Sacred Precinct and would not be pursued. It is related from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Even if I found the killer of al-Khattab (my father) within it, I would not touch him until he leaves it." Accordingly Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: whoever is liable to be killed outside the Sacred Precinct, for retaliation (qisas), apostasy, or adultery, and then takes refuge in the Sacred Precinct, shall not be molested; however, he is not to be sheltered, but is to be fed and given drink, and no one may trade with him until he is compelled to leave. It was also said: its security means safety from the Fire. And from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever dies in one of the two sanctuaries (Makkah or Madinah) will be raised on the Day of Resurrection in security." And from him, upon him be prayer and peace: "Al-Hajun and al-Baqi' are taken by their edges and scattered into Paradise." These two are the cemeteries of Makkah and Madinah. From Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood at the Thaniyyat al-Hajun, and there was no cemetery there at that time, and he said: 'Allah the Exalted will raise from this plot and from this whole sanctuary seventy thousand whose faces are like the full moon on the night of the full moon; they will enter Paradise without reckoning; each one of them will intercede for seventy thousand, whose faces are like the full moon on the night of the full moon.'" And from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever endures the heat of Makkah for an hour of the day, Hell will be removed from him a distance of two hundred years' journey."

﴿وَلِلَّهِ عَلى النّاسِ حِجُّ البَيْتِ﴾ [And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by people]: a sentence composed of a subject (mubtada'), which is ḥajj (ḥajj, the pilgrimage), and a predicate (khabar), which is lillah [owed to Allah]. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿عَلى النّاسِ﴾ [by people] is related to what the predicate is related to, namely the sense of being established (al-istiqrar), or to an omitted element which is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed within the preposition; the governing element for it is that sense of being established. It is permissible that ﴿عَلى النّاسِ﴾ be the predicate and "lillah" be related to what the predicate is related to. There is no way for it to be related to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause from the concealed pronoun in ﴿عَلى النّاسِ﴾, because this would require placing the circumstantial clause before its governing element of meaning (al-'amil al-ma'nawi), and this is something the majority (al-jumhur) find inadmissible; Ibn Malik permitted it when the circumstantial clause is an adverb of place or time or a prepositional phrase and its governing element is likewise, unlike the adverb and the prepositional phrase, which may precede their governing element of meaning. The lam in ﴿البَيْتِ﴾ [the House] is for specific reference (al-'ahd). Its ḥajj (ḥajj) is the intention to visit it in the specific known manner. The vowelling of the ḥa' as kasrah (ḥijj) is the dialect of Najd. It was also said: it is a noun for the verbal noun (ism lil-masdar). It has also been read with a fatḥah (ḥajj).

﴿مَنِ اسْتَطاعَ إلَيْهِ سَبِيلا﴾ [for whoever is able to make his way to it]: in the place of a genitive (jarr) on the basis that it is a substitute (badal) for "people," a substitute of part for whole (badal al-ba'd min al-kull), specifying its generality, so the pronoun referring back to the substituted element is omitted, meaning: "whoever among them is able." It was also said: it is a substitute of the whole (badal al-kull), with "people" meaning the part who are able, so there is no need for a pronoun. It was also said: it is in the place of a nominative (raf') as the predicate of a concealed subject (mubtada' mudmar), meaning: "they are whoever is able, etc." It was also said: it is in the place of an accusative (nasb) by estimating "I mean" (a'ni). It was also said: the word "man" is conditional (shartiyyah), and the response (jaza') is omitted because what is mentioned indicates it; and likewise the pronoun referring to "people," meaning: "whoever among them is able to make his way to it, then for Allah upon him is the pilgrimage to the House." This has been preferred on the basis that "man" after it is conditional, and the pronoun in the prepositional phrase "ilayhi" refers either to "the House" or to "ḥajj." The prepositional phrase is related to "the way" (al-sabil), and it has been placed before it to draw attention to its importance, as in His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فَهَلْ إلى خُرُوجٍ مِن سَبِيلٍ﴾ [Is there any way out?] and ﴿هَلْ إلى مَرَدٍّ مِن سَبِيلٍ﴾ [Is there any way of return?], because it carries the meaning of arriving at and reaching (al-ifda' wal-iysal). How could it not? For it is an expression for the means, whether of wealth or otherwise. Anas ibn Malik related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: "The way is provision and a mount." Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, related that "a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is the way?' He said: 'Provision and a mount.'" This is what is meant by what is related: that he, upon him be peace, interpreted ability (al-istita'ah) as provision and a mount. Likewise it is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them, and most scholars hold this view. However, al-Shafi'i took its apparent meaning and obliged the appointment of a proxy upon the disabled person who is able to pay the wages of one who will perform it on his behalf. The apparent point is that his, upon him be peace, not mentioning physical health was because the matter is evident; how could it not be? For what is actually explained is the way that brings the one who is able to the House himself, and that cannot be conceived without physical health. It is related from Ibn al-Zubayr that it is "according to the measure of strength." The position of Malik is that if a man trusts in his strength, it is obligatory upon him; and it is also related from him that it is "according to the measure of capacity." Provision and a mount may be found by one who is unable to travel, and one may be able to travel without a mount or provision. It is related from al-Dahhak that if one is able to hire himself out, then he is able.

﴿وَمَن كَفَرَ﴾ [And whoever disbelieves]: the phrase "whoever disbelieves" is placed in the position of "whoever does not perform the pilgrimage," as emphasis of its obligation and as severe warning against one who abandons it. For this reason he, upon him be peace, said: "Whoever dies without having performed the pilgrimage, let him die, if he wishes, as a Jew or a Christian." It is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he, upon him be peace, said in his sermon: "O people, Allah has enjoined the pilgrimage upon whoever is able to make his way to it; and whoever does not do so, let him die in whatever state he wishes, as a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian."

﴿فَإنَّ اللَّهَ غَنِيٌّ عَنِ العالَمِينَ﴾ [then indeed Allah is free of need of the worlds], and of their worship. Since whoever disbelieves is among them, entering them as a first-level inclusion, this suffices in place of the resumptive pronoun linking the condition and the response. This noble verse has achieved, from the various modes of consideration, what expresses complete concern for the matter of the pilgrimage and the utmost severity against one who abandons it: the form of a declarative statement, which indicates certainty, was chosen, or it appears in the form of a nominal sentence, which indicates permanence and continuity, in a manner that conveys that it is a right and a binding duty owed to Allah, glorified is He, upon the necks of people, from which they cannot be released, nor free of its obligation. He led them through the path of generality, then specification and ambiguity, then clarification and summary, then detail, because of the additional affirmation and confirmation this brings. He expressed abandoning it by disbelief, which has no worse thing beyond it, and made its recompense His independence, the Exalted, which indicates intense detestation and great wrath, not only against the one who abandons it, for He has turned away from him entirely, dropping him from the level of consideration and disdaining to mention him, but against all the worlds of those who perform and those who abandon, to indicate the utmost intensity of anger. Furthermore, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and 'Ata', may Allah be pleased with them, said: ﴿وَمَن كَفَرَ﴾ means: whoever denies the obligation of the pilgrimage and claims that it is not obligatory. It is related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that it was revealed concerning the Jews, for they said: "The pilgrimage to Makkah is not obligatory." It is also related that when the saying of the Exalted: ﴿وَلِلَّهِ عَلى النّاسِ حِجُّ البَيْتِ﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gathered all the people of the religions and addressed them, saying: "Indeed Allah has prescribed the pilgrimage upon you, so perform it." A single community believed in it, namely the Muslims, and five communities disbelieved in it, saying: "We do not believe in it, nor do we pray towards it, nor do we perform it." Then ﴿وَمَن كَفَرَ﴾ was revealed. From the Prophet ﷺ: "Perform the pilgrimage before you are prevented from performing it, for the House has been demolished twice, and it will be raised to heaven in the third (instance)." It is also related: "Perform the pilgrimage before the land prevents its way." From Ibn Mas'ud: "Perform the pilgrimage to this House before there grows in the desert a tree of which no animal eats without perishing." From 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "If people abandoned the pilgrimage for a single year, they would not be granted respite."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 98:

﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the verses of Allah, while Allah is witness over what you do?"﴾ They are the Jews and the Christians. (p-63) They were addressed by the title "People of the Scripture" (ahl al-kitab), which necessitates belief in it and in what confirms it of the Great Qur'an, as an exaggeration in censuring their state in their disbelief in them. His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Why do you disbelieve in the verses of Allah?﴾ is a rebuke and a denunciation of there being any cause among the causes for their disbelief in them, and an affirmation of what requires total avoidance of it. By "His verses, Exalted is He," is meant what encompasses the Qur'anic verses, among which are those recited concerning the Hajj and other matters, and what is in the Torah and the Gospel of the evidences of his prophethood, peace be upon him. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿while Allah is witness over what you do﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿you disbelieve﴾, serving to intensify the rebuke and to emphasize the denunciation. The mention of the Divine Name (al-Jalalah) in the place where a pronoun would be expected is to instill awe and to magnify the gravity of the matter. The intensive form in "shahid" (witness) is for intensifying the threat. The word "ma" (what) either refers to their disbelief, or is on its general meaning, and [their disbelief] is included within it as a primary inclusion. The meaning: For what reason do you disbelieve in the verses of Him, Mighty and Majestic, when the state is that He, Exalted is He, is exceedingly aware of all your deeds and of recompensing you for them? And there is no doubt that this closes off every manner of what you do and cuts off its causes entirely.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 99:

﴿Say: O People of the Scripture﴾. This is a command to rebuke them for misguiding others, following on from the rebuke for their own misguidance. The repetition serves to intensify the rebuke and censure. The clause is not joined by a conjunction to the previous command, to indicate that each rebuke stands on its own. Likewise, the phrase ﴿Why do you avert﴾ is separated from ﴿Why do you disbelieve﴾, to show that each of their disbelief and their averting is a grave offence in its own right, deserving blame and censure. The address is repeated with the title "people of the Scripture" to emphasise the independence of each charge and to intensify the condemnation. This title calls for belief in what confirms what is with them, and it also calls for encouraging people towards it. Therefore, their averting others from it is at the extreme of ugliness. Their averting in some cases was by distorting the Scripture and disbelieving in the verses that indicate the prophethood of the Prophet, peace be upon him. It is also read as "tusiddūna" from "asadda" (to cause to turn away).

﴿from the way of Allah﴾, that is, His true religion, which leads to eternal happiness, namely monotheism and the religion of Islam.

﴿those who believe﴾ is the object of ﴿you avert﴾, and the prepositional phrase is placed before it for emphasis on it.

They used to tempt the believers, scheme to turn them away from it, and by all their efforts prevent anyone who wished to enter it. They would say that his description, peace be upon him, is not in their Scripture and that good news of him had not come before among them. It was also said: the Jews came to the Aws and the Khazraj and reminded them of the enmities and wars that had existed between them in the pre-Islamic period (jahiliyya), so that they would return to what they had been in.

﴿seeking it﴾ is in the sense of dropping the preposition and having the verb reach the pronoun, as in his words:

*So his young man turned and called out: "Is it a male ostrich I hunt for you, or a donkey?"*

With the meaning "I hunt for you", that is, you seek for the way of Allah, which is the most upright of ways, ﴿crookedness﴾, meaning deviation, by confusing people and making them imagine that there is in it a deviation from the truth, through denying abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by a later one) and altering the description of the Messenger (ﷺ) from its true form, and the like. The clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of ﴿you avert﴾. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from ﴿the way of Allah﴾.

﴿while you are witnesses﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of ﴿you avert﴾, in view of its being restricted by the first circumstance, or from the subject of ﴿seeking it﴾, meaning: while you are witnesses who testify that it is the way of Allah, in which no trace of crookedness hovers, and that averting from it is misguidance. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: that is, witnesses that in the Torah the religion of Allah, which no other is accepted, is Islam; or: while you are upright among yourselves, whom people trust in your sayings and who are asked to bear witness in judicial matters (p-64) and in grave affairs.

﴿Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ is a concluding parenthetical sentence, containing a severe threat and warning. It was said: since their averting of the believers was done secretly, the noble verse concludes with what cuts off the root of their stratagem, namely the comprehensive knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, of their deeds. Likewise, since their disbelief in the signs of Allah was done openly, the preceding verse concluded with His witnessing of what they do.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 100:

﴿O you who have believed, if you obey a party of those who were given the Scripture, they will return you, after your belief, to disbelief.﴾ This is a shift (taltwin) in the mode of address, turning it toward the believers, as a warning to them against obeying the People of the Book and being seduced by their temptation, right after the rebuke directed at them for misleading and leading astray. It is a deterrent for them from that. The attribution of the return to disbelief to obeying a party from among them serves to intensify the warning against obeying them and to make it obligatory to avoid associating with them altogether, for it has the force of saying: "Do not obey a party..." and so on. Likewise, the generalization of the rebuke in what precedes it serves either to intensify the reprimand or to preserve the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul). It is narrated that a group of the Aws and Khazraj were sitting and talking, when Shas ibn Qays, a Jew who was extremely disbelieving and intensely envious of the Muslims, passed by them. He was angered by what he saw of their harmony of hearts, unity of word and agreement of opinion, after the enmity and hatred that had been between them. So he ordered a young Jewish man who was with him to sit with them, remind them of the Day of Bu'ath (a great day on which the two clans fought, and victory on it was for the Aws), and recite to them what had been said about it of poetry. He did so, and the people boasted and grew angry until they leapt upon one another, and they said: "The weapons! The weapons!" Thereupon a great multitude from the two tribes gathered. At that point the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions came to them and said: "Do you call to the Jahiliyya while I am among you, after Allah the Exalted has honored you with Islam, cut off from you the affair of the Jahiliyya, and joined your hearts together?" They realized that it was a prick from Satan and a plot of their enemy. So they threw down their weapons, sought forgiveness, embraced one another, and departed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Imam al-Wahidi said: They had lined up for battle, and then the verse was revealed up to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿that you may be guided﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) came and stood between the two rows, recited these verses and raised his voice. When they heard the voice of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they fell silent for him and began to listen to him. When he finished, they threw down their weapons, embraced one another, and began to weep.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿disbelievers﴾ (kafirin), it is either a second object of ﴿yaruddukum﴾ (they will return you), with the meaning of "return" implicitly carrying the sense of "make" (tadmin al-tasyir), as in the verse of the poet:

*Time has struck the women of the family of Sa'd*
*with a decree they have stayed awake for.*

*So it turned their black hair white,*
*and turned their white faces black.*

Or it is a circumstantial state (hal) of its object. The first is more effective in absolving the believers from being ascribed to disbelief, because it explicitly states that the disbelief is imposed upon them by way of compulsion (qasr). The mention of the adverbial phrase (zarf), though there is no need for it, is because the address has already preceded under the title of "believers," and because a return to disbelief is impossible without prior belief. Its placement between the two objects serves to show the complete ugliness of disbelief and the extreme remoteness of its occurrence, either to increase its repulsiveness, which turns the sane person away from engaging in it, or because belief resists it. It is as if it were said: "After your firm belief." In this there is so much of the strengthening of the believers that it cannot be hidden.

(p-65) ﴿How can you disbelieve?﴾ This is an interrogative of denial (istifham inkari), meaning the denial of the occurrence of the act, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How can there be a covenant with the polytheists?﴾ and so on. It is not a denial of the reality of the act, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead?﴾ and so on. Directing the denial and the astonishment at the manner of disbelief carries an emphasis that is absent when it is directed at the act itself, as in saying: "Do you disbelieve, given that every existent must exist in some state?" When one denies and negates all the states of its existence, its existence is negated entirely, by way of demonstrative proof (al-burhani).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while the verses of Allah are recited to you﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) occupying the position of a state of the pronoun of the addressees in "you disbelieve." It reinforces the denial and astonishment by what it contains of matters that call to steadfastness in faith and restrain from disbelief. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and among you is His Messenger﴾ is conjoined to it and falls under its same ruling. The recitation of Allah's verses to them, and the presence among them of His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, who teaches them the Book and wisdom and purifies them by establishing the truth and removing doubts, are among the strongest deterrents from disbelief. The recitation is not attributed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, to indicate that each of the two is independent in this matter.

﴿And whoever holds fast to Allah﴾ means: whoever adheres to His true religion, which He has made clear through His verses upon the tongue of His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. This is Islam and monotheism, which was referred to earlier as the way of Allah.

﴿then he has been guided﴾ is the answer to the conditional. The particle "qad" (قَدْ) serves to express confirmation, as if the guidance has already been attained; so it reports of it as already accomplished. The sense of expectation in it is evident, for the one who holds fast to Him, exalted is He, is expecting guidance, just as the one who seeks the generous is expecting bounty.

﴿to a straight path﴾ that leads to the desired goal. The indefinite form (tanwin) is for magnification, and the description with "straightness" is to make explicit the refutation of those who seek crookedness in it. Although this is in reality His true religion, and being guided to it is the same as holding fast to it, nonetheless, since the two aspects differ, and the latter designation is one that competitors vie for, it was presented in the context of the answer to urge and encourage, following the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into the Garden has indeed triumphed﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 102:

﴿O you who believe﴾: repeating the address with the title of faith is an honour upon an honour.

﴿Fear God﴾: *al-ittiqa'* (guarding oneself) is a reflexive form (*ifti'al*) derived from *al-wiqaya*, which means extreme protection.

﴿with the fear due to Him﴾: that is, with the fear due to Him and what is obligatory from it. This means exerting one's full effort in fulfilling what is required and in avoiding what is forbidden, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So fear God as much as you are able﴾. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, that it means: to be obeyed and not disobeyed, to be remembered and not forgotten, to be thanked and not ungrateful. It has been related as a hadith traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ). It has also been said that it means: that one is not deterred in God's cause by the blame of any blamer, and that one upholds justice even against oneself, one's son, or one's father. It has been said that it means: that one purifies obedience from turning to it (for its own sake) and from expecting a reward for it. The precise truth of this matter has already been discussed under His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾. The word *al-tuqat* is from *ittaqa*, like *al-tu'ada* from *it"ada*; its root is *wuqya*, in which the initial *waw* when vowelled with a *damma* was changed into a *ta'*, as in *tuhma* and *tukhama*, and its *ya'* when vowelled with a *fatha* was changed into an *alif*.

﴿and do not die except as Muslims﴾: that is, sincerely devoted of your souls to God, exalted is He, not admitting any association with anything other than Him at all, as in His saying: ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to God﴾. This is an *istithna' mufarragh* (exceptive construction with the excluded element omitted) relating to the most general of circumstances. That is: you must not die in any state except the state of the firm realization of your Islam and your steadfastness upon it, as the nominal sentence (*jumla ismiyya*) indicates. Had it been said "except as Muslims," it would not have conveyed its purpose. The element governing the circumstantial clause (*hal*) is what precedes *illa* after the negation. Although the apparent sense of the noble composition is a prohibition against dying under a restricted condition, namely being in any state other than the state of Islam, the real intention is the prohibition of that restriction at the moment of death, which entails the command to its opposite, namely being in the state of Islam at that time. Since the address is to the believers, the meaning is the obligation of steadfastness in Islam until death. Directing the prohibition at death itself serves to intensify the prohibition against its stated restriction. A prohibition against a restricted thing of this kind is a prohibition against the restriction, and the complete removal of it at its root, which conveys what a prohibition against the restriction itself does not convey. For your saying, "Do not pray except while being humble," conveys an intensification in the obligation of humility in prayer that your saying, "Do not abandon humility in prayer," does not convey, because the latter is a prohibition only against abandoning humility, whereas the former is a prohibition against it and against what accompanies it, and it conveys that humility is the essential element of prayer, and that prayer without it should not be performed at all. There is in this a kind of warning against what lies beyond death.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 103:

And His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And hold fast, all of you together, to the rope of Allah﴾, i.e., to the religion of Islam or to His Book, due to His saying, upon him be prayer and peace: "The Qur'an is the firm rope of Allah; its wonders never cease, and it does not wear out from much repetition. Whoever speaks by it speaks truly, whoever acts by it is rightly guided, and whoever holds fast to it is guided to a straight path." This is either a metaphor (tamthil) for the state resulting from their seeking support in it and their confidence in its protection, likened to the state of one who hangs from a high place by a strong rope that is safe from snapping, without considering a metaphor in the individual words; or it is a metaphor (isti'arah) for the rope, referring to the religion or the Book mentioned, and "holding fast" (i'tisam) is a complement (tarshih) to it, or it is borrowed for trusting in it and relying upon it.

﴿Jami'an﴾ (all together) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "i'tasimu" (hold fast), i.e., gathered together in holding fast.

﴿And do not separate﴾, i.e., do not separate from the truth by the occurrence of disagreement among you, like the People of the Book, or as you were divided in the Jahiliyyah, when some of you fought against others; or do not create what necessitates division and removes the harmony in which you are.

﴿And remember the favor of Allah﴾: a verbal noun (masdar) annexed to its agent. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿upon you﴾ is related to it, or to something omitted that functions as a circumstantial clause from it. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿when you were﴾ is an adverbial complement (zarf) of it, or of the stability (istiqrar) in "upon you," i.e., remember His bounty upon you, or remember His bounty established upon you at the time when you were ﴿enemies﴾ in the Jahiliyyah, with enmities (ihan), hostilities and continuous wars among you.
