It is said that they were al-Aws and al-Khazraj, who were two brothers of one father and one mother, but enmity and hatred occurred between their descendants, and the wars among them lasted one hundred and twenty years.

﴿And He joined your hearts﴾ by your being guided by Him to Islam.

﴿So you became﴾, i.e., you became.

﴿by His favor﴾, which is that joining.

﴿brothers﴾ is the predicate of "you became", i.e., brothers loving one another, gathered in brotherhood in God, showing mercy to one another, giving sincere counsel to one another, agreed upon the word of truth. It is said that the meaning of ﴿you became﴾ is: you entered upon the morning, so the preposition "bi" (by) is then related to something omitted that functions as a circumstantial clause from the subject, and likewise "brothers", i.e., you became (p-67) engaged in a state of being brothers.

﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire﴾: the shafa (brink) of the pit and its shafah is its edge, i.e., you were overlooking falling into the Fire of Hell because of your disbelief, for if death had overtaken you in that state you would have fallen into it.

﴿Then He saved you﴾ by guiding you to Islam.

﴿from it﴾: the pronoun refers to the pit, or to the Fire, or to the brink; and the feminine form is due to the annexed noun, as in his saying: "As the spear's chest was stained with blood," or because it carries the sense of shafah (edge), since the shafa of a well and its shafah is its side, like al-janib and al-janibah; its root is shafaw, the waw being changed to alif in the masculine and dropped in the feminine.

﴿Thus﴾ is a reference to the verbal noun of the verb that follows it, and the distance implied in it is to indicate the elevated rank of the one referred to, the remoteness of his station in excellence, and the perfection of his being distinguished thereby from others, and his being integrated through it into the series of visible matters. The particle "ka" (kaf) is inserted to emphasize the grandeur indicated by the demonstrative noun, and its position is accusative as it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., like that clear explanation.

﴿Allah makes clear to you His signs﴾, i.e., His proofs.

﴿so that you may be guided﴾, seeking your steadfastness upon guidance and your increase in it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 104:

﴿Let there be among you a community that invites to good﴾. Allah, glorified is He, commanded them to perfect others and guide them, after commanding them to perfect and refine themselves through the commands and prohibitions that precede it. This is to establish all of these in their observance of the rulings they contain: that some of them should perform their obligations, preserve their rights and limits, remind people of them all, and restrain them from violating them.

The majority of readers pronounce the lam of the imperative with a sukun (*sukun*, the vowel-less marking). It was also read with a kasra (*kasra*, the vowel i) according to the original form, and this is from *kana al-tammah* (the complete "to be," *kāna al-tāmmah*, where the verb needs no predicate). The word ﴿مِن﴾ (*min*, "from") is partitive (*tab'idiyyah*, indicating a part of a whole) and is connected either to the imperative or to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the subject, which is ﴿أمة﴾ (*ummah*, "community"). ﴿يدعون﴾ (*yad'una*, "they invite") is its qualifier. That is: let there be among you a community that invites to good. The *ummah* is the group toward which the various kinds of people turn, meaning that they aim at it and take it as a model. Alternatively, it is from the *naqisah* (the incomplete "to be," *kāna al-nāqiṣah*, which requires a predicate), in which ﴿أمة﴾ is its subject and "yad'una" its predicate. That is: let there be among you a community who are inviters to good. In any case, directing the address to everyone while attributing the invitation to some serves to affirm that it is a communal obligation (*fard kifayah*, a duty fulfilled by some on behalf of all), and that it is obligatory upon all, but in such a way that if some establish it, it lapses from the rest. If all neglect it, all are sinful together. It is not that it becomes binding on each individual to establish it, as indicated by His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿And the believers should not go forth all together﴾, the verse.

It is also because it is among the great and resolute matters which only those who know Allah's rulings, the stages of *ihtisab* (the duty of enjoining what is right, *ihtisab*), and the manner of establishing it take up. Whoever knows these is likely to enjoin what is wrong, to forbid what is right, to be harsh where gentleness is needed, to be gentle where harshness is needed, and to rebuke those whom rebuke only increases in persistence and obstinacy.

It was also said that ﴿مِن﴾ is explanatory (*bayaniyyah*, specifying what is meant), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds among them﴾, the verse. The imperative is from the *naqisah* "to be," and the meaning is: be a community who invite, the verse, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾, the verse. This does not require that the invitation be a *fard 'ayn* (an individual obligation, *fard 'ayn*, binding on each person). Jihad (struggle, *jihad*) is among the communal obligations even though it is established by general addresses. Calling to good is an expression for calling to what contains religious or worldly welfare. Joining the enjoining of what is right and the forbidding of what is wrong to it, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾, though both are included within it, is by way of mentioning the specific after the general, to show their excellence and their superiority over all other goods, like the joining of Gabriel and Michael to the angels, peace be upon them.

The omission of the explicit object from the three verbs is either to indicate that it is evident, meaning: they invite people, command them, and forbid them, or to intend the establishment of the act itself, as in your saying: "So-and-so gives and withholds," meaning: they perform the invitation to good, the enjoining of what is right, and the forbidding of what is wrong.

[p-68] ﴿And those﴾ is a pointing to the aforementioned community, in consideration of their being characterized by the excellent qualities mentioned, and their being perfectly distinguished by that from others, and their being organized by it into the thread of visible affairs. The sense of distance in it is to signal the loftiness of their rank and the remoteness of their station in excellence. The singular form in the "kaf" of address is either because the one addressed is everyone who is fit to be addressed, or because specifying an individual is not intended, meaning: those described with those complete attributes.

﴿They are the successful﴾, meaning: they are the ones specially singled out for complete success. "Hum" (*hum*, "they") is a *damir al-fasl* (separating pronoun, *ḍamīr al-faṣl*) that separates the predicate from the qualifier, affirms the attribution, and indicates the restriction of the predicate to the subject. Or it is a subject whose predicate is "the successful," and the clause is the predicate of "those." The definiteness of ﴿the successful﴾ is either for a known reference, or for pointing to what everyone knows of the reality of the successful.

It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he was asked about the best of people, and he said: "The one who enjoins them most in what is right, forbids them most from what is wrong, is most fearful of Allah, and keeps ties of kinship best." And from him, peace be upon him: "Whoever enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong is the khalifah (deputy, *khalīfah*) of Allah on His earth, the khalifah of His Messenger, and the khalifah of His Book." And from him, peace be upon him: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, you will surely enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, or else Allah will soon send upon you a punishment from Himself, then you will supplicate Him and you will not be answered." And from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "The best jihad (struggle) is enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, and whoever hates the wicked and is angry for the sake of Allah, Allah will be angry on his behalf."

As for enjoining what is right, its being obligatory or recommended follows what is commanded. As for forbidding what is wrong, it is entirely obligatory, for everything the Law (*shar'*) has disapproved of is forbidden, and the sinner is obligated to forbid what he himself has committed, since it is obligatory upon him to abandon it and to disapprove of it. So the obligation of neither of the two is dropped by neglect of the other.

The rebuke in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon people while you forget yourselves?﴾ is only upon their forgetting themselves, not upon their commanding righteousness. It is also reported from the early generations (*salaf*): "Command good, even if you do not do it yourselves."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 3, verse 105:**

﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾: they are the People of the Two Books (Ahl al-Kitab), when the Jews split into sects and the Christians split into sects.

﴿and differed﴾: by drawing out deviant interpretations (ta'wilat, sing. ta'wil, "interpretation") and concealing the clear verses and distorting them, for the sake of the base goods of this lowly world that they clung to.

﴿after the clear proofs had come to them﴾: that is, the manifest verses that make the truth clear, which necessitate agreement upon it and unity of word. The prohibition is therefore directed primarily at those who undertake the call (to the faith), and secondarily at their followers. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "the relative pronoun") may be generalised to include those of the earlier nations who differed, to whom He, Mighty and Majestic is He, refers in His words: ﴿And none differed concerning it except those who were given it, after the clear proofs had come to them﴾. It has also been said: they are the innovators (mubtada'a, sing. mubtadi', "innovators in religion") of this community. It has also been said: they are the Harurites (al-Haruriyya, the early Kharijite group). In any case, what is forbidden is only differing concerning the fundamentals (usul, "fundamental principles of the faith"), not the subsidiary matters (furu', "derivative legal rulings"), unless the difference contradicts clear texts or consensus (ijma', "scholarly consensus"), based on his ﷺ saying: "The difference of my community is a mercy," and his ﷺ saying: "Whoever exerts himself in ijtihad and is correct has two rewards, and whoever errs has one reward."

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the ones mentioned, considered in terms of their being characterised by what is in the relative clause (sila, "the clause following the relative pronoun"), and it is the subject (mubtada'). His, Exalted is He, words ﴿for them﴾ are its predicate (khabar). His, Exalted is He, words ﴿a great punishment﴾ are raised by the adverbial phrase, functioning as the agent (fa'il) because it depends on the subject; or it is a subject, with the adverbial phrase as its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of the first subject. In this there is what is not hidden of emphasis and exaggeration in the threat against those who divide, and of severity in warning those who resemble them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 106:

(p-69) ﴿On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black﴾. That is: many faces (will turn white). It has also been read as "tabyaad" (تَبْياضِ).

﴿And [many] faces will turn black﴾. It has also been read as "taswaad" (تَسْوادِ). It is reported from ʿAta': "The faces of the Emigrants (muhajirun) and the Helpers (ansar) will turn white, and the faces of the Banu Qurayzah and the Banu al-Nadir will turn black." The word ﴿Day﴾ is in the accusative, either as an adverbial of place (zarf) for the verb of settledness in ﴿for them﴾, meaning: for the establishment of the great punishment for them; or as an object (maf'ul) of an implied verb addressed to the believers, as a warning to them about the consequence of division after the clear proofs have come, and as an encouragement to unity in holding fast to the religion. That is: remember the Day when some faces will turn white, etc. The whiteness and blackness of the face are metaphors (kinayatan) for the manifestation of the radiance of joy and the gloom of fear in it. It has also been said: the people of truth will be marked by white faces and white scrolls, radiant complexions, and light running before them and in their right hand, while the people of falsehood will be marked by the opposites of these.

﴿As for those whose faces have turned black﴾: a detailed account of the conditions of the two groups after an general allusion to them, and the mention of these first is because the context is one of warning against resembling them, together with what it contains of combining general and detailed description and of concluding the discourse with the good state of the believers, as it began with that in the general statement.

﴿Did you disbelieve after your faith?﴾ This is according to the implied speech: that is, it will be said to them. The interrogative particle (hamza) is for rebuke and for expressing wonder at their state. Apparently, they are the People of the Book, and their disbelief after their faith is their disbelief in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after the faith of their predecessors, or the faith of themselves in him before his mission (peace be upon him). Or it refers to all the disbelievers, since they disbelieved after they had acknowledged monotheism on the Day of the Covenant, or after they had been enabled to have faith through correct reflection, clear proofs and manifest signs. It has also been said: the apostates. It has also been said: the people of innovations and desires.

The fa' in His words, Mighty and Exalted, ﴿So taste the punishment﴾: that is, the known punishment described as great, to indicate that the command to taste the punishment, in the manner of humiliation, is consequent upon their aforementioned disbelief, just as His words, exalted be He, ﴿because you used to disbelieve﴾ are explicit that the very tasting is caused by that. The combination of the past and the present forms is to indicate the continuity of their disbelief, or that it was in the past in the world.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 107:

﴿As for those whose faces turn white, they shall be in the mercy of Allah﴾ — I mean Paradise and everlasting bliss. It is expressed by "mercy" as a reminder that the believer, even if he spends his entire life in the obedience of Allah the Exalted, will not enter Paradise except by the mercy of Allah the Exalted. It is also read as "ابْياضَّتْ" (ibyaddat, with the doubled ض). Likewise it is read as "اسْوادَّتْ" (iswaddat, with the doubled د).

﴿They will abide therein forever﴾ — this is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) answering a question arising from the context, as if it were said: "How will they be therein?" So it was answered: "They will abide therein forever, not departing from it, and not dying." The placing of the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) "therein" first serves to preserve the rhyme of the verses (ru'us al-ayy).

The term "that" (﴿تِلْكَ﴾) is a demonstrative referring to the verses that include the bliss of the righteous and the punishment of the disbelievers. The sense of distance (in the demonstrative) is to signal the elevated status and lofty rank of these verses. It is the subject (mubtada', "subject") and the phrase ﴿آياتُ اللَّهِ﴾ ("the signs of God") is its predicate (khabar, "predicate"). The phrase ﴿نَتْلُوها﴾ ("We recite them") is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya, "clause of circumstance") referring back to "the verses," and its governing element is the sense of the demonstrative. Alternatively, it is itself the predicate, and "the signs of God" is a substitute (badal, "apposition") for the demonstrative.

The shift to the first-person plural ("We") with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azama, "the nun of majesty"), even though the recitation is carried out through Jibril (peace be upon him), serves to show the full extent of care given to the recitation. It is also recited as ﴿يَتْلُوها﴾ ("He recites them"), with the verb attributed to the pronoun of God, may He be exalted.

The phrase ﴿عَلَيْكَ﴾ ("to you") is connected to ﴿نَتْلُوها﴾. The phrase ﴿بِالحَقِّ﴾ ("in truth") is an emphatic circumstantial phrase (hal mu'akkida, "emphatic circumstantial") referring to the subject of ﴿نَتْلُوها﴾ or its object. That is, they are (or it is) connected with truth and justice, such that there is no trace of injustice in their judgment, whether by diminishing the reward of the one who does good, by increasing the punishment of the one who does evil, or by punishing without a crime. Rather, each of these is given to them according to what they deserve by their deeds, in accordance with the requirement of the promise and the threat.

The phrase ﴿وَما اللَّهُ يُرِيدُ ظُلْمًا لِلْعالَمِينَ﴾ ("and God does not desire any injustice to the worlds") is a concluding statement (tadhyil, "concluding statement") that confirms what precedes it in the most eloquent and emphatic way. The indefinite form of "injustice," the directing of the negation to the desire for it with the present tense rather than to the act itself, the attaching of the judgment to individual members of the definite plural, and the shift to the majestic name (God) to indicate the reason for the judgment, all together establish the complete freedom of His exalted and majestic essence from injustice in the most complete manner. That is, He does not desire even a single instance of injustice toward a single one of the worlds at any time, let alone that He should wrong them. The present tense, as it indicates continuity in affirmation, also indicates continuity in negation according to the context. Likewise, the nominal sentence indicates, with the aid of context, the permanence of the state, and when the particle of negation enters, it indicates the permanence of the absence, not the absence of permanence.

The construction of the sentence also contains a kind of allusion, by implication, that the disbelievers are the wrongdoers: they wronged themselves by exposing themselves to everlasting punishment, as in His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed God does not wrong people at all, but people wrong themselves﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 109:

﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. That is: to Him, the Exalted, alone, without any partner at all, belongs whatever creatures are in them, absolutely, by ownership and by creation, by giving life and causing death, by granting reward and inflicting punishment. The mention of the word "ma" (whatever), which is used for non-rational beings, is either to give precedence to non-rational beings over rational ones (taghlib), or to place the rational beings in the position of non-rational ones, to show their insignificance in the context of describing His greatness, may He be exalted.

﴿And to Allah﴾: that is, to His judgment and decree, not to anyone else, whether as a partner or independently.

﴿All matters are returned﴾: that is, their affairs. So He recompenses each of them according to what He promised them and threatened them with, without anyone having any interference in that whatsoever. Thus the sentence confirms the content of what was mentioned concerning the recompense of the two groups. It was also said: it is coordinated with what precedes it, confirming its content, for the fact that the worlds are His servants, His creation and His provision requires that He wills good for them.

﴿You are the best nation﴾ is a resumptive statement (*kalam mustaʾnaf*), brought to strengthen the believers in what they are upon of agreement on the truth and of calling to good. The verb "kuntum" is from *kana* (the "incomplete" *kana*, a verb that indicates that something was realized with a certain attribute in past time, without indicating that it was non-existent before or after), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has ever been Forgiving and Merciful﴾. It has been said: "You were such in the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, or in the Preserved Tablet, or among the earlier nations." It has also been said: its meaning is "You are the best nation."

﴿brought forth for mankind﴾ is an attribute of ﴿nation﴾, and the *lam* is connected to ﴿brought forth﴾, meaning: it was made manifest to them. It has been said: it is connected to ﴿best﴾, meaning: you were the best of people to people. This is explicit that being "best" means benefit to people, even though this is also understood from the bringing forth for them; that is, you were brought forth for their sake and their welfare. Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said: its meaning is: you were the best of people, bringing them in chains and then admitting them into Islam. Qatada said: they are the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), to whom no prophet before him was commanded to fight, so they fight the disbelievers and admit them into Islam, and thus they are the best nation for mankind.

﴿You enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ is a continuation (*istiʾnaf*) explaining your being the best nation, as one says: "Zayd is generous; he feeds people, clothes them, and attends to their interests." Or it is a second predicate of ﴿you were﴾. The form of the present tense indicates continuity. Although the address in direct speech is specific to those among the believers who witnessed the revelation, its ruling is general to all. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: he means the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Zajjaj said: the original address is to the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it includes the rest of his nation. Al-Tirmidhi related from Bahz ibn Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather, that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say, concerning His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾: "You complete seventy nations; you are the best of them and the most honored of them before Allah, exalted is He." It is evident that what is meant by "every nation" is their earliest and their latest, not only the earliest, so the descendants of this nation must also be included in the ruling. Likewise is the case with what is reported: that Malik ibn al-Sayf and Wahb ibn Yahudha, two Jews, passed by a group of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) among whom were Ibn Masʿud, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Muʿadh ibn Jabal, and Salim, the freedman of Hudhayfa, may the good pleasure of Allah be upon them, and they said to them: "We are better than you, and our religion is better than what you call us to." Saʿid ibn Jubayr related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that ﴿You were the best nation﴾ refers to those who emigrated with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Medina. It is reported from al-Dahhak that they are the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) specifically, the transmitters and the callers whom Allah commanded the Muslims to obey.

﴿and you believe in Allah﴾ means: a belief connected to everything that must be believed in, of messenger, book, reckoning, and recompense. He did not state it explicitly in detail because it is evident that it is what the believers believe in, and to indicate that it is in truth faith in Allah, exalted is He, and that whatever is devoid of any part of that, such as the faith of the People of the Book, is not of faith in Him, exalted is He, in any way. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others," and they intend to adopt a way in between. Those are the disbelievers in truth﴾. This [belief] was placed after enjoining right and forbidding wrong, although it precedes them both in existence and rank, because their indication of your being best for mankind is clearer than its indication of that, and so that there may be joined to it His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed, it would have been better for them﴾, meaning: if they had believed as you believe, that would have been better for them than what they have of leadership and of commanding the common people; and their leadership would have increased, and they would have enjoyed worldly pleasures, along with attaining what they were promised for belief, namely the giving of their reward twice. It has been said: "better" than what they are in of disbelief; so the "best" is only by their own assumption, and in this there is a kind of mockery of them. He did not mention what is believed in at all, to signal that it is evident that it is what the name "faith" is applied to, so that the mind does not go to anything else; and if the object of belief had been specified here or earlier, it might have been understood that the People of the Book also have some faith in general, but the faith of the believers is better than theirs—and far is that from the truth.

﴿Among them are the believers﴾ is a resumptive sentence brought as an answer to what arises from the conditional clause indicating the negation of their being best, because of the negation of faith among them. As if it were said: "Is there among them anyone who believed, or are all of them upon disbelief?" So it was said: "Among them are the believers"—the known ones who attained the good of both abodes, such as ʿAbdullah ibn Salam and his companions.

﴿but most of them are defiant wrongdoers﴾: those who are persistent in disbelief and who go beyond the limits.

﴿لَنْ يَضُرُّوكم إلا أذًى﴾ *istithna' mufarragh* (an exception in which the excluded element is left unstated, here drawn from the general noun) *min al-masdar al-'amm* (the general verbal noun, i.e. "harm" in its unrestricted sense), meaning: they will never harm you at all with any harm, except the harm of *adha* (mere annoyance) that is not worth heeding, such as taunting and threatening that leave no effect.

﴿وَإنْ يُقاتِلُوكم يُوَلُّوكُمُ الأدْبارَ﴾ meaning: they will turn and flee without managing to gain anything from you, whether killing or capture.

﴿ثُمَّ لا يُنْصَرُونَ﴾ *'atf* (conjunction) upon the conditional clause (*al-shartiyya*, the conditional sentence), and *thumma* (then) here denotes *al-tarakhi fi al-rutba* (delay in rank, i.e. a greater degree of significance rather than a delay in time). Meaning: they will not be helped by anyone, nor will they be prevented from you, whether in killing or in seizing. In this there is a reinforcement for those among them who believed, for they used to be harmed by them through mockery, reproach, misguidance and threats. It is also good news for them that the Jews cannot go beyond verbal harm to an injury that matters, even though He had promised them victory over them and vengeance upon them, and that the final outcome of their affair is abasement and humiliation. The negation of their being helped was not conjoined to the response (*al-jaza'*) because the intended meaning is the promise of the absolute negation of victory. Had it been conjoined to it, it would have been restricted to their fighting you, like turning their backs, and how great the difference between the two promises. It is as if it were said: then their condition, about which I inform you and give you good news, is that they are forsaken, victory is withheld from them, and strength is denied them. They will not rise up thereafter with any wing, nor stand upon any leg, nor will their affair be set right. And so it was, when the Banu Qurayza, the Nadir, the Banu Qaynuqa' and the Jews of Khaybar met what they met.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 112:

﴿Humiliation was decreed upon them﴾, i.e., the wasting of their souls, wealth and families, or the humiliation of clinging to falsehood.

﴿Wherever they are found﴾, i.e., wherever they are found.

﴿Except with a rope from Allah and a rope from the people﴾: this is an exception from the most general of circumstances, i.e., humiliation was decreed upon them like a dome over the one it covers, in all circumstances, except when they are holding fast to the protection of Allah, or His Book which came to them, and the protection of the Muslims, or to the protection of Islam and following the way of the believers.

﴿And they returned with wrath from Allah﴾, i.e., they came back deserving it. The indefiniteness (of "wrath") is for magnification and awe, and "from" (min) is connected to an omitted element which occurs as a description of "wrath," emphasizing what the indefiniteness conveys of grandeur and terror, i.e., it is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And poverty was decreed upon them﴾: so it encompasses them from all their sides. The Jews are likewise, for the most part, needy under the authority of the Muslims and the Christians.

﴿That﴾: a reference to what was mentioned of the decreeing of humiliation and poverty upon them and the returning with great wrath.

﴿Because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾, i.e., that which was mentioned is due to their continuous disbelief in the signs of Allah, which speak of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), their distortion of them, and of all the other Qur'anic verses.

﴿And they killed the prophets without right﴾, i.e., in their belief as well. Attributing the killing to them, although it was the act of their ancestors, is because they were pleased with it, just as distortion, though it was the act of their rabbis, is attributed to everyone who follows their conduct.

﴿That﴾: a reference to what was mentioned of disbelief and killing.

﴿Because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾, i.e., it is due to their disobedience and their continuous transgressing of the limits of Allah, the Exalted. For persistence in minor sins leads to committing major sins, and persistence in these leads to disbelief. It has been said: its meaning is that the decreeing of humiliation and poverty in this world and the deserving of wrath in the Hereafter, as it is caused by their disbelief and killing, is also a consequence of their disobedience and transgression, insofar as they are addressed with the branches of the law in terms of being held accountable.

﴿لَيْسُوا سَواءً﴾ ("They are not all alike") is a resumptive sentence (*jumlah mustaʾnifah*, a sentence that begins a new point) introduced as a preface to enumerating the virtues of the believers among the People of the Book, and as a reminder of God's words: ﴿مِنهُمُ المُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ("among them are believers"). The pronoun in ﴿لَيْسُوا﴾ refers to the People of the Book as a whole, not only to the wicked among them. It is the subject of *laysa* (the negative verb "is not"), and its predicate (*khabar*) is "*sawāʾan*" ("alike"). It is singular because it is originally a verbal noun (*maṣdar*). (p-73) The intended meaning of negating equality is the negation of participation in the basic state of having the aforementioned vile qualities, not the negation of equality in degrees of having them while participation in the basic state is established. That is, not all of the People of the Book share in the attribute of the aforementioned vices and in suffering the punishments that follow from them.

God's words ﴿مِن أهْلِ الكِتابِ أُمَّةٌ قائِمَةٌ﴾ ("Among the People of the Book is a community standing [upright]") are a resumptive sentence explaining how they are not equal, and removing the ambiguity in what precedes it, just as what came before, God's words ﴿تَأْمُرُونَ بِالمَعْرُوفِ﴾ ("you enjoin what is right"), and the verse as a whole, explains God's words ﴿كُنْتُمْ خَيْرَ أُمَّةٍ﴾ ("you are the best community") and so on. The placing of "People of the Book" in the position of a pronoun referring back to them serves to establish what the two groups have in common, and to signal that this community is among those who were given a abundant share of the Book, not among their lowest. "*Qāʾimah*" means upright and just, from *aqamtu al-ʿūd* ("I straightened the stick"), so that *qāma* means *istaqāma* (to be upright). These are those among them who embraced Islam, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, Thaʿlabah ibn Saʿid, Usayd ibn ʿUbayd, and their like. It is said that they were forty men from the people of Najran, thirty-two from Abyssinia, and three from Rome, who were upon the religion of ʿIsa (Jesus) and affirmed Muhammad, peace be upon them both. Among the Ansar there were a number of them before the arrival of the Prophet (ﷺ), including As'ad ibn Zurarah, al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur, Muhammad ibn Maslamah, and Abu Qays Sirmah ibn Anas. They were monotheists, performed ritual bathing from major impurity, and practised whatever they knew of the laws of the *Ḥanīfiyyah* (the pure monotheistic religion of Abraham), until God sent the Prophet (ﷺ), whereupon they affirmed him and supported him.

God's words ﴿يَتْلُونَ آياتِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("they recite the verses of God") occupy a nominative position, as a second attribute of "*ummah*" (community). It is also said that they occupy an accusative position, as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from it, since it has been specified by the qualifier. The governing element is the stability (*al-istiqrār*, the implied sense of "being located") contained in the prepositional phrase, or it is from the pronoun in ﴿قائِمَةٌ﴾, or from the hidden element in the prepositional phrase, since it occurs as the predicate of "*ummah*." The intended meaning of ﴿آياتِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("the verses of God") is the Qur'an.

God's words ﴿آناءَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ ("during the hours of the night") are an adverb of time (*ẓarf*) governing ﴿يَتْلُونَ﴾, meaning: during its periods. It is the plural of *anā* on the pattern of *ʿaṣā*, or *innī* on the pattern of *miʿan*, or *anyin* on the pattern of *ẓabyin*, or *inyin* on the pattern of *niḥyin*, or *inwin* on the pattern of *jirwin*. ﴿وَهم يَسْجُدُونَ﴾ ("while they prostrate") means: they pray, since there is no recitation during prostration. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Verily I have been forbidden to recite while bowing or prostrating." Singling out prostration from among the other pillars of prayer is because it is more indicative of complete humility. The explicit mention of their reciting God's verses in prayer, although the prayer necessarily includes them, serves to emphasise the opposition and to clarify the inequality between them and those who were described just before as disbelieving in them. This is the reason for placing this attribute before the attribute of faith. By "their prayer" is meant the night prayer (*tahajjud*), since it is more fitting for praising them, and in it recitation is readily possible for them, whereas in the obligatory prayer recitation is the duty of the imam. Considering their state during prayer as an individual act is incompatible with the context of praise, and this is the most fitting, along with the shift from mentioning it by the generic noun, which in common usage refers to the obligatory prayer, and expressing its time by the indefinite *ānāʾ* (periods of the night).

It is also said that it refers to the night (ʿishāʾ) prayer, because the People of the Book do not perform it. This is based on what is narrated: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) delayed it one night, then went out and found people waiting for the prayer. He said: "Indeed, there is no one among the followers of other religions who remembers God at this hour except you," and then he recited this verse.

Presenting the clause as a nominal sentence indicates continuity, and repeating the predication strengthens and emphasises the ruling. The form of the present tense indicates renewal. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the subject of "*yatlūna*" (they recite). It is also said that it is a resumptive sentence, and the meaning is: they stand at times and prostrate at other times, seeking God's bounty and mercy through the various forms of humility toward God, Mighty and Majestic, as in God's words ﴿والَّذِينَ يَبِيتُونَ لِرَبِّهِمْ سُجَّدًا وقِيامًا﴾ ("those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing"). It is also said that by prostration is meant humility, as in God's words ﴿وَلِلَّهِ يَسْجُدُ مَن في السَّماواتِ والأرض﴾ ("To God prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth").

(p-74)﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ is another attribute of "a community" (ummah), specifying that they differ from the Jews in another respect. That is, they believe in them in the manner that the divine law (al-shar', the revealed law) has articulated. The absolute form is used to signal that no restriction is needed, since it is evident that this is the belief to which the term "belief in them both" applies, and no other understanding comes to mind. It also implies a rebuke: the Jews' belief in them, together with their saying that ʿUzayr is the son of Allah, their disbelief in some of the Books and Messengers, and their description of the Last Day in a way that differs from its true nature, is not belief in them at all. Had it been restricted by what was mentioned, one might have supposed that the negated element was only the mentioned restriction, while belief in the basic principle would still be permissible for them. But far be that!

﴿They enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ are two further attributes of "a community," applied to them to confirm their difference from the Jews in the virtues related to guiding others, following the description of their difference in the qualities related to perfecting the self. It also implies a rebuke of the Jews' laxity in enforcing accountability (al-ihtisab), or rather, their reversal of this duty by leading people astray and turning them away from the path of Allah. For that is an enjoining of what is wrong and a forbidding of what is right.

﴿And they hasten to good works﴾ is another attribute of "a community," comprehensive of all kinds of excellence related to the self and to others. Hastening to good (al-musara'ah fi al-khayr) means an extreme eagerness for it, because whoever desires a matter hastens to undertake it and to carry it out, and prefers immediacy (al-fawr) over delay (al-taraakhi). That is, they hurry, with complete eagerness, to do all kinds of good, both those that are obligatory and those that extend to others. There is also a rebuke here of the Jews' sluggishness in these matters, or rather, their hastening toward evils. The use of the word "fi" (in) instead of what occurs in His saying, ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [3:133], etc.... signals that they are firmly established in the root of goodness, moving within its many branches that rank in levels of excellence, not that they are outside of it, merely arriving at it.

﴿And those﴾ is a reference to the community, in view of their being characterized by what has been detailed of noble qualities. The sense of distance in the demonstrative signals the elevation of their rank and the loftiness of their level in excellence. Using it rather than a pronoun indicates the reason for the judgment and the praise. That is: those described with those excellent attributes, because of their being characterized by them.

﴿Among the righteous﴾ means: among the number of those whose conditions are made good in the sight of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and who deserve His good pleasure and praise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 115:

﴿And whatever good they do﴾, in whatever form it is, whether it has been mentioned or not.

﴿Then they will not be denied it﴾, i.e., they will by no means be deprived of its reward at all. He expressed it this way, just as He expressed the full giving of reward by "thanks" (shukr), to display the perfect exaltation of Him, glory be to Him and exalted, above withholding their recompense, by depicting it in the form of something whose occurrence from Him, exalted be He, is impossible, namely the ugly deeds. He made it transitive to two objects by including the meaning of deprivation (hirman). The choice of the passive form is to proceed in accordance with the customs of majesty. The two verbs have also been read in the second-person form (khitab).

﴿And Allah is Knowing of the al-Muttaqin (the God-conscious)﴾: this is a concluding remark (tadhyil) confirming the content of what precedes it, for His knowledge, exalted be He, of their conditions necessarily calls for the full payment of their wages. By "the muttaqin" is meant either the known community (al-umma al-ma'hudah), placed in the position of the pronoun referring back to them, as praise for them, as a specification of the basis on which knowledge is attached to them, and as an indication of the ground of their reward, which is God-consciousness (taqwa), encompassing the previously mentioned qualities; or it means the genus of the God-conscious in general, and they are included under His judgment by an initial inclusion (indiraj awwali).

(p-75) ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾, i.e., in what must be believed in.

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: They are the Banu Qurayza and the Banu al-Nadir, for their opposition was for the sake of wealth. It has also been said: They are the polytheists of Quraysh, for Abu Jahl used to boast greatly of his wealth. It has also been said: Abu Sufyan and his companions, for he spent much wealth on the disbelievers on the day of Badr and Uhud. It has also been said: They are all the disbelievers, for they boasted of wealth and children when they said: "We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, refuted them and said: ﴿will not avail them﴾, i.e., will not ward off from them.

﴿Their wealth nor their children will avail them at all against Allah﴾, i.e., against His punishment, exalted is He.

﴿anything﴾, i.e., any small amount of it, or any measure of benefit.

﴿And those are the companions of the Fire﴾, i.e., its close associates and those who remain constantly in it.

﴿They will abide therein eternally﴾, forever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 117:

﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life﴾ is an explanation of the manner in which their wealth, on which they relied for bringing about benefits and averting harms, and to which they attached their empty hopes, fails to be of any benefit. The ﴿mā﴾ here is a noun-relative (mawṣūlah ismiyyah) whose returning pronoun has been omitted, meaning: the condition of what the disbelievers spend out of a desire for nearness (to God), or out of boasting and ostentation, or what the hypocrites spend out of showing off and fear. Its story is wondrous, and it has become a proverb for strangeness.

﴿Like the likeness of a wind in which is ṣirr﴾ — that is, a severe cold. It is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar), though its use has become common for a cold wind, like ṣarṣar. It has been said that the word ﴿fī﴾ here is the one of abstraction (tajrīdiyyah), as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed there has been for you in the Messenger of God an excellent pattern﴾.

﴿It struck the tilth of a people who wronged themselves﴾ by disbelief and sins, so they incurred anger from God. They were described thus because destruction that comes from wrath is more severe and more dreadful.

﴿And it destroyed it﴾ as a punishment for them, and it left no trace of it nor any dust. The intended meaning is to liken what they spent, in its being lost and gone entirely without any benefit ever returning to them, to the crop of disbelievers that the cold struck and uprooted, leaving them with no benefit from it in any way whatsoever. This is a compound simile (tashbīh murakkab), whose detailed explanation has passed in the commentary on His words, exalted is He: ﴿The likeness of one who kindled a fire﴾. For this reason, the word of comparison "al-rīḥ" was not troubled by being placed before "al-ḥarth" (the tilth) rather than the tilth itself. It is also permissible that what is intended is: the likeness of the destruction of what they spend is like the likeness of the destruction by a wind, or: the likeness of what they spend is like the likeness of something destroyed by a wind, namely the tilth. It is also read as "tunfiqūn" (with the second person).

﴿And God did not wrong them﴾ by what has been explained of the loss of the wealth they spent.

﴿But they wronged themselves﴾ because they squandered it by spending it not in the manner that befits it. The placement of the object before the verb is for the sake of the rhyme (ri'āyat al-fawāṣil), not for specification (takhṣīṣ), since the discourse concerns the verb in relation to its agent, not its object. That is: God did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. The imperfect form (muḍāri') indicates renewal and continuity. It has also been permitted that the meaning is: God, exalted is He, did not wrong the owners of the tilth by destroying it, but they wronged themselves by committing what made them deserve punishment; and this is contradicted by the fact that it has already been addressed explicitly and by implication. It is also read as "wa-lākinna" with the doubled nun, on the basis that ﴿anfusahum﴾ is its subject and "yaẓlimūn" is its predicate, with the returning pronoun omitted for the sake of the fāṣilah, meaning: but their souls wrong them (yaẓlimūnahā). As for estimating a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), there is no way to it, since it is specific to poetry by necessity, as in the verse:

*But whoever looks upon your eyelids will fall in love.*

(p-76) ﴿O you who have believed, do not take as intimate friends (biṭāna) those other than your own.﴾ The biṭāna of a man (waliyyatuhu) is the one who is given his secrets out of trust in him. It is likened to the lining of a garment (biṭānat al-thawb), just as it is likened to the undergarment (al-shi'ār). He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "The Helpers are the undergarment (shi'ār) and the people are the outer garment (dithār)." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: Some of the believers used to associate with the Jews because of the kinship, friendship and alliance between them, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning a group of believers who used to associate with the hypocrites, so they were forbidden from that. What supports this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When they meet you they say, "We believe," but when they are alone they bite the tips of their fingers at you out of rage﴾, which is the description of the hypocrite. Whichever is the case, the ruling is general to all disbelievers without exception.

﴿other than your own (min dūnikum)﴾ means: other than the Muslims. It is connected either to ﴿do not take﴾ or to an implied word that serves as an attribute of ﴿biṭāna﴾, meaning: one who is from other than you, going beyond you.

﴿They do not spare you corruption (lā ya'lūnakum khabalan)﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining their condition and calling for keeping away from them, or it is an attribute of "biṭāna". It is said: "alā fī al-amr" when one falls short in it; then it is used with two objects in their saying: "lā ālūka nuṣḥan wa lā ālūka juhdan (I do not withhold from you sincere advice or effort)", by way of including the meaning of withholding and lessening. Khabal means corruption, i.e., they do not fall short in causing corruption to you.

﴿They wish that you suffer (waddū mā 'anittum)﴾ means: they wish your distress (ʿanat), i.e., your hardship and the severity of your harm. This is also a resumptive clause emphasizing the prohibition, requiring still greater keeping away from what is forbidden.

﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths (qad badat al-baghḍā' min afwāhihim)﴾ is another resumptive clause, conveying greater keeping away from what is forbidden. That is: hatred has already shown in their speech, because, despite their great effort in controlling their selves and forcing themselves upon it, they cannot prevent what indicates their hatred of the Muslims from slipping from their tongues. It is also read "qad badā al-baghḍā'". "Afwāh" is the plural of "fam" (mouth), and its root is "fūh", so its third radical is hā'; this is shown by its plural "afwāh", its diminutive "fuwayh", and its relative form "fūhī".

﴿What their breasts conceal is greater (wa mā tukhfī ṣudūruhum akbar)﴾ than what has appeared, because its appearance is not from deliberation and choice.

﴿We have indeed made the signs clear to you (qad bayyannā lakumu al-āyāt)﴾ which indicate the obligation of sincerity in religion, loyalty to the believers, and enmity toward the disbelievers.

﴿If you have understanding (in kuntum ta'qilūn)﴾ means: if you are among the people of intellect, or if you understand what has been made clear to you of the signs. The answer is omitted, its meaning being indicated by what has been mentioned.

﴿Here you are, these are you﴾ is a sentence made of a subject (mubtada') and a predicate (khabar), introduced by the particle of alerting (harf al-tanbih), to show the great concern with its content. That is: you are those who are mistaken in their allegiance to them. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You love them, and they do not love you﴾ explains their error in this matter. It is a second predicate of ﴿you﴾, or a predicate of ﴿these﴾, and the sentence is the predicate of ﴿you﴾, like your saying: "أنْتَ زَيْدٌ تُحِبُّهُ" ("You are Zayd, you love him"). Or it is a relative clause (ṣilah) for it, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), with the governing element being the meaning of pointing (al-ishārah). It is also permissible for "أُولاءِ" to be in the accusative, governed by a verb that is explained by what follows it, and the sentence would then be the predicate.

﴿And you believe in the Book, all of it﴾ means: in the whole category of books. It is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the object in "they do not love you." The meaning is: they do not love you, while you believe in their book. So what is the matter with you, that you love them while they do not believe in your book? This contains a rebuke: they are more steadfast in their falsehood than you are in your truth.

﴿And when they meet you, they say: "We believe"﴾ out of hypocrisy.

﴿And when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾ means: because of it, out of regret and grief, since they find no way to satisfy their anger.

﴿Say: "Die in your rage"﴾ is a supplication against them that the rage should continue

(p-77) and increase with the growing strength of Islam and its people, until they perish by it, or that it should intensify until it destroys them.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is in the chests﴾, so He knows what is in your breasts of enmity, hatred and fury. This may be part of what is said, meaning: and say to them that Allah, exalted is He, knows what is more hidden than what you conceal, namely the biting of fingertips out of rage. It may also be separate from what is said, meaning: do not be surprised that I inform you of their secrets, for I am Knowing of what is in the chests. It was also said: this is a command to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to be content of soul, to have strong hope, and to rejoice in the promise of Allah, exalted is He, that they will die of rage at the honouring of Islam and their humiliation by it, without there being any actual speech. It is as if it were said: tell yourself this.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 120:

﴿If good touches you, it grieves them; but if evil befalls you, they rejoice at it.﴾ This explains that their enmity has reached the point that they envy whatever good and benefit reaches you, and they gloat over whatever harm and hardship befalls you. The mention of "touch" (massa) with good and of "befall" (asaba) with evil is either to indicate that the basis of their displeasure is the lowest degree of attaining good, while the basis of their joy is the full attainment of evil; or because "touch" is used figuratively in the sense of "befall."

﴿But if you are patient﴾ i.e., patient toward their hostility, or patient in the face of the hardships of the obligations.

﴿and God-fearing﴾ i.e., by avoiding what God Most High has forbidden you and prohibited you from.

﴿their scheming will not harm you﴾ their plotting and their stratagem which they devised against you. It is read "lā yiḍrukum" (with a kasra on the ḍād and a jazm on the rā’), as a jussive answer to the conditional, from ḍārahu yaḍīruhu, meaning ḍarrahu yaḍurruhu (to harm him). The ḍamma on the rā’ in the well-known reading is for ease of pronunciation (ittibā‘), like the ḍamma of the madd.

﴿in the least﴾ is put in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: it will not harm you in the least degree of harm, by the grace of God and His protection promised to those who are patient and God-fearing; and because the one who is earnest in the matter and trained through God-fearing and patience becomes bold against the adversary.

﴿Indeed, God is encompassing of what they do﴾ of the scheming they engage in against your enmity.

﴿Encompassing﴾ in knowledge, so He will punish them for that. It is also read with a tā’ (taʿmalūn, "what you do"), i.e., of the patience and God-fearing you practice, and so He will reward you with what you deserve.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 121:

﴿And when you set out early in the morning﴾ is a resumptive sentence (kalam mustaʾnaf) brought in as evidence, by what it contains of the consequence of not being patient and mindful of God (taqwa) for harm, that their existence entails the deliverance promised from the harm of the enemies' scheming. The word "idh" (when) is in the accusative as an object (maf'ul bihi) governed by a hidden verb (mudmar), addressed specifically to the Prophet ﷺ, although the address before and after it is general to him and to the believers, because the content of the statement pertains specifically to him, peace be upon him. That is: "And mention to them the time when you set out early," so that they may recall the circumstances that befell them, which arose from not being patient, and thus know that if they adhere to patience and mindfulness of God, the scheming of the disbelievers will not harm them. The directing of the command to remember towards the time, rather than towards the events that occurred in it, although the events are the primary intended matter, is for emphasis in making the remembrance obligatory and bringing the incident to mind with its details, as its explanation has already passed in the commentary on His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels﴾, etc. What is meant by it is his, peace be upon him, going out to Uhud, and that was from the house of 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, and this is what is meant by His words, exalted is He: ﴿from your household﴾, that is: from the presence of your household.

﴿You were stationing the believers﴾, that is: you were lodging them, or preparing and arranging places for them.

﴿at their positions﴾. The reading of one who recites "tubawwi'" (you station) with "lil-mu'minin" (for the believers) is supported by this, and the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "ghadawta" (you set out), but not in the sense of a prospective circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara), meaning: intending and purposing the stationing, as has been said, (p-78) but rather in the sense that the intended matter is the mention of the extended, broad period of time that includes the beginning of the departure and the stationing and what follows from them, since it is this that reminds of the story. It was expressed by "ghuduw" (setting out early), which is the departure in the morning, even though his, peace be upon him, departure was after the Friday prayer, as you will come to know, because at that time the stationing occurred, which is the principal matter in the affair; since the purpose of reminding of the time is to remind them of their disobedience to the command of the Prophet ﷺ, their departing from their assigned places at the time of the stationing, and their lack of patience. By this it becomes clear that the view of the one who argued from it for the permissibility of performing the Friday prayer before midday (zawal) is flawed. The "lam" in His words, exalted is He: ﴿for the fighting﴾ is either connected to "tubawwi'" (you station), meaning: for the sake of fighting, or it is connected to an omitted element which functions as an adjective for "maq'ad" (position), meaning: positions for fighting, its places and stations. The use of "maq'ad" and "maqam" in the sense of "place" is a widespread and well-known figurative extension, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿in a seat of truth﴾ and His words, exalted is He: ﴿before you rise from your station﴾. It is narrated that the polytheists descended at Uhud on Wednesday, and the Messenger of God ﷺ consulted his companions and summoned 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, whom he had not summoned before that, and consulted him. 'Abd Allah and most of the Ansar said: "O Messenger of God, remain in Medina and do not go out to them. By God, we have never gone out from it to any enemy except that they inflicted harm upon us, and they have never entered it against us except that we inflicted harm upon them. So how much more so, when you are among us! Leave them. If they stay, they will stay in the worst of confinements; and if they enter, the men will fight them face to face, and the women and children will pelt them with stones; and if they return, they will return disappointed." Some of them said: "O Messenger of God, lead us out against these dogs, lest they see that we have been cowardly towards them." The Prophet ﷺ said: "I have seen in my dream cows slaughtered around me, and I interpreted them as good. I saw a notch in the edge of my sword, and I interpreted it as a defeat. And I saw that I had put my hand into a strong coat of mail, and I interpreted it as Medina. So if you see fit to remain in Medina and leave them, then do so." Some men among the Muslims, who had missed Badr and whom God, exalted is He, had honoured with martyrdom on that day, said: "Lead us out against our enemies." Al-Nu'man ibn Malik al-Ansari, may God be pleased with him, said: "O Messenger of God, you would deprive me of Paradise! By the One who sent you with the truth, I will surely enter Paradise." Then he said, in his own words: "I bear witness that there is no god but God, and that I will not flee from the battle line." They did not cease to press him, peace be upon him, until he entered and put on his armour. When they saw him thus, they regretted and said: "We have done wrong; we advised the Messenger of God while revelation was coming to him." They said: "Do as you see fit, O Messenger of God." He said: "It is not fitting for a prophet, once he has put on his armour, to take it off until he has fought." He went out on Friday after the Friday prayer, and he arrived in the ravine of Uhud on Saturday, in the middle of Shawwal in the third year after the Hijra. He walked on foot, and began arranging his companions for battle, as if he were straightening an arrow with them; if he saw someone protruding from the line, he would say: "Step back." His encampment was on the slope of the valley, and he placed his back and his army towards Uhud. He appointed 'Abd Allah ibn Jubayr over the archers and said to them: "Shoot at them with arrows on our behalf, so that they do not come at us from behind, and do not leave your place. We will not cease to be victorious as long as you remain in your place."

﴿And God is All-Hearing﴾ of your words.

﴿All-Knowing﴾ of your inner thoughts. The sentence is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraḍ), to announce that there issued from them there (on that occasion) sayings and deeds which should not have issued from them.

﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for ﴿when you set out early﴾, specifying what the reminder is really about. Or it is a *zarf* (adverbial complement) modifying ﴿All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, in the sense that He, exalted is He, combines hearing their words with knowing their inner thoughts at that time, since there is no point in restricting His being All-Hearing and All-Knowing to that moment. Al-Farra' said: The meaning of your saying "I struck and honored Zayd" is that Zayd is in the accusative governed by both verbs, and that both of them acted upon him together.

﴿Two parties among you⁠﴾ [who were about to] ﴿lose heart﴾: *an-tafshala* is governed by *hammat*, with the preposition *bi* omitted, meaning *bi-an tafshalā*, i.e., they would lose courage and become weak. They were two clans of the Ansar: Banu Salama of the Khazraj and Banu Harithah of the Aws. They were the two wings of the army of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they numbered one thousand men. It is also said they were nine hundred and fifty. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had promised them victory if they remained steadfast. When they drew near the army of the disbelievers, which numbered three thousand, Abd Allah ibn Ubayy withdrew with a third of the people, saying: "O people, why should we kill ourselves and our children?" Amr ibn Hazm al-Ansari followed them and said: "I adjure you by Allah regarding your Prophet and yourselves!" Abd Allah said: "If we knew there would be fighting, we would have followed you." The two clans were then about to follow Abd Allah, but Allah preserved them, and they went on with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they intended to turn back, but Allah resolved them upon right guidance, so they remained firm. The apparent meaning is that this was merely an impulse and a passing thought of the soul, which the soul is rarely free of in times of hardship.

﴿And Allah is their Protector⁠﴾: that is, the One who preserves them from following that passing impulse. This clause is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*). It may also be a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier) of the subject of ﴿hammat﴾, or of its pronoun in ﴿tafshalā﴾, serving to show how unlikely it was that they would lose heart or entertain such a thought, given that they were under the protection of Allah, exalted is He. It has also been read as ﴿And Allah is their Protector﴾ with the pronoun in the plural, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight one another⁠﴾ (Q 49:9).

﴿And upon Allah⁠﴾ alone, to the exclusion of anything else, absolutely, whether independently or in association.

﴿let the believers put their trust⁠﴾ in all their affairs, for He is sufficient for them. The mention of the Exalted Name here serves both for blessing and as a reason: divinity is among the things that necessitate trusting in Him, exalted is He. The *lam* in ﴿the believers⁠﴾ is generic, so the two clans are included in it from the outset. In this there is an indication that the attribute of faith is one of the motivations for trust and one of its requirements.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 123:

﴿And Allah had already helped you at Badr﴾ This is a resumptive clause (jumla musta'nifa), brought to establish the obligation of patience and piety (taqwa) by reminding them of the victory that follows from these two, immediately after reminding them of the harm that follows from their absence. It has also been said: it is brought to establish reliance upon Allah the Exalted by reminding them of what necessitates it. "Badr" is the name of a water-place between Makkah and Madinah, which belonged to a man named Badr ibn Kildah, and so it was named after him. It has also been said: it was named for its clarity (safa'ihi), like the full moon (al-badr), and its roundness (istidaratihi). It has also been said: it is the name of a place or a valley. The Battle of Badr took place on the seventeenth of the month of Ramadan in the second year of the Hijra.

﴿And you were humble (adhilla)﴾ This is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the object of "nasarakum" (helped you). "Adhilla" is the plural of dhalil (humble, weak), and it was put in the plural form of paucity (jam' qilla) to signal that they were, at that time, characterized by both the attributes of paucity and humility. They were three hundred and some odd men (bid'a 'ashar), and their condition was at its weakest extent: they went out on water-camels (nawadih), with several men taking turns on a single camel, and there was not in the army except one horse. It has also been said: there were two horses, for al-Miqdad and Marthad, and ninety camels, six coats of mail, and eight swords. The enemy numbered about a thousand, and with them were one hundred horses, along with full equipment and might (shawka).

﴿So fear Allah﴾ He confined himself to the command of piety, although it was accompanied by patience both before and after, in order to indicate its primacy and that patience is among its necessary beginnings; for this reason it was mentioned first, and the placing of the command to piety after the report of victory signals that their aforementioned victory was due to their piety. That is: since the matter is so, then fear Allah as you feared Him on that day.

﴿That perhaps you may be grateful﴾ That is: hoping that you will give thanks for the bounty which He bestows upon you through your piety, namely victory, as you gave thanks before; or, "that perhaps Allah will bestow upon you victory as He did before." Thus gratitude (shukr) has been placed in the position of its cause, which is the bestowal of favor (in'am).

(p-80)

﴿When you said﴾: this is a shift in address (*talwin al-khitab*, a change of grammatical person from the general to the particular), singling out the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to honour him and to indicate that the victory came about through his good tidings, peace be upon him. The word ﴿when﴾ is an adverb of time governed by ﴿He helped you﴾. The command to ﴿be mindful of Allah﴾ was placed before it to show the full extent of concern for it. What is meant by the time is the extended period in which what is mentioned after it occurred, and what has been omitted from mention, relying on the testimony of the circumstances (*shahadat al-hal*) regarding what the existence of the victory depends on. The use of the present tense is for narrating a past situation (*hikayat al-hal*) in order to bring its image to mind, meaning: He helped you at the time you said it.

﴿to the believers﴾: when they showed their inability to fight. Al-Sha'bi said: news reached the believers that Kurz ibn Jabir al-Hanafi intended to reinforce the polytheists, and this weighed heavily upon the believers, so this was revealed at that time, and then it is related here.

﴿Is it not sufficient for you that your Lord should reinforce you with three thousand﴾: sufficiency (*al-kifaya*) is filling a need and undertaking the matter. Reinforcement (*al-imdad*) originally means giving a thing gradually, one state after another. Al-Mufaddal said: what is by way of strengthening and assistance is said of as *amadahu yumiduhu imdadan*, and what is by way of increase is said of as *madahu yamudduhu madan*, and from it is ﴿and the sea, after it, is extended by seven seas﴾. It was also said: *al-madd* is used for evil, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and He extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ and His words: ﴿and We will extend for him of the punishment an extension﴾; and *al-imdad* is used for good, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and We reinforced you with wealth and children﴾. The mention of the title of Lordship (*rububiyya*) here and in what follows, along with its addition to the pronoun of the addressees, is to show concern for them and to indicate the cause of the reinforcement. The meaning is: a denial and negation that reinforcement with that amount is not sufficient. The word ﴿will not﴾ (*lan*) indicates that they were at that time like those who had despaired of victory, because of their weakness, their small number, the strength of the enemy and its multitude.

﴿from the angels﴾: this is an explanation, or a qualifier of ﴿thousands﴾ or of what it is added to, meaning: being from the angels.

﴿sent down﴾: a qualifier of ﴿three thousand﴾. It was also said that it is a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the angels. It was read as *munazzalin* with the doubled letter for intensification or for gradualness. It was said: Allah reinforced them first with a thousand, then they became three thousand, then five thousand. It was also read as an active participle (*mabniyyan lil-fa'il*) in both forms, meaning: sending down victory.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 3, verse 125:**

﴿Yes﴾ is an affirmation of what follows "lan" (never), and a confirmation of it, i.e.: Yes; that is sufficient for you. Then He promised them the increase on condition of patience and piety, urging them to them both and strengthening their hearts. So He said: ﴿if you are patient﴾ in facing the enemy and contending with them.

﴿and fear [Allah]﴾ disobedience to Allah and opposition to His Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace.

﴿and they come upon you﴾ i.e., the polytheists.

﴿from their immediate [fawr] this﴾ i.e., from this very moment. Fawr is, originally, the verbal noun of "fara al-qidr" (the pot boiled), meaning its boiling intensified; it was then borrowed for speed, and then applied to every state in which there is no delay at all. Describing it with this is to emphasise the speed, by increasing its specification and proximity. The arrangement of their coming swiftly within the frame of the two conditions for the support, which entail it in existence and in non-existence, I mean: patience and piety, together with the certain realisation of the support regardless of whether they hasten or delay, is for the realisation of the swiftness of the support, not for the realisation of its basic occurrence, or to show its realisation in whatever state it is supposed, in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, by linking it to the most remote of the possibilities, so that its realisation in all the others is known by a fortiori. For the assault of the enemies and their coming swiftly is from the places where support does not customarily reach, so the realisation of the support has been linked to it, as a notice that where it is realised together with what customarily contradicts it, it is all the more fitting and more certain that it will be realised without it. Just as when you wish to describe a coat of mail as being of utmost protection, you say: if you wear it and confront the enemies with it, and they strike you with strong hands and sharp swords, you will certainly not be affected by them.

﴿your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels, marked [musawwimin]﴾. It derives from "taswim", which is the showing of the mark of a thing, i.e., marking themselves or their horses. It has been narrated that they had white turbans, except Jibril (peace be upon him), who had a yellow turban in the manner of al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam. It has also been narrated (p-81) that they were upon piebald horses. ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr said: The angels were upon piebald horses, wearing white turbans whose ends they had let hang between their shoulders. Hisham ibn ʿUrwa said: yellow turbans. Qatada and al-Dahhak said: They had marked the forelocks and tails of the horses with wool. It has been narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to his companions: "Mark yourselves, for the angels have marked themselves." It was also read as "musawwamin" in the passive form, meaning: marked by Him, glory be to Him. It was said: sent forth, from "taswim" in the sense of "isama" (letting loose).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 126:

﴿And Allah did not make it﴾ is a independent sentence, not included within the scope of the preceding speech, and is directed from Him, exalted is He, to explain that apparent causes have no real effect, and that the true reality of victory belongs exclusively to Him, mighty and majestic, so that the believers may place their trust in Him and not despair of Him when its causes and signs are absent. It is coordinated with (ma'tuf 'ala) an implied verb that the speech extends to and that the context requires. The announcement of the occurrence of victory in general, the reminder of its time, and the recounting of the promise of its occurrence in a particular manner, namely the reinforcement by angels again and again, and the specification of its time in the past, necessarily entail that it occurred at that time with certain decisiveness. However, this was not stated explicitly, relying on the convergence of the proofs and the interlocking of the signs and indications, and as a notice of the complete independence from it. Rather, it was to avoid the taint of repetition, or the appearance of the possibility of a breach in the binding promise. It is as if it were said after His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels, distinguished﴾, then He reinforced you with them (﴿And Allah did not make it...﴾ etc.). The verb "made" (ja'l) is transitive to one object, which is the pronoun referring back to the verbal noun of that implied verb. As for its referring back to the verbal noun mentioned, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that He reinforce you﴾, or to the verbal noun indicated by His saying: ﴿will reinforce you﴾, as has been said, this is not worthy of the eloquence of the revelation, because the simple state precedes the compound state. Therefore, the explanation of the final cause of the existence of the reinforcement, which is what is intended by the noble composition, should come after the explanation of its existence in itself. There is no doubt that the two mentioned verbal nouns are not considered in terms of existence and occurrence, like the verbal noun of the implied verb, so as to undertake explaining the rulings of their existence. Rather, the first is considered in terms of sufficiency, and the second in terms of the promise. Moreover, the first is the reinforcement with three thousand, while what actually occurred was the reinforcement with five thousand. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except as good news for you﴾ is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of causes. The shift in address serves to honor the believers and to indicate that they are the ones in need of good news and of the calming of hearts through the facilitation of apparent causes, and that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is independent of it by virtue of his spiritual support. That is: Allah did not make your reinforcement by the sending down of angels visible, for anything among things, except as good news for you that you will be victorious.

﴿And so that your hearts may be assured thereby﴾, that is, by the reinforcement, and be at rest in it, just as there was tranquility for the Children of Israel in that manner. Both of them are final causes of the making. The first was put in the accusative because its conditions were met, namely the unity of the agent and the time, and that it is a verbal noun brought as a reason. The second remained in its original state because these conditions were absent. It has been said that it is also to indicate its originality in causation and its importance in itself, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and horses, mules, and donkeys, for you to ride and as adornment﴾. In restricting the reinforcement to these two, there is an indication that the angels, peace be upon them, did not engage in fighting that day. Rather, their reinforcement was by strengthening the hearts of those who fought, by increasing the number and the like, as is the view of some of the early generation (al-salaf), may Allah be pleased with him. It has been said: the making is transitive to two objects (ithnayn), and His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿except as good news for you﴾ is an exceptive construction from the most general of objects. That is: Allah, exalted is He, did not make anything among things except as good news for you. Thus the lam in His saying: ﴿and so that﴾ is connected to an omitted element whose estimate is: "and so that your hearts may be assured thereby, He did that."

﴿And victory is not﴾, that is, the true reality of victory in its absolute sense, so that the victory known to people falls under its ruling by primary inclusion.

﴿except from the presence of Allah﴾, that is: except that it is existing from His presence, exalted is He, without there being any partnership in it from the side of causes or numbers. Rather, these are manifestations of Him through the way of the operation of His custom, exalted is He. Or: the victory known to people is not except from Him, exalted is He, not from the presence of the angels, for they have no effect at all. Their utmost role is only what has been mentioned of good news and strengthening of hearts.

﴿the Mighty﴾, that is, the One who cannot be overcome in His judgment and decrees. The application of this attribute to Him, exalted is He, is to indicate the reason for the restriction of victory to Him, exalted is He, just as His description with His saying: ﴿the Wise﴾, that is, the One who does everything He does according to what wisdom and benefit require, is to indicate the reason for making victory through the sending down of angels, for that is among the requirements of far-reaching wisdoms.

**[That He may cut off]** (*li-yaqta'a*) is connected to His saying: ﴿And Allah had already helped you﴾, and what lies between them confirms the reality of that help and explains how it occurred. The restriction of causation to what was mentioned, namely the glad tidings and the assurance, applies only to the reinforcement by the angels in the manner described. That does not undermine the causation of the victory itself by the "cutting off" and what is joined to it, or by what the predicate is linked to in His words, Mighty and Exalted: ﴿And victory is only from Allah﴾. This holds on the assumption that it refers to the known victory. It has been indicated that what is caused by the glad tidings and the assurance is only the outward reinforcement, not the inward victory it contains, which is the essence of the matter. As for linking it to the victory itself, as has been said, then, apart from the separation between the verbal noun and its complement by a foreign element, namely the predicate, it damages the soundness of the meaning. How could it not? Its meaning would be restricting the specific victory, which is caused by specific causes, to what comes from the direction of Allah. The intent is nothing other than restricting the reality of victory, or the known victory, to that. The meaning is: Allah indeed helped you that day, or: the apparent victory at the time of the angels' reinforcement is established only from Allah, ﴿that He may cut off﴾, i.e., destroy and diminish.
