﴿a portion of those who disbelieved﴾: that is, a group of them, by killing and capture. This happened when seventy of their chiefs and leaders were killed and seventy were taken captive.

﴿or subdue them﴾: that is, disgrace them and enrage them by defeat. *Al-kabt* means intense rage, or a weakness that enters the heart, from *kabatahu*, meaning he struck his liver with rage and burning anguish. It was also said that *al-kabt* means being struck by something hateful. It was also said that it means throwing down onto the face and hands. In that case the *tā'* is not replaced, and *aw* (أوْ) is for enumeration (*li-l-tanwī'*).

﴿so that they turn back frustrated﴾: that is, so that they are routed, with their hopes cut off, failing to attain anything of what they sought, as in His saying, Exalted: ﴿And Allah repelled those who disbelieved in their rage; they gained no good﴾.

﴿لَيْسَ لَكَ مِنَ الأمْرِ شَيْءٌ﴾ (You have no say in the matter at all) is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) placed between the item conjoined with what precedes, which is related to the immediate result, and the item conjoined with what follows, which is related to the future result. Its purpose is to establish that the victorious have no influence, immediately after stating that the helpers have no influence. The negation is restricted to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) through a shift in address (talwin al-khitab), to indicate by a stronger inference that it is negated for anyone else. The clause is placed at this point because what precedes it, namely the cutting off and humiliation of the disbelievers, is something that might lead one to think that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and all those engaged in fighting have some role in it.

﴿أوْ يَتُوبَ عَلَيْهِمْ أوْ يُعَذِّبَهُمْ﴾ (or He turns to them in forgiveness or punishes them) is conjoined with "yakbitahum" (He humiliates them). The meaning is: the absolute Owner of their affair is God, Mighty and Majestic. He grants you victory over them so that He may destroy them, or humiliate them, or turn to them in forgiveness if they embrace Islam, or punish them if they persist (in disbelief). You have no say whatsoever in their affair; you are only a servant commanded to warn them and to fight them. By "their punishment" is meant the severe punishment of the Hereafter, specific to the most extreme of disbelievers in disbelief. Otherwise, punishment in the Hereafter in general is also realized for the first two groups. The arrangement of the repentance and the mentioned punishment within the chain of the ultimate cause of the victory, which is consequent upon it in existence, is because the acceptance of their repentance is a branch of its realization, which arises from their knowledge of the truth of Islam through the dominance of its people, which is consequent upon the victory. And their punishment with the mentioned chastisement is consequent upon their persistence in disbelief after the truth has become clear, in the manner mentioned. This is it.

It has been said: "Utba ibn Abi Waqqas struck the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud and broke his incisor. He (ﷺ) began wiping the blood from his face, while Salim, the freed slave of Hudhayfah, was washing the blood from his face and saying: 'How can a people prosper who have stained the face of their Prophet with blood while he is calling them to their Lord?'" Then this verse was revealed: ﴿لَيْسَ لَكَ مِنَ الأمْرِ شَيْءٌ﴾, etc. It is as if it were a kind of rebuke for his (ﷺ) denial of their prosperity.

It has also been said: he (ﷺ) intended to invoke curses upon them, so God the Exalted forbade him, knowing that among them there are those who will believe. Thus His statement, "or He turns to them in forgiveness," is then conjoined either to "the affair" or to "anything," with "an" (that) understood. That is: you have no say in their affair, or in God's turning to them in forgiveness, or in their punishment; or: you have no say in their affair or in turning to them in forgiveness or in punishing them. It is related from al-Farra' and Ibn al-Anbari that "aw" here means "illa an" (except that), and the meaning is: you have no say in their affair except that God turns to them in forgiveness, so that you rejoice in it, or He punishes them, so that you take satisfaction from them.

In any case, this is a resumed statement brought in to explain some matters related to the Battle of Uhud, following the explanation of some matters related to the Battle of Badr, because of the evident connection between them, since each of them is founded on the exclusive attribution of the whole affair to God the Exalted and indicates its negation from anyone else. As for the claim that the whole story relates to the Battle of Uhud, on the basis that His statement, "when you said," is a second substitute for "when you set out in the morning," and that what is reported from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) occurred on the day of Uhud, and that the promised reinforcement was conditional upon patience and piety, so when they did not do so, the promise was not realized, as has been said, this is not supported by the noble text. First: because what was conditional upon patience and piety was the reinforcement with five thousand, not with three thousand, and moreover the reinforcement did not occur that day, nor with a single angel. Second: because in that case it would have been necessary to censure them for their offenses and for their being deprived, by reason of them, of that great blessing. The claim that this is apparent, despite the lack of indication from the preceding and following context, and indeed despite their indicating the opposite, is something hardly to be heard. Third: because there is no way to make the pronoun in His statement, "and God did not make it," etc., refer to the promised reinforcement, since it was not realized, so how could it explain its final cause? Nor can it refer to the promise of it, in the sense that God only made that promise as glad tidings for you and to reassure your hearts, but you did not do what He required of you of patience and piety, so the promised thing was not fulfilled, because His statement, "And victory is only from God, the Mighty, the Wise," is explicit that the promised reinforcement did occur, but its effect was merely glad tidings and reassurance, and both were attained. As for true victory, it is only from Him, the Exalted. And to make it a resumed statement confirming that the reinforcement did not occur, in the sense that the promised victory is specific to Him, so He does not grant victory to one who opposes His command by abandoning patience and piety, is a clear distortion which the revelation must be exalted above. Moreover, His statement, "that He might cut off a part," etc., is then connected to what His statement, "from God," is connected to, of firmness and stability. And it is necessary that its connection to His statement, "And God had already helped you at Badr," etc., while the intervening detail is connected to the Battle of Uhud, is like separating the wood from its bark. Therefore it is necessary to consider the existence of the victory with certainty, because the detail of the rulings consequent upon the existence of a thing is in the position of explaining its non-existence, which is not found in human speech, let alone in the glorious Book. So the truth from which there is no escape is that His statement, "when you said," is an adverbial complement (zarf) of "He helped you," and that what is related within it, up to His statement, "defeated," is definitely connected to the day of Badr, and what follows it admits of the two aforementioned possibilities. His statement, "for they are wrongdoers," is in any case a cause for His statement, "or He punishes them," clarifying that this is from their side and a requital for their wrongdoing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 129:

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ This is a resumptive statement (kalam mustanaf), brought to explain that the dominion (malakut) of all created beings belongs exclusively to Him, glory be to Him, following the explanation that a portion of that belongs exclusively to Him, glory be to Him. It serves to confirm what preceded and to complete it. The fronting of the prepositional phrase (taqdim al-jarr) is for restriction (li'l-qasr), and the word "ma" (whatever) also includes rational beings by way of predominance (taghlib). That is: to Him belongs whatever exists in them of beings, by creation and by ownership, with no share for anyone whatsoever at all; so to Him belongs the entire command.

﴿He forgives whomever He wills﴾ to forgive him, by a will founded upon wisdoms and interests.

﴿and punishes whomever He wills﴾ to punish him for his deed, by a will likewise. The use of the word "man" (whoever) in both places is for restricting forgiveness and punishment to rational beings. The placing of forgiveness before punishment is to signal that His mercy precedes His wrath, and that forgiveness is among the requirements of His essence, whereas punishment is among the requirements of the evil deeds of the disobedient. This is an explicit negation of the obligation of punishment, and the restriction by repentance or its absence is, as it were, incompatible with it.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ a concluding statement (tadhyil) confirming the content of His words, "He forgives whomever He wills," with an addition. In restricting the concluding statement to this, without an indicator, there is, as is evident, great concern for the matter of forgiveness and mercy.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 130:

﴿O you who have believed, do not consume usury, doubled and redoubled.﴾ This is an independent statement that comprises that which is the essence of the matter in every chapter, especially in the chapter of jihad (struggle in the way of God), namely taqwa (God-consciousness) and obedience, and the other matters mentioned after them, which are presented in the manner of encouragement and warning. It was brought in the midst of the narrative, hastening to guide the addressees to what is in it, and as a declaration of the complete obligation of observing it in what they are engaged in of jihad. For the matters mentioned in it, along with their being the criterion for success in both abodes absolutely, are a pillar in the matter of jihad, upon which turns the sphere of victory and triumph. How could it not be so? For if they had maintained patience, taqwa and obedience to the Messenger (ﷺ), they would not have suffered what they suffered. Perhaps the prohibition of usury was included in the midst of these matters because encouragement to spend in ease and in hardship, whose foremost form is spending in the way of jihad, entails encouragement to acquire wealth, and so it was a likely occasion for people to rush to means of earning, of which usury is one; therefore they were forbidden from that. What is meant by "consuming" it is taking it, and it was expressed by "consuming" because it is the greater part of what is sought by taking, and because of its currency in foodstuffs, along with the added severity of censure. As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿doubled and redoubled﴾, it is not to restrict the prohibition to it, but to take into account the custom they were accustomed to, as a rebuke to them for it; for a man would lend at interest until a term, and when it fell due he would say to the debtor: "Increase the money for me and I will increase the term for you," and he would do so, and likewise at the due date of each term, so that a trifling thing would eventually consume all his wealth entirely. Its position is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of "usury." It has also been read as "muda"aafah" (with the doubling of the ʿayn).

﴿And fear God﴾ regarding what you have been forbidden of matters, of which usury is one.

﴿That you may prosper﴾, hoping for success.

Translation:

﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾, by guarding oneself against following them and against engaging in what they engage in. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, used to say: "It is the most frightening verse in the Qur'an, since Allah threatens the believers with the Fire prepared for the disbelievers if they do not fear Him by avoiding His prohibitions."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 132:

﴿And obey Allah﴾ in everything He has commanded you and forbidden you from.

﴿And the Messenger﴾ who conveys to you His commands and His prohibitions.

﴿That you may be shown mercy﴾, hoping for His mercy.

He follows the threat with the promise, as a warning against opposition and an encouragement toward obedience. The use of "la'alla" (perhaps; that you may) in both places indicates that attaining success and mercy is difficult to reach. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: this verse is a rebuke to those who disobeyed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he commanded them with what he commanded them on the Day of Uhud.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 133:

﴿And hasten⦆ is coordinated (ʿatf) with "obey" (aṭīʿū). It was also read without the conjunction "wa", on the basis of resumption (istiʾnāf), meaning: hurry and turn toward. It was also read "sābiqū" (vie with one another).

﴿To forgiveness from your Lord and a garden﴾ meaning: toward that which leads to both of them. It was said: toward Islam. It was said: toward repentance. It was said: toward sincerity. It was said: toward jihad. It was said: toward the performance of all obligations and the abandonment of all prohibited acts, so that within this fall primarily all the matters commanded and forbidden that have passed. The mention of forgiveness before the garden is because clearing (takhliyah) precedes adorning (tahliyah). "From" (min) is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of "forgiveness", meaning: existing from your Lord. The mention of the attribute of lordship (rubūbiyyah), together with its attachment to the pronoun of the addressees, is to show increased kindness toward them.

As for the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿whose breadth is the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: like their breadth, is a qualifier of "garden". The specific mention of breadth is for emphasis in describing it with vastness and expansiveness, in the manner of illustration (tamthīl), since breadth is customarily less than length. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both: "like seven heavens and seven earths joined one to another."

﴿prepared for the God-fearing﴾: it is in the place of a genitive as another qualifier of "garden", or in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from it, because it is specified by the qualifier, meaning: it has been made ready for them. In this there is evidence that the Garden is now created and that it is outside this world.

﴿Those who spend﴾ is in the genitive case (*al-jarr*) as a descriptive modifier (*na't*) of "the God-fearing" (*al-muttaqin*), either as praise for them (*madih*), or as an apposition (*badal*) or an explanatory clarification (*bayan*). It may also be in the accusative (*nasb*) or nominative (*raf'*) case, as an implied praise (*al-madh*). The object of "spend" (*yunfiquna*) is omitted so that it covers everything that is fit to be spent, or it is left entirely unstated, as in your saying: "He gives and withholds" (*yu'ti wa yamna'*).

﴿In prosperity and adversity﴾ means in times of ease and hardship, in times of comfort and difficulty, or in all circumstances, since a person is never free of either joy or harm. That is, in no state do they refrain from spending of whatever they have the means to give, whether little or much.

﴿And those who restrain their anger﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with the relative clause. The shift to the active participle form (*sigha al-fa'il*) indicates continuity. As for spending, since it is an action that recurs, it is expressed with a form that indicates occurrence and renewal. "Kazm" means restraint, as in the saying "he restrained his anger" (*kazama ghayzahu*), that is, he held it back. Al-Mubarrad said: its interpretation is that he suppressed it while being full of it, as in the saying: "I filled the water-skin and tied it tight" (*kazamtu al-siqa'*), that is, those who hold it in and refrain from carrying it out while having the power to do so. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever restrains his anger while he is able to act upon it, Allah will fill his heart with security and faith."

﴿And those who pardon people﴾, that is, those who abandon the punishment of one who deserves to be held accountable. It is narrated that on the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: "Where are those whose reward is with Allah, the Exalted?" Then none will stand except those who pardoned. The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "Indeed, such people among my community are few, except for those whom Allah protects, though they were many among the nations that passed before." In these two attributes there is an indication of the perfect appropriateness of the Prophet's (ﷺ) pardon of the archers (*al-rumat*) and his leaving off holding them accountable for disobeying his command, peace be upon him, and an exhortation to him, peace be upon him, to abandon what he had resolved upon, namely to repay the polytheists for what they had done to Hamza, may Allah be pleased with him, when he said upon seeing him: "He has been mutilated, so I will mutilate seventy in your place."

﴿And Allah loves the good-doers﴾. The article *al-* (in *al-muhsinin*) is either for the genus, in which case they are included in it as the first and foremost of its members, or it is for a specific reference (*al-'ahd*), in which case it refers to them. He expressed them as "the good-doers" to indicate that the qualities enumerated are of the category of *ihsan* (excellence), which is performing actions in the proper manner, whose descriptive excellence (*husn al-wasfi*) necessarily entails their intrinsic excellence (*husn al-dhati*). The Prophet (ﷺ) explained it with his saying: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you." The sentence is a concluding summary (*tadhyil*) confirming the content of what came before it.

﴿Those who﴾ is in the nominative case, as the subject of a new sentence (mubtada'). It has also been said that it is in the genitive case, conjoined to what precedes it among the attributes of the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). God's words ﴿and God loves the good-doers﴾ are a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) placed between them, pointing to the disparity between the two groups: the rank of the former in piety is higher than the rank of these, and their share is more abundant than theirs. Or it refers to the God-fearing themselves, in which case the disparity is greater and more evident.

﴿When they commit an indecency﴾, that is, a deed grievous in its ugliness, such as fornication.

﴿Or wrong themselves﴾ by committing a sin, whatever sin it may be. It has been said: indecency refers to major sins and wronging oneself to minor sins. Or: indecency is that which extends to others, and wronging oneself is that which does not. It has been said that the believers said: "O Messenger of God, the Children of Israel were more honored by God Most High than we are. If one of them sinned, the expiation of his sin would be written on the threshold of his house: Do such-and-such." So God Most High revealed this verse. It has also been said that Nabhan al-Tammar (the date-seller) was approached by a beautiful woman seeking dates from him. He said to her: "These dates are not good, but inside the house there are better ones." He took her to his house, embraced her and kissed her. She said to him: "Fear God!" So he left her, regretted this, went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned it to him, and this verse was revealed. It has also been said that something similar occurred between an Ansari man and a woman, and a Thaqafi man who had a bond of brotherhood (mu'akhah) with them; the Ansari regretted it, threw dust on his head, wandered aimlessly, and began roaming the mountains repentant and seeking forgiveness. Then he came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the verse was revealed. Whichever of these is the case, the unrestricted wording of the expression encompasses what the fornicators did, encompassing it in the first instance.

﴿They remember God﴾, that is, they recall His great right and His majesty, which requires awe and shame, or His threat, or His judgment and His punishment.

﴿And seek forgiveness for their sins﴾ through repentance and regret. The fa' (and so) indicates that remembering Him Most High necessarily entails seeking forgiveness.

﴿And who forgives sins but God?﴾ This is a rhetorical question of denial (istifham inkari), and what is meant by "sins" is their kind, as in your saying: "So-and-so wears clothes and rides horses," not all of them, so as not to undermine what is intended, namely the impossibility that forgiveness of any single one of them proceed from anyone other than God Most High. God's words ﴿but God﴾ are a substitute (badal) for the pronoun hidden in yaghfiru ("forgives"), meaning: none forgives the kind of sins except God. However, the implication of negation through the interrogative is stronger and more emphatic, because it signals that everyone who has a share of address (khitab) knows that negation and so hastens to answer with it. What is meant by it is describing Him, glorified be He, with the utmost breadth of mercy and the generality of forgiveness. The clause is parenthetical between the two conjoined elements, or between the circumstantial phrase and its referent, to affirm the seeking of forgiveness, to urge it, and to imply the promise of acceptance.

﴿And they do not persist﴾ is conjoined to "they sought forgiveness." Its placement after it, although non-persistence logically precedes seeking forgiveness in rank, serves to show concern for the matter of seeking forgiveness and its deserving to be hastened to immediately after the mention of God Most High. Or it is a circumstantial phrase (hal) of its subject, meaning: "while not persisting" (aw ghayra muqimin).

﴿In what they did﴾, that is, in the sins they committed, whether an indecency, an act of wronging, or in their deed. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "One who seeks forgiveness does not persist, even if he returns to the same sin seventy times a day, and there is no major sin with seeking forgiveness, nor minor sin with persistence." ﴿While they know﴾ is a circumstantial phrase of the subject of "they do not persist": that is, they do not persist in what they did while knowing its ugliness, the prohibition against it, and the threat for it. The qualification by this is because one who does not know this may be excused, provided that the failure to acquire knowledge of it was not due to negligence.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 136:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to those mentioned last, in view of their being characterized by the praiseworthy attributes that have preceded, and the sense of distance contained in it (the demonstrative "those," rather than "these") signals the remoteness of their rank and the exalted level of their excellence. It is the subject (mubtada'), and His exalted words ﴿their recompense﴾ are a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from it. His exalted words ﴿forgiveness﴾ are its predicate (khabar), or "their recompense" is a second subject (mubtada' thani) and "forgiveness" is its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of ﴿those﴾. And this clause is the predicate of His exalted words ﴿and those who, when they commit﴾ etc.... According to the first aspect, which is the most evident and the most suited to the arrangement of forgiveness, which indicates a prior sin, within the category of recompense; for according to the last two aspects, His exalted words ﴿those﴾ etc. would be a resumptive clause (jumla mustani'afa) explaining what precedes it and disclosing the condition of both groups, the good-doers and the penitents. The attributes of the first group that contain any trace of sin were not mentioned, so that forgiveness, which encompasses them, would be mentioned at the outset of the recompense; and restricting the demonstrative to the latter two, despite their both sharing the ruling of the preparation of Paradise for them, is evident far-fetchedness.

﴿from their Lord﴾ is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier (sifa) of ﴿forgiveness﴾, confirming what the indefiniteness (tanwin) conveyed of intrinsic grandeur with relational grandeur, meaning: it proceeds from His direction, exalted is He. The mention of the title of Lordship together with its attachment to their pronoun is to signal the reason for the ruling and the honouring.

﴿and gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ is conjoined to "forgiveness," and the indefiniteness, which signals that they are lower than the previously mentioned Paradise, supports the preference for the first aspect.

﴿abiding therein﴾ is a provisional circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara) from the pronoun in ﴿their recompense﴾, because it is in meaning an object; for it is equivalent to: God will recompense them with gardens, abiding therein. It is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from "gardens" in wording, while in meaning it belongs to their owners, for if it were so, the pronoun would have appeared.

﴿and excellent is the reward of the workers﴾: the element specified for praise is omitted, meaning: and excellent is the reward of the workers that, namely what was mentioned of forgiveness and the gardens. The expression of them by "reward," which signals that they are deserved in exchange for work, even though it is by way of bounty, is for the sake of greater encouragement to acts of obedience and deterrence from sins. The sentence is a concluding summation (tadhyil) specific to the penitents, according to the specificity of the earlier concluding summation to the first group. Its content suffices as evidence of the clear disparity and manifest difference between the two groups: how far apart are the good-doers, who attain the love of God, mighty and majestic, and the workers, who receive their wage and their hire.

(p-88) This is a return to detailing the rest of the account, after laying the groundwork of the beginnings of right guidance and righteousness and arranging the preliminaries of success and prosperity. *Khuluww* means passing away, and *sunan* means occurrences and events. It is also said that *sunan* means nations. The adverbial phrase (*al-zarf*) is either connected to *khalat* ("have passed"), or to an omitted element that serves as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of *sunan*. That is, "they have passed before your time," or "existing before you are occurrences that God Most High established concerning the denying nations," as in His words: ﴿And they will be killed with thorough killing﴾ and ﴿[It is] the way of God concerning those who passed before﴾, etc.

The *fa'* (the "so") in His words ﴿So travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers﴾ indicates that their having passed is the cause for the travel and observation, or it is for commanding both. It is also said that the meaning is conditional, i.e., "if you doubt, then travel," etc. *Kayfa* ("how") is the predicate (*khabar*) placed before *kana* ("was"), and it suspends the verb of seeing (*al-nazar*). The clause is in the position of an accusative after the removal of the preposition, because the original usage of the verb is with a preposition.

This (﴿This﴾) refers to what preceded it in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Ways have passed before you﴾, to its end.

﴿A clarification for mankind﴾, meaning: a making clear for them. The lām is either connected to the verbal noun (maṣdar, the noun of action), or it is connected to an omitted word that functions as an adjective (ṣifah) for it, so that the meaning is: a clarification that is for them. The definite article in "al-nās" (the people) is for a known referent (ʿahd), namely the deniers. That is, this is an explanation of the evil outcome of what they are upon of denial. Although the command to travel and reflect is specific to the believers, acting upon its implication is not restricted to one group over another. Thus it includes the deniers too, so that they should look into the outcomes of those before them among the people of denial and take heed from what they witness of the traces of their destruction, even though the speech was not directed at them.

﴿And guidance and admonition﴾, meaning: and an increase in insight and admonition for you. It was said ﴿for the God-fearing﴾ to indicate the cause of the ruling, since the basis of it being guidance and admonition for them is only their God-consciousness (taqwā). It is also permissible that "the God-fearing" (al-muttaqūn) means those who are heading towards God-consciousness, and "guidance" and "admonition" are taken in their literal sense. That is: this is an explanation of the end of the people's affair and the evil of its final outcome, and guidance for those among them who are God-conscious, and a restraint for them from what they are upon of denial. It is also permissible that it refers to what includes them and others among the actually God-conscious, and that "guidance" and "admonition" refer to what includes their beginning and the increase in them. The clarification being mentioned as for the deniers, though it was not directed at them, is placed before its being guidance and admonition for the God-fearing, although the latter is the intended aim of the context, because the first thing that follows from seeing the traces of the destruction of their predecessors is the manifestation of the condition of their successors. As for the increase in guidance, or its origin, it is a matter that follows from this. The restriction of the clarification to the people, despite its including the God-fearing as well, is because what is meant by it is merely clarification, free of guidance and admonition. Restricting the two to the God-fearing, although they follow from the clarification, is because they are the primary objective. It is also permissible that the definite article in "al-nās" is for the class (jins), meaning: this is a clarification for people in general, and guidance and admonition for the God-fearing among them specifically.

It has been said: the word "this" (hādhā) refers to what was summarized of the matter of the God-fearing, the penitent and the persistent. His words, exalted is He, ﴿Ways have passed before you﴾, to the end of the verse, are a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ) that urges belief and what is deserved by it of the reward mentioned for the doers. You know that a parenthetical clause must confirm the content of what occurred within it, and witnessing the traces of the destruction of the deniers is not connected to the condition of any of the three categories of believers, although it inspires belief and restrains from denial. It has also been said that it refers to the Qur'an, but its remoteness is not hidden.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 139:**

﴿And do not weaken, nor grieve﴾. This is an encouragement for the believers, a strengthening of their hearts, and a consolation for what befell them on the Day of Uhud of killing and wounding. Five of the Emigrants (muhajirun) were killed that day: Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, Mus'ab ibn Umayr, the bearer of the banner of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abdullah ibn Jahsh, the cousin of the Prophet (ﷺ) through his paternal aunt, Uthman ibn Shammas, and Sa'd, the freedman of Utbah, may the good pleasure of Allah the Exalted be upon them all. And seventy men from the Helpers (Ansar) were killed, may Allah be pleased with them. That is: do not become weak in jihad because of the wounds that have reached you, and do not grieve over those among you who were killed.

﴿And you will be the superior ones﴾. This is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) from the subject of the two verbs, meaning: while the state is that you are the superior ones, the victors, over your enemy, for their affair will end in destruction, as you have witnessed from the conditions of their predecessors. This is therefore an explicit promise of victory and triumph, after an earlier allusion to it. Or: and you are those known for the utmost loftiness of station, because you are upon the truth, your fighting is for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and your slain are in Paradise, whereas they are upon falsehood, their fighting is for Satan, and their slain are in the Fire. It has also been said that "and you will be the superior ones" is a circumstantial clause relating to them, since you inflicted on them at the Day of Badr more than what they inflicted on you today.

﴿If you are believers﴾. This is connected either to the prohibition or to "the superior ones," and its response is omitted, being indicated by what it is connected to. That is: if you are believers, then do not weaken and do not grieve, for faith requires strength of heart, confidence in the workings of Allah the Exalted, and indifference to His enemies. Or: if you are believers, then you are the superior ones, for faith necessarily entails superiority. Or: if you are believers in the promise of Allah the Exalted, then you are the superior ones. In any case, the purpose is to affirm the conditioned matter on the basis of affirming the condition, as in the words of the hired worker: "If I have worked for you, then give me my wage." Accordingly, it has been said that its meaning is: "since you are believers." It has also been said that its meaning is: "if you remain upon faith."

﴿If a wound has touched you, a wound has certainly touched the other people as well, like it.﴾ "Al-qarḥ" (wound) is read with a fatḥah or a ḍammah on the qāf, and both are dialectal forms, like "al-ḍaʿf" and "al-ḍuʿf" (weakness). Both readings are transmitted. It is said that the fatḥah form means the wound itself, and the ḍammah form means its pain. It is also read with two fatḥahs, and it is said that "al-qarḥ" and "al-qaraḥ" are like "al-ṭard" and "al-ṭaradd" (expulsion). The meaning is: if they inflicted [a wound] upon you on the day of Uhud, then you had inflicted [one] upon them before it, on the day of Badr. Yet that did not weaken their hearts, nor did it deter them from returning to fight you. So you are more deserving not to become weak, for you hope from God for what they do not hope for. It is also said that both touches occurred on the day of Uhud, for the Muslims inflicted [wounds] upon them before they disobeyed the command of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). They killed some twenty-odd men among them, including the bearer of their banner, wounded a great number, and hamstrung almost all of their horses with arrows.

﴿And those days﴾ is a reference to the days that pass among the nations, past and future, all of them, and not only to the particular known days of the Battle of Badr and the Battle of Uhud. Rather, those are included in them as a primary inclusion. What is meant by them is the times of victory and dominance.

﴿We alternate them among the people﴾ means: We turn them around among them, granting victory to these at one time and to those at another time, like the saying of one who said:

*"One day against us, and one day for us,
and one day we are grieved, and one day we are gladdened."*

"Al-mudāwalah" (alternation) is like "al-muʿāwarah" (taking turns). It is said: "I alternated it among them, and they alternated it," meaning: "I passed it around, and they passed it around." The demonstrative ﴿those﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and "the days" is either an attribute (ṣifah) of it, or an appositive substitute (badal) of it, or an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayān) of it, and "We alternate them" is its predicate (khabar), or the predicate is "We alternate them" and it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "the days," with its governing element being the meaning of the demonstrative, or it is a predicate after a predicate. The present tense form, which indicates renewal and continuity, is used to announce that this alternation is a established practice among all nations, past and future, and in it there is a kind of consolation.

As for the saying of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿and that God may know those who believe﴾, it is either by way of figurative representation (tamthīl), meaning: He deals with you in the manner of one who wishes to know the sincere ones who are steadfast in faith from others. Or "knowledge" in it is a figurative usage (majāz) for distinguishing, by way of naming the cause for the effect, meaning: that He may distinguish those steadfast in faith from others, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the wicked from the good﴾ (p-90). Or it is in its literal sense, considered from the standpoint of its relation to the known, insofar as it exists actually, for it is that upon which the sphere of recompense revolves, and not insofar as it exists potentially. The mention of "faith" while what is meant is firmness and sincerity in it is to announce that the name of faith does not apply to anything else. The shift to the third person (iltifāt ilā al-ghaybah) by attributing the knowledge to the proper name (God), which comprises all the attributes, is to cultivate awe, and to indicate that the issuance of each of the things mentioned as a cause is from His actions, exalted is He, with respect to a specific source among His attributes that differs from the source of the other. The clause is a cause for what is one of the individual instances of absolute alternation, which was expressed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We alternate them among the people﴾, from the known alternation occurring between the two groups, the believers and the disbelievers. The particle "li-" (in order that) is connected to what the absolute verb indicates, restricted by occurring between the two mentioned groups, or to the absolute verb itself with respect to its occurring between them. The clause is conjoined to another cause for it, which is considered, either specifically and definitively deleted, because what is mentioned indicates it, as it is among its beginnings, as if it were said: "We alternate them between you and your enemy, so that your affair may become manifest, and that it may be known..." etc. For the manifestation of their deeds and their emergence from potentiality into actuality is among the beginnings of distinguishing them from others, and among the requirements of the eternal knowledge's relation to them from that aspect. The same holds in the matter of figurative representation, so reflect. Or it is general and indefinite, to alert that the causes are not confined to these, but include a number of other matters, and that the servant is distressed by what befalls him of calamities, and does not realize that God, exalted is He, has placed in that subtle kindnesses that do not occur to the mind. It is as if it were said: "We alternate them among you so that there may be such and such benefits, and so that He may know..." etc. In this there is, of course, much emphasis on consolation and an increase in insight. The specification of the explanation to the cause of this individual instance out of the absolute alternation, rather than the rest of its individual instances occurring among the rest of the nations, whether specifically or indefinitely, is because the purpose of knowledge does not relate to explaining them. You may also make the deleted indefinite element an expression for the causes of all the rest of its individual instances, to allude in general to the fact that each individual instance of them has a cause that motivates it. As if it were said: "We alternate them among the people, all of them, so that such and such may be among the wisdoms motivating those individual instances, and so that He may know..." etc. In that case the first "li-" is connected to the absolute verb with respect to its restriction to those individual instances, and the second with respect to its restriction to the known individual instance. It is also said: it is connected to a deleted postponed element whose estimate is: "and so that God may know those who believe, He did that."

﴿and that He may take martyrs from among you﴾. "Shuhadāʾ" is the plural of "shahīd" (martyr), meaning: and that He may honor some people among you with martyrdom, and they are the martyrs of Uhud. So "min" (from) is either for the beginning of the scope (ibtidāʾiyyah) or partitive (tabʿīḍiyyah), connected to "yattakhidh" (take), or to a deleted element that occurred as a circumstantial clause from "shuhadāʾ." Or "shuhadāʾ" is the plural of "shāhid" (witness), meaning: and that He may take from among you witnesses who are vouched for by what appeared from them of steadfastness upon the truth, patience in hardships, and other evidences of truthfulness, so that they may bear witness against the nations on the Day of Resurrection. So "min" is explanatory (bayāniyyah), because that witnessing is the duty of all, not only of those who are called upon to witness. Whichever it is, the word "take" (ittikhādh), which indicates selection and drawing near, contains much honor for them and exaltation of their status.

﴿and God does not love the wrongdoers﴾ is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ) that confirms the content of what precedes it. The negation of love is an expression (kināyah) for hatred. Placing it upon the wrongdoers contains an allusion to His love for their opponents. By "the wrongdoers" is meant either those who are not steadfast in faith, so the confirmation is in that His hatred for them is one of the motives for removing the sincere and chosen ones for martyrdom from among them. Or it means the disbelievers to whom the victory was alternated, so the confirmation is in that this is not by way of support for them, for support is specific to His friends, but rather for the benefits mentioned that return to the believers.

وَقَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَلِيُمَحِّصَ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ (p-91) أيْ: لِيُصَفِّيَهم ويُطَهِّرَهم مِنَ الذُّنُوبِ، عَطْفٌ عَلى "يَتَّخِذَ" (*yattakhidha*, "that He may take") وتَكْرِيرُ اللّامِ لِتَذْكِيرِ التَّعْلِيلِ لِوُقُوعِ الفَصْلِ بَيْنَهُما بِالِاعْتِراضِ (*i'tiraḍ*, a parenthetical clause interposed in the sentence) وإظْهارُ الِاسْمِ الجَلِيلِ في مَوْقِعِ الإضْمارِ لِإبْرازِ مَزِيدِ الِاعْتِناءِ بِشَأْنِ التَّمْحِيصِ، وهَذِهِ الأُمُورُ الثَّلاثَةُ عِلَلٌ لِلْمُداوَلَةِ المَعْهُودَةِ بِاعْتِبارِ كَوْنِها عَلى المُؤْمِنِينَ قُدِّمَتْ في الذِّكْرِ، لِأنَّها المُحْتاجَةُ إلى البَيانِ ولَعَلَّ تَأْخِيرَ العِلَّةِ الأخِيرَةِ عَنِ الاعْتِراضِ لِئَلّا يُتَوَهَّمَ انْدِراجُ المُذْنِبِينَ في الظّالِمِينَ أوْ لِيَقْتَرِنَ بِقَوْلِهِ عَزَّ وجَلَّ: ﴿وَيَمْحَقَ الكافِرِينَ﴾ فَإنَّ التَّمْحِيصَ فِيهِ مَحْوُ الآثارِ وإزالَةُ الأوْضارِ كَما أنَّ المَحْقَ عِبارَةٌ عَنِ النَّقْصِ والإذْهابِ. قالَ المِفْضَلُ (al-Mufaḍḍal): وهو أنْ يَذْهَبَ الشَّيْءُ بِالكُلِّيَّةِ حَتّى لا يُرى مِنهُ شَيْءٌ، ومِنهُ قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿يَمْحَقُ اللَّهُ الرِّبا﴾ أيْ: يَسْتَأْصِلُهُ، وهَذِهِ عِلَّةٌ لِلْمُداوَلَةِ بِاعْتِبارِ كَوْنِها عَلى الكافِرِينَ، والمُرادُ بِهِمُ: الَّذِينَ حارَبُوا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ (ﷺ) يَوْمَ أُحُدٍ وأصَرُّوا عَلى الكُفْرِ وقَدْ مَحَقَهُمُ اللَّهُ عَزَّ وجَلَّ جَمِيعًَا.

Abu al-Su'ud, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*, on Surah 3, verse 142:

﴿Or did you think﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*), brought to explain what the ultimate goal and outcome is of the alternation of fortunes and of what has been mentioned about distinguishing the sincere believers, testing them, taking martyrs, and showing the honour of attaining them. The address is to those who fled on the day of Uhud. The *am* here is disjunctive (*munqati'ah*), and the *bal* contained in it is for turning away (*idrab*) from consolation by explaining the causes of the hardship they suffered, toward establishing that these are among the beginnings of attaining the sought-after reward. The hamza is for denial and disapproval, meaning: "Rather, did you think?"

﴿that you would enter Paradise﴾ and attain its bliss. His words, exalted is He, ﴿while God has not yet known those of you who struggled﴾, form a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *tadkhulu* ("you enter"), reinforcing the denial. Hoping for reward without action from one whom one knows is bound to action is considered unreasonable by minds. The non-knowledge is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for the non-existence of what is known, because of the necessary connection between them, which rests on the necessity that the first (knowledge) be realized in order for the second (the object) to be realized, since it is impossible for anything to exist without God's knowledge of it. Using this form instead of stating it explicitly serves to intensify the establishment of the intended meaning, for it is a proof that their striving did not occur. It also signals that the basis on which reward is attached to deeds is only God's knowledge of them. It is as if it were said: "And the situation is that those of you who struggled have not come into being." The negation was directed at the qualified persons, although what is negated is only the attribute. It would have sufficed to say, "while God has not yet known your striving," as a metonymy for the meaning of "while you have not yet struggled," to intensify the demonstration that the attribute is absent and not realized at all. The word *lamma* indicates that striving is expected from them in the future, but it is not taken into account in reinforcing the denial.

It was also read as *ya'lama* with a fatha on the mim, either because its original form was *ya'lamanna* and the nun was dropped, or by the method of assimilating the mim to the vowel before it, in order to preserve the glorification of God's name. ﴿of you﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *alladhina* ("those who").

﴿and know the steadfast﴾ is in the accusative by the implied *an* (*idmar an*), with the waw being for conjunction, as in your saying: *la ta'kul al-samaka wa tashrab al-laban* ("do not eat the fish and drink the milk"), meaning: let there not be from you the eating of fish and the drinking of milk. The meaning is: "Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while the struggle and the steadfastness have not been realized from you," i.e., their combination. The use of the active participle (*ism al-fa'il*) rather than the relative clause indicates that what is considered is continuance in steadfastness, and also serves to preserve the rhyme (*fawasil*). It was also said that it is jussive, conjoined to the jussive preceding it, and its final consonant was given a fatha because two unvocalized consonants met (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*), for lightness and by assimilation, as already mentioned. The reading with a kasra supports this, being the original form for vocalizing an unvocalized consonant.

It was read as *ya'lamu* with a damma, the waw being for the circumstantial clause, and its subject being the relative pronoun, with the implied subject, meaning: "And He knows the steadfast," as if it were said: "While you have not struggled and you are steadfast."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 143:

(p-92) ﴿And you certainly used to wish for death﴾. That is, you used to wish for battle, for it is among the beginnings of death, or [you wished for] death by martyrdom. The address is to those who did not witness Badr, and they used to wish that they could witness [a battle] with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that they might attain the honour that the martyrs of Badr had attained. So they insisted upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to go out [to fight], and then there appeared from them the opposite of that.

﴿Before you met it﴾: this is connected to ﴿you used to wish﴾, explaining the reason for their eagerness to wish, [namely] before you had seen it and known its terror and its severity. It has also been read as "tulaqqūhu" (you encounter it).

﴿Then indeed you have seen it﴾: that is, what you wished for of the causes of death, or death itself, by witnessing its causes. The words of the Exalted, ﴿while you were looking on﴾, are a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the addressees. The choice of "seeing" (ru'yah) over "meeting" (mulaqah), and restricting it to "looking" (naẓar), adds further emphasis to their witnessing of it. The fa' [in "fa-qad"] is eloquent (faṣīḥah), as if it were said: "If you were truthful in your wish for that, then you have seen it, observing it directly when those among your brothers and relatives were slain before your eyes, and you were close to being slain yourselves. So why did you do what you did?" This is a rebuke for them regarding their wishing for war and their causing it, and then their cowardice and flight, not a rebuke for wishing for martyrdom, on the basis that it implies the victory of the disbelievers, since the aim of one who wishes for it is to attain the honour of the martyrs, and nothing else comes to his mind; therefore he does not deserve blame from that direction.

﴿Muhammad is only a Messenger﴾: a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate). The particle *ma* (negative) does not govern the predicate (*la 'amal li-ma*) by agreement of the scholars, because its negation is broken by *illa* ("except").

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Messengers have passed away before him﴾, is a ṣifah (qualifying clause) for ﴿Messenger﴾. It indicates that he holds the honour of having passed away (*sharaf al-khuluww*), since the passing away of those who shared his station of messengership is certainly one of the proofs that he too will pass away, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him. It is as if it were said: "Messengers like him have passed away before him, so he will pass away just as they passed away." The restriction (*qaṣr*) here is *qalbī* (a restriction that corrects a mistaken belief). They had turned back on their heels, as though they believed that he, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, was a messenger unlike the other messengers in that he would not pass away as they did, and that adherence to his religion would be obligatory after him just as adherence to their religions was obligatory after them. So He refuted them by saying that he is nothing but a messenger like the other messengers, so he will pass away as they passed away, and adherence to his religion is obligatory just as adherence to their religions is obligatory.

It has also been said that it is a restriction of *ifrād* (a restriction that corrects a belief in a combined attribute). When they regarded his not remaining among them, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, as a grave matter, they were treated as though they were those who thought his destruction unlikely. It is as though they believed that he, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, had two attributes: messengership and distance from destruction. So He refuted them by saying that he is restricted to messengership and does not go beyond it to distance from destruction. In that case, it is necessary to take His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Messengers have passed away before him﴾ etc., as a new independent statement, brought to establish that he was not exempt from destruction and to explain that he is an example for the messengers before him, peace be upon them.

In any case, the speech departs from what the apparent meaning requires.

﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾ This is a denial of their apostasy and their turning away from the religion upon his passing away through death or killing, after they had knowledge that the messengers before him had passed away and that their religion remains to be held fast.

It has also been said that the *fa'* is causal (*sababiyyah*) and the *hamzah* is for denying that they should make the passing away of the messengers before him a cause of their turning back after his death, even though in reality it is a cause for their steadfastness in the religion. The mention of death with the word *in* ("if"), although they know it with certainty, is to treat the addressees as if they were doubtful about it, because of their magnification of it, as stated. The situation is the same in all other instances, for the word *in* in the speech of Allah, exalted is He, never operates on its apparent meaning, since He knows with certainty whether something occurs or does not occur (p-93). Rather, it is interpreted in light of the state of the listener or some other matter that suits the context. The mention of death first, although it was the killing that caused the strife and in which the trial was great, is because death is of the more honourable kind of occurrence, so restraining people from turning back at his death and urging them to remain steadfast then is more important. Also, the attribute that unites him and the messengers, peace be upon them, is passing away by death, not by killing.

It is reported that when the two groups met, Abu Dujanah charged with a number of Muslims against the polytheists and fought a fierce battle. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, fought a great battle until his sword bent, and likewise Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. They killed a group of the polytheists and routed them. When the archers saw them and saw that they had been routed, they turned to plunder and did not heed the prohibition of their commander 'Abd Allah ibn Jubayr, so that only eight men remained with him. When Khalid ibn al-Walid saw them busy with the spoils, he charged against them with two hundred and fifty polytheist horsemen from the direction of the mountain pass, killed those of the archers who remained, entered behind the backs of the Muslims, scattered them and routed them, and attacked the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and fought them until about thirty men were struck down there. Each of them would kneel before him, saying: "My face is a shield for your face, my soul is a ransom for your soul, and upon you be the peace of Allah, without farewell." 'Abd Allah ibn Qami'ah al-Harithi threw a stone at the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, breaking his front tooth and wounding his noble face. Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, may Allah be pleased with him, who was the standard-bearer, defended him until Ibn Qami'ah killed him, and Ibn Qami'ah claimed that he had killed the Prophet ﷺ. He said: "I have killed Muhammad." A crier cried out, said to be Iblis: "Truly Muhammad has been killed!" The people dispersed, and the Messenger ﷺ began calling: "To me, servants of Allah!"

Ka'b ibn Malik said: "I was the first of the Muslims to recognise the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so I called out at the top of my voice: 'O assembly of Muslims, this is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ!' Thirty of his companions gathered around him, protected him, and drove the polytheists away from him, while the rest scattered." Some of them said: "Would that Ibn Ubayy would take safe-conduct for us from Abu Sufyan!" And some of the hypocrites said: "If he had been a prophet he would not have been killed. Return to your brothers and to your religion!" Anas ibn al-Nadr, who was the uncle of Anas ibn Malik, said: "O people, if Muhammad has been killed, the Lord of Muhammad is living and does not die. What good is life after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ? Fight for what he fought for, and die nobly for what he died for." Then he said: "O Allah, I apologise to You for what these people say, and I disavow to You what these people have brought." Then he drew his sword, fought until he was killed.

Their permitting his killing, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, is contrary to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾. This is because not every verse is heard by everyone, nor does everyone who hears it recall it in every situation, especially in such a terrifying situation. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, forgot this noble verse at the time of his death, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, and stood among the people and said: "Some hypocrites claim that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has died. The Messenger of Allah has not died, but he has gone to his Lord just as Moses son of 'Imran went, and was absent from his people for forty nights, then returned. By Allah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ will return, and I will cut off the hands and feet of men who claim that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has died." He kept repeating this until Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up, praised Allah, exalted and majestic is He, and extolled Him. Then he said: "O people, whoever used to worship Muhammad, then Muhammad has indeed died. And whoever used to worship Allah, then Allah is living and does not die." Then he recited: ﴿Muhammad is only a Messenger; messengers have passed away before him﴾, the verse. The narrator said: "By Allah, it was as if the people had not known that this verse had been revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ until Abu Bakr recited it." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "By Allah, it was only that I heard Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, reciting it, and I was struck down, so that my legs could not carry me, and I knew that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had indeed died."

﴿And whoever turns back on his heels﴾: by turning away from what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to devote himself to, such as the matter of jihad and other things.

(p-94) It has also been said: by his apostasy from Islam. No one among the Muslims apostatised on that day except those who were among the hypocrites.

﴿Then he will not harm Allah﴾ by what he did of turning back.

﴿at all﴾: that is, not any harm. He harms only himself by exposing himself to wrath and punishment.

﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾: that is, those who remain steadfast upon the religion of Islam, which is the greatest blessing and the most excellent favour. They were called grateful because remaining steadfast upon it is thankfulness to Him and acknowledgement of His right. In this there is an allusion to the ingratitude of those who turned back. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that by them is meant: those who obeyed Allah, exalted is He, from among the Emigrants and the Helpers. And from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: Abu Bakr and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them. And from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Abu Bakr is among the grateful and among the beloved ones of Allah, exalted is He." The use of the noble Name in the place of the pronoun is to highlight greater attention to the matter of their reward.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 145:

﴿And it is not for any soul to die except by permission of Allah﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf) brought forth to draw attention to their error in what they did, out of fear of their being killed, and on the basis of the rumour spread about his being killed (ʿalayhi al-salatu wal-salam), by clarifying that the death of every soul is bound to the will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; it hardly occurs without its being attached to Him, even if souls plunge into the places of fear and force their way into the straits of every terrifying calamity. By this it is indicated that its death was not attached to the time in which they feared it, and for this reason they were not killed at that time, not because of their reluctance to engage directly in fighting. The word "kana" (was) is defective (naqisa), its subject (ism) is "an tamuta" (that it should die), and its predicate (khabar) is the adverbial phrase (al-zarf), understood as being related to an elided element (mahdhuf). The saying of the Exalted: ﴿except by permission of Allah﴾ is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of causes, meaning: death does not come to any soul among souls through any cause among causes except by His will, Exalted is He. The "permission" is a metaphor for it, since it is one of its necessary consequences; or [it means] except by His permission to the Angel of Death in seizing its spirit. The discourse is framed as an illustration by depicting death in relation to souls in the form of voluntary actions which the agent cannot bring about or undertake without the permission of Allah, Exalted is He; or by treating their undertaking of its beginnings, namely fighting, as if it were the undertaking of death itself, for the sake of intensifying the establishment of the aim. For if their death is impossible to occur when they undertake it, or its beginnings and their striving to bring it about, then it is all the more impossible, and more evident, when that is absent. In this there is an incitement to fighting that is not hidden.

﴿a decree﴾ is an infinitive (masdar) emphasising the meaning of what precedes it, meaning: Allah decreed it as a decree.

﴿a term appointed﴾ means determined by a known time that does not advance or delay even by an hour. It is read "mu'ajjalan" with a waw in place of the hamza, according to the analogy of lightening (takhfif). And after establishing that the pivot of death and life is purely the will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, without any entry for anyone at all, it is indicated that the fulfilment of the fruits of deeds depends on their intentions, so that they may turn them from base aims to lofty objectives. Thus it is said: ﴿And whoever desires﴾, meaning: by his deed.

﴿the reward of this world, We shall give him﴾ with the plural of majesty (nun al-ʿazama), by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

﴿of it﴾ meaning: of its reward, whatever We will to give him of it, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Whoever desires the hasty [life], We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We desire﴾. This is an allusion to those whom the spoils preoccupied on that day, and its detailed explanation has passed.

﴿And whoever desires﴾ meaning: by his deed.

﴿the reward of the Hereafter, We shall give him of it﴾ meaning: of its reward, what We will of multiplications, according to what the gracious promise has established.

﴿And We shall reward the thankful﴾: those who give thanks for the blessing of Islam, who remain steadfast upon it, turning what Allah, Exalted is He, has given them of powers and capacities toward that for which they were created, namely the obedience of Allah, Exalted is He, no turner whatsoever turning them from that at all. By "them" is meant either the known fighters among the martyrs and others, or the class of the thankful, of whom they are included in the first instance. The clause is a parenthetical statement confirming the meaning of what precedes it and a promise of an increase upon it. In beginning it with "sa-" (surely) and leaving the reward indefinite, there is emphasis and an indication of the magnitude of the reward's rank, such that speech falls short of it, which is not hidden. The three verbs are also read with the letter ya' (third-person form).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 146:

﴿And how many﴾ is an independent (mubtada') statement that censures them for their shortcoming and the evil of their conduct in turning away from the ways of the godly (rabbaniyyun) who strove in the way of Allah alongside the earlier Messengers, peace be upon them. "Ka'ayyin" is a compound word made of the kaf of comparison (kaf al-tashbih) and ayyin, and after the compounding the word acquired the meaning of multiplicity, as in "kadha wa kadha." The nun is a tanwin (nunation) that was written in the script contrary to analogy (qiyas). There are five dialectal forms (lughat) of it, of which this is the first. The second is "ka'in," like "kha'in." The third is "ka'yin," like "ka'yin." The fourth is "kay'in," with a sukun-ed ya followed by a kasra-ed hamza, which is a transposition (qalb) of what precedes it. The fifth is "ka'n," like "ka'an." All of these have been read. Its position (mahall) is nominative (raf') by virtue of being the subject (ibtida'). His words, exalted is He: ﴿from a prophet﴾ are a specifier (tamyiz) for it, because it is like "kam" (how many) in its declarative use. Its tamyiz has also come in the accusative, as in the verse:

"I drive away despair with hope, so how many a hope—its ease has been decreed after hardship."

His words, exalted is He: ﴿there fought with him many godly men﴾ are the predicate (khabar) for it, on the basis that the verb is attributed to an explicit noun, and the linking element (rabit) is the genitive pronoun in "ma'ahu" (with him). It has been read "qutila" and "quttila" in the passive form, both light and emphatic. "Al-Ribbiyyun" is a relative adjective derived from "al-Rabb," like "al-Rabbani," and the kasra on the ra' is one of the changes of the relative form. It has also been read with a damma and a fatha, on the original pattern. It has been said that it is derived from "al-Ribbah," which means a group, meaning: many prophets fought alongside him, to raise the word of Allah and strengthen His religion, pious scholars, or worshippers, or many groups. The adverbial phrase is then connected to "fought," or to an omitted element that falls as a circumstantial clause (hal) from its subject, as in the last two readings, since there is no possibility in them of its being connected to the verb. That is, they were killed or were slain, being with him in the fighting, not in the killing. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "We have not heard of a prophet being killed in battle." Al-Hasan al-Basri and a group of the great scholars said: "No prophet was ever killed in war." It has been said: the verb is attributed to the pronoun of the prophet, and the adverbial phrase is connected to an omitted element that falls as a circumstantial clause from him, and the linking element is the genitive pronoun referring back to him. This is clear according to the well-known reading without disagreement. That is: how many a prophet fought, being with him in the fighting, many godly men. As for the last two readings, it is not apparent, especially according to the reading with the emphatic form, though some have permitted it and supported it on the grounds that the core of the rebuke is their faltering because of the rumour of his death, peace be upon him. That is: how many a prophet was killed, being with him in the killing or in the fighting, godly men, etc.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿so they did not weaken﴾ are coordinated (ataf) with "fought," on the basis that what is meant is the absence of the weakness that would be expected from fighting, as in your saying: "I admonished him and he did not heed, and I shouted at him and he did not desist." The bringing of a thing after the occurrence of what requires abandoning it, although on the surface it is a continuation of it, is in reality a fresh act, which justifies the entry of the fa' that orders it after what precedes it. That is: they did not slacken, and their resolve was not broken.

﴿For what befell them﴾ in the course of fighting. It is the cause of the negated element, not of the negation. Indeed, his words, exalted is He: ﴿in the way of Allah﴾ hint at its cause, for the fact that this is in His way, glorious and majestic is He, is among the things that strengthen their hearts and remove their weakness. The "ma" is either a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun. If the two pronouns are taken to refer to all the godly men, then it is an expression for what is other than being killed, such as wounds and all the other hardships that befall everyone. If the two are taken to refer to the remaining ones after the others were killed, as is most suitable to the context of rebuking those who gave way after the martyrs were martyred, then it is an expression for what was mentioned together with what befell them of the killing of their brothers, from fear, grief, and other things. This is according to the well-known reading. As for the last two readings: if the verb is attributed to the godly men, then the two pronouns necessarily refer to the remaining ones among them; and if it is attributed to the pronoun of the prophet, as is most suitable to the rebuke for giving way because of the rumour of his death, peace be upon him, then the two also refer to the remaining ones, if it is taken that the godly men were with him in the killing, and to all of them if it is taken that they were with him in the fighting.

﴿And they did not become weak﴾ before the enemy. It has been said: before the struggle. It has been said: in religion.

﴿And they did not submit﴾, that is, they did not yield to the enemy. Its root is "istakanna," from "sukun" (stillness), because the one who submits becomes still before his master so that he may do with him what he wishes. The alif is from lengthening the fatha, or it is "istakawna," from "kawn" (being), because it seeks to be for one to whom it submits. This is an allusion to what befell them of weakness and breaking when the unbelievers gained power over them and spread the rumour of the death of the Prophet ﷺ, and to their weakness at that time in striving against the polytheists and their submission to them, when they wished to seek the support of Ibn Ubayy the hypocrite in seeking safety from Abu Sufyan.

﴿And Allah loves the patient﴾, that is, those who endure hardships and bear adversities in the way of Allah, so He helps them and magnifies their station. By "the patient" is meant either those already mentioned, with the explicit noun used in place of the pronoun to praise them for the goodness of their patience and to indicate the reason for the ruling, or the category in general, into which they enter as a first and primary inclusion. The sentence is a concluding summation (tadhyil) of what precedes it.

﴿وَما كانَ قَوْلَهُمْ﴾ is a statement explaining their verbal virtues, conjoined to the preceding clauses that explain their physical virtues. The accusative ﴿قَوْلَهُمْ﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of kana (the verb "was"), and its subject (ism) is "an and what follows it" in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿إلا أنْ قالُوا﴾. The exception here is an incomplete exception (istithna' mufarragh, an exception whose excluded element is not stated, so it is read against the most general category), from the most general of things. That is: their saying, at any encounter with the enemy, in the entering of the narrow passes of war, and in the afflictions of the various kinds of hardship and terrors that befell them, was not anything at all, except that they said: ﴿رَبَّنا اغْفِرْ لَنا ذُنُوبَنا﴾ ("Our Lord, forgive us our sins"), meaning our minor sins.

﴿وَإسْرافَنا في أمْرِنا﴾ ("and our excess in our affair") means our going beyond the limit in committing major sins. They attributed the sins and the excess to themselves, although they were rabbaniyyun (devoted worshippers of the Lord), free from negligence toward God, in order to belittle them, to regard their aspirations as small, and to ascribe what had befallen them to their own deeds. They put before this the supplication for forgiveness of these, since that was the more important matter given the circumstances, among their supplications, with their saying: ﴿وَثَبِّتْ أقْدامَنا﴾ ("and make our feet firm"), meaning in the places of war, by strengthening and supporting them from Your presence, or make us firm upon Your true religion.

﴿وانْصُرْنا عَلى القَوْمِ الكافِرِينَ﴾ ("and help us against the disbelieving people") is a means of bringing the supplication near to acceptance, for a supplication accompanied by humility and issuing from purity and cleanness is closer to being answered. The meaning is that they continued to be constant in this supplication, without any utterance issuing from them that would suggest a trace of anxiety, weakness, or wavering in the positions of war and the watch-posts of religion. In this there is an implicit reproach of those who fled, which is not hidden.

Ibn Kathir and 'Asim, in one narration from them, read ﴿قَوْلُهُمْ﴾ with the nominative, taking it as the subject, and the predicate is "an and what is in its scope, meaning: their saying at that time was not anything at all except this saying which indicates the finest of virtues. This, as you see, is more firmly grounded in meaning and better suited to the requirement of the context, because the information that their absolute saying is characterized by the particular saying of theirs related in detail, as their reading of it indicates, gives the listener more benefit than the information that the particularity of their mentioned saying is their saying. This is because the locus of benefit and the position of clarification in declarative sentences is the predicate, so what is more deserving of the predicate role is what gives more benefit and more clearly indicates the event, and what contains more specific relations that are remote from occurrence in external reality and in the hearer's mind. It is not hidden that this is more complete and perfect here with "an and what is in its scope. As for what the genitive construction indicates of the general, absolute, comprehensive relation, since it is easy to attain both externally and mentally, its proper treatment is to be considered in an aesthetic manner and made a heading for the subject, not something intended in itself in the domain of clarification. The majority chose what they chose on account of a technical rule: that when two definites are combined, the more definite of them deserves the role of the nominal (ism). There is no doubt about the greater definiteness of "an qalu," because it indicates the mode of the relation and the time of the event, and because it resembles a pronoun in that it is described but is not itself used as a descriptor, while qawluhum is a construct attached to a pronoun, so it is in the position of a proper noun. So reflect.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 148:**

﴿So Allah gave them﴾ because of their supplication that (said).

﴿the reward of this world﴾, i.e., victory, spoils, honour, and a good remembrance.

﴿and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾, i.e., the good reward of the Hereafter, which is the Garden and everlasting bliss. The specification of the attribute of goodness (husn) to it is to announce its excellence and distinction, and that it is what is reckoned of value in His sight, exalted is He.

﴿And Allah loves the good-doers﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) confirming the content of what precedes it. For Allah's love toward the servant is an expression of His being pleased with him and His willing good for him, so it is the source of every happiness. The lam (in al-muhsinin) is either for specification (al-'ahd), referring to those previously mentioned, and the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun of those referred to in order to indicate that what was related of their actions and words is from the category of good-doing; or it is for the genus (al-jins), and they are included in it as primary inclusion. This latter is more suitable to the context of encouraging the believers to attain the noble virtues related of them.

﴿O you who have believed﴾: this begins the warning against following the disbelievers, showing that such following leads to the loss of both this world and the Hereafter. It comes after encouraging them to emulate the helpers of the prophets, peace be upon them, by showing that such emulation leads to their success in the happiness of both abodes. The address opens with the vocative and the attention-drawing particle to show concern for what falls within its scope. Describing them with faith reminds them of their state and firms them up in it, by showing how it contrasts with the state of their enemies. Likewise, describing the hypocrites with disbelief in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿If you obey those who disbelieve﴾, serves this same purpose, intending greater aversion from them and warning against obeying them.

Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: It was revealed concerning the saying of the hypocrites to the believers at the time of the defeat, "Return to your brothers and enter into their religion." Accordingly, the placement of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿they will turn you back on your heels﴾ as the answer to the conditional clause, although it is in effect as if it were said: "If you obey them in their saying, 'Return to your brothers and enter into their religion,' they will bring you into their religion," is by considering it a preparation for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and you will turn back as losers﴾, meaning, losing both this world and the Hereafter, gaining nothing of either, and falling into the everlasting punishment. Turning back on one's heels is also a sign of the reversal of affairs and a proverb for reverting after having advanced (al-hawr ba'da al-kawr, lit. "reverting after wrapping," i.e., regression after progress).

It was also said: the intended people are the Jews and Christians, since they used to seduce them, cast doubts into their religion, and say, "If he were truly a prophet, he would not have been defeated, and what befell him and his companions would not have befallen them. He is merely a man whose state is like that of other people: a day for him and a day against him."

It was also said: they are Abu Sufyan and his companions, and obeying them means seeking their safe-conduct and submitting to them.

It was also said: the relative pronoun is general, and the meaning is the prohibition of the believers from obeying them in any matter, so that they do not lead them step by step to apostasy from the religion. (p-98) According to these interpretations, there is no need for the explanation that has passed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 150:

﴿Nay, Allah is your Protector﴾. This is a turning away (idrab) from what is understood from the content of the conditional clause, as if it were said: "They are not your helpers, so that you should obey them. Rather, Allah is your Helper, none other, so obey Him and dispense with them through Him, having no need of their alliance." It is also read with the accusative (nasb), as if it were said: "So do not obey them, but obey Allah." And "Protector of you" (mawlakum) is in the accusative as an attribute (sifah) of Him.

﴿And He is the best of helpers﴾. So single Him out for obedience and for seeking help.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 151:

﴿We shall cast﴾ with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azamah), by way of iltifat (the shift from one grammatical person to another), in keeping with the manner of Divine majesty, so as to cultivate awe. It is also read with the ya' and the sin, to emphasise the casting.

﴿terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ with the 'ayn pronounced with a sukun (al-ru'b). It is also read with a damma on it, according to the original form, and it refers to the fear that was cast into their hearts on the Day of Uhud, so that they abandoned the fighting and returned without any cause, while they had the strength and the upper hand.
