It is also said: they went towards Mecca, and when they were part of the way they said: "We have accomplished nothing. We killed some of them and then left them, while we were the conquerors. Return and utterly destroy them." At that point Allah the Exalted cast terror into their hearts, so they held back. Therefore it must be that the revelation of the verse occurred in the midst of the battle or immediately after its conclusion. It is also said: it is what was cast into their hearts of terror on the Day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab).

﴿because they associated partners with Allah﴾ is connected to "We shall cast," not to "terror," and "ma" is a verbal-masdar particle (masdariyyah), i.e., "because of their associating partners with Him, the Exalted," for it is one of the causes of their being forsaken and of the believers' victory over them, and both of these are among the motivations for terror.

﴿for which He had sent down no authority﴾ i.e., for their associating partners with Him.

﴿authority (sultan)﴾ i.e., proof (hujjah). It is so named because of its clarity, its brilliance, its strength, or its penetrating force. Mentioning that it was not sent down, despite the impossibility of its realisation in itself, belongs to the type of the saying:

"And you do not see the lizard (dabb) being cornered by it,"

i.e., there is no lizard and no cornering. In this there is an indication that what is to be followed in this matter is heavenly evidence, not opinions and baseless desires.

﴿Their abode﴾ is an explanation of their state in the Hereafter following the explanation of their state in this world, which is terror; i.e., that to which they retreat in the Hereafter.

﴿is the Fire﴾ there is no refuge for them other than it.

﴿and evil is the abode of the wrongdoers﴾ i.e., their abode. The explicit noun mentioned was placed in the position of the pronoun for the sake of intensification (taghlizh), causation (ta'lil), and the indication that they are wrongdoers in their associating partners, placing a thing in other than its proper place. The one to whom blame is attributed is omitted, i.e., "evil is the abode of the wrongdoers: the Fire." In making it "their abode" after making it "their refuge" there is a kind of allusion to their eternal dwelling therein, for the mathwa is the place of residence which indicates lingering, whereas the ma'wa is the place to which a person retreats.

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 3, verse 152:

﴿And Allah did indeed fulfil His promise to you﴾. It is in the accusative as the second object (maf'ul thani) of "sadaqa" (fulfilled) directly. It was also said that it is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning "in His promise." It was revealed when some of the believers said, upon their return to Madinah: "From where has this befallen us, when Allah the Exalted has promised us victory?" This refers to what He had promised them, through the tongue of His Prophet ﷺ, of victory, when he said to the archers: "Do not leave your place. We will not cease to be victorious as long as you remain in your place." In another narration: "Do not leave this place. Indeed, we will not cease to be victorious as long as you remain in this place." And so it was: when the polytheists advanced, the archers began shooting at them, and the rest struck them with swords until they fled, while the Muslims pursued them, slaying them in a devastating slaughter. This is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿when you were routing them﴾, that is, killing them in great numbers, widespread, from "hassa" (to eliminate its sensation), when one destroys its sensation. It is an adverbial of time (zarf) governed by "sadaqakum." His saying, the Exalted: ﴿by His permission﴾, that is, by His facilitation and granting of success in realising that their slaying was by what Allah the Exalted had promised them of victory. It was also said that it refers to what He promised them by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿if you endure and fear Allah﴾, and the verse. It has already been established that this was on the day of Badr. How could it not be, since what was promised with the aforementioned is His, the Mighty and Majestic's, support by sending down the angels, peace be upon them? And restricting the truth of His promise, the Exalted, to the time of their slaying by His permission is explicit that what was promised is the spiritual victory and the facilitation, not the support by the angels. It was also said that it refers to what He, the Exalted, promised by His saying: ﴿We shall cast﴾, and so on.

You should know that the casting of terror occurred at the time they abandoned fighting and returned without cause, or afterwards on the road, according to the two differing narrations. In any case, there is no way for it to be the object of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿until, when you lost courage﴾, that is, you became cowardly and your judgement weakened, or you inclined towards the spoils, for greed stems from weakness of heart.

﴿and you disputed concerning the matter﴾. When the polytheists were routed and turned fleeing, while the Muslims were upon their heels slaying and striking them, some of the archers said: "What is our position here after this?" Their commander, 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "We will not oppose the command of the Messenger ﷺ." So he remained in his place with a group of fewer than ten of his companions, while the rest rushed out for plunder. This is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and you disobeyed after He had shown you what you love﴾, that is, of victory, spoils, and the rout of the enemy. When the polytheists saw this, they attacked them from the direction of the mountain pass, and slew the commander of the archers and those with him of his companions, as detailed in the explanation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾. The answer to "idha" (when) is omitted, and it is: "He withheld His support from you." It was also said that the answer is: "He tested you." This is rejected by making the beginning (ibtida') the limit of the turning away which results from the withholding of support. It was also said that the answer is: "You divided into two groups," as indicated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Among you are those who desire this world﴾, namely those who abandoned the position and turned to plunder, ﴿and among you are those who desire the Hereafter﴾, namely those who remained in their place until they attained the honour of martyrdom. This is on the assumption that "idha" is conditional and "hatta" is inceptive (ibtida'iyya), entering upon the conditional sentence. It was also said that "idha" is a noun, as in their saying: "Idha yaqumu Zayd yaqumu 'Amr" (when Zayd stands, 'Amr stands), and "hatta" is a preposition meaning "until," governing His saying, the Exalted: ﴿sadaqakum﴾ by virtue of its implying the meaning of victory, as if it were said: "Allah had indeed given you victory until the time of your failure and your disputing," and so on. On this view, His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then He turned you away from them﴾ is conjoined to that, and on the first view it is conjoined to the omitted answer, as has been indicated. The two adverbial clauses are a parenthetical insertion between the two conjoined elements, meaning: He restrained you from them until the situation changed and the state turned. And in this there is of gentleness towards the Muslims what is not hidden.

﴿that He might test you﴾, that is, He treats you as one who tests you with calamities, so that your steadfastness in faith may become manifest at that time.

﴿And He has certainly pardoned you﴾ out of bounty, and because He knew of your regret for disobeying.

﴿And Allah is full of bounty toward the believers﴾. This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) that affirms the content of what precedes it, and indicates that this pardon was by way of grace and benevolence, not as an obligation upon Him, meaning: it is His nature to bestow grace upon them with pardon; or He is bounteous towards them in all circumstances, in that the trial was also a mercy, "and He gave them a turn," or "a turn was given against them." The indefiniteness of "fadl" is for magnification. By "the believers" is meant either those addressed, and the use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is for honour and to indicate the reason for the ruling, or the category in general, in which case they are included in the ruling by primary inclusion.

(p-100) ﴿إذْ تُصْعِدُونَ﴾ (when you were going up) is related to "صَرَفَكُمْ" (He turned you away), or to His saying ﴿لِيَبْتَلِيَكُمْ﴾ (that He might test you), or to an implied verb (muqaddar) as they have mentioned. And al-ita'ad (إصعاد, going up) means going away and going far into the land. It has been read as "تَصْعَدُونَ" from the triliteral (ثلاثي) form, meaning: up the mountain. It has been read as "تَصَعَّدُونَ" from the tafa'ul (تفعّل) form by dropping one of the two tas. It has been read as "يَصْعَدُونَ" with iltifat (التفات, shift) to the third person (الغيبة).

﴿وَلا تَلْوُونَ عَلى أحَدٍ﴾ means: you do not turn to what is behind you, and not one of you stops for another. It has been read as "تَلُونَ" with a single waw, by changing the damma-ed waw into a hamza and then dropping it for lightness (تخفيفًا). It has been read as "يَلْوُونَ" like "يَصْعَدُونَ".

﴿والرَّسُولُ يَدْعُوكُمْ﴾ The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was calling them: « "To me, servants of Allah! To me, servants of Allah! I am the Messenger of Allah. Whoever turns back (يَكُرّ), for him is Paradise"». And mentioning him, peace be upon him, by the title of messengerhood (الرسالة) is to indicate (لِلْإيذانِ) that his call, peace be upon him, was by way of messengerhood from Him, glorified is He, to fully rebuke (إشباعًا في توبيخ) the fleeing (المنهزمين).

﴿فِي أُخْراكُمْ﴾ in your rear (ساقة) and your other group (جماعة).

﴿فَأثابَكُمْ﴾ is conjoined (عطف) to "صَرَفَكُمْ", meaning: then Allah, exalted is He, recompensed you for what you did ﴿غَمًّا﴾ (grief) ﴿بِغَمٍّ﴾ (with grief) joined to it, from being saddened (الاغتمام) by the killing, the wounding, the victory of the polytheists, the rumour (الإرجاف) of the killing of the Messenger ﷺ, and the missing of the spoils. So the indefinite form is for magnification (للتكثير). Or, "غمًّا" is in exchange for (بمقابلة) "غمٍّ" that you caused the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to taste by your disobedience to him.

﴿لِكَيْلا تَحْزَنُوا عَلى ما فاتَكم ولا ما أصابَكُمْ﴾ That is: so that you would train yourselves in patience during hardships, so that you would not grieve over a benefit that had passed or a harm that had come. It was also said: "لا" is superfluous (زائدة), and the meaning is: so that you would feel regret over what had escaped you of victory and spoils, and over what had befallen you of wounds and defeat, as a punishment for you. It was also said: the pronoun in "أثابَكُمْ" refers to the Messenger ﷺ, meaning: he consoled you in the grief, so he grieved over what had descended upon you, just as you grieved over what had descended upon him, and he did not rebuke you for your disobedience, as consolation for you and relief from you, so that you would not grieve over what had escaped you of the victory and what had befallen you of wounds and other things.

﴿واللَّهُ خَبِيرٌ بِما تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ That is: He is aware of your deeds and of what you intended by them.

ثُمَّ أنْزَلَ عَلَيْكُمْ: a conjunction of coordination (ʿaṭf) on His saying, ﴿فَأثابَكُمْ﴾ (then He rewarded you). The address is to the believers in truth.

مِن بَعْدِ الغَمِّ: that is, the grief mentioned. The explicit statement that the sending-down came after it, though "thumma" (then) already indicates this and its remoteness from it, serves to add clarification and to remind of the magnitude of the blessing, as in His saying, ﴿ثُمَّ تابُوا مِن بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ وأصْلَحُوا﴾ (then they repented after that and made amends), and so on.

أمَنَةً: that is, security (amn). It is in the accusative as an object (mafʿūl). His saying, ﴿نُعاسًا﴾ (drowsiness), is either a substitute (badal) for it or an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān). It has been said that it is an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), or that it is the object itself, and ﴿أمَنَةً﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from it, placed before it; or it is a circumstantial clause of purpose, or a circumstantial clause from the addressees on the assumption of an omitted noun, meaning "those possessing security"; or it is the plural of āmin (secure), like barr and baraera. It was also read with the letter mīm vowelless, as if it were a single instance of security (amn). The fronting of the two adverbial phrases before the direct object is for the reason mentioned more than once: the emphasis on what is placed first and the building of anticipation for what is delayed. The singling out of fear from among the kinds of grief for removal is because it was the most important concern for them at that time, since when the polytheists withdrew they kept threatening the Muslims that they would return, so the believers did not feel safe from their renewed attack. They were under their shields, ready for battle, so Allah the Exalted sent down security upon them, and drowsiness overtook them. Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "He gave them security on that day through drowsiness that covered them after fear, for only one who feels secure dozes off, and the one in fear does not sleep." Al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) when fear grew intense, and Allah sent down sleep upon us. By Allah, I was hearing the words of Muʿattib ibn Qushayr while drowsiness was covering me; I heard them only as in a dream, as he said: 'If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here.'" Abū Ṭalḥa (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I raised my head on the day of Uhud, and I did not see anyone among the people except that he was swaying beneath his shield from drowsiness." He said: "I was among those overcome by drowsiness that day; the sword would fall from my hand and I would pick it up, then the whip would fall from my hand and I would pick it up." In this is an indication that among the believers there were some upon whom drowsiness did not fall, as His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, indicates: ﴿يَغْشى طائِفَةً مِنكُمْ﴾ (He covers a group of you). Ibn ʿAbbās said: "They are the Emigrants and most of the Helpers." This does not undermine the generality of the sending-down for all. The clause is in the accusative place, as it is a qualifier (ṣifa) of "nuʿāsan" (drowsiness). It was also read with the letter tāʾ, as a qualifier of ﴿أمَنَةً﴾. In this reading there is the point that the qualifier ought to precede the substitute and the explanatory apposition, and should not be separated from the qualified noun by the object of purpose, and that the customary practice is to speak about the substitute rather than the thing substituted for.

﴿وَطائِفَةٌ قَدْ أهَمَّتْهم أنْفُسُهُمْ﴾ (and a group, their own selves had distressed them): that is, their selves had brought them into anxieties and sorrows; or, there was nothing troubling them except the concern of their own selves. The intent of its being freed from it comes from their saying, "the matter concerned me" (hammanī al-shayʾ), meaning it was of my resolve and aim. The restriction is derived with the help of the context. "Ṭāʾifa" (group) is the subject (mubtadaʾ), and what follows it is either its predicate (khabar), and that is permissible despite its being indefinite because it relies on the conjunction "wāw" of circumstance, as in the verse:

*We travelled while a star had shone, but since your face appeared, its light has hidden every dawn-star.*

Or because it occurs in a position of detailing, as in the verse:

*When she weeps behind her, she turns toward him with one half [of her face], and the other half, with us, has not turned.*

Or its qualifier is what follows, and the predicate is omitted, meaning: "and with you is a group," or "there is," and it has been said its supposed form is: "and among you is a group." In this there is the implication that it requires the hypocrites to be included in the address with the sending-down of security. In any case, the clause is either circumstantial, explaining the horror of the terror and emphasizing the magnitude of the blessing of deliverance from it, as in His saying, ﴿أوَلَمْ يَرَوْا أنّا جَعَلْنا حَرَمًا آمِنًا ويُتَخَطَّفُ النّاسُ مِن حَوْلِهِمْ﴾ (Do they not see that We made a secure sanctuary while people are being snatched away all around them?); or it is a new clause (istiʾnāf) brought to explain the state of the hypocrites. His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿يَظُنُّونَ بِاللَّهِ﴾ (they think about Allah), is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿أهَمَّتْهُمْ﴾, or from "ṭāʾifa," because it is specified by the description, or it is another qualifier of it, or a predicate after a predicate, or a new clause explaining what precedes it. His saying, ﴿غَيْرَ الحَقِّ﴾ (other than the truth), is in the sense of a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: they think about Him, Exalted is He, a thought other than the true thought that ought to be held concerning Him, glorified is He. His saying, Exalted is He,

﴿ظَنَّ الجاهِلِيَّةِ﴾ (the thought of the Age of Ignorance) is a substitute from it, and it is the thought particular to the pagan creed. The construction is like "Ḥātim al-Jūd" (Ḥātim of generosity) and "rajul ṣidq" (a man of truth). His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿يَقُولُونَ﴾ (they say), is a substitute from "yaẓunnūn" (they think), because their questioning proceeded from that thought; that is, they say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the form of seeking guidance:

﴿هَلْ لَنا مِنَ الأمْرِ﴾ (Do we have any say in the matter?): that is, in the command of Allah Exalted and His promise of victory and triumph.

﴿مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ (anything): that is, any share at all; or, "do we have any part in the planning?" His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿قُلْ إنَّ الأمْرَ كُلَّهُ لِلَّهِ﴾ (Say: Indeed the entire matter belongs to Allah), means: ultimately the victory belongs to Allah Exalted and to His allies, for the party of Allah are the victors; or, indeed all the planning belongs to Allah, for He Exalted has ordered the matter as it occurred in His prior decree, so there is no turning it back. "Kulluhu" (all of it) was also read in the nominative as a subject (mubtadaʾ). His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿يُخْفُونَ في أنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ (they conceal within themselves): that is, they harbor it within them, or they say among themselves secretly.

﴿ما لا يُبْدُونَ لَكَ﴾ (what they do not reveal to you): a new clause or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "yaqūlūn." His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿إنَّ الأمْرَ﴾ (Indeed the matter...) and so on, is a parenthetical interjection between the circumstantial clause and its subject, meaning: they say what they say while showing that they are seeking guidance and seeking victory, while concealing denial and rejection. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿يَقُولُونَ﴾ (they say), is a new clause that came as an answer to a question arising from what precedes it, as if it were said: "What is it they conceal?" So it was answered: they speak to themselves, or some of them say to others among themselves in secret.

﴿لَوْ كانَ لَنا مِنَ الأمْرِ شَيْءٌ﴾ (If we had any say in the matter): as Muḥammad (peace be upon him) promised, that victory belongs to Allah Exalted and His allies, and that the entire matter belongs to Allah; or, if we had any say in planning and opinion.

﴿ما قُتِلْنا ها هُنا﴾ (we would not have been killed here): that is, we would not have been defeated, or those of us who were killed would not have been killed in this battle. The negation refers to the killing itself, not merely to its occurrence in that place. "And we would not have left our dwellings," as Ibn Ubayy saw it. This is supported by the specifying of the place of killing, and likewise His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿قُلْ لَوْ كُنْتُمْ في بُيُوتِكُمْ﴾ (Say: even if you had been in your houses), that is, even if you had not gone out to Uhud and had stayed in Medina, as they say.

﴿لَبَرَزَ الَّذِينَ كُتِبَ عَلَيْهِمُ القَتْلُ﴾ (those destined for killing would have gone forth): that is, written in the Preserved Tablet, by some cause among the causes that impel one to go forth.

﴿إلى مَضاجِعِهِمْ﴾ (to their places of falling): to their places of death, where Allah Exalted had decreed their killing, and they were definitely killed there; the resolve to remain in Medina would certainly not have availed, for the decree of Allah Exalted is not turned back and His judgment is not overturned. In this there is exaggeration in refuting their false statement, since it was not limited to establishing the act of killing itself, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿أيْنَما تَكُونُوا يُدْرِكْكُمُ المَوْتُ﴾ (Wherever you may be, death will overtake you), but its place was also specified. And there is no doubt that its time is also specified, by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿فَإذا جاءَ أجَلُهم لا يَسْتَأْخِرُونَ ساعَةً ولا يَسْتَقْدِمُونَ﴾ (So when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor advance it). It is narrated that the Angel of Death came to the assembly of Solomon (peace be upon him) and looked at a man among the people of the assembly with a terrifying gaze. When he rose, the man said, "Who is this?" Solomon (peace be upon him) said, "The Angel of Death." He said, "Send me with the wind to another world, for I have seen from him a terrifying sight." So he (peace be upon him) commanded the wind, and it cast him into a remote region of the regions of the world. Then the Angel of Death returned to Solomon (peace be upon him) and said: "I had been commanded to take the soul of that man at this hour in such-and-such a land. When I found him in your assembly, I said, 'When will he reach it, when you have sent him with the wind to that place?' Then I found him there." Thus the decree of Allah the Mighty and Majestic was fulfilled in its time and place without any alteration in any of that. "Kataba" (He wrote) was also read in the active voice with "al-qatl" (killing) in the accusative. "Kutiba ʿalayhimu al-qitāl" (battle was prescribed for them) was also read. "Lubarriza" with the doubled letter was also read, in the passive voice.

﴿وَلِيَبْتَلِيَ اللَّهُ ما في صُدُورِكُمْ﴾ (and that Allah may test what is in your breasts): that is, that He may deal with you as one who tests what is in your breasts of sincerity and hypocrisy, and bring out what is in them of hidden inner states. This is a purpose (ʿilla) of an omitted verb before it, joined by conjunction to other omitted purposes, indicating their multitude. It is as if it were said: "He did what He did for many benefits, and in order to test..." Making these purposes of "barraza" (went forth) is rejected by sound taste, for the context requires explaining the wisdom of what occurred that day of hardship and horror, not the wisdom of the imagined going forth. Or it is a purpose of a verb supposed after it, meaning: and for the aforementioned testing He did what He did, not out of neglect of the affairs of the believers or the like. Supposing the verb in front is free of this virtue.

﴿وَلِيُمَحِّصَ ما في قُلُوبِكُمْ﴾ (and that He may purify what is in your hearts): from hidden matters, and reveal them, or cleanse them from whisperings.

﴿واللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِذاتِ الصُّدُورِ﴾ (and Allah is All-Knowing of what is in the breasts): that is, the secrets and hidden inner thoughts that scarcely leave the breasts but rather remain with them and accompany them. The sentence is either a parenthetical interjection to alert that Allah Exalted is free of need for testing, and He only displays the appearance of testing to train the believers and to make manifest the state of the hypocrites; or it is a circumstantial clause from the object of the two verbs, meaning: He did what He did for testing and purification, while He is free of need of them both, encompassing hidden matters. In this is both a promise and a warning.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 155:

﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two armies met﴾, and they are those who fled on the day of Uhud, as their account has passed.

﴿It was only that Satan caused them to slip﴾, i.e., the cause of their defeat was only that Satan sought to make them slip.

﴿because of some of what they had earned﴾ of sins and disobediences, which are the violation of the command of the Prophet (ﷺ), the abandoning of the post (al-markaz), and greed for booty or for life. Thus they were deprived of support (al-ta'yid) and firmness of heart. It has also been said: the slipping caused by Satan was their turning away, and this was due to sins that had preceded in them, for sins draw one another along, just as obedience does. It has also been said: he caused them to slip through sins that had come before from them, and they disliked being killed before sincerely repenting and leaving the wrongful deed (al-maẓlima).

﴿And certainly Allah has pardoned them﴾ for their repentance and their apology.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾ of sins,

﴿Forbearing﴾, who does not hasten to punish the sinner so that he may repent. The clause is an explanation of what precedes it, in the manner of confirmation, and the displaying of the Divine Name (al-jalala) in it serves to cultivate awe and to emphasize the explanation.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 156:**

﴿O you who have believed, do not be like those who disbelieved﴾. They are the hypocrites (munafiqun) who said: "If we had had any say in the affair, we would not have been killed here." He mentioned their disbelief at the beginning of the relative clause (sila) explicitly, to make clear how different their state is from the state of the believers, and to repel the believers from resembling them, [saying that their condition is like] a trace with a trace (athar dhi athir). His words, exalted is He, ﴿and said of their brothers﴾, specify the aspect of the resemblance and likeness that they were forbidden from, that is: they said it on account of them and concerning them. The meaning of "their brothers" is that they agreed with them in lineage or in creed (madhhab).

﴿when they traveled in the land﴾, that is, they journeyed in it and went far away for trade or for other purposes. The choice of "idha" (when), which indicates the future, over "idha" with the past sense, is to narrate a past situation, since what is meant by it is the continuous time that organizes the state upon which the matter of evoking the image revolves. Al-Zajjaj said: "Idha" here stands in place of past and future time; that is, it is for the mere time, or it is intended to express continuity. Its being a adverbial of place (zarfiyya) for their saying is only in regard to what happened within it. Rather, the verification is that it is an adverbial of place for what happened, not for their saying; as if it were said: They said, on account of what befell their brothers when they traveled, etc.

﴿or were raiders﴾, that is, their brothers.

﴿ghuzzan﴾ is the plural of ghazin, like 'ufan, the plural of 'afin. He said:

*"And a dust-darkened horizon, its landmarks humbled, / for it is a heart of 'ufan, the watering-troughs, a dark-colored one."*

It was also read with the letter zay lightened, by dropping the taa' from ghuzat. The singling out of their being raiders by mention, though it is included under "traveling in the land," is because it is what is intended to be explained in this context. The mention of traveling in the land is a preparation for it, and its being placed first is due to the frequency of its occurrence, though it may occur without traveling in the land, since what is meant by it is long-distance travel. He did not say "or ghazwan" (as a verbal noun) to indicate the continuation of their being characterized by the title of raiders, or the conclusion of that, that is: they were raiders in the past. His words, exalted is He, ﴿if they had been with us﴾, that is, residing [at home].

﴿they would not have died, nor been killed﴾ is the object of "they said," and it is evidence that there is an implied element that has been omitted, relying on its certainty, that is: when they traveled in the land and so died, or were raiders and so were killed. The prohibition does not aim at not resembling them in uttering this statement, but in believing its content and judging by its consequence, just as the one who denies it is the one who denies it upon its speakers. Do you not see His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿so that God may make that a regret in their hearts﴾? For He is the one who certainly placed regret in them. To this it was pointed, as it is transmitted from al-Zajjaj, that it is an indication of their supposition that if they had not attended the fighting, they would not have been killed. Its connection to "they said" is not in terms of their uttering that statement, but in terms of what it contains of judgment and belief. The lam is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾, that is: they said that and believed it, so that it would become a regret in their hearts. What is meant by the aforementioned causal clause is to show that no benefit whatsoever results from that. It has been said: it is a causal clause for the prohibition, in the sense of "do not be like them in uttering that statement" and believing it, so that God, exalted is He, may make it a regret in their hearts specifically, and may protect your hearts from it. That, as has passed, is an indication of what their statement indicates of belief. It may also be an indication of what the prohibition indicates, that is: do not be like them, so that God may make the absence of your being like them a regret in their hearts, for your opposition to them in statement and belief is among what grieves and enrages them.

﴿And God gives life and causes death﴾ is a refutation of their false saying after explaining its harm, that is: He alone is the one who has influence over life and death, without residing or traveling having any role in that. For He, exalted is He, may give life to the traveler and the raider even though they plunge into the sources of death, and may cause death to the resident and the one who sits even though they possess the means of safety.

﴿And God is seeing of what you do﴾ is a warning to the believers not to resemble them. It was also read with the letter ya' (yaʿmalūna, "they do"), so that it becomes a threat to those who disbelieved. "What they do" is general, encompassing their aforementioned statement, its source which is their belief, and the actions that follow from that. For this reason it addressed the title of sight, not the title of hearing. The placing of the noble Name in the position of the pronoun is to cultivate awe, to instill dread, and to intensify the threat and the severity of the warning.

This is the beginning of the discussion on establishing that what they fear, namely being killed or dying in the cause of God Most High as a result of going out to fight and travel, is not something to be feared. Rather, it is something that those who compete should compete for, once its being a consequence of those two things has been negated. The *lam* here is the *lam al-muwatti'ah lil-qasam* (the preparatory lam that introduces an oath), and the *lam* in His words ﴿a forgiveness from God and mercy﴾ is the *lam al-ibtida'* (the lam of inception). The tanwin in both places is for minimization (*lil-taqlil*). The word "min" (from) is attached to an omitted element that functions as an adjective of the subject (*mubtada'*), and the adjective of "mercy" has been omitted because the mentioned element indicates it. The clause is the answer to the oath and takes the place of the answer to the conditional (*sadd masadd jawab al-shart*). The meaning is: travel and fighting are not, in principle, among the things that bring about death or hasten the appointed term. And even if that happens by the command of God Most High, it is only a slight breath of forgiveness and mercy, both from God Most High, in exchange for it.

﴿is better than what they amass﴾, that is, what the disbelievers gather of the benefits and good things of this world for the duration of their lives. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it means "better than the filling of the earth with red gold." It has also been read with the *ta'* (second person), meaning: what you yourselves gather, had you not died. Limiting the statement to the comparison of their superiority, without addressing the actual attainment of the two by them, signals that there is no need to mention it, on the basis that it is impossible for Him to disappoint after raising hopes. It has been said that another omission is necessary, namely: "surely a forgiveness for you from God, etc.," and in that case the omitted element is again placed as an adjective rather than a predicate, for the same reason mentioned, namely the claim that it is evident and needs no statement. The change in order found in their saying "they did not die and were not killed," which is built upon frequency and infrequency of occurrence, is for emphasis in encouraging jihad, by showing the greater excellence of being killed in the cause of God and its superiority in securing forgiveness and mercy. There is clear evidence in this for what was previously mentioned, that the prohibition is aimed only at not resembling them in believing the content of the said statement and acting upon its implications, not at merely uttering it or misleading people with it.

And if you die or are killed, [it is all the same, for] to Allah you will be gathered, [whatever manner of your death may be, according to the operation of the Divine will].

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim):

﴿وَلَئِنْ مُتُّمْ أوْ قُتِلْتُمْ﴾ That is: in whatever manner your destruction comes about, in accordance with the connection of the Divine will. It is also read "mittum" with a kasra on the mim, from "mata yamatu" (to die).

﴿لإلى اللَّهِ﴾ That is: to the Worshipped One (al-Ma'bud) in truth, the One of great station, vast mercy and abundant beneficence.

﴿تُحْشَرُونَ﴾ not to anyone else, so that He will pay you your rewards in full and bestow upon you your gifts abundantly. The discussion concerning the two lams of the sentence (lam al-qasam and lam al-jawab, i.e. the two lams of the oath and its answer) is as it was mentioned in its sister (passage).

﴿So by a mercy from Allah, you were gentle with them﴾ This is a shift of address (iltifat, a change from third person to second person) directed at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The fa' (fa, "so") marks the sequence of the statement according to what the context indicates: that they deserved blame and rebuke by virtue of human nature, or from the vastness of the scope of His forgiveness and mercy, may He be exalted. The ba' (bi, "by") is connected to *linta* ("you were gentle"), and it has been placed before it for restriction (qasr, limiting the meaning). *Ma* is either extra (mazidah) for emphasis or a noun meaning "some." *Rahmah* ("mercy") is a substitute (badal) from it, specifying its indefinite meaning, and the tanwin (nunation) is for magnification. *Min* ("from") is connected to an omitted element that functions as a descriptive modifier of *rahmah*. The meaning is: "So by a great mercy from Allah, you were gentle with them," which is His steadying of your heart and His singling you out for noble character. You were soft-hearted toward them and dealt with them with kindness and gentleness, when you grieved for them after what they did of opposing your command and of your being exposed to the enemy.

﴿And if you had been harsh﴾ (and had not been so, but rather) ﴿harsh﴾ rude in social dealings, in speech and in action. Al-Raghib said: *al-fazz* is one who is ill-natured. Al-Wahidi said: it is one who is hard-sided and bad in character.

﴿hard-hearted﴾ cruel. Al-Kalbi said: harsh in speech and hard-hearted in action.

﴿they would have scattered from around you﴾ they would have dispersed from your presence, would not have remained at ease with you, and would have fallen into the pits of destruction. The fa' in His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿so pardon them﴾ marks the sequence of the pardon, or the command to it, upon what came before. That is: since the matter is as mentioned, pardon them in what concerns your rights, just as Allah has pardoned them.

﴿and ask forgiveness for them﴾ from Allah concerning what relates to His rights, to complete the compassion toward them and to perfect kindness to them.

﴿and consult them in the matter﴾ that is, in the matter of war, since that is what is customary; or in it and in similar matters in which consultation is ordinarily practiced, seeking support from their opinions, comforting their hearts, and preparing the way for the sunnah (practice) of consultation within the community. It has been recited as "and consult them in some of the matter."

﴿And when you have decided﴾ that is, after consultation, upon something, and your soul has become settled in it.

﴿then rely upon Allah﴾ in carrying out your affair in what is most right and best for you, for His knowledge is exclusive to Him, glorified and exalted is He. It has been recited as "then when I have decided" in the first person, meaning: I have decided for you upon something and guided you to it, so rely upon Me and do not consult anyone after that. The shift (iltifat) serves to cultivate awe and to give the reason for, or command of, reliance; for the title of divinity (uluhiyyah), which comprises all attributes of perfection, calls for reliance upon Him, exalted is He, or the command to it.

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who rely [upon Him]﴾ upon Him, exalted is He, so He will support them and guide them to what is good and right for them. This clause gives the reason for relying upon Him, exalted is He.

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿If Allah helps you, none can overcome you﴾ is a resumed sentence (jumlah musta'nifah), brought in through a shift of address (talwin al-khitab, a change in the mode of address) to honour the believers, to make their reliance upon Him obligatory, to urge them to turn to Him, and to warn them against what would lead to His forsaking them. That is: if Allah helps you as He helped you on the Day of Badr, then no one can overcome you. This is by way of negating the genus (nafy al-jins, the negation that encompasses every individual of the category of "one who overcomes"), both in essence and in attribute. Had it been said, "None of you shall be overcome by anyone," it would only indicate the negation of the attribute. Then, the meaning that arises from the apparent wording of the noble verse (p-106), although it is the negation of their being defeated without any reference to the negation of equality, is also what the context requires. Yet what is understood from it with certain understanding is the negation of equality and the affirmation of superiority for the addressees. Thus, when you say, "No one is more generous than so-and-so," or "No one is more excellent than him," what is necessarily understood is that he is more generous than every generous person and more excellent than every excellent person. This is a principle consistent across all languages, and it is not restricted to explicit negation; rather, it applies also to what occurs in the form of a rhetorical interrogation of denial, as in His saying: ﴿And who is more wicked than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ in many places in the Revelation. Among what is a decisive text for what we have mentioned is what occurs in Surah Hud, where after it was said concerning them: ﴿Without doubt, they will be the greatest losers in the Hereafter﴾, for their being greater losers than every loser necessarily entails their being more wicked than every wrongdoer.

﴿And if He forsakes you﴾, as He did on the Day of Uhud. It has also been read as "yukhdhilkum" (yukhdhilkum), from akhdhalahu, meaning when one makes him forsaken (makhdhul).

﴿Then who is there who can help you﴾ is an interrogation of denial, conveying the absence of any helper, in essence and attribute, by way of emphasis.

﴿after Him﴾, that is, after His forsaking you, or after Allah, meaning if you transgress Him.

﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the verb serves to restrict reliance to Him, the Exalted. The "fa" (then) indicates either the consequence of this, or the consequence of the command to rely upon Him, from what has preceded: the addressees' victory if He helps them, and their defeat if He forsakes them. For knowledge of this necessarily requires restricting reliance to Him, the Exalted, without doubt. By "the believers" is meant either the category in general, with the addressees included in it by primary inclusion, or the addressees specifically by way of iltifat (shift in grammatical person). Whichever it is, there is in it an honouring of them through the title of faith, either jointly or individually, and a reason for the necessity of relying upon Him, the Exalted, since the attribute of faith certainly requires it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 161:

﴿And it is not for a prophet﴾ i.e., it is not valid for any prophet of the prophets, nor is it proper for him.

﴿to commit ghulul (embezzlement)﴾ i.e., to betray in the booty. Prophethood is clearly incompatible with it. It is said: ghalla shay'an min al-maghnam, yaghullu ghululan, and aghalla, ighlalan, when one takes it secretly. The intended meaning is either: to absolve the sanctity of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of what the archers suspected of him on the day of Uhud, when they left their position and rushed to the spoils, saying, "We fear that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ will say: whoever takes anything, it is his, and he will not distribute the spoils, as he did not distribute them on the day of Badr." The Prophet ﷺ said to them: "Did I not remind you that you should not leave your position until my command reaches you?" They said: "We left our brothers standing." He, peace be upon him, said: "Rather, you thought that we would embezzle and not distribute among you."

Or it is an emphasis in the prohibition for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, according to what is reported: that he sent out advance units, and the Prophet ﷺ then gained spoils after them, and he distributed them among those present and left nothing for the advance units, so this verse was revealed. The meaning is: it is not for a prophet to give to one group of the army and withhold from others; rather, he must distribute among all equally. The deprivation of some warriors was expressed as ghulul for emphasis.

As for what has been said, that the intended meaning is to absolve him, peace be upon him, of what some hypocrites uttered, since it is reported that a red woolen garment was lost on the day of Badr, and some hypocrites said: "Perhaps the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took it," this is very far-fetched.

It has been read in the passive form, and the meaning is: it is not for him to be found as one who embezzles or to be attributed with embezzlement.

﴿And whoever embezzles will come on the Day of Resurrection with what he embezzled﴾ he will come bearing the very thing he embezzled, carrying it upon his neck, as occurs in the noble hadith. It is reported that he, peace be upon him, said: "Certainly, let me not find any of you coming with a camel that bellows, or a cow that lows, or a sheep that bleats, calling out, 'O Muhammad! O Muhammad!' and I will say: I possess nothing for you from Allah; I have indeed conveyed to you." Or he will come bearing what he has taken of his sin and its burden.

﴿Then every soul will be paid in full for what it earned﴾ i.e., it will be given in full the recompense of what it earned, good or evil, much or little. Placing the earned deed in the position of its recompense is to establish justice, by showing the complete proportion between them, quantitatively and qualitatively, as if they were one thing. In attributing the full payment to every earner and linking it to every deed, although the intended purpose is to explain the condition of the embezzler when he comes on the Day of Resurrection with what he embezzled, there is an indication of the greatness of the matter of that Day and the terror of its arrival, and an exaggeration in explaining the abhorrence of the embezzler's condition, which is not hidden. For since every earner is paid in full the recompense of what he earned, and nothing is diminished from it, even if his offense is very small and insignificant, then it is all the more evident and manifest that nothing should be diminished from the recompense of the embezzler, whose offense is among the greatest of crimes.

﴿And they﴾ i.e., all people, indicated by "every soul."

﴿will not be wronged﴾ by an increase in punishment or a decrease in reward.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 162:

﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾ That is: one who strives to attain it and sets his course toward it wherever he is, by performing acts of obedience and abstaining from what is forbidden, like the Prophet (ﷺ) and whoever walks in his way.

﴿like one who returns﴾ That is: returns.

﴿with wrath﴾ great, whose extent cannot be measured, existing

﴿from Allah﴾ the Exalted, because of his acts of disobedience, like the one who embezzles (ghall) and whoever follows his religion. The purpose is to affirm the negation of embezzlement (ghulul) from the Prophet (ﷺ), and to establish it by confirming the complete contrast between him and the embezzler, since each of the two is described with the opposite of what the other is described with: His pleasure (Allah's) is matched with His wrath, and following (ittiba') with returning (ba'). The combining of the interrogative hamzah and the fa' is to direct the denial toward the supposition of equivalence between the two and the judgment of that equivalence in light of what was mentioned about the state of the embezzler, as if it were said: After the manifestation of his condition, can one who has risen to the highest of the high (ʿIlliyyin) be like one who has sunk to the lowest of the low (Asfal Safilin)? The placing of the noble Name (Allah) in the position where a pronoun would ordinarily stand serves to instill awe and to cultivate reverence.

﴿and his refuge is Hell﴾ Either it is a new independent statement, brought to explain the outcome of the one who returns with the wrath of Allah, the Exalted; or it is conjoined to His words, the Exalted, ﴿returns with wrath﴾, as a conjunction of a nominal clause upon a verbal clause. In either case, it has no place in terms of grammatical case (i'rab).

﴿and evil is the destination﴾ is a concluding parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ tadhyili), and the element specified for blame is omitted, meaning: "and evil is the destination, Hell." The difference between this (maṣir) and (marji') "return/destination" is that the former implies a return contrary to the original state, unlike the latter.

﴿They﴾ refers back to the two groups introduced by the relative pronoun (*al-mawṣūlayn*, "the two connected/relative ones"), according to meaning.

﴿are degrees with Allah﴾ means: they are distinct ranks in His knowledge and judgment. Their differing conditions and states are likened to degrees (*darajāt*) for emphasis, and to signal that there is an inherent difference among them, like degrees, or that they are people possessing degrees.

﴿And Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾ of the deeds and their degrees, so He will recompense them according to them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 164:

﴿Indeed, Allah has bestowed favor﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, meaning: "By Allah, indeed He has bestowed favor," i.e., He has bestowed blessing (an'ama).

﴿upon the believers﴾, i.e., from among his people, peace be upon him.

﴿when He sent among them a messenger from themselves﴾, i.e., from their lineage or from their kind, an Arab like them, so that they could easily understand his speech and be aware of his state in truthfulness and trustworthiness, taking pride in him; and in this there is great honor for them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾. It has also been read as "min anfusihim" (from their noblest), i.e., from their most honorable, for he, peace be upon him, (p-108) was of the most noble of the tribes of the Arabs and their lineages. It has also been read as "lamin manni Allahi ʿala al-mu'minina idh ba'atha" etc., as a predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "His favor is when He sent," etc., or with idh in the place of nominative case as the subject, meaning: "Indeed, the favor of Allah upon the believers is from the time of His sending," etc. Singling them out for the favor, despite the generality of the blessing of the mission for the black and the red, is due to the greater benefit they derive from it, as has passed. His, the Exalted's, statement ﴿from themselves﴾ is related to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of "messenger," meaning: "being from themselves." His, the Exalted's, statement ﴿reciting to them His verses﴾ is another qualifier, meaning: he recites to them the Qur'an after they were people of ignorance, and nothing of the revelation had reached their ears.

﴿And He purifies them﴾ is a conjunction with "reciting," i.e., He purifies them from the filth of natures, the corruption of beliefs, and the burdens of sins.

﴿and teaches them the Book and the wisdom﴾, i.e., the Qur'an and the Sunnah. This is another qualifier of "messenger," arranged in existence after the recitation. He placed purification between them, which is an expression for the perfecting of the soul in accordance with the practical faculty and its refinement, branching from its perfecting in accordance with the theoretical faculty, which is attained through teaching that follows recitation, to indicate that each of the matters arranged is a great blessing in its own right, deserving of gratitude. Had the order of existence been observed, as in His, the Exalted's, statement ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses and teach them the Book and the wisdom and purify them﴾, the understanding would immediately count all of them as one blessing. This is the secret in expressing the Qur'an sometimes as "verses" and other times as "the Book and the wisdom," as a symbol that, with regard to each title, it is a blessing in its own right. This does not conflict with the inclusion of wisdom in the noble hadiths' contents of the sharia rulings, as has passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

﴿And indeed they were before﴾, i.e., before his, peace be upon him, mission, purification, and teaching.

﴿in manifest error﴾, i.e., clear, with no doubt that it was error. "In" is the lightened form of the heavy one, the pronoun of the matter is omitted, and the lam distinguishes it from the negating "in." The first adverbial phrase is superfluous, connected to "kana," and the second is its predicate; together with its predicate, it is the predicate of the lightened "inna" whose noun is omitted, namely the pronoun of the matter. It has been said: it is a negating "in," and the lam means "illa" (except), i.e., "and they were not before except in manifest error." In either case, the clause is either a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object pronoun in "yu'allimuhum," or a new independent clause, and under both assessments it clarifies the completeness and perfection of the blessing.

(p-109) Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 3, verse 165:

﴿Why, when a calamity afflicted you, though you had inflicted twice as much (on the enemy), do you say, "How is this?"﴾ This is an independent statement, brought in to refute some of the corrupt suppositions and false sayings that issued from them, arising after the refutation of some other of them. The hamza (the interrogative particle, here "a") is for rebuke and affirmation, and the waw (the conjunction "wa") is coordinating, its complement being attached to something omitted before it. "Lamma" (when) is an adverbial term governing ﴿qultum﴾ ("you said"), and it is put in the genitive by what follows it. ﴿Qad asabtum﴾ ("you had inflicted") is in the nominative position, being a qualifier of ﴿musibah﴾ ("calamity"). What is meant by it is what afflicted them on the day of Uhud, namely the killing of seventy of them; and by "twice as much" (mithlayha) is meant what afflicted the polytheists on the day of Badr, namely the killing of seventy of them and the capture of seventy. "How is this?" (anna hadha) is the speech that is said by "you said." The placing of the adverbial term and what is connected to it between the hamza and it, although it is the thing whose denial is intended, and the conjunction waw being in reality for emphasizing the denunciation and intensifying the rebuke, since doing an ugly act at an improper time is uglier, and denouncing its doer is more fitting. The meaning is: at the time when a portion of what they had inflicted on you from the polytheists had been inflicted on them by you before that, you became distressed and said, "From where has this befallen us?!" The promise of victory had already preceded, so the denial and rebuke are directed at the utterance of that saying from them at that particular time, on the basis that it was not a context that would prompt it, but rather a context that would prompt its absence; for the fact that the calamity of their enemy was twice their calamity is something that eases the matter and produces consolation. Or (the meaning is): "Did you do what you did, and when its harm afflicted you, you said, 'How is this?'", with the denial directed at their finding the occurrence strange while they were directly involved in its cause. The demonstrative "this" (hadha) in "how is this?" is masculine, although it refers to the calamity, not because the calamity is an expression for killing or the like, but because their pointing was only to what they had witnessed on the battlefield as it was, without the thought of naming it by any name, let alone by the name "calamity"; that naming occurred only at the time of narration.

﴿Say: it is from yourselves.﴾ His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, is a command to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he should answer their corrupt question after establishing its corruption through denial and rebuke, and should silence them: that what befell them came to them only from their own side, through their abandoning the post and their greed for booty. It is said: through their choosing to leave Medina. This is repudiated by the fact that the promise of victory came after that, as mentioned at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And God had indeed fulfilled His promise to you﴾ (the verse), and by the fact that the Prophet's (ﷺ) acting upon its requirement removed the danger from him and lightened their offense in it; moreover, the choice to go out and insistence upon it came from those whom God honored with martyrdom on that day, and where are they from uttering such a word? It is also said: through their taking ransom on the day of Badr before they were permitted. The first is the more evident and stronger, and what supports it is the placement of the address to the Messenger (ﷺ) between the two addresses directed to the believers, and the delegation of the rebuke to him, peace be upon him, for the rebuke of the doer for an act, when it comes from one who had forbidden him from it, is more forceful in its effect.

﴿Indeed God is over all things Competent.﴾ Among that is victory upon obedience and abandonment upon opposition; and since you departed from obedience, there befell you from Him, Exalted is He, what befell you. The sentence is a concluding statement confirming the content of what precedes it, included under the command.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 166:

﴿And what afflicted you﴾ is a return to address the believers, following the address to him (peace be upon him) with a secret that calls for it, and a guidance for them to the path of truth regarding what they asked about, and an explanation of some of the wisdoms and benefits in it, and a repelling of what might be imagined from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is from yourselves﴾, namely their independence in the occurrence of the event. The turning away from the pronoun to what has been mentioned serves to magnify the matter and to increase its affirmation by stating its time with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿on the day the two hosts met﴾, that is, your host and the host of the polytheists.

﴿By the permission of Allah﴾, that is, it occurred by His decree and by His leaving the disbelievers free; this is called permission because it is one of its necessary consequences.

﴿And that He might make evident the believers﴾ is conjoined to His saying, ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, as the conjunction of the effect to the cause, and what is meant by knowing (ʿilm) is distinguishing (tamyiz) and making manifest (izhar) among the people.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 3, Verse 167**

﴿And that He might know those who were hypocrites﴾. It is conjoined (ʿaṭf, coordination) to what precedes it, with the same kind of verb. The verb is repeated to honour the believers and to free them from being grouped with the hypocrites. It also signals that the knowledge differs according to its relation to the two groups. For it relates to the believers in the same manner as its earlier relation, and to the hypocrites in a new way. This is the reason the first group is introduced with the active participle (ism al-fa'il), which indicates continuity, and the second with a relative clause (mawsul) whose predicate (silah) is a verb indicating occurrence (ḥudūth). The meaning is: "And what afflicted you on that day was by the will of God, in order to distinguish those who remained steadfast in faith from those who displayed hypocrisy."

﴿And it was said to them﴾. It is conjoined to "they were hypocrites" and is included with it within the scope of the relative clause, or it is an independent statement. Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: "When ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions turned away from the Messenger of God ﷺ on the day of Uhud, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn Haram said to them: 'I remind you of God, do not forsake your Prophet and your people.' He called them to fight, and this is the meaning of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Come, fight in the way of God, or defend﴾." Al-Suddi said: "Defend us against the enemy by increasing our numbers, if you will not fight with us." It was also said: "Or defend your families, your land and your sanctuary, if you will not fight in the way of God, exalted is He." The omission of the conjunction between ﴿تَعالَوْا﴾ ("come") and "قاتِلُوا" ("fight") is because the intended object of both is one, namely the second. The first is mentioned as a preparation for it and an encouragement towards it, because it implies mutual support and cooperation.

﴿They said﴾. This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), given as an answer to a question that the discourse implies, as if it were said: "What did they do when they were offered the two options mentioned?" It was answered: they said: ﴿If we knew how to fight, we would certainly follow you﴾. That is, "If we were skilled at fighting and were able to do it." They said this out of deceit and mockery. The negation of the ability to fight is expressed through the negation of knowledge of it, because the ability to perform voluntary acts entails knowledge of them. Alternatively, the meaning is: "If we knew what could be called fighting, we would have followed you. But what you are engaged in is not fighting at all; it is only casting oneself into destruction." In their making the consequence merely "following" rather than "fighting," which is the actual aim of the call, there is evidence of the complete extent of their discouragement from fighting, since their souls would not accept making it the consequent of a premise that is impossible to occur.

﴿They were, on that day, nearer to disbelief than to faith﴾. The pronoun is the subject (mubtada'), and "aqrab" ("nearer") is its predicate. The prepositional phrases ﴿لِلْكُفْرِ﴾ ("to disbelief"), ﴿لِلإيمانِ﴾ ("to faith"), ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾ ("on that day") and "minhum" ("than them") are all related to it. The rule that two particles identical in form and meaning cannot be governed by one operator without a conjunction or apposition applies only to operators other than the elative (af'al al-tafdil), because the operating aspect is one. As for the elative, since it indicates the basic act together with its increase, it functions as if it were two operators. It is as though it were said: "Their nearness to disbelief exceeds their nearness to faith." It was also said that the two prepositional phrases are related to it because they resemble the two adverbs of time and place, meaning: "They were nearer to disbelief than to faith on the day when they said what they said, for before that they used to display faith, and no sign appeared from them indicating their disbelief. When they withdrew from the army of the Muslims and said what they said, they moved away thereby from the faith ascribed to them and drew near to disbelief." It was also said: "They were nearer, in terms of support, to the people of disbelief than to the people of faith, because diminishing the number of the Muslims by withdrawal strengthens the polytheists."

﴿They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts﴾. This is a resumptive sentence that confirms the content of what precedes it. The mention of the mouths and the hearts is a depiction of their hypocrisy and a clarification of the difference between their outward and inward states. "Ma" (what) refers to the speech, and what is meant by it is either the very statement, which appears on the tongue at one time and in the heart at another, so that the affirmed and the negated are identical in essence though different in manifestation. Or it refers to the spoken utterance alone, and then the negated element is its source, which the utterance never separates from at all. It is expressed by the utterance only to show the close connection between them. That is: they utter a statement for which there is no existence, or whose source is absent from their hearts altogether, from among the falsehoods of which the earlier-reported words are a part. In these words they displayed two things of which there was nothing in their hearts: first, the lack of knowledge of fighting; second, following on the supposition of knowing it. In both they lied a clear lie, for they knew it, and were not intending to follow, but rather they were persisting, along with that, in withdrawing, determined to apostatize.

﴿And God knows best what they conceal﴾. This is an addition for the confirmation of their disbelief and hypocrisy, by explaining that their hearts are occupied with what contradicts their words, of the various kinds of evil and corruption, following the statement of their being empty of what would agree with them. The elative form is used because some of what they conceal, concerning the rulings of hypocrisy, the disparagement of the believers, the criticism of their opinions, the rejoicing at their misfortune, and other things, is known to the believers in general terms, while the details and the modes of these matters are exclusive to the divine knowledge.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 168:

﴿Those who said﴾ is in the nominative case, either as a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for the *waw* of "yaktumuna" (they conceal), or as the *khabar* (predicate) of an omitted *mubtada'* (subject). It is also said that it is a *mubtada'* whose *khabar* is ﴿Say: "Avert﴾, with the returning pronoun omitted, its full sense being "Say to them," and so on. It may be in the accusative case as a *dhamm* (expression of censure), or as a *na't* (qualifier) of "those who were hypocrites," or as a *badal* of it. It is also said that it is in the genitive case as a *badal* of the pronoun in "their mouths" or "their hearts," as in the line of verse:

"Upon his generosity, Hatim would indeed be stingy with water."

By them is meant 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions.

﴿concerning their brothers﴾, i.e., on their account. The brothers are those among their own kind or relatives who were killed on the day of Uhud, so that some of the martyrs are included among them.

﴿and sat back﴾ is a *hal* (circumstantial clause) relating to the pronoun in "said," with "qad" implied, meaning: they said while they had sat back from fighting by abandoning the army.

﴿Had they obeyed us﴾, i.e., in what we ordered them to do, and agreed with us in that.

﴿they would not have been killed﴾, just as we were not killed. This indicates that they had instructed them to abandon the fight when they themselves abandoned it, and had led them astray just as they themselves had gone astray. To take "sitting back" as referring to what Ibn Ubayy approved during the consultation, namely remaining in Madinah at the outset, and to take "obedience" as meaning acceptance of his opinion and acting upon it, is refuted by the fact that the clause is circumstantial, since its purpose is to specify what constitutes disobedience and opposition. Moreover, Ibn Ubayy was not among those who sat back in that sense. Furthermore, restricting the non-obedience to their brothers points to the restriction of the command to them as well, so it is impossible that it should be taken as referring to what the Prophet ﷺ was addressed with during the consultation.

﴿Say﴾, as a rebuke to them and to expose their lie.

﴿Avert from yourselves death﴾ is the answer to a condition that has been omitted, relying on what follows it, namely the words of the Exalted: ﴿if you are truthful﴾. Just as the condition has its answer omitted, so too the conditional clause is omitted with its answer indicated by the answer that is mentioned. The meaning is: if you are truthful in what your statement implies, that you are able to repel killing from those for whom it has been decreed, then repel from yourselves the death that has been decreed for you, tied to a particular cause, limited to a specific time, by averting its cause. For the causes of death are equally capable of being averted by stratagems and incapable of it. Your own selves are dearer to you than your brothers, and their affair is more important to you than theirs. The meaning is that your not being killed was because it had not been decreed for you, not because you repelled it by sitting back while it was decreed for you; for that is something that has no way of being. Rather, fighting may be the cause of salvation, and sitting back may lead to death.

It is related that seventy hypocrites died on the day they said what they said. It is also said that ﴿if you are truthful﴾ refers to the content of the conditional statement, and the meaning is: had they obeyed you and sat back, they would have been killed while sitting, just as they were killed while fighting. Then the words of the Exalted, ﴿Avert from yourselves death﴾, in that case are mockery of them, meaning: if you are men who repel the causes of death, then repel all its causes so that you do not die, just as in your claim you repelled this particular cause.

﴿وَلا تَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ قُتِلُوا في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ أمْواتًا﴾ ﴿And do not think that those who have been killed in the way of Allah are dead.﴾ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought to explain that the killing which they fear, and which they warn people against, is not something to be feared. Rather, it is among the goals for which the competitors compete. This follows the explanation that caution does not avail and does not suffice. It is also read as "وَلا تَحْسِبَنَّ" with a kasra on the sin. The intended people are the martyrs of Uhud, who were seventy men: four from the Muhajirun, namely Hamzah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr, ʿUthman ibn Shihab, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh, and the rest from the Ansar, may the pleasure of Allah be upon them all. The address is either to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. It is also read with the yaʾ (يَحْسَبَنَّ), attributing the verb to his pronoun (ﷺ) or to the pronoun of the one who thinks. It has been said that it is attributed to "those who were killed." The first object is omitted, because it was originally a subject (mubtada), which may be omitted when there is an indication. The estimate is: "and let those who were killed not think them dead," meaning: let those who were killed not think themselves dead. The purpose of directing the prohibition to them is to alert the listeners that they are deserving of being consoled by this, and of being given the good news of eternal life, noble honor, and lasting bliss. But this is not at all times, only at the beginning of the killing; for after their state becomes clear to them, there is no benefit in considering their consolation and good news, nor any point in alerting and reminding the listeners. It is also read as "قُتِّلُوا" with shaddah, because of the large number of those killed.

﴿بَلْ أحْياءٌ﴾ ﴿Rather, they are alive.﴾ That is: rather, they are alive. It is also read in the accusative, meaning: rather, consider them alive, with "al-husban" (thinking) in the sense of certainty (al-yaqin), as in the verse of the poet:

I have considered piety and glory the best trade,
profitable when a man wakes up burdened.

Or it is used by way of al-mushakalah (a stylistic correspondence of form).

﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ﴿with their Lord﴾ It is in the nominative position, as a second predicate of the implied subject, or an attribute of "ahyaʾ," or in the accusative position, as a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun in "ahyaʾ." It has been said that it is an adverb of place, modifying "ahyaʾ" or the verb after it. By "nearness" is meant closeness and proximity. Mentioning the title of Lordship, which indicates nurture and bringing to perfection, together with its attribution to their pronoun, is an additional honor for them.

﴿يُرْزَقُونَ﴾ ﴿they are provided for﴾ That is, from Paradise. This emphasizes that they are alive and confirms the meaning of their life. Imam al-Wahidi said: "The most correct view about the life of the martyrs is what is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), that their spirits are in the crops of green birds, and that they are provided for, eat, and enjoy themselves." It is also narrated from him (ﷺ) that he said: "When your brothers were struck at Uhud, Allah placed their spirits in the crops of green birds that roam the rivers of Paradise." It is also narrated: "They come to the rivers of Paradise, eat of its fruits, roam in Paradise wherever they wish, and take refuge in lamps of gold hanging in the shade of the Throne." In this there is evidence that the human spirit is a subtle body that does not perish with the ruin of the body, and that its perception, pain, and pleasure do not depend on the body. As for the one who holds that human souls are immaterial, he says the meaning is that the souls of the martyrs take the form of green birds, or are attached to them, and so they enjoy what has been mentioned. It has also been said that the meaning is that they are attached to the spheres and the stars, and so they enjoy that and gain an increase in perfection.

﴿Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾, which is the honour of martyrdom, the attainment of eternal life, nearness to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the enjoyment of everlasting bliss in this world at once.

﴿And they rejoice﴾: they are gladdened by good tidings.

﴿concerning those who have not yet joined them﴾: that is, concerning their brothers who have not yet been killed in the way of Allah and so have not yet joined them.

﴿from behind them﴾: this is connected to "yalhaquu" (join them). The meaning is that they remain behind after them, though they have already preceded them. Or it is connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject of "yalhaquu", meaning: they have not joined them while remaining behind them and still alive in this world.

﴿No fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾: this is a substitute (badal) for "alladhīna" (those who), a badal ishtimāl (substitution of an inclusive part), which specifies that their rejoicing concerns the state of their brothers and not their persons. The "an" here is the lightened form (al-mukhaffafa) of "inna", its noun being an omitted pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and its predicate being the negated clause. That is: they rejoice at what has become clear to them of the good state of their brothers whom they left behind, namely that when they are killed they attain an eternal life which is not troubled by fear of an undesired event or grief over the loss of a sought-after thing. Alternatively, "no fear shall be upon them" refers to the present world, namely fear of being killed, since that is precisely the life which one ought to desire, let alone fear and beware of. That is, nothing befalls them that would necessitate such fear, not that such fear befalls them while they do not actually fear or grieve. The purpose is to state the continuous absence of fear and grief, not to state the absence of their continuity, as might be suggested by the predicate in the second clause being in the present tense (muḍāri'), for although negation, when it enters upon the present tense itself, conveys continuity and persistence according to the context.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 171:

﴿They rejoice in a favour﴾ is repeated to show that the rejoicing mentioned is not merely the absence of fear and grief, but rather it is with that and with what accompanies it of a great favour, whose magnitude cannot be measured, namely the reward of their deeds. It has also been permitted that the first [clause] be connected to the state of "their brethren," and this [clause] to the state of themselves, as an explanation of some of what was summarized in His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾.

﴿from Allah﴾ is connected to a omitted [element] which occurs as a qualifier of "a favour," confirming what the indefiniteness conveyed of intrinsic grandeur with relational grandeur; i.e., [a favour] proceeding from Him, may He be exalted.

﴿and bounty﴾, i.e., a great increase, as in His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿For those who do good is the best [reward] and an increase﴾.

﴿and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers﴾: with the "that" (anna) pronounced with a fatha, it is conjoined to "bounty," being included with it in the thread of what is rejoiced in. The intended "believers" is either the martyrs, and the expression of them as "believers" is to indicate the loftiness of the rank of faith and that it is the basis of the happiness they attained; or it is all the people of faith, martyrs and others, [their] recompense for their faith being mentioned as fulfilled and counted among what the martyrs rejoice in, by virtue of the brotherhood in religion. It has also been read with a kasra [on the "inna"], as an interposed resumptive clause indicating that this is a reward for them for their faith, implying that for one who has no faith his deeds are nullified and have no reward. And in it is an exhortation to jihad, an encouragement toward martyrdom, an incitement to increase in obedience, and a glad tidings to the believers of success, which is not hidden.

﴿Those who responded to God and the Messenger after injury had befallen them﴾ is a laudatory qualifier (ṣifa madiha) for the believers, not a restrictive one (mukhaṣṣiṣa). It may also be in the accusative in the sense of praise (naṣb ʿalā al-madḥ), or in the nominative as an inchoative (mubtadaʾ, subject of a nominal sentence). The predicate (khabar) is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿For those among them who did good and were mindful of God is a great reward﴾, taken as a whole. The ﴿مِن﴾ (min) here is explanatory (lil-bayān). The purpose of combining the two attributes is praise and giving the reason, not restriction, because all of those who responded were doers of good and mindful of God.

It is narrated that «Abu Sufyan and his companions, when they turned back from Uhud and reached al-Rawḥāʾ, regretted it and resolved to return. This reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so he wished to frighten them and to show them the strength of himself and his companions. He summoned his companions to set out in pursuit of Abu Sufyan and said: "None shall go out with us except those who were present with us yesterday." So he (ﷺ) went out with a group until they reached Ḥamrāʾ al-Asad, which is eight miles from Medina. His companions were suffering from their wounds, but they forced themselves onward so that the reward would not escape them. God Most High cast terror into the hearts of the polytheists, so they departed. Then it was revealed.»

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 173:

﴿Those to whom the people said﴾ meaning the caravan (rakb) who met them from ʿAbd Qays, or Nuʿaym ibn Masʿud al-Ashjaʿi. The application of "the people" (al-nas) to him is because he was of their kind and his speech was their speech. It is said: "So-and-so rides horses and wears garments, while he has nothing except a single horse and one garment." Or because some people from Medina joined him and spread his words.

﴿Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them﴾. It is narrated that Abu Sufyan called out when he was departing from Uhud: "O Muhammad, our appointment is the season of Badr next year, if you wish." He (peace be upon him) said: "If God the Exalted wills." When the following year came, Abu Sufyan set out with the people of Mecca until he halted at Marr al-Zahran. God the Exalted cast terror into his heart, and it seemed good to him to turn back. Then a caravan from the Banu ʿAbd Qays passed by him, wanting to go to Medina for provisions, and he stipulated for them a camel-load of raisins if they would dissuade the Muslims. It was also said: he met Nuʿaym ibn Masʿud, who had come as a pilgrim (muʿtamir), and asked him this, and committed to him ten camels, which Suhayl ibn ʿAmr guaranteed from him. So Nuʿaym set out and found the Muslims preparing to go forth, and said to them: "They came to you in your homes and not one of you escaped except as a fugitive. Do you think you should go out when they have gathered against you? So flee." He (peace be upon him) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, I will certainly go out even if no one goes out with me." He went out with seventy riders, all of them saying: "God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Guardian." It was said: this is the phrase that Abraham (peace be upon him) said when he was cast into the fire.
