﴿So it increased them in faith﴾. The hidden pronoun refers to what was said, or to the verbal noun of "said," or to its subject if by it is meant Nuʿaym alone. The meaning: they did not pay attention to that; rather, their certainty in God the Exalted was confirmed by it, their tranquility increased, they displayed zeal for Islam, and they sincerely purified their intention before Him. This is evidence that faith varies in increase and decrease, for the increase of certainty through familiarity, frequent reflection, and the support of proofs is beyond doubt. It is reinforced by the saying of Ibn ʿUmar (may God be pleased with them both): "We said: O Messenger of God, does faith increase and decrease?" He said: "Yes; it increases until it brings its possessor into Paradise, and it decreases until it brings its possessor into the Fire."

﴿And they said: God is sufficient for us﴾. That is, "Our reckoner (muhsibuna) is God, and our sufficiency," from "ahsabahu" when it suffices him. The evidence that it has the sense of the one who suffices is that it does not gain definiteness by being annexed, in your saying: "This is a man sufficient for you" (hadha rajulun hasbuka).

﴿And excellent is the Disposer of affairs﴾. That is, excellent is the one to whom affairs are entrusted (al-mawkul ilayhi), and the object of praise is omitted, i.e., God, Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 174:

﴿So they returned﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to an implied clause that the discourse presupposes, meaning: they went out to them (the enemy) and kept the appointment. It is narrated that he (ﷺ) arrived at Badr with his army and remained there for eight nights, and they had merchandise with them, so they sold it and gained much good.

The preposition bāʾ in His words, exalted is He, ﴿with grace﴾ is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "fa-nqalabū" (so they returned). The tanwīn here is for magnification (tafkhīm), meaning: they returned from their objective, accompanied by a great grace whose measure cannot be estimated.

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿from Allah﴾ are connected to an omitted element that occurs as an attribute (ṣifah) of "niʿmah" (grace), confirming its intrinsic magnificence, which the indefiniteness conveys, with the magnificence of annexation (idafah). That is: originating from Allah, exalted is He. It is the well-being, the steadfastness upon faith, the increase in it, and the protection of them from the enemy.

﴿And bounty﴾ means: profit in trade, and its indefiniteness is also for magnification.

﴿No harm touched them﴾ is another circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿fa-nqalabū﴾, or from the concealed pronoun in the circumstantial clause, as if it were said: blessed while they were safe from evil. When the circumstantial clause is a present-tense verb negated by "lam" and contains the pronoun of the one it qualifies, the conjunction wāw may be used before it, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Or he says, "It has been revealed to me," while nothing has been revealed to him﴾; and it may be omitted, as in this noble verse and in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah turned back those who disbelieved in their rage; they gained no good﴾.

﴿And they followed﴾ in everything they did of word and deed.

﴿the pleasure of Allah﴾, which is the basis of success in the good of both abodes.

﴿And Allah is the possessor of great bounty﴾, in that He bestowed upon them steadfastness, increase in faith, success in hastening to jihad, firmness in religion, displaying boldness against the enemy, and keeping them from everything that would harm them, together with attaining the great benefit. In this there is a reproach (taḥsīr) for those who stayed behind from them and a demonstration of the error of their opinion, since they deprived themselves of what these men gained. It is narrated that they said: "Would this be considered a military expedition (ghazw)?" So Allah, exalted is He, gave them the reward of a military expedition and was pleased with them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 175:

﴿That is only the Satan﴾ [i.e., the one who discourages]. The demonstrative refers to the discourager (al-muthabbit), or to the one who incited him to discouragement. The address is to the believers. "Dhalikum" (that) is the subject (mubtada'), and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the Satan﴾, may be its predicate (khabar). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿frightens his allies﴾, is either a resumptive clause (jumla mustani'a) explaining his being a satan, or a circumstantial clause (hal), as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So those are their houses, empty﴾ (Qur'an 27:52), and so on. Or it may be his attribute (sifa), with the clause being the predicate.

It is also permissible that the demonstrative refers to the saying, with an elided noun (mudaf) understood, meaning: "That is only the saying of the Satan," i.e., Iblis. The pronoun concealed in "yukhawwifu" (frightens) either refers to the matter (al-miqdar), or to the Satan, with the returning pronoun to the understood antecedent omitted, meaning: he frightens by it. By "his allies" is meant either Abu Sufyan and his companions, in which case the first object is elided, meaning: he frightens you with his allies, as is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So do not fear them﴾, i.e., his allies.

﴿But fear Me﴾ in opposing My command. Or, if by "his allies" are meant those who stayed behind (al-qa'idun), then the second object is elided, meaning: he frightens them from going out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The explicit pronoun in ﴿So do not fear them﴾ refers to the people, the second [interpretation], i.e., "So do not fear them, so that you sit back from fighting and become cowardly, and fear Me, so fight with My Messenger and hasten to what he commands you." The address is to both groups, those who went out and those who stayed behind. The fa' (so) indicates the consequence of the prohibition or the cessation on what precedes it, for the fact that the one feared is a satan necessitates not fearing him, and the prohibition against it.

﴿If you are believers﴾, for faith requires preferring the fear of Allah, exalted is He, over the fear of anyone else, and it calls for security from the evil of the Satan and his allies.

And ﴿let not grieve you﴾ is a shift of address (*iltifat*, a change in the grammatical person addressed), turning the address to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), to honour him by singling him out for consolation, and to signal that he is the principal authority in managing the affairs of the religion and in attending to its concerns.

﴿Those who hasten into disbelief﴾: that is, they fall into it swiftly, because of their extreme eagerness for it and their intense desire for it. The choice of the preposition "fi" (in) here, rather than what occurs in His saying, ﴿And hasten to forgiveness﴾ and the verse that follows, indicates their being settled in disbelief and the continuity of their involvement with it at both the beginning and the end of their hastening. This is like His saying, ﴿Those hasten in the good works﴾, for that indicates their involvement with good works and their turning among its varieties at both the beginning and end of the hastening and throughout it. As for the choice of "ila" (to) in His saying, ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a garden﴾ and the verse that follows, it is because forgiveness and the garden are the final point and goal of the hastening.

The relative clause (*silah*) refers to the hypocrites among those who stayed behind and a group of the Jews, as specified in His saying, ﴿O Messenger, let not grieve you those who hasten into disbelief, of those who say "We believe" with their mouths but their hearts have not believed, and of those who are Jews﴾. It has also been said that the reference is to a people who apostatized from Islam. Expressing them by this description indicates, through what is contained in the relative clause, the likely existence of the forbidden matter and its befalling the Messenger of God (ﷺ). That is: do not let them grieve you by their hastening into disbelief, their rushing to carry out its rulings, and their supporting its people. The prohibition is directed at them, while the intended meaning is to prohibit him (peace and blessings be upon him) from being affected by them, for the sake of emphasis, since a prohibition of influence is a prohibition of being affected in its very essence and a total negation of it. The prohibition may also be directed at the consequence while the intended meaning is the thing that entails it, as in your saying: "Let me not see you here."

He (one reader) read "لا يُحْزِنْكَ" (*la yuḥzinka*) from *aḥzana*, which is the causative of *ḥazina* with a kasra on the *zay*, and the meaning is the same. It has been said that the meaning of *ḥazanahu* is: he caused grief in him, as in *dahanahu*, meaning he put oil on him; and the meaning of *aḥzanahu* is: he made him grieved. It has also been said that the meaning of *ḥazanahu* is: he produced grief in him, and the meaning of *aḥzanahu* is: he exposed him to grief.

﴿Indeed they will not harm God﴾: this is a causal explanation for the prohibition and a completion of the consolation, by affirming the absolute negation of their harm. That is: they will by this never harm the friends of God at all. The attribution of the negation of harm to God (exalted is He) is to honour them and to signal that their harming them is equivalent to harming Him, glorified is He. In this there is further emphasis in the consolation. His saying, ﴿anything﴾ (*shay'an*), is in the accusative position as a verbal noun (*masdariyya*), meaning: any harm at all. The indefiniteness serves to emphasise the smallness and insignificance of what is involved. It has been said that it is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning: with anything at all. It has also been said that the meaning is: by this they will not diminish anything of His dominion and authority, as Abu Dhar related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "God says: If your first and last, your jinn and your humans, were upon the most pious heart of a man among you, that would not increase My dominion by anything. And if your first and last, your jinn and your humans, were upon the most wicked heart of a man among you, that would not diminish My dominion by anything." The first interpretation is more appropriate to the context of consolation and causal explanation.

﴿God desires not to give them any share in the Hereafter﴾: this is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) explaining the secret of their being tested with their immersion in disbelief. The mention of "desire" indicates the complete sincerity of the one who calls them to deprivation and punishment, given that the desire of the Most Merciful of the merciful is attached to these two things, which is not hidden. The future form of the verb indicates the continuity and persistence of the desire. That is: God desires by this that He not give them any share of reward in the Hereafter. For this reason He has left them in their transgression, wandering blindly, until they perish in disbelief.

﴿And for them﴾: together with that total deprivation.

﴿is a great punishment﴾, beyond measure. It has been said: since hastening toward a thing indicates the greatness of its importance and the splendour of its value in the eyes of the one who hastens, their punishment is described as great in keeping with this correspondence, and to draw attention to the baseness of what they hastened toward and its lowliness in itself. The clause is either an independent sentence explaining their portion of punishment immediately after explaining that they have no portion of reward, or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in "lahum" (for them), meaning: God desires their deprivation from reward, while a great punishment is prepared for them.

**Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 3, verse 177:**

﴿Indeed, those who have bought disbelief in exchange for faith﴾: that is, they took it (disbelief) in place of it (faith), out of desire for what they took and aversion to what they left behind. The full explanation of this figure of speech (*istiʿara*, metaphor) has already been given in the commentary on His words, Exalted and Majestic: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾.

﴿They will not harm Allah at all﴾: its explanation is as previously stated, except that it contains a clear implication that the harm is limited to themselves, as if it were said: "They only harm themselves." If the relative clause is taken to refer to the specific hastening ones who are known (*al-musariʿun al-maʿhudun*), so that buying disbelief in exchange for faith means preferring it over faith, either by taking it in place of faith that has actually been attained, as is the case with apostates, or by taking it in place of the near potential for faith attained through witnessing its proofs in the Torah, as is the case with the Jews and their hypocrites, then the repetition serves to establish the ruling and confirm it by stating its cause, with a change in the subject's designation. What is mentioned in the relative clause concerning the aforementioned buying is clear in showing that its harm falls only upon themselves and does not extend to others at all. How could it not be so? It is a sign of total loss and everlasting deprivation, indicating the complete foolishness of their minds and the weakness of their opinions. How could they accomplish what depends on the strength of resolve, the soundness of judgment, and the firmness of planning, namely harming the party of Allah, the Exalted? That party is more rare than the single piebald (horse) and more inaccessible than the eagle of the sky.

If the relative clause is taken in its (p-117) generality, so that the aforementioned buying means the common element encompassing both of the above meanings, and taking disbelief in place of what has been placed in the position of faith itself, namely the near readiness for it attained through witnessing the explicit revelation and observing the proofs set out in the horizons and in the souls, as is the practice of all disbelievers, then the sentence serves to confirm the content of what precedes it, establishing the general principles for the particular rulings subsumed under them. Moreover, it has been permitted that the first relative pronoun be general, referring to all disbelievers, and the second be specific, referring to the known individuals.

You know well that this, despite being free of the aforementioned subtleties, is unbefitting the grandeur of the status of the Revelation, since the occurrence of hastening into disbelief in the stated sense, and its being a likely cause of grief for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as is understood from the prohibition against it, can only be conceived of in those known to be characterized by it. As for those disbelievers whose condition is not known, who are located in distant places, attributing the aforementioned hastening to them, on the basis that it is among the beginnings of his grief, peace be upon him, is without justification.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾ is an independent sentence, clarifying the complete severity of their punishment by mentioning the extreme degree of its painfulness after mentioning the extreme degree of its magnitude. It has been said: since it is the custom for a buyer to rejoice in what he has bought and to be pleased at obtaining it when the transaction is profitable, and to be pained when it is a loss, their punishment is described as painful in consideration of this.

﴿Let not those who disbelieve think that the respite We grant them is good for their souls﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with His saying, ﴿And let not those [who hasten to disbelief] grieve you﴾, the verse. The verb is attributed to the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl, "those who"), and "anna" with what follows it fills the place of its two objects according to Sibawayh, because the intended meaning is complete with it, namely the attachment of the mental verb to the predication between the subject and the predicate. Or it fills the place of one of them according to al-Akhfash, with the other omitted. "Mā" is either verbal (maṣdariyya, forming a verbal noun) or relative (mawṣūla), its returning pronoun omitted, and its connection is written as it is in the script to follow the Imam (the standard 'Uthmanic codex). The meaning is: let not the disbelievers think that Our granting them respite, or that what We grant them, is good for their souls, or let not the disbelievers think that the goodness of Our granting them respite, or the goodness of what We grant them, is established or occurring. Its implication is a prohibition against them rejoicing in the outward appearance of His granting them respite, on the basis of their assuming it is good for them, and a disgracing of them by explaining that it is pure evil and sheer harm. Just as the implication of the coordinated clause is the prohibition of the Messenger ﷺ against grieving over the outward state of the disbelievers, on the basis of supposing harm from them, and the consolation of him, peace be upon him, by explaining their complete inability to do that.

The relative pronoun may refer either to the class of disbelievers, so that the judgments of the specific ones fall under its general ruling by primary inclusion, or to specific known individuals only. In the latter case, the use of the explicit noun rather than a pronoun serves to maintain the constant concomitance between the relative clause and the respite, which is a expression of their being given time, left alone and left to their affairs for a long age. For what constantly accompanies the respite is the persistent disbelief, not the hastening mentioned nor the purchasing mentioned, for these are among the renewed states that pass within the course of the persistent disbelief.

It has been read as "lā taḥsabanna" with the letter tāʾ, the address being to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this is more suitable to the context of consolation, or to every person who is capable of such assumption, intending to spread the enormity of their condition. The relative pronoun is the object, and "annamā numlī lahum" is either a substitute (badal) for it. Since reliance is placed upon the substitute, which fills the place of the two objects, as in His saying, ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear?﴾, it is restricted to one object, as in your saying, "I placed the goods, some of them upon others." Or it is a second object, with a noun omitted, either in it, meaning: let not those who disbelieve (p-118) be people who think that the respite is good for their souls, or in the first object, meaning: let not the condition of those who disbelieve be such that you think the respite is good for their souls. The meaning of preference is in terms of their own assumption.

﴿Indeed, We grant them respite only that they may increase in sin﴾ is a resumed clause (istiʾnāf) explaining the wisdom of the respite. "Mā" is a restrictive particle (kāffa), and the lām is the lām of intention. According to the Muʿtazila, it is the lām of consequence (lām al-ʿāqiba). It has been read with a fatḥa on the hamza here, to make the verb govern it, and with a kasra on it in what preceded, as a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ) between the verb and its object, which gives additional emphasis to refuting the assumption. Its meaning is: let not the disbelievers think that Our granting them respite is for the increase of sin, as is their habit, but rather it is for making up what they have neglected through repentance and entering into faith.

﴿And for them﴾ in the Hereafter.

﴿is a humiliating punishment﴾. Since the respite includes enjoyment of the good things and adornments of the world, and that calls for arrogance and haughtiness, their punishment is described as humiliating, so that their recompense is an equal recompense. The sentence is either an independent clause explaining their state in the Hereafter after explaining their state in this world, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the waw, meaning: so that they may increase in sin, a humiliating punishment being prepared for them. This is the necessary reading according to the last recitation.

﴿It is not for God to leave the believers in the state you are in﴾ is a resumed statement (kalām mustaʾnaf), brought to promise the believers and to threaten the hypocrites with worldly punishment, namely disgrace and humiliation, after the mention of their punishment in the Hereafter. By "the believers" are meant the sincere ones. As for the address (al-khiṭāb), it has been said that it is directed to the general body of those who affirm faith, both the sincere and the hypocrites, so there is an iltifāt (shift in grammatical person) within a talwīn (variation of address). By "what you are in" is meant the mixing of some of them with others and their being equal in the application of the rulings of Islam to them, since this is the common ground shared by both groups. It has also been said that the address is to the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Muqātil, al-Kalbī, and most exegetes (mufassirūn). In that case there is only talwīn. Perhaps "the hypocrites" is an explanatory conjunction (ʿaṭf tafsīrī) for "the disbelievers," since otherwise there is no sharing between the believers and the hypocrites in any matter. By "what they are in" is meant the common ground mentioned above, for just as it may be attributed to both groups together, it may be attributed to each of them separately. It is not the disbelief and hypocrisy, as has been said, for the believers were not sharing with them in that, so that they would be left in it. It has also been said that the address is to the believers alone, and this is the view of most of the scholars of rhetoric (ahl al-maʿānī). In that case there is talwīn and iltifāt as mentioned. The mention of their faith before the address serves to indicate the reason for the ruling. By "what they are in" is meant what has been mentioned more than once. The first view is the closer one, and the verifying scholars (al-muḥaqqiqūn) of the exegetes inclined to it, because it is explicit that what is meant by "what they are in" is the common ground mentioned between the two groups, insofar as it is shared between them. This is unlike the last two views, which are far from that. How could it not be? For what is understood from the state of the hypocrites is disbelief and hypocrisy, and what is understood from the state of the believers is faith and sincerity, not the common ground between them. And if that is understood, it is understood only insofar as it is attributed to one of them, not insofar as it is attributed to both together. On this turns the matter of the mixing that necessitates separation (ifrāz).

The lām in ﴿liyadhara﴾ is either connected to a predicate supplied for kāna (the verb "to be"), as is the view of the Basran grammarians (al-Baṣriyya), and the verb after it is in the subjunctive by an implied ʾan. That is: "It is not that God is willing or intends to leave the believers..." In this case, directing the negation to the will to do the act gives emphasis and intensification which it would not have if directed to the act itself. Or it is an additional particle (zāʾida) for emphasis, governing the verb itself, as is the view of the Kufan grammarians (al-Kūfiyya). The additional nature of the particle does not undermine this, just as the additional nature of the prepositions does not undermine their government.

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿until He distinguishes the wicked from the good﴾ are a limit (ghāya) for what the negation mentioned implies, as if it were said: God does not leave them in that mixing, but He arranges affairs and establishes causes until He separates the hypocrite from the believer. In expressing the two groups with what the noble composition has used, there is a recording (tasjīl) against each of them of what befits it, and an indication of the reason for the ruling. The singular "the wicked" and "the good," despite the multiplicity and abundance of what is meant by each, especially after the mention of what is meant by one of them, namely the believers, in the plural form, is to announce that the basis for separating one of the two groups from the other is their attribution of their qualities, not the particular nature of their essences or the multiplicity of their individuals. This is as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿That is nearer to your not deviating﴾, and similar to it His words, Exalted is He: ﴿every nursing mother will forget what she nursed﴾, where the intent is to indicate the attribution of the quality without regard to whether the described is rational or otherwise. The linking of the distinguishing to "the wicked," expressed to refer to the hypocrite, although what is immediately understood from the preceding is the non-leaving of the believers in the mixing, is because the distinction that occurs between the two groups happens only through acting upon the hypocrites and changing them from one state into a state different from the first, while the believers remain in what they were in of the basic faith, though their increased sincerity becomes manifest. It is not by acting upon them and changing them from one state to another state while the hypocrites remain in their concealment. Also, because in this there is greater emphasis on the threat, as is indicated in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿God knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾. The non-leaving was not attributed to them because it implies concern for the matter of the one to whom it is attributed, for what is immediately understood from it is that they are not left in an unsuitable condition, as sound taste bears witness.

It has been read as ﴿yumayyiza﴾ from tamyīz (distinguishing).

The words of the Exalted: ﴿and God would not inform you of the unseen﴾ are a preparation for the explanation of the promised distinction, by way of turning the address exclusively to the sincere ones in honour of them. The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿but God chooses of His messengers whom He wills﴾ are an indication of the manner in which it occurs in general terms. The manifestation of the august Name in both places is to cultivate awe. So the meaning is: God would not leave the sincere ones in mixing with the hypocrites, but He arranges the beginnings until He brings the hypocrites out from among them. He does not do that by making you aware of what is in their hearts of disbelief and hypocrisy, but God reveals to His messenger, upon him be peace, and informs him of that and of what appeared from them of statements and actions, as partly related about them earlier, and so He exposes them before all witnesses and rescues you from the baseness of the partners and the evil of their company. The mention of choosing (ijtibāʾ) is to announce that standing upon such hidden secrets is not possible except for one whom God, Exalted is He, has designated for a lofty rank, beyond which the aspirations of nations fall short, and has chosen above the masses for their guidance. The generalization of choosing to all the other messengers, upon them be peace, serves to show that his, upon him be peace, condition in this matter is a firm affair with an original root, proceeding according to the practice of God, Exalted is He, followed among the earlier messengers, upon them be peace.

The generalization of the command in the words of the Exalted: ﴿So believe in God and His messengers﴾, although the arrangement of the noble composition is for faith in the Prophet ﷺ, is to make faith in him obligatory by way of proof, and to indicate that this entails faith in all of them, because he confirms what is before him of the messengers, and they are witnesses to the soundness of his prophethood, upon him be blessings and peace. The thing commanded is faith in everything the Prophet ﷺ brought, and so it includes, as a primary entry, belief in his truthfulness in what he informed about the states of the hypocrites. This is what the eloquence of the noble composition requires. It has also been permitted that the meaning is: He does not leave you mixed until He distinguishes the wicked from the good, by imposing on you difficult obligations which only the sincere can endure, whose hearts God, Exalted is He, has tested, such as sacrificing lives in jihād and spending wealth in the way of God, Exalted is He, (p-120) and so He makes that a test (ʿiyār) of your beliefs and a witness to your inner thoughts, until some of you know what is in the heart of another by way of inference, not by standing upon the essence of the breasts (dhāt al-ṣudūr), for that is among what God, Exalted is He, has reserved for Himself. You know that the istidrāk (corrective addition) through the choosing of messengers, which indicates their greater excellence and superior knowledge over creation, after the explanation of the inadequacy of their rank in standing upon the hidden recesses of hearts, is explicit that what is meant is the manifestation of those secrets by way of revelation, not by way of imposing obligations that would lead to the removal of their secrets from the rank of concealment. Closer to this is to take the noble verse as being given to explain the wisdom in God's granting respite to the disbelievers after explaining their evil state. So the meaning is: God would not leave the sincere ones in mixing forever, as He left them thus until now, for a secret that requires it. Rather, He separates the hypocrites from them. For this reason He did it on that day, when He left the disbelievers to themselves, and so He displayed the appearance of victory, and those in whose hearts is a sickness were exposed to the wickedness within them, and they were disgraced before all witnesses.

It has been said: The disbelievers said, "If Muhammad is truthful, let him inform us who among us will believe and who will disbelieve," and so this was revealed.

﴿And if you believe﴾, that is: in what has been mentioned, with true faith.

﴿and fear God﴾, that is: not neglecting the rights of Him, or hypocrisy.

﴿then for you﴾, in exchange for that faith and piety, there is a great reward whose full extent cannot be reached.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 180:

﴿Let not those who are niggardly with what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them﴾. This explains the state of stinginess (bukhl) and the gravity of its outcome, and it corrects its people for supposing that it is good for them, in line with the explanation of the state of respite (imla'). The matter they were stingy with is presented as something Allah the Exalted has given them of His bounty, in order to intensify the explanation of how evil their conduct is, since that is one of the things that calls for spending it in His way, as in His saying: ﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾. The verb (al-fi'l) is attributed to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who"), and the first object is omitted because the relative clause (al-sila) indicates it. The separating pronoun (damir al-fasl, the pronoun of separation, "huwa") refers back to it. That is, "Let not the stingy think that what Allah has given them of His bounty, without any role or entitlement of theirs in it, is good for them compared with spending it." It has also been said that the verb is attributed to the pronoun of the Prophet ﷺ, or to the pronoun of whoever is doing the thinking, and the first object is the relative pronoun with an implied noun (mudaf) understood, and the second object is what was mentioned. This is also the case according to the reading in the second person. That is: "Let not the stinginess of those who are stingy with what Allah has given them of His bounty be thought good for them."

﴿Rather, it is evil for them﴾. Stating explicitly that it is evil for them, though it is already implied by the negation of its goodness, is for emphasis, and the tanwin (nunation) on "sharr" is for magnification (tafkhim). His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will be encircled with what they were stingy with on the Day of Resurrection﴾ explains the manner of its evil. That is: they will be bound with the burden of what they were stingy with, in the manner of the binding of a collar (tawq). The noun that was omitted (mudaf) is dropped, and the noun in the genitive (mudaf ilayhi) takes its place, to indicate the complete suitability between the two. It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "No man who does not pay the zakat on his wealth will have Allah make for him a serpent (shuja') around his neck on the Day of Resurrection." It has also been said: "What he was stingy with of zakat will be made into a snake around his neck, biting him from his horn to his foot and pecking at his head, and it will say: I am your wealth."

﴿And to Allah belongs﴾ alone, not to anyone else, either independently or in partnership.

﴿the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾. That is: what the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth inherit of wealth and other things, and of the sovereignties which the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth inherit. So what is the matter with them, that they are stingy toward Him with His own dominion and do not spend it in His way? Or it means that He inherits from them what they withhold and do not spend in His way, the Exalted, at the time of their death, and regret and remorse remain upon them.

﴿And Allah is well-acquainted with what you do﴾, of withholding and stinginess.

﴿All-Aware﴾, so He will recompense you for that. Mentioning the Glorious Name in a place where a pronoun would be expected serves to cultivate awe, and it is an iltifat (shift in grammatical person) for the sake of intensifying the warning, and to indicate the intensification of the wrath of the Most Merciful, arising from the mention of their ugly deeds. It has also been read with the ya' (third person, "He"), in keeping with the apparent sense.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 181:

﴿Indeed, Allah has heard the saying of those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich."﴾ This was said by the Jews when they heard the words of His Exalted saying: ﴿Who is it that would lend to Allah a goodly loan?﴾. It is narrated that "he (ﷺ) wrote, together with Abu Bakr (رضي الله عنه), to the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa', inviting them to Islam, to the establishment of the prayer, the giving of zakat, and to lend to Allah a goodly loan. Finhas said: 'Indeed, Allah is poor, to the point that He asks us for a loan.' Abu Bakr (رضي الله عنه) then slapped him on the face and said: 'Were it not for the covenant between us and you, I would strike off your neck.' He complained about him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but he (Finhas) denied what he had said, so this verse was revealed." The use of the plural here, though the speaker was one, is because the rest were content with that statement. The meaning is: nothing about them was hidden from Allah, and He has prepared for them a punishment equal to their deed. The expression "hearing" is used to indicate that the saying is so grave and vile that its speaker would not be pleased for any listener to hear it. The oath-form of emphasis is for intensifying the threat and magnifying the warning.

﴿We will record what they have said﴾, i.e., We will record what they uttered of this monstrous and hideous speech in the scrolls of the recording angels, or We will preserve it and fix it in Our knowledge, never forgetting it or neglecting it, just as what is written is fixed. The sin (*sin*) is for emphasis, i.e., it will never escape Our recording and fixing it, because it is of extreme magnitude and horror. How could it not be so? For it is disbelief in Allah Most High and mockery of the Great Qur'an and the Noble Messenger. Therefore, His saying is conjoined to it: ﴿and their killing of the prophets﴾, to indicate that the two are brothers in magnitude, and to draw attention to the fact that this is not their first crime, but they have precedents in it, and that whoever dares to kill the prophets is not to be thought unlikely to commit such monstrous acts. By "their killing of the prophets" is meant their approval of the deed of their forefathers. His saying ﴿without right﴾ is connected to an elided element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "their killing", i.e., existing without right in their own belief as well as in reality. "Sa-yaktubu" is also read in the active voice, "sa-yuktabu" in the passive voice, and "qatluhum" in the nominative.

﴿And We will say: "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ i.e., We will take vengeance upon them after the recording by saying to them: "Taste the burning punishment, just as you made the Muslims taste distress." It contains emphases that are not hidden. It is also read "wa-yaqulu" with the yā' (third person), and it may be read in the passive voice.

﴿That﴾ refers to the punishment mentioned, and the sense of distance in it (in Arabic, the demonstrative ﴿dhalika﴾ "that") indicates the greatness of its importance and the remoteness of its rank in terror and dreadfulness. It is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is the words of the Exalted: ﴿for what your hands have sent forth﴾, i.e., because of what you have committed of the killing of the prophets and of uttering such a great matter and other sins. The expression of the selves (anfus) by the hands is because most of their deeds are carried out by them.

The position of "anna" (that) in His words, the Exalted: ﴿and that Allah is not unjust to the servants﴾, is in the nominative case, as it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is a parenthetical concluding remark (i'tiraq tadhyili) confirming the meaning of what precedes it, i.e., the matter is that He, the Exalted, does not punish His servants without any sin on their part. The expression of this by the negation of injustice, although punishing them without sin is not injustice according to the established principle of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah), let alone being gross injustice, is to demonstrate the perfection of His purity, the Exalted, from that by depicting it in the form of what cannot possibly proceed from Him, glorified is He, of injustice, just as the withholding of reward for deeds is expressed as their loss, although deeds do not necessitate reward, such that His withholding of it would entail their being lost. The intensive form (sigha al-mubalagha) is for emphasizing this meaning, by presenting the mentioned punishment without sin in the form of exaggeration in injustice. It has been said: it is for observing the plurality of the servants, from the saying: "So-and-so is unjust to his servant" and "a great doer of injustice to his servants," the intensive form being for magnitude in number and not in quality.

Furthermore, it has been said: the position of "anna" is in the genitive case by conjunction with what has already passed, and its causality for the punishment is in that the negation of injustice necessitates justice, which requires rewarding the good-doer and punishing the evil-doer. Its corruption is evident, for leaving punishment of one who deserves it is not injustice, either according to the law or by reason, such that the negation of injustice would stand as a cause for punishment, as the one who stated this said in Surat al-Anfal. It has also been said: the causality of their sins for their punishment is restricted by the addition of the negation of His injustice, the Exalted, to it, since without it, it would be possible for Him to punish them without their sins. And you know well that the possibility of His punishing His servants without sin, indeed its actual occurrence, does not contradict that the punishment of these disbelievers is because of their sins, such that one would need to consider its absence along with it; it would only need that if the claim were that all of His punishments, the Exalted, are due to the sins of those punished.

﴿Those who said﴾ is in the accusative or nominative, as a form of censure. They were Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Malik ibn Sayfi, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, Finhas ibn Azura, and Wahb ibn Yahudha.

﴿Indeed, Allah has made a covenant with us﴾ That is, He commanded us and enjoined us in the Tawrat (Torah).

﴿That we should not believe in any messenger until he brings us an offering (qurban) that fire devours﴾ As was the practice of the prophets of the Children of Israel, when an offering was brought forward, the prophet would stand and supplicate, and fire would descend from heaven and consume it. That is, it would reduce it to its own nature by burning. This is one of their fabrications and falsehoods, for the fire consuming the offering did not necessitate faith except insofar as it was a miracle, so it and all other miracles are equal. Since the essence of their false statement was that their non-belief in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was due to his not bringing what they mentioned, and that if he had brought it, faith would have been realized, Allah answered them with His words, ﴿Say﴾, that is, to rebuke them and expose their lie.

﴿Messengers have certainly come to you﴾ numerous in number and great in rank,

﴿before me with clear proofs﴾ that is, with evident miracles,

﴿and with what you have mentioned﴾ precisely, the offering that fire devours.

﴿Why then did you kill them, if you are truthful?﴾ concerning what your statement indicates, that you would believe in a messenger who comes to you with what you have proposed. For Zakariyya, Yahya, and other prophets, peace be upon them, have come to you with what you mentioned, along with other miracles. So what is the matter with you that you did not believe in them, until you dared to kill them?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 184:

﴿And if they deny you﴾: a beginning of consoling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), following what was revealed to him that would grieve him, peace and blessings be upon him, from the statements of the disbelievers among the polytheists and the Jews. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Messengers before you were indeed denied﴾ is a justification for the answer of the conditional, meaning: so be consoled, for messengers before you were indeed denied, etc. And "from" (min) is related to ﴿were denied﴾, or to an omitted adjective of ﴿messengers﴾, meaning: existing from before you.

﴿They came with the clear proofs﴾: meaning the evident miracles, as an adjective of "messengers".

﴿And the scriptures﴾: is the plural of zabur (psalter/writing), and it is the book restricted to wise sayings, from "zabartahu" when you made it good (hassanta). It was said: the scriptures of admonitions and deterrents, from "zabartahu" when you rebuked him (zajartahu).

﴿And the illuminating Book﴾: it was said: meaning the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms. And "the Book" in the usage of the Qur'an is what contains the laws and rulings, and for this reason "the Book" and "the Wisdom" came joined by conjunction in most occurrences. And it was recited "wa-bi-l-zuburi" with the preposition repeated, indicating that they are different in essence (p-123) from the clear proofs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 185:

﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾ is both a promise and a warning, for the believer and the disbeliever alike. It has also been recited as ﴿ذائِقَةُ المَوْتِ﴾ with and without tanwin (nunation), as in the line of poetry:

"Nor one who remembers God, except a little."

﴿And you will only be paid your rewards in full﴾, meaning you will be given the recompense for your deeds completely and perfectly.

﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning the day you rise from the graves. The use of the word "payment" (tawfiyah) indicates that some of their rewards reach them before that day, as the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) indicate about the grave: "It is either a garden from the gardens of Paradise or a pit from the pits of the Fires." ﴿Whoever is drawn away from the Fire﴾, meaning moved far from it on that day and saved. Linguistically, zahzahah (being drawn away) originally means repeating the zahh, which is pulling with haste.

﴿And is admitted into Paradise, he has indeed triumphed﴾ by being saved and attaining what he sought. Fawz (triumph) is gaining one's desired goal. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever loves to be drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise, let his death come to him while he believes in God and the Last Day, and let him treat people as he would like to be treated."

﴿And the life of this world is nothing but﴾, meaning its pleasures and adornments.

﴿except the enjoyment of delusion﴾. It is likened to goods that are passed off deceptively on a buyer and presented attractively so that he purchases them. This applies to those who prefer it over the Hereafter. As for one who seeks the Hereafter through it, it is for him a provision for reaching the goal. Ghuroor (delusion) may be a verbal noun or the plural of ghar (deceiver).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 186:**

﴿You will surely be tested﴾ is the beginning of consoling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those believers with him, regarding what they will encounter from the disbelievers of hardships. This follows their consolation regarding what has already befallen them, so that they may prepare themselves to bear it when it occurs, ready themselves to meet it, and confront it with good patience and steadfastness. Indeed, the onslaught of terrors shakes the feet of men, while readiness for calamities makes afflictions easier to bear.

The root of *ibtila'* (trial, testing) is *ikhtibar* (examination), meaning you seek knowledge of the state of the one being tested by exposing him to a matter that is generally difficult for him to undergo and to commit. This is truly conceivable only in the case of one who does not know the outcomes of affairs. As for the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, it occurs only figuratively, through His empowering the servant to choose one of two matters, or several matters, before He sets upon him something that is among its ordinary beginnings, as has already passed. The sentence is the answer to an omitted oath, meaning: *By Allah, you will surely be tested*, that is, you will be treated as one being tested, so that what you have of steadfastness upon the truth and good deeds may become manifest. The purpose of the emphasis is either to affirm the meaning of testing, to make the matter easier to bear, or to affirm that the one tested will indeed encounter it, as an intensification in urging them toward the readiness and preparation that is intended from them.

﴿in your possessions﴾: through the various kinds of afflictions that occur in them and lead to their destruction. As for spending them in the way of good in general, it is not appropriate, in terms of composition, to place it within the category of testing, because it belongs to the category of diminishing (*al-id'af*), not to the category of destruction (*al-itlaf*).

﴿and in your selves﴾: through killing, captivity, wounds, and what befalls them of various kinds of hardships, fears, and calamities, and the like. The mention of possessions first is due to the frequency with which ruin occurs in them.

﴿And you will surely hear from those who were given the Book before you﴾: that is, before your being given the Qur'an. They are the Jews and the Christians. He referred to them by this description to indicate the basis of the enmity (*madar al-shiqaq*), and to announce that some of what they say to you is grounded, in their claim, in the Book, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Allah has covenanted with us﴾ and so on. The explicit statement of priority is to reinforce this indication and strengthen this basis, for the antiquity of the revelation of their Book is something that supports their adherence to it.

﴿and from those who associated partners [with Allah] much harm﴾: such as reviling the upright religion, disparaging the rulings of the noble Law, obstructing whoever wishes to believe, condemning whoever has believed, and what occurred from Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his like of satirizing the believers and inciting the polytheists to oppose the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the like of that, which contains no good.

﴿And if you are patient﴾: that is, under those hardships and trials when they arrive, and you confront them with good forbearance.

﴿and fear Allah﴾: that is, you devote yourselves wholly to Allah, the Exalted, turning away entirely from all else, to the point that the arrival of what is loved and the encounter with what is disliked are equal in your sight.

﴿then indeed that﴾: a reference to patience and God-consciousness, and what carries in it the sense of distance, to announce the elevation of their rank and the lofty status of both. The singular form of the address particle may be either in consideration of each one of those addressed, or because the intended address is merely to draw attention, without regard to the particular circumstances of those addressed.

﴿is of the resolve of affairs﴾: among the matters that are resolved upon, for which the competitors compete, that is, among what everyone ought to resolve upon, because of its perfection of excellence and nobility; or among what Allah, the Exalted, has resolved upon, commanded, and emphasized. The meaning is that this is one of the firm resolutions of Allah, the Exalted, that you must be patient and fear Allah. The sentence serves as a justification for the answer to the conditional clause, occupying its place, as if it were said: *And if you are patient and fear Allah, then it is better for you*, or *then do so*, or *then you have done well*, or *then you have been correct*, for indeed that is... And it is permissible that *that* refers to the patience and God-consciousness of those addressed, in which case the sentence is then the answer to the conditional clause. In presenting the command to patience and God-consciousness in the form of a conditional, there is a manifestation of the perfection of kindness toward the servants that is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 188:

﴿Do not think﴾: the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to be addressed.

﴿those who rejoice in what they have brought﴾: i.e., in what they have done, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, His promise is ever fulfilled﴾. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b), "who rejoice in what they have done" (yafrahūna bi-mā fa'alū). It was also read "bi-mā ātaw", meaning "given", and "bi-mā ūtū", i.e., "in what they were given of knowledge of the Torah". Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: They are the Jews, who distorted the Torah, rejoiced in that, and loved to be described as possessing religious knowledge and virtue. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked the Jews about something in the Torah, and they concealed the truth (p-126) and informed him of the opposite, showing him that they had told him the truth, seeking his praise, and rejoicing in what they had done. It was also said: They rejoiced in concealing the explicit texts that bear witness to his prophethood, peace be upon him, and loved to be praised for following the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him. So the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) refers to those mentioned, or to their notables, and is placed in the position of their pronoun. The sentence is brought to explain the punishment in the Hereafter that follows from their deeds described here, after explaining how ugly those deeds are. Also incorporated into it is an explanation of another of their abominations: their persistence in the vices they are engaged in, their rejoicing in that, and their love of being described with attributes of goodness they do not possess. This is arranged within the relative clause (ṣila), which should be something known to be true of the relative pronoun for the addressee, to announce that their being characterized by this is well known. It was also said: They are a group who stayed behind from the military campaign, then made excuses, claiming they saw benefit in that, and sought praise for it. It was also said: They are all of the hypocrites, and this is most appropriate to the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿and love to be praised for what they have not done﴾, because it is well known that they used to rejoice in what they did, namely displaying faith while their hearts were settled in disbelief, seeking praise from the Muslims for faith while being far from practising it, and they used to show love for the believers while being in the utmost extreme of enmity. So the relative pronoun refers to a specific group known among those mentioned and others, for most of the hypocrites were from the Jews. Perhaps the better course is to take the relative pronoun in its general sense, including everyone who performs any good deed and rejoices in it with self-admiration, and wishes people to praise him for virtues he lacks, while it is initially included among those previously known. Whatever the case, it is the first object of "do not think" (taḥsabanna).

His saying: ﴿So do not think them﴾ is an emphasis on it, and the fa' is extra (zā'ida), and the second object is His saying: ﴿to be safe from the punishment﴾, i.e., connected with deliverance from it, on the basis that mafāza is a mīmī verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī). Its feminine ending with the tā' does no harm, because it is predicated upon it and is not there to indicate singularity, as in the verse:

Were it not for the hope of victory from you and the fear
Of your punishment, they would have been for us among the watering places.

There is no way to make it a noun of place (ism makān), on the basis that the preposition phrase is related to an omitted word that occurs as an adjective for it, i.e., "a safety that is from the punishment," because it is not from the punishment. Positing a specific verb to make the meaning correct, i.e., "a safety that saves from the punishment," despite it being contrary to the original rule, is far-fetched and unnecessary. It was read with a ḍamma on the bā' in both verbs, on the basis that the address includes the believers too. It was read with the third-person yā' and a fatḥa on the bā' in both, on the basis that the verb belongs to him, peace be upon him, or to everyone who is capable of supposing, and its two objects are as mentioned. It was read with a ḍamma on the bā' in the second verb only, on the basis that the verb belongs to the relative pronoun, and the first object is omitted because it is the same as the subject, and the second is "to be safe", i.e., "let not those who rejoice think themselves successful." His saying: ﴿So do not think them﴾ is an emphasis on the first, and the fa' is extra as already mentioned. It is also permissible to take the first verb as having both objects omitted together for brevity, since the second verb's objects indicate them, in reverse of what is in the verse:

By what book or by what sunnah
Do you see their love as a shame for me, and suppose it?

Here both objects of the second verb are omitted because the objects of the first verb indicate them. Or it is said that the first verb belongs to the Messenger (ﷺ) or to every supposer, its first object is the relative pronoun, and the second is omitted because the object of the second verb indicates it. The second verb is attributed to the pronoun of the relative pronoun, the fa' is for coordination, because it is evident that the non-supposing of them is a consequence of the non-supposing of him, peace be upon him, and its two objects are the attached pronoun. His saying: ﴿to be safe﴾. The opening of the threat with their prohibition from the supposition mentioned is to draw attention to the falsehood of their feeble opinions and to cut off their empty hopes, since they used to claim that they would be saved from the punishment of the Hereafter by what they had done, just as they were saved from worldly accountability, and their rejoicing was built upon this. As for his prohibition, peace be upon him, it is for an allusion to their supposing mentioned, not because supposing could arise from him, peace be upon him.

﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾: after it was indicated that they will not be saved from punishment in general, it confirms that for them is a specific kind of it, without limit in its duration or severity, as the nominal sentence, the indefinite noun in its emphatic sense, and the descriptive adjective indicate (p-127).

﴿For Allah﴾ i.e., exclusively. ﴿is the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ i.e., the overpowering sovereignty over them, by which He disposes of them and what is in them as He wills and desires: bringing into existence and annihilating, giving life and causing death, punishing and rewarding, without anyone else having any share of involvement in any of that in any way whatsoever. Thus the clause confirms what precedes it. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and Allah is over all things competent﴾ confirms the exclusivity of the dominion of the corporeal world, expressed by its two regions, to Him, glorified and exalted is He. For His being capable of everything, such that nothing in His dominion escapes Him, necessitates that whatever else exists, whatever it may be, is something over which He has power. And it necessarily entails the exclusivity of power to Him, exalted is He, and the impossibility that any thing should share with Him in power over any thing, let alone share in the dominion of the heavens and the earth. In it is also a confirmation, as an effect of confirmation, of what has passed concerning the painful punishment for them and their not being saved from it. The use of the noble Name in the place of a pronoun serves to inspire awe and to indicate the basis of the ruling, for the comprehensiveness of power over all things is among the rulings of divinity, along with what it implies of the independence of each of the two clauses in confirmation.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 3, Verse 190:**

﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*jumlah mustaʾnafah*), brought to confirm what preceded concerning God's exclusive possession of overpowering sovereignty and complete power. It is introduced by the emphatic particle (*inna*), out of concern for establishing its content, meaning: in their origination, as they are in their essences and attributes, among the matters whose most manifest aspects the intellects are bewildered in trying to comprehend.

﴿and the earth﴾, as it is in its essence and attributes.

﴿and the alternation of the night and the day﴾: meaning, in their succession over the face of the earth, and in each of them being a replacement (*khilfah*) for the other, according to the rising and setting of the sun, which follow the motions of the heavens and the stillness of the earth. Or it means in their variation, with each one increasing as the other decreases and decreasing as the other increases, according to the changing position of the sun relative to us in nearness and distance across the seasons. Or it means in their difference and variation according to places: either in length and shortness, for the lands close to the North Pole have longer summer days and shorter summer nights than the lands far from it; or in themselves, for the sphericity of the earth requires that at some times in some places it is night while in the opposite place it is day, and in some places it is morning, in others noon or afternoon, or other times.

As for "*al-layl*" (the night), it is said to be a collective noun (*ism jins*), whose singular is distinguished from its plural by the feminine *tāʾ*, like *tamr* (dates) and *tamrah* (a date). *Al-layālī* (the nights) is a plural of a plural, though the correct view is that *layl* is a singular noun for which no plural is recorded. *Al-layālī* is the plural of *laylah* (a night), and it is an irregular plural, as if they imagined that it was *laylāh*, as in *kaykah* and *kayākī*, as though it were the plural of *kaykāh*.

As for "*al-nahār*" (the day), it is a name for the period between the break of dawn and the setting of the sun, as stated by al-Raghib. Ibn Faris said: it is the light between the two.

The mention of the night before the day is either because it is the origin, since the crescents of the months appear in the nights, or because it precedes in succession, as indicated by His saying: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day, and then they are in darkness﴾ (Qur'an 36:37). That is: We remove it from it, and so it is replaced by it.

﴿are indeed signs﴾: the noun of *inna* (*ism inna*, the subject of *inna*) is preceded by the *lām* (of emphasis) because it is delayed beyond its predicate. The indefiniteness is for magnification, in quantity and quality, meaning: truly many great signs whose extent cannot be measured, indicating the wondrous aspects of His affairs, among which is the aforementioned exclusive possession of great sovereignty and complete power by Him, glorified is He. The verse does not address what is mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah concerning the ships, the rain, the directing of the winds and the clouds, because the purpose here is to demonstrate His independent dominion over what has been mentioned of sovereignty and power, so it suffices with the greatest part of the evidences indicating that. As for there, it was intended, within demonstrating His exclusive divinity, to demonstrate His attribute of vast mercy. Thus the indications of bounty and mercy were woven into the thread of the indications of monotheism, for what was detailed there of the signs of His mercy, exalted is He, are also signs of His divinity and oneness.

﴿for people of understanding (*ulu al-albab*)﴾: meaning, for those with intellects that are polished and pure, free from the impurities of sense and imagination, detached from worldly attachments, freed from the dark obstacles, contemplating the realities of things and the rulings of attributes, watching over the stages of dominion and the secrets of the realm of divine power, reflecting upon the marvels of the works of the Creator, the King, pondering the wondrous wisdoms He has deposited in the souls and the horizons, looking at the world with the eye of consideration and witnessing, searching into the reality of the secret of the Truth in every existing thing, persevering in watching over Him and remembering Him, not turning to anything other than Him except insofar as it is a mirror for witnessing His beauty and an instrument for contemplating the attributes of His perfection. For everything that has appeared in the loci of origination and has been present in the places of creation and invention is a straight path to the world of monotheism and a strong proof of the glorious Maker, speaking through the signs of His power. So is there any hearer who listens attentively, and any informer who relates the news of His knowledge and wisdom? Is there any caller who speaks to people according to the measure of their intellects, and responds to their answers according to what they say, conversing at times with the clearest expression and at other times hinting with the subtlest allusion, taking into account in the dialogue both their ambiguity and their explicitness? And ﴿there is not a thing but that it glorifies Him with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ (Qur'an 17:44). So reflect upon these affairs and secrets: ﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for those of vision﴾ (Qur'an 59:2).

«From ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Would you permit me, O ʿĀʾishah, tonight to worship my Lord?" I said: "O Messenger of Allah, I truly love your nearness and I love what pleases you; I have given you permission." So he rose to a water-skin in the house, performed ablution, and did not pour much water. Then he stood to pray, and he recited from the Qur'an and began to weep until the tears reached his lap. Then he sat, praised Allah the Exalted and extolled Him, and began to weep. Then he raised his hands and wept until I saw his tears had wet the ground. Then Bilal came to him to call him to the dawn prayer, and he saw him weeping, and said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, do you weep when Allah has forgiven you what preceded of your sin and what followed?" He said: "O Bilal, should I not be a grateful servant? And why should I not weep, when Allah the Exalted has revealed to me this night: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth…﴾ etc." Then he said: "Woe to whoever recites it and does not reflect upon it."»

It is also related (in another version): "Woe to whoever chews it between his jaws and does not contemplate it."

And from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, that "when the Prophet ﷺ rose at night, he would clean his teeth with the siwak, then look at the sky, then say: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth…﴾."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 191:

﴿Those who remember Allah﴾. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) may be attached to "ulu al-albab" (people of understanding) in the genitive, as a descriptive qualifier (na't kashif) that clarifies it through what lies within its relative clause (hayyiz al-silah). Alternatively, it may be separated from it and be in the nominative or accusative as a mark of praise (madh), or in the nominative as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf). It has also been said that it is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is the saying implied before the words of the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord﴾. There is, in this, a disruption of the sublime structure of the verse that is not hidden. In any case, through what lies within its relative clause it is indicated (p-129) that the intended ones are those who do not neglect Him, the Exalted, at most times, because their hearts are at rest in His remembrance and their inner selves are absorbed in watching over Him, since they are certain that everything other than Him flows from Him and returns to Him. So they do not witness any state of affairs, within themselves, and this is what is indicated by the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿standing, sitting and upon their sides﴾; nor in the horizons, and this is what is indicated by what follows, except that they perceive in that some aspect of His, the Exalted, manifestations. The intended meaning, then, is His remembrance absolutely, whether it is in respect of His essence or in respect of His attributes and acts, and whether it is accompanied by verbal remembrance or not.

As for what is related from Ibn 'Umar, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr and a group, may Allah be pleased with them, that they went out on the day of the festival to the musalla (place of prayer), and began to remember Allah, the Exalted, and some of them said: "Did not Allah, the Exalted, say ﴿those who remember Allah, standing and sitting﴾?" So they stood and remembered Allah on their feet. Their intention in this was not to interpret the verse or to establish its fulfilment specifically; rather, they intended a blessing through a kind of conformity with it, by performing an instance of what it denotes. As for interpreting remembrance as prayer in these states according to ability, as he, peace be upon him, said to 'Imran ibn Husayn: "Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; if you cannot, then on your side, making a sign (with your head)", this is among what the immediate context (siyaq) and the sublime structure of the verse do not support. "Standing" (qiyam) and "sitting" (qu'ud) are plurals of "qa'im" and "qa'id", like "niyam" and "ruqud" are plurals of "na'im" and "raqid". Their accusative case is as circumstantial qualifiers (hal) of the pronoun in "yadhkurun" (they remember), meaning: they remember Him standing and sitting. The words of the Exalted: ﴿and upon their sides﴾ are connected to an omitted element coordinated with the two circumstantial qualifiers, meaning: and lying upon their sides, that is, reclining. The intended meaning is the generalisation of remembrance to all times, as has passed. The specification of the mentioned states by mention is not to restrict remembrance to them; rather, these are the customary states that a person is generally never free from.

﴿And they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. This is coordinated with "yadhkurun" and shares with it the same position within the relative clause, so it has no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis). It has been said that its place is accusative, as coordinated with the preceding states, but this is not apparent. It is an explanation of their reflection upon His acts, glorified be He, following the explanation of their reflection upon His essence, the Exalted, in an absolute sense, and an indication of its outcome, which leads to knowledge of the states of the Return, as the tongues of the messengers and the verses of the scriptures have declared. Just as those verses are legislative signs guiding creation to knowledge of Him, the Exalted, and the obligation of obeying Him, so also created things are cosmic signs guiding them to that. The former alert them to the latter and are calls to take them as evidence, like this noble verse and similar verses that occur in countless places in the revelation. The latter are confirmations of the former and witnesses indicating the soundness of its content and the truth of its hidden meaning. For whoever contemplates the details of the creation of the world in this wondrous pattern judges that its Creator, the Exalted, possesses all that the messengers and scriptures have declared: necessary existence in Himself, essential unity, sovereign dominion, complete power, all-encompassing knowledge, far-reaching wisdom and other attributes of perfection. He judges that whoever is able to originate it without a model to imitate or a law to follow is more able to restore it through resurrection. And he judges that this is for nothing but a dazzling wisdom, which is the recompense of the responsible according to their deserving, which is bound to their deeds, that is, their knowledge and beliefs that follow from their reflection upon the proofs, evidences, signs and indications set out for them, and their other deeds that branch from these. For deed is not restricted to deeds of the limbs; it encompasses the deed of the heart, and indeed is its noblest kind, because each of the heart and the body has a deed specific to it, and it follows from the fact that the first is nobler than the second that its deed is also nobler than its deed. How could it not be so, when there is no deed without knowledge of Him, the Exalted, which is the first of the obligations upon the servants and the ultimate purpose of creation, as He, the Mighty and Majestic, declared: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾, meaning: that they should know Me, as His words, peace and blessings be upon him, make clear: "Allah, the Exalted, says: I was a hidden treasure, so I loved to be known, and I created the creation so that I might be known." Its path is only reflection and contemplation upon the aspects of Him, the Exalted, that have been mentioned. It has been related from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "Do not prefer me over Yunus ibn Matta, for every day there was raised for him the like of the deeds of the people of the earth." They said: that was only reflection upon the matter of Allah, the Exalted. For this reason he, peace be upon him, said: "There is no worship like reflection." You have understood that it entails the realisation of what the true Law has brought, for otherwise the Prophet ﷺ would not have explained the words of the Exalted: ﴿And He it is who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ by his words, peace and blessings be upon him: "Which of you is best in intellect and most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of Allah, the Exalted." For scrupulousness regarding His prohibitions, glorified be He, depends on knowledge of the lawful and the unlawful, which is bound to the Book and the Sunnah. Then the cosmic signs agree with one another and the transmitted and rational proofs are in harmony. This is the secret in the arrangement of what is related of the reflecting ones, of matters that call for belief in the Law, in the line of the outcome of their reflection, as you will come to know. The manifest mention of the creation of the heavens and the earth, even though pronoun reference would have sufficed, is to show the complete care in describing their state and to announce that their reflection is in a manner of verification and detail. The non-mention of the alternation of night and day within the series of reflection, although it was mentioned earlier, is either to announce that its inclusion in it is clear, because that belongs to the circumstances that follow the states of the heavens and the earth, as has been indicated, or to signal their haste in judging the outcome merely through their reflection upon some of the signs, without need for others of them in establishing the sought matter. "Creation" (khalq) is a verbal noun in its own right, meaning: they reflect upon the bringing into being and originating of the two with what is in them of wondrous made things. It has also been said that it means "the created thing", with the genitive construction in the sense of "in", meaning: they reflect upon what has been created in the two, more general whether by way of being a part of them, or by way of residing in them, or that it is explanatory.

﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾. The word "this" (hadha) is a reference to the heavens and the earth, containing a kind of glorification, as in His words: ﴿Indeed this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾. The masculine form is used because they, with respect to the creation being related to them, are in the sense of "the created thing". "In vain" (batilan) is either an adjective of an omitted verbal noun for emphasis, or a circumstantial qualifier of the object, meaning: You did not create this marvellous, greatly significant creation purposelessly, empty of wisdom and devoid of benefit, as the condition of the heedless who are unaware of that and who turn away from reflecting upon it indicates. Rather, it is arranged for great wisdoms and mighty benefits, among which is that it be a source of sustenance for the servants and a beacon guiding them to knowledge of the states of the origin and the Return, as the messengers and divine scriptures have made clear, as you have fully verified in detail. The whole sentence, in its entirety, occupies an accusative position through an implied saying. This, if the relative clause is a qualifier of "ulu al-albab", is a resumptive clause explaining the outcome of the reflection and the meaning of the signs, arising from what has preceded. For the soul, upon hearing that the signs set up in the creation of the world are specified for people of understanding, then their being described by the mention of Allah, the Exalted, and reflection upon the locations of those signs, remains expectant of what appears from them of their effects and rulings, as though it were said: What then occurs when they reflect upon that? And what outcome results from it? So it is said: they say such-and-such, which indicates that they have come to understand the secret of the creation, leading to knowledge of the truthfulness of the messengers and the truth of the scriptures that express the details of the legal rulings in the detail that you have now come to know. As for making it a circumstantial qualifier of the hidden pronoun in the verb, as the majority has agreed, this is something the eloquence of the noble structure does not support, because what lies within the relative clause, and what is a condition attached to it, should properly be among the grounds of the ruling that is predicated of the relative pronoun and the motives for its establishment for him, such as their remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, at most times, and their reflection upon the creation of the heavens and the earth, for these are among the things that lead to the perception of those signs and to deducing from them the sought matter. There is no doubt that their saying this is not among the grounds of the aforementioned inference, but rather among its results that follow from it. Therefore, treating it as a condition for what lies within the relative clause is not fitting for the sublimity of the noble revelation. Yes, it is a circumstantial qualifier of that, on the assumption that the relative pronoun is in the nominative or accusative as a mark of praise, or nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, since there is no doubt that their saying this is among the grounds of their praise and the excellent qualities of their character. In presenting this saying in the position of a circumstantial qualifier rather than a predicate, there is an indication of its coincidence with their reflection, without hesitation or wavering in that.

His words, exalted be He: ﴿Glory be to You﴾, meaning: exalted are You above what is unfitting for You of matters, among which is the creation of what has no wisdom, form a parenthetical clause that confirms the content of what precedes it and paves the way for what follows, namely His words, the Exalted: ﴿so protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾. For knowledge of the secret of the creation of the world and what it contains of profound wisdom and praiseworthy purpose, the performance of the righteous deeds it requires, and the glorification of the Maker, the Exalted, above futility, are among the motives for seeking refuge from what befalls those who neglect these, from two aspects. One is standing upon the realisation of the punishment, so the "fa'" (so) is for the ordering of the supplication upon what has been mentioned. The second is preparation to accept the supplication, so the "fa'" is for the ordering of what is requested, namely protection, upon that. It is as though it were said: Since we have come to know Your secret, obeyed Your command and glorified You above what is unbecoming, then protect us from the punishment of the Fire, which is the recompense of those who do not know that.

﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit into the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾. This is an emphatic (mubalaghah) plea for protection and an explanation of its cause. The sentence opens with the address "Our Lord" to intensify the supplication and entreaty, and it is emphasized with "indeed" to show complete certainty in its content and to signal intense fear. The Fire is named explicitly where a pronoun would be expected, to magnify its terror.
