The mention of admission into the Fire, as the place of punishment, specifies the manner of the punishment and makes clear the extreme severity of its harshness.

Al-Wahidi said: The word *ikhza'* (disgrace) has several closely related meanings. It is said, "Allah disgraced him," meaning He removed him far away. It is also said that it means to humiliate him, to destroy him, or to expose him. Ibn al-Anbari said: *Khizy* (disgrace) linguistically means ruin through loss, through the cutting off of an argument, or through falling into affliction. The meaning here is: "You have certainly disgraced him with a disgrace beyond which there is no further end," like the saying, "Whoever reaches the pasture of al-Simman has reached the best of pastures, beyond which there is no other pasture." This carries an indication of the severity of spiritual punishment, which is not hidden.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾, are a concluding statement (tadhyil) that reveals the utmost severity of their condition by showing that their punishment is eternal, since there is none to help them or to rescue them. Its purpose is to reinforce the plea. The word "wrongdoers" is placed in the position of the pronoun referring to those who are admitted, in order to censure them and to indicate that their entry into the Fire is due to their wrongdoing and their placing of things in other than their proper places. The plural "helpers" is used in view of the plurality of "wrongdoers," meaning: no wrongdoer among the wrongdoers has a helper among helpers. What is intended by "helper" is one who gives support through repelling and overpowering. Therefore, the verse contains no indication negating intercession. Moreover, the intended "wrongdoers" are the disbelievers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 193:

﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith﴾ This is a report of another supplication of theirs, based on their reflection on the revealed evidence (al-dalil al-sam'i), following the report of their earlier supplication, which was based on reflection on the rational evidences. The opening of the supplication with the call (al-nida') serves to show the completeness of humility and earnest entreaty. The emphasis (al-ta'kid) signals that the speech came from them with intense desire and complete eagerness. By "the call" is meant the supplication (al-du'a'). The two verbs are followed by "ila" because they include the sense of conveying (al-inha'), and by "li-" because they include the sense of exclusivity (al-ikhtisas). By "the caller" is meant the Messenger (ﷺ). The indefinite form (tanwin) of "munadiyan" is for magnification, and the choice of "caller" over "one who calls" indicates his complete concern for the matter of the call and its conveyance to those near and far, since it implies raising the voice. "Yunadi" is an attribute (sifah) of "munadiyan" according to the majority (al-Jumhur), as in your saying: "I heard a man saying such and such." Had it been definite, it would have been a circumstantial clause (hal) from it, as when you say: "I heard Zayd saying etc." According to al-Farisi (Abu Ali al-Farisi) and his followers, it is a second object (maf'ul thani) of "sami'na" (we heard). This is a wonderful construction, employed for the sake of emphasizing the certainty of the hearing and indicating that it occurred without intermediary when the heard words came directly from the speaker, and for the means of detailing it and calling its image to mind. The noble composition is further distinguished by an added excellence: it describes the one heard as "the caller," then characterizes him with the call to faith, in the manner of your saying: "I heard a speaker speaking with wisdom," because detail after vagueness and specification after generality fall more effectively upon the soul and are more worthy of acceptance. It has been said: the caller is the Great Qur'an.

﴿that believe﴾ That is: believe, where "an" is either explanatory (tafsiriyyah), or with "an ﴿amanu﴾" where it is verbal (masdariyyah).

﴿in your Lord﴾ in your Owner, the one who manages your affairs and brings you to perfection. In the unrestricted mention of faith followed by its restriction there is magnification of its importance.

﴿so we believed﴾ That is: we complied with His command and answered His call.

﴿Our Lord﴾ a repetition for the sake of supplication, a display of complete submission, and a presentation of acknowledgment of His lordship together with belief in Him.

The "fa" in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so forgive us﴾ is for the sequencing (tarattub) of forgiveness, or of the supplication for it, upon belief in Him, exalted is He, and acknowledgment of His lordship, for that is among the causes of forgiveness and of supplicating for it.

﴿our sins﴾ That is: their major ones (kaba'iraha), for faith wipes out what came before it.

﴿and remove from us our misdeeds﴾ That is: our minor ones (saghair), for these are expiated for one who avoids the major ones.

﴿and cause us to die with the righteous﴾ That is: singled out for their companionship, benefiting from their proximity, counted among their company. In this there is an indication that they used to love meeting God, and whoever loves meeting God, God loves to meet him. "Al-abrar" is the plural of "barr" or "barr," like "ashab" and "arbab."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 194:

﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ This is a report of another supplication of theirs, preceded by what came before it and joined to it by a conjunction, because the adornment (al-tahliyah) is delayed relative to the clearing away (al-takhliyah). The repetition of the address (al-nida') is for what has passed many times. By "what was promised" is meant the reward. "Upon" (ʿalā) may be connected to the promise, as in your saying, "God promised Paradise upon obedience," meaning: You promised us upon the confirmation of Your messengers. Or it may be connected to a omitted element that serves as an attribute of an omitted emphatic infinitive (maṣdar), meaning: You promised us a promise that was conveyed upon the tongues of Your messengers. It has been said: the estimate is "sent down upon Your messengers," or "carried upon Your messengers." It is not hidden that estimating specific verbs in such positions is forced (taʿassuf). The plural "messengers" is used even though the one who calls is the Messenger ﷺ alone, because his call, peace be upon him, especially in the matter of monotheism and what all the sacred laws agreed upon, encompasses the call of all of them. So confirming him is confirming them, peace be upon them. How could it not be so, when the covenant was taken from them to believe in him, peace be upon him, according to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever Book and wisdom I have given you…"﴾ (Q. 3:81), and likewise the reward promised upon his tongue is promised upon the tongues of all. The choice of the plural is to show complete confidence in the fulfilment of the promise, based on the abundance of witnesses.

﴿And do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾ By this they intended to remind Him of His promise in His saying: ﴿On the Day when God will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believe with him﴾ (Q. 66:8), showing that they are among those who believed with him, hoping to be counted in their line on that day. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, You do not break the promise﴾ is a reason establishing what they included in the line of supplication. These supplications, and what is within them of complete humility and entreaty, are not out of fear that the promise would be broken, but out of fear that they might not be among those promised, through a change of state and an evil end and outcome. So their return is to a supplication for steadfastness, or it is for intensifying worship and humility. (al-mi'ad): the promise. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it refers to resurrection after death. In the transmitted reports from Ja'far al-Sadiq: whoever is afflicted by a matter and says "Our Lord" five times, Allah will save him from what he fears and give him what he wishes, and he recited this verse.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 195:

﴿So their Lord responded to them﴾. Al-istijaba (ٱلِاسْتِجَابَة, responding) has the same meaning as al-ijaba (ٱلْإِجَابَة, answering). Taj al-Qurra (Taj al-Qurra, "Crown of the Reciters") said: al-ijaba is general, while al-istijaba is specific to granting what is asked. It is transitive both with the preposition al-lam and directly, as in the line:

*"So the one who answers does not answer him at that time."*

This clause is coordinated (ʿatf) with an implied resumption (istinaf muqaddar) in what came before, and it is consequent upon the supplications contained within its scope, just as the Exalted's words ﴿Then it was said to those who did wrong﴾ and so on are coordinated with an implied qila (قِيلَ, "it was said") that precedes "now" (الآن), meaning: it was said to them, "Do you believe in it now?" Then "it was said," the verse. Likewise, the Exalted's words in Surat al-A'raf ﴿upon their hearts﴾ are coordinated with what is indicated by the meaning of ﴿Does it not guide﴾ and so on, as if it were said: they are heedless of guidance, and We seal [their hearts], and so on. There is no harm in their differing in form, because the future form there indicates continuity, which suits the context of supplication, while the past form here indicates the certainty and establishment of the response. Likewise there is no harm in the difference between the Exalted's words ﴿when you sought help from your Lord﴾ and what is coordinated with it, the Exalted's words ﴿so He responded to you﴾, as will come. It is also permissible that it be coordinated with an implied element that the mind is led to, meaning: they called upon Him with these supplications, so He responded, and so on. As for the view that the implied element is a circumstantial clause (hal), then it is coordinated with ﴿they reflect﴾ in view of its being contemporaneous with what occurred as a circumstance of its subject, namely the Exalted's words ﴿Our Lord, our Lord﴾ and so on. The response is consequent upon their supplications, not merely upon their reflection. Since it is one of their beautiful attributes that follow from their deeds in the Hereafter, it deserves to be included among their praiseworthy qualities mentioned in the course of their praise. As for the view that the relative clause is a description of ﴿those of understanding﴾, then there is no basis at all for this coordination, because, as you know, what lies within the relative clause's scope should be among the beginnings of the judgment passed upon the relative pronoun, and you know that their earlier supplications are not such. So where is the response that comes later than them? In the mention of the title "Lordship" (al-rububiyya), which indicates the complete delivery [of the promise], together with its being attributed to their pronoun, there is an honouring of them and a manifestation of kindness toward them, which is not hidden.

﴿That I do not waste the work of any worker among you﴾. That is, "that I [do not]", and thus Ubayy (رضي الله عنه, may Allah be pleased with him) recited it. The preposition ba' (الباء) here is causal (sababiyya), as if it were said: "So their Lord responded to them because He does not waste the work of any worker among them." That is, His noble practice is continuous in this. The shift (iltifat, a shift in grammatical person) to the first person and to the second person serves to show complete concern for the matter of the response and to honour the supplicants by the honour of direct address. The intent is to confirm it by stating its cause, and to indicate that its basis is their deeds, which they offered before the supplication, not the supplication alone. The promise is generalised to all other workers, even if they have not reached the rank of those of understanding, in order to confirm the response to the aforementioned supplications. The expression of withholding reward as "wasting" is used although it is not real wasting, since deeds do not necessitate reward such that their non-fulfilment would entail their being wasted. It is to demonstrate the perfect purity of Him, exalted is He, from that, by depicting it in the form of what is impossible for Him to do of the ugly kinds, and by presenting the granting of reward in the guise of matters obligatory upon Him. It has also been read with a kasra on the hamza, according to the intention of speech, meaning: saying "Indeed I..." and so on; in that case there is no iltifat. It has also been read as "la uddayyi'" with tashdid, and "min" (مِنْ) is connected to an omitted element that functions as a description of "worker", meaning: a worker who is from among you. The Exalted's words ﴿male or female﴾ are an explanation of "worker" and an emphasis on its generality. The Exalted's words ﴿some of you are from others﴾ are an intervening clause (jumla mu'tarida) explaining the reason for including women within the scope of men in the promise. For each of the two being "from the other," whether because they both branch from a single origin, or because of the intense connection between them, or because they agree in religion and action, is something that calls for sharing and unity in this matter.

It is related that Umm Salama (رضي الله عنها, may Allah be pleased with her) said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I hear Allah, the Exalted, mention men in regard to emigration, and He does not mention women." So this was revealed. The Exalted's words ﴿So those who emigrated﴾ are a form of detailed explanation of what was summarised in the deed, and an enumeration of some of the finest of its instances, in the manner of praise and glorification, that is: those who emigrated from polytheism, or from homelands and clans, for the sake of religion. The Exalted's words ﴿and were expelled from their homes﴾ are, on the first interpretation, an expression for the very act of emigration, and on the second, an expression for its manner, namely that it occurred by compulsion and necessity.

﴿and were harmed in My way﴾, that is, because of their faith in Allah and for His sake. It encompasses every harm that befell them from the polytheists.

﴿and fought﴾, that is, fought the disbelievers in the way of Allah, the Exalted.

﴿and were killed﴾, that is, were martyred in battle. It has also been read in reverse order, since the conjunction waw (و) does not require sequence; or because the intent is: some of them were killed and others fought. For the meaning is not that each individual of the aforementioned relative pronoun is characterised by each one of the things mentioned in the relative clause, but rather that all of them are characterised by all of them in some respect, whether this is by each individual being characterised by one of the mentioned attributes, or by two of them, or by more, either by way of distribution (tawzi', distributing the attributes among the individuals), or by way of omitting some of the relative pronouns from between them, as is the view of the Kufan grammarians. How could it not be so? For if the judgment were applied to each individual being characterised by all of them, then the work of one who was characterised by only some of them would have been wasted. It has also been read as "wa-qutthilu" (وَقُتِّلُوا) with tashdid (intensive doubling).

﴿Certainly I shall expiate their misdeeds from them﴾: this is the answer to an omitted oath, meaning: "By Allah, I shall certainly expiate..." The oath clause is the predicate of the subject, which is the relative pronoun. This is an explicit statement of the promise of what the supplicants asked for specifically, after having promised it in general. The Exalted's words ﴿and certainly I shall admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ refer to what the supplicants had expressed earlier with their words "and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers," and they explain it.

﴿as a reward﴾: a verbal noun (masdar) emphasising what precedes it, since the expiation of misdeeds and the admission into the Garden are included in the meaning of reward. The Exalted's words ﴿from the presence of Allah﴾ are connected to an omitted element which is a description of it, clarifying its nobility, meaning: "I shall reward them with a reward that is from Him, the Exalted, reaching the furthest degree of nobility." The Exalted's words ﴿and with Allah is the finest reward﴾ are a concluding parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ tadhyili) confirming the content of what came before. The noble Name is the subject (mubtada'), its predicate is "with Him" (ʿindahu), and "the finest reward" (ḥusn al-thawab) is raised by the adverbial phrase as its agent, since it depends on the subject; or it is a second subject, with the adverbial phrase as its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of the first subject. Being "with Him" (al-ʿindiyya) is an expression for exclusive belonging to Him, the Exalted, like His being by His power and bounty in such a way that no one other than Him can bring about anything of the kind, like something that is in the presence of someone who has no hand in it for anyone else. Thus exclusivity is derived from the figurative expression, whether "ʿindahu" is made a fronted predicate of "ḥusn al-thawab" or not. In opening the noble promise with the non-wasting of deeds and then following it with such a kindness whose worth cannot be measured, there is a gentleness of manner indicating the greatness of the status of the one who bestows kindness, which is not hidden.

(p-135) ﴿Let not the turning about of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾. This is an explanation of the ugliness of what the disbelievers are given of the portions of worldly life, and a disclosure of the insignificance of its status and the badness of its outcome, following the explanation of the goodness of what the believers are given of reward. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, on the basis that the intent is to make him firm in what he is upon, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾. Or, on the basis that the intent is a prohibition of the believers, just as the address is directed to the people's gatherings (madar) and their leaders, and the intent is their annihilation. Or it is for every person among the believers who is fit to be addressed. The prohibition is for the one addressed, and the turning about is made into an intensification (mubalaghah), meaning: do not look at what the disbelievers have of abundance and great fortune, and do not be deceived by the outward appearance of what you see of them in their expansion in gains, trade and farms.

It is narrated that some of the believers used to see the polytheists in ease and softness of living, and they would say: "The enemies of God, exalted is He, are in good, as we see, while we have perished from hunger and hardship." So this was revealed. It has also been read as "wa-la yaghurrannaka" with the light nun (nun al-khafifah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 197:

﴿مَتاعٌ قَلِيلٌ﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), i.e., "it is a little enjoyment, which has no worth in comparison with what has been mentioned of the reward of Allah, the Exalted." He (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of this world compared to the Hereafter is nothing but the likeness of one of you dipping his finger into the sea; let him look at what it brings back." Therefore, its existence does not benefit those who possess it, and its loss does not harm those who lose it.

﴿ثُمَّ مَأْواهُمْ﴾ means: their destination, the place to which they resort and from which they do not depart.

﴿جَهَنَّمُ﴾ whose punishment cannot be described. And the words of the Exalted, ﴿وَبِئْسَ المِهادُ﴾ ("and what an evil resting-place"), are a condemnation of it and an announcement that their destination is to it, because of what their souls have earned and what their hands have acquired. The object of the blame (al-makhsus bil-dhamm) is omitted, i.e., "Evil is what they have prepared for themselves: Jahannam."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 198:

﴿But for those who fear their Lord, there are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein﴾ is an explanation of the perfection of the good state of the believers, after an explanation, and a repetition of it following an affirmation, along with the added point of their abiding in the gardens, so that their joy is completed, their delight increases, and the bad state of the disbelievers is thereby made complete. The mention of taqwa (God-consciousness) within the relative clause serves to indicate that the qualities mentioned are of the category of taqwa, and what is meant by it is guarding oneself against shirk (associating partners with God) and sins. So the relative pronoun (al-ladhina) is the subject (mubtada'), and the prepositional phrase is its predicate, and "gardens" is raised by it as its agent, owing to its reliance on the subject; or the prepositional phrase is the predicate of "gardens," and the whole clause is the predicate of the relative pronoun. "Abiding therein" means: in the gardens, is a presumptive circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) from the pronoun or from ﴿gardens﴾, since it is specified by the description, and the governing element is the sense of settledness (istiqrar) contained in the prepositional phrase.

﴿An provision from God﴾. It has been read with a sukun on the zay (nuzl, with sukun), and it is what is prepared for the guest of food, drink, and other things. Abu al-Shi'r al-Dabbi said:

؎ When a tyrant came against us with an army as a guest, we made the spears and the sharp swords his provision

Its accusative case is as a circumstantial clause from ﴿gardens﴾, since it is specified by the description, and the governing element in it is the sense of settledness contained in the prepositional phrase. It was said: it is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar), as if it were said: a provision or a gift from God.

﴿And what is with God is better﴾ is a subject and predicate. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for the righteous﴾ is attached to an omitted element which is a description of "better," meaning: what is with Him, exalted is He, of the aforementioned enduring matters, is a better thing existing for the righteous, that is, than the scant, passing enjoyments in which the wicked wallow. The expression of them as "the righteous" serves to indicate that the qualities counted as works of piety are, just as they are of the category of taqwa, and the sentence is a concluding summary (tadhyil) of what precedes it.

(p-136) ﴿And among the People of the Book there are indeed those who believe in God﴾. This is a resumptive sentence (*jumlah mustanfa'a*, a new sentence that begins a fresh point), brought to show that the People of the Book are not all like those whose faults were recounted, such as breaking the covenant, distorting the Book, and other things. Rather, among them are those who possess sublime virtues. It is said: they are 'Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions. It is also said: they were forty people from Najran, thirty-two from Abyssinia, and eight from Byzantium, who had been Christians and then embraced Islam. It is also said: the intended person is Ashamah al-Najashi (the Negus), for when he died, Gabriel informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of his death. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Go out and pray over a brother of yours who has died in a land other than your own." So he went out to al-Baqi' (the cemetery), looked toward the land of Abyssinia, saw the bier of al-Najashi, prayed over him, and asked forgiveness for him. The hypocrites said: "Look at this man, praying over a Christian barbarian whom he has never seen and who is not of his religion!" Then the verse was revealed. The emphatic lam (*lam al-ibtida'*, the lam of commencement) entered upon the particle *inna* in order to separate the adverbial phrase between them, as in God's words: ﴿And indeed among you is one who will certainly lag behind﴾ (4:72).

﴿and what has been sent down to you﴾: that is, the Qur'an.

﴿and what has been sent down to them﴾: that is, from the two Scriptures (the Torah and the Gospel). The mention of their belief in these two after their belief in the Qur'an, although in terms of existence the matter is the reverse, is because the Qur'an is the criterion (*'iyar*, the standard by which other scriptures are measured) and the overseer (*muhaymin*, the guardian and witness) over them. Their belief in those two is considered only insofar as it follows their belief in the Qur'an, since there is no value in their rulings that have been abrogated (*mansukha*, cancelled by later revelation). What has not been abrogated among them is valued only in terms of its being established by the Qur'an, and because what follows is connected to them. By their belief in these two is meant: their believing in them without distortion or concealment, as is the practice of the distorters and their followers among the common people.

﴿humbly submissive to God﴾: a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject of "believe," and the plural form is used in view of the meaning.

﴿They do not sell the signs of God for a small price﴾: an explicit statement of their opposition to the distorters. This clause is a circumstantial clause, like the preceding one, and its inclusion among their admirable qualities is not merely because they do not sell (the signs), but because it includes the manifestation of the evidences of his prophethood (ﷺ) found in the two Scriptures.

﴿Those﴾: a demonstrative referring to them in respect of their possessing the praiseworthy qualities already enumerated. The distance implied by it indicates the elevation of their rank and the remoteness of their station in nobility and excellence. It is the subject (*mubtada'*), whose predicate is God's words: ﴿for them﴾. And His words: ﴿their reward﴾, that is, the reward specifically belonging to them, promised to them by God's words: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾ (28:54), and His words: ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾ (57:28). It is raised by the adverbial phrase as the agent, or as the subject with the adverbial phrase as its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of "those." God's words: ﴿with their Lord﴾ are in the accusative as a circumstantial element (*hal*) of "their reward," and the intended meaning is honor, functioning like a qualifier.

﴿Indeed God is swift at reckoning﴾: because His knowledge penetrates all things, so He knows what each doer deserves of reward without any need for reflection. The intended meaning is to explain the speed with which the promised reward reaches them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 3, verse 200:

﴿O you who have believed﴾ after what has been explained within the course of this noble surah of the various kinds of wisdom and rulings, it is concluded with what necessitates preserving them. So it is said: ﴿Be patient﴾, i.e., in the hardships of acts of obedience and other than that of the hardships and calamities.

﴿And endure﴾, i.e., overcome the enemies of Allah, the Exalted, through patience in the places of war; and the most hostile of your enemy (is overcome) through patience in opposing one's desire. The specifying of endurance (muṣābara) with a command after the command of general patience is because it is more intense and more difficult than it.

﴿And stand guard﴾, i.e., remain on the frontiers, stationing your horses there, watching for the raid and prepared for it. The Exalted said: ﴿And from the stationing of horses, by which you terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy﴾. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever stations himself (on guard) for a day and a night in the way of Allah, it is as if he had fasted the month of Ramadan and prayed its night vigil, and he does not break his fast, and he does not turn away from his prayer except for a need."

﴿And fear Allah﴾ in opposing His command absolutely, so that what has been mentioned within the course of this noble surah is included in it at the first level of inclusion.

﴿So that you may succeed﴾, so that you may be counted among the group of the successful, those who attain every sought-after thing and are saved from every distress. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah Al 'Imran will be given, for every verse of it, security upon the bridge of Hell."

And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the surah in which Al 'Imran is mentioned on Friday, Allah and His angels will send blessings upon him until the sun is veiled."

And Allah knows best.
